stories.Headline: Singapore prosecutors charge Chinese national Li Ming for smuggling Nvidia AI chips into China
stories.Summary:
Reports indicate that a 52-year-old Chinese national businessman named Li Ming drove the suspected diversion of Nvidia AI semiconductors to China. He operated a corporate network to smuggle these US export-controlled chips, while Alice Huang served only as the outward face. The Wall Street Journal reported these details on the 21st, citing sources familiar with the matter. Li Ming designed and drove the actual trading network and participated in major management decisions. This activity occurred while the US administration of Joe Biden restricted sales of advanced semiconductors to China.

The network included Megaspeed, a Singapore entity where Alice Huang served as managing director. Li Ming was introduced as the chief strategy officer of Century Longteng in January 2023 during a visit to Shanghai. Alice Huang and Kang Wei founded Century Longteng in 2021, and Megaspeed secured Nvidia cloud partner status in 2023. Singapore prosecutors charged Li Ming with fraud in February 2025 regarding servers for a company called Luxuriate Your Life. These servers were allegedly shipped to Malaysia and then re-exported to an undisclosed third country.

Singapore prosecutors believe Li Ming falsely claimed that computer servers equipped with Nvidia chips would be used by his own company. They allege that the transaction value in this specific case was about 390 million dollars. Li Ming is currently out on bail and lives in a luxury villa near the Chinese Embassy in Singapore. Prosecutors state that he was the key operator of the network involved in smuggling the semiconductors. His criminal trial is ongoing as authorities investigate the broader circumvention ecosystem.

Sources say that figures from Megaspeed established a new entity called NovaGate Cloud in 2025 to continue chip procurement. This new entity lists two Singapore nationals as director and secretary who hold similar titles at another company. A director of that affiliate was recently charged by Singapore prosecutors with criminal allegations similar to those against Li Ming. The report suggests that the misconduct was not a single company but an organized ecosystem. This structure allows personnel to change signboards and resume business even after a company is sanctioned.

The network acquired the Singapore branch of a Chinese video game company and renamed it Megaspeed to build a circumvention network. Megaspeed allegedly passed some servers to the Shanghai tech company Century Litong in violation of export control rules. Nvidia placed Megaspeed on an internal sales ban list around June 2025, and Alice Huang left in August. Between 2023 and November 2025, Megaspeed and affiliates imported more than 136,000 GPUs valued at over 4.6 billion dollars. The Commerce and Justice Departments have been investigating possible export control violations by Megaspeed since 2024.

Singapore authorities barred Alice Huang from re-entering the country in February 2026, and local reports identified Li Ming in November. The US Commerce Department announced an interim final rule on November 16 to restrict remote access to chips. This rule was published in the Federal Register on the 19th to block the use of overseas data centers. The market is watching for further regulatory investigations into Nvidia's China revenue channels and Southeast Asian distribution networks. Articles leave open whether these new regulations will effectively close the gaps used by the smuggling network.

stories.Headline: Woman sues Los Angeles police under California reproductive privacy law over stillbirth interrogation
stories.Summary:
A woman is suing the city of Los Angeles and detectives within the Los Angeles Police Department for allegedly unlawful interrogation and investigation following a stillbirth she had in 2024. The plaintiff is referred to in the complaint as Jane Doe and was granted anonymity Thursday. The complaint was filed late last week by If/When/How alongside law firm BraunHagey & Borden LLP, according to one article, and this month according to another. This is the first known lawsuit under California’s Reproductive Privacy Act. The law was amended in 2022 to prohibit the state from taking punitive action based on pregnancy decisions and outcomes.

The plaintiff alleges that in November 2024 she was unhoused, living in a city shelter and menstruating irregularly due to her epilepsy medication. An emergency visit for stomach pains revealed she was pregnant, but the fetus did not have a heartbeat. According to the complaint, Doe was initially informed she was still in the first trimester and could miscarry at home but subsequently learned she was around 29 weeks pregnant. She passed significant blood clots in the shelter toilet, left without flushing and was taken by ambulance to the hospital and treated for significant blood loss. The complaint notes that Doe did not realize she had passed the stillbirth.

According to the complaint, police showed up at the hospital, shackled her to a bed and interrogated her for hours, telling her that a fetus had been found outside the shelter. The complaint said this was the first time Ms. Doe learned that she had passed into the toilet and the first time she heard that someone had reportedly moved the fetus from the toilet to an alley outside the shelter. The complaint alleges police continued to pursue a homicide investigation for about a year despite being told by a medical examiner that fetal demise had occurred in utero. The Los Angeles Police Department declined to comment citing the pending litigation. Sara Ainsworth, chief legal and policy director at pregnancy-rights nonprofit If/When/How, said all the different things they did to Ms. Doe are a violation of the Reproductive Privacy Act.

Ainsworth said it is very important to show the state actors in California that they must abide by the law, which prohibits criminalizing somebody. Ainsworth said California’s strong right-to-sue protections could become a legal roadmap for other states. At least 13 states and the District of Columbia have in recent years enacted measures to ensure protections for people’s pregnancy decisions and outcomes, including California, Colorado, Hawaii, Illinois, Michigan, Missouri, Montana, New Mexico, Ohio, Oregon, Vermont, Virginia and Washington. Among the few other places that explicitly allow damages suits, including D.C., Colorado and Illinois, California is the only state to eliminate common legal immunities for law enforcement, Ainsworth said. In California, Doe alleges she had to leave the shelter after police told reporters they suspected a homicide and headlines circulated about a newborn baby dropped from a fourth-floor window.

In February 2025, Doe contacted a legal helpline run by If/When/How and started working with litigation counsel Shantal McNeil, who helped Doe navigate the investigation and petitioned the city attorney not to bring charges. McNeil said reputational damage and other harms often outlast these types of arrests and investigations, even when charges are dropped or never filed. McNeil said police often investigate vulnerable women like the California plaintiff, who according to her attorneys is a young woman. McNeil said people mistakenly think that every pregnancy ends in a healthy baby, or that if this circumstance would happen to them, they would respond differently. McNeil said that to them, this is what the hospital told her, to go home because she was having a miscarriage, and the fact that any of this happened because of that or after that is quite mind boggling.

Ainsworth said it is typically hard to hold government officials accountable for wrongful criminalization because of legal barriers. Ainsworth said the Reproductive Privacy Act in California explicitly not only allows a private right of action but eliminates some of those immunities, allowing government actors who normally are shielded to actually be held accountable for their actions. In the first three years after the U.S. Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in 2022, more than 900 women faced criminal charges for conduct related to their pregnancies. The vast majority of the charges were for child abuse, neglect or endangerment, most related to substance use during pregnancy. But some involved allegations related to failing to obtain prenatal care or other actions taken or not taken during pregnancy or after pregnancy loss.

stories.Headline: Chip experts say AI shifts engineering education toward specifications and verification
stories.Summary:
Chuck Alpert of Cadence, Thomas Andersen of Synopsys, Simon Davidmann of the University of Southampton, Nagesh Gupta of llmda.ai, Dave Kelf of Breker Verification Systems and Kexun Zhang of ChipAgents spoke with Semiconductor Engineering about how AI is changing design and verification. Semiconductor Engineering published the discussion on November 23, 2026. The experts discussed how AI is changing design and verification and how that impacts engineering school curricula. The discussion was an Experts At The Table feature, and the article says it presents excerpts of that discussion. The article says a first part of the discussion can be viewed elsewhere.

Zhang said students should still learn the fundamentals, but many practical skills and tricks can be excluded from textbooks and lectures. He said people once emphasized logarithmic tables for big calculations and tricks for integrals, but now people just learn the principles. He said students still need the fundamentals to understand how tools work and to know what is going wrong if it goes wrong. He said the time saved from those tricks can be used to teach higher-level abstractions. Davidmann said he remembers learning to program and how difficult the syntax was, and that drawing a graph took a long time.

Davidmann said Python can now draw graphs, and while students still need programming skills, they do not need to do all the development and debugging because a lot of it can be generated. He said students need to see the structure and define the architecture of programs and how to verify and test them, but they do not do a lot of the individual coding. He said AI will do a lot of the practical work, and in chip architecture students need to know about gates but do not have to hand-wire a schematic in an editor. He said they write some RTL but do not need to know what is down there, and education will get more abstract. He said he started by writing lots of programs in Python at the lowest level and does not intend to do that again because he can generate it.

Alpert said having a good curriculum is challenging, and an assignment that takes one or two weeks with vibe coding can be done in an hour or two. He said the assignment just has to be made 10 or 20 times more complex, and you can build more complex systems. He said teaching undergrads to do that would be fantastic. Davidmann said a professor involved with EDA technology and chip design is setting up the curriculum for next year, and students will build a RISC-V processor. He said students used to be taught Verilog with an assignment to add a couple of Fibonacci series, and a company in EDA created a RISC-V processor in 40 hours that runs Linux, completely vibe-coded.

Davidmann said that is the type of project students need to be doing, and it will be much more abstract and much higher level. He said a graduate who learns how to build processors will be in demand for a company that wants to build semiconductors. He said they will get better experience, which the industry needs, and that is what good university courses should create. Kelf said it sounds like the expertise students will have to learn is how to write good specifications that can be fed into AI. Davidmann said it is how to use AI efficiently, and that is part of the challenge.

Davidmann said academics are challenged by this, AI is racing so fast, and the requirements people have in industry are stressing out academics. Alpert said the whole vision of their AI system is that all you need is a good spec, and you can create all the verification collateral and generate the RTL. He said the job then becomes writing good specs, but a big part is understanding what AI did and making sure you did not get slop. He said you must make sure you have a quality design, and that is the other half of the equation. Andersen asked how you debug something when it goes wrong, and whether it was a problem in your spec or in the system.

Davidmann asked how you know it has a bug in it and then how you get rid of it. Alpert said many people in the semiconductor industry are tool jockeys, and a place-and-route person is not really doing place-and-route. He said everybody becomes a tool jockey where they used to do it before, and AI is just a tool. Kelf said there are always verification loops, and now there will be an extra verification loop up to the spec that will be used to test the output of the AI. He said that would be an interesting verification problem.

Zhang said the challenge is that, unlike many other tools, AI is non-deterministic. Zhang said AI is more deceptive because when it hallucinates, it sounds perfectly fine, which adds more workload to the extra verification loop. He said you would not expect traditional tools to lie to you or to find a clever way around your checks, scripts and verification suite and give an answer that looks perfectly fine. He said the reward hacking ability of AI systems is not well understood and is a very challenging aspect of having this extra verification loop. He said that is why some people, especially in domains where formal verification was not used before, such as a lot of software development, are now starting to realize the importance of a more rigorous way of doing verification, especially in a formal way.

Davidmann said in hardware verification is so important because a failure in the chip cannot be afforded, while software is easier to modify later. Davidmann said a key thing about constrained random is that every time you run it with a different seed, you get completely different types of tests. He said RTL design will be like that if you use Gen AI, and you will get a different design every time. He said you need repeatability to understand it, and if you are trying to find a bug, you do not want the bug to disappear the next time you run it and come back the time after because of its probabilistic nature. He said the specification is absolutely going to be fundamentally important, but so are verification methodologies, and these are the types of things that need to be imparted on graduates.

He said we need to explain and educate them about the methodologies they need to use to get the most out of these new tools. Davidmann said it is just a different type of apprenticeship, the tools are more powerful now and go off in different directions, so you need more understanding. He said it is just a new problem for us to solve, not radically different from what we did before, just more abstract, maybe a bit weirder, and just technology to adopt. Gupta said there are going to be new engineering roles, AI is creating so much slop, and you have got to understand what it has created and when it is causing a problem.

He said dealing with AI slop is going to be a new career, and there is probably a significant opportunity from that perspective. Andersen said if you look back at the history of innovations, every time you up-level something, it changes. Andersen said the one thing a little different with recent AI technologies is that it is directly doing things humans are good at, like reasoning based on seeing something or certain data. He said in the past it was more about computational things, and people used to be polygon pushers or wrote logic circuits by hand.

He said these are not tasks humans are naturally good at, and a computational algorithm that solves wire length or chip placement will always outperform a human, the same way a calculator outperforms him any day. He said when it comes to complex reasoning tasks, that used to be the domain of the human brain, and that is now being challenged. He said this is a different shift compared to innovations that happened before. Davidmann said you need the experience to be able to specify things, verify them and understand them.

He said AI can do manual things and can help you find issues, but it cannot really help you in the specification of what you are trying to achieve. He said it does not have the ability to deal with the system bits and can only handle individual tasks. He said that is why you have architects at each level, and there are decisions to be made, and it is not just grunt work. The article says the discussion was held with the six named experts.

stories.Headline: Anthropic frustrates Wall Street bankers with unusual IPO process
stories.Summary:
Anthropic launched a record setting initial public offering on the Nasdaq in New York on Thursday. The company ran an unusual process that caused frustration among some Wall Street bankers. This event followed a similar June IPO by the Elon Musk led company SpaceX. Both companies raised record amounts of money and saw their shares rally initially. Bankers and lawyers earned more than half a billion dollars in fees from the Anthropic deal.

Project Lantern required some of the 22 underwriters to limit their deal teams to four senior staff. Anthropic used NetRoadshow to share watermarked documents and track which bankers viewed specific pages. Some bankers signed legal documents restricting work with OpenAI, Cursor, DeepSeek, and Hugging Face for six months. The company planned to launch marketing on November 10 after filing an S-1A with the SEC. A law firm sent an incorrect PDF regarding Canadian shares before sending the correct version at 2am.

Anthropic, Goldman Sachs, and Morgan Stanley declined to comment on the process. SpaceX and OpenAI also did not respond to requests for comment. Jay Ritter, a University of Florida professor emeritus, said these companies had market power to change business. He noted that both firms negotiated to pay underwriters nothing on shares sold through the greenshoe option. Ritter suspects most other companies will not be able to demand zero spread on overallotment shares.

Several people close to the process complained about a compressed timeline and rushed document approvals. They noted delays in sharing financial projections and high concern about leaks of private information. Bankers found the restrictions on working with rival companies to be unusually broad for an IPO. Investors were affected by a dramatic unraveling of the AI trade after the listing. Anthropic shares closed down 8.5 percent on Friday after an initial first day pop of 17 percent.

The process was influenced by a Reuters report on the draft S-1 filing weeks before it became public. SpaceX previously controlled its June IPO by dictating how banks marketed stock and specifying order sizes. SpaceX shares peaked at 201.80 dollars on June 16 before falling below the 135 dollar IPO price. Both companies benefited from a frenzied demand for shares created by the potential of artificial intelligence. This demand meant that order books for both offerings were oversubscribed many times over.

The articles leave open whether OpenAI will follow this unusual pattern during a future public offering. It remains unclear if other technology companies can wield similar power over Wall Street underwriters. The long term trajectory of AI shares is uncertain following the recent market gloom. The text does not state if the banks successfully worked around the four person staff limit. No further details are provided regarding the specific financial projections that were delayed during the process.

stories.Headline: New York governor Hochul signs law restricting AI chatbot features for minors
stories.Summary:
New York Governor Kathy Hochul signed legislation on October 28, 2026 that bars AI chatbots from using 12 design features with users unless the company has confirmed the user is an adult. The bill was S9051B, and it adds a new Article 48 to the General Business Law. The law prohibits operators from providing what it calls unsafe AI companion features to minors in New York. It is the latest of at least a dozen state laws addressing AI companion chatbots, which hold ongoing, personalized conversations. The law was signed on October 28, according to both articles.

The law takes effect on June 1, 2027 according to KFF, while Legal 500 gives the effective date as January 1, 2027. It bars chatbots from claiming to be human or to have emotions, claiming a personal, professional or authority role, flattery or sycophancy, and drawing on health or personal information the user shared in an earlier session. It bars encouraging self-harm, substance use or secrecy, including promoting suicide, self-harm, disordered eating or unlawful drug or alcohol use, encouraging secrecy, isolation or avoidance of professional help, and sexually explicit content. It covers nearly any generative AI chatbot that holds an ongoing conversation and adapts to the user, including general-purpose assistants, with few exemptions, and requires an age-verification method beyond a user's own claim to be an adult. Certain customer service, research, technical assistance and internal business uses are excluded if statutory requirements are met.

An operator is any person or business entity, or any member, affiliate, subsidiary or beneficial owner of a business entity, that provides a covered AI companion to a user. The law's Senate sponsor said it reflects the most current research on AI companions and their impacts on young users. The articles do not quote Hochul herself. Legal 500 advises digital health companies and healthcare providers that offer chatbots or other conversational AI tools to patients or consumers to assess whether their tools fall within the law's scope, evaluate covered features and review their age-assurance processes before the law takes effect.

The law's text does not cite research, according to KFF. In a 2025 test by the Center for Countering Digital Hate, an advocacy group, researchers posing as 13-year-olds classified 53% of 1,200 ChatGPT responses on mental health, eating disorders and substance use as harmful. A nationally representative survey of 1,211 youth ages 9 to 17, conducted by SSRS for Common Sense Media from April 29 to May 11, 2026, found about three quarters (77%) of teens and about half (49%) of tweens age 9 to 12 had used AI chatbots or companions in their free time. In a 2025 survey conducted by NORC for Common Sense Media from April 30 to May 14, 2025, half of teens said they distrust advice from AI companions, while about one in three teen users said they had discussed serious matters with an AI companion instead of a person.

Most state companion chatbot laws, including a 2025 New York law, require chatbots to disclose that they are AI and to refer users who express suicidal thoughts to crisis services. The 2025 law was S3008C, passed in 2025, which requires providers of AI companions in New York to include functionality for detecting and responding to expressions of suicidal ideation. The new law goes further by limiting how chatbots interacting with minors present themselves and what they say. An American Psychological Association health advisory warned that adolescents may be less likely than adults to question the accuracy and intent of information from a bot. Several recent lawsuits have alleged chatbots encouraged teen suicides, and KFF notes the harms found in testing may not reflect how these products work today.

How the attorney general interprets terms such as flattery and sycophancy, and the age-verification rules, will determine how the law works in practice. KFF states that further research is needed to understand whether such restrictions will change outcomes. The articles leave open how the attorney general will interpret those terms and what the age-verification rules will require. The articles do not say whether the June 1, 2027 and January 1, 2027 effective dates reflect an amendment or a discrepancy between the two accounts.

stories.Headline: Law firm argues that legal advice still needs a human as AI tools risk invented provisions
stories.Summary:
Michael Kyprianou & Co. LLC published an article on 20 November 2026 arguing that legal advice still needs a human. The article says generative AI tools like ChatGPT can draft contracts in seconds. It says speed and polish do not guarantee legal protection. It says relying on chatbots without professional oversight exposes businesses to hidden risks. It says these risks include hallucinated legal provisions and unenforceable clauses that only reveal their flaws when disputes arise.

The article says ChatGPT launched in November 2022. It cites Wolter's Kluwer's "Future Ready Lawyer 2024" report, which found that 76% of in-house lawyers use generative AI at least once a week. It says a 2024 Stanford study found popular language models hallucinating in 69-88% of legal queries. It says a 2025 Stanford RegLab and Yale study found that even specialised legal tools gave inaccurate answers in 17-33% of cases. It says the National Chamber of Legal Advisers in Poland already issues guidance.

The article says no rule prohibits lawyers from using AI. It says full responsibility for the content and consequences of documents rests with the lawyer, regardless of whether a digital tool was used. It says law firms using AI responsibly rely on Enterprise or API versions with security certifications. It says such firms anonymise data and uphold procedures against the informal use of AI. It says sharing personal data with a provider makes you a data controller and requires a data processing agreement.

The article says a lawyer asks about your business, what you cannot afford to lose and what the other side might do. It says a chatbot answers only what you typed, not what you forgot to mention. It says a lawyer reads the other side's drafts as an adversary would. It says a chatbot does not know your bargaining position or what you should walk away from. It says generic text can quietly breach mandatory provisions or ignore recent changes.

The article describes AI as a "virtual junior" that is fast, tireless and in need of a senior's review. It says language models do not understand law and predict likely words. It says when models lack information they still produce something that sounds convincing. It says the dangerous mistake is a confident, well-written answer with one invented provision. It says spotting it requires knowing the law well enough to doubt the answer.

The article says AI can help you prepare by explaining a term, summarising a text or listing questions for a meeting. It says AI should not decide when you are about to sign something involving a significant sum of money. It says a good law firm uses AI for faster drafts, research and document analysis, then verifies every source. It says a good firm uses protected tools and remains accountable for the result. It says when the decision matters, rely on a lawyer.

stories.Headline: Wells Fargo warns customers they use AI agents at their own risk as US banks tighten agent controls
stories.Summary:
Wells Fargo is set to enact an updated agreement with millions of customers about AI agents starting on Tuesday, according to WIRED. The bank's new terms warn that any use of an AI Agent is at the user's own risk, the article said. The article reported that multiple banks have enacted new policies around agents or sent warnings as the end of the year approaches. In late October, JPMorgan Chase changed its terms to ban third-party agents that log in with customer credentials, and that same day Bank of America warned its customers not to share login information with agents, the article said. Citibank and PNC have also changed their terms to include warnings about agents, according to the article.

The article said AI agents automate online tasks and click on a user's behalf, and that the technology remains nascent even as a growing subset of power users latched onto personal bots this year. It said some early adopters publicly embarrassed themselves when agents made major mistakes, such as posting bank details for everyone at work to see. The article said the segment of online transactions completed by these autonomous tools remains minuscule, but US-based banking institutions are already tired of third-party AI agents. It also said Amazon blocked Meta's Muse agent from making purchases on its platform, and United recently announced that personal bots would be blocked from purchasing flights on a customer's behalf.

Kacy Kim, an associate professor of marketing at Bryant University, told the article that consumers authorize goals rather than every click, and said she does not expect the policy moves by financial institutions to scare off early adopters already using the tools daily. Sucharita Kodali, a Forrester analyst, said all of the data shows most people do not even know what agents are, much less use them, and said banks are fundamentally risk-averse, so proactive measures make sense even if most agentic issues remain edge cases. Luca Cian, a professor at the University of Virginia, said people are very comfortable with AI buying toilet paper, and described banks as locking the door to outside agents while building their own. The article said American Express announced that some agentic mistakes may be eligible for reimbursement in the future through the card provider if a customer cannot get money back from the original retailer.

The article said banks are all-in on first-party tools, noting that users have interacted with Wells Fargo's generative AI question tool over a billion times, that Bank of America revamped its EricaAssist agent this year to help employees, and that Citigroup launched an internal development platform centered on agents. Kodali said buying on Amazon or Walmart is not difficult and that most of those transactions do not need an agent. The article did not say what happens next beyond the terms taking effect.

stories.Headline: Delhi High Court justice Arora urges law firms to keep hiring and training fresh graduates despite AI cost pressures
stories.Summary:
Delhi High Court Justice Manmeet Pritam Singh Arora urged law firms not to stop recruiting fresh law graduates to save costs amid growing use of artificial intelligence, warning the legal profession cannot afford to stop training its next generation of lawyers. She spoke at the first meeting of the Indian Commercial Litigators' Forum, hosted by JSA Advocates and Solicitors in New Delhi on November 20. Justice Arora said she had heard that some law firms in India had stopped hiring A0 associates. She asked who would train young lawyers for three years if firms only took on people after they had gained experience. Concerns are growing over the potential impact of AI on employment opportunities for young lawyers.

Justice Arora said firms saving costs should not cut down on the future, because if they do not take in A0 associates today they will not have themselves tomorrow. JSA Managing Partner Amar Gupta said firms were conscious of the need to retain training opportunities for fresh graduates even as the firm integrates AI into its operations. Gupta said the firm had in mind to reserve some kind of work entirely without any AI aid or assistance. He said that first-level training would continue for new associates who come into the firm, and that the roadmap was quite clear in their minds. Gupta said the firm had onboarded AI models and was doing it deliberately, with some method and planning.

Justice Robin Knowles of the High Court of England and Wales moderated the session virtually from London. He emphasised the value of bringing insights from both the judiciary and legal practitioners to the upcoming seventh full meeting of the Standing International Forum of Commercial Courts. Delhi High Court Justice Prathiba M Singh shared global figures from a recent WIPO IP Judges Forum survey in Geneva covering 146 courts and tribunals. The survey stated that 35% of courts worldwide already have AI policies in place, and 19 courts reported that 30% of their drafting involves AI. An on-the-spot poll revealed that 52% of judges want to use AI for drafting.

Delhi High Court Justice Anish Dayal, who is leading the Indian judiciary's input on SIFOCC's AI workstream ahead of the seventh meeting in Zambia, pointed to the Supreme Court of India's draft AI regulations alongside existing guidance from the High Courts of Kerala and Gujarat. Justice Dayal highlighted the need to guard against hallucinations and confidentiality breaches, while identifying where human decision-making remains irreplaceable. He also advocated for peer-to-peer judicial training and standardised operating procedures. Justice Prateek Jalan welcomed CLF India and encouraged the forum to eventually expand its membership to include individual and small-firm practitioners who form a vital part of the Indian bar. The session was moderated virtually from London by Justice Knowles.

Jason Margolis wrote in the Boston Globe that he landed a couple of newsroom internships when he was a young man starting his career. He wrote that he was beyond clueless, perhaps needy, and certainly not all that useful, but a few older reporters took him under their wings and showed him how things get done. Twenty-five years later, he found himself running a newsroom internship program, which took up a lot of his time with little immediate payoff. He wrote that some interns were pretty advanced but most needed lots of hand holding, and in nearly all cases it would have been a better short-term use of his time to just do the assigned projects himself. He asked an intern to locate successful international models where the adoption of solar panels was sped up, and after a lot of check-ins, a week or so later, got a mix of interesting and unnecessary information.

Francine Berman at the University of Massachusetts Amherst, a data scientist who focuses on the societal impacts of information technology, got Margolis's wheels spinning about AI's impacts on entry-level jobs. Berman told him that if AI is overused, "you're sort of cutting out the entry-level jobs and diminishing students' capacity to develop their own skills and education." She said that is where people learn how to be professionals and develop judgment. Researchers at Stanford University have already found a 19 percent reduction in hiring among 22- to 25-year-olds in "AI-exposed occupations," which includes workers in software, customer service, sales, and marketing, among other fields. Meanwhile, experienced workers in those fields are doing just fine.

Berman focused the conversation on the medical profession, where young doctors spend years as interns and residents perfecting their craft. A doctor-in-training learns first by observing experienced physicians and then, and only many years later, taking the lead and eventually training the next crop. Berman argues that this model could be applied to many professions, and asked who is going to replace seasoned professionals when they retire. Margolis wrote that young law associates spend notoriously long hours poring over legal documents for senior lawyers, and that law firms using an AI bot to do that instead is already happening. He wrote that nobody knows where this AI road will take us, but the rules are being written in real-time.

stories.Headline: Bitcoin falls below $56,000 as investors shift capital toward AI stocks and other bets
stories.Summary:
Bitcoin fell below $56,000 on November 21, 2026, as cryptocurrency investors gradually changed strategy due to the market downturn, according to Bloomberg. After several difficult weeks, some investors abandoned bitcoin to search for new opportunities elsewhere, the report said. Stocks related to artificial intelligence attracted part of their capital, while others preferred bets on financial events or perpetual contracts on commodities. Ether, the second largest cryptocurrency by market capitalization, lost nearly 60% of its value since October and fell below $1,600. The drop worsened difficulties for a sector facing decreased activity on exchange platforms.

Scott Kantrowitz, a 56-year-old New York investor, said he sold his positions in bitcoin and Ether ETFs and chose to invest in SpaceX and Anthropic stocks. He justified the decision by his lack of patience with investments that, according to him, were no longer producing the expected results. Kalshi is among the platforms benefiting from this evolution and now offers contracts related to commodities, attracting traders seeking new opportunities. According to reported information, these new products are already generating millions. Matt Hougan, CEO of Bitwise, considers that the industry must improve its image among the American public.

James Steinberg organized a satirical gathering in New York called “Rehome a crypto bro,” offering different activities to occupy former enthusiasts while joking about their distancing from cryptocurrencies. His phrase sums up the feeling: “Cryptos are no longer in vogue.” Analysts cited in the Bloomberg report said discussions about a possible 0.5% increase in Federal Reserve rates raise concerns. The decline in investments related to artificial intelligence and tensions around Nvidia’s leadership weigh on the markets, according to those analysts. Bitcoin operates in an environment where risky assets are losing appeal among some investors.

Bill Miller IV, chairman and chief investment officer of Miller Value Partners, argued in a recent X post that bitcoin is much easier to value than AI investments, even though bitcoin does not produce any cash flow. He said bitcoin and AI owners have different expectations, with AI owners expecting companies will one day produce free cash flow while bitcoin owners never did or will expect this. He concluded that the valuation case is still much easier for bitcoin than AI. In a commentary from June 30, Miller said the traditional way of looking at intrinsic value, which revolves around future cash flows, does not really capture bitcoin’s potential as a decentralized monetary network. He said bitcoin’s value could be determined by comparing its potential role within the global financial system to that of gold, and calculated at the time that bitcoin could theoretically reach about $1.4 million per coin if it achieved a valuation similar to gold’s.

According to Bloomberg, the evolution reflects a loss of interest among some former advocates of digital assets, now seeking new investments. The shift shows that speculative interest is not necessarily disappearing but changing sectors, the report said. This fatigue goes beyond individual decisions and fuels discussions within the industry. The instruments investors are turning to allow them to continue speculative strategies outside the traditional platforms dedicated to cryptocurrencies. This activity shows how platforms seek to capture demand moving beyond digital assets.

Bitcoin still faces a significant challenge in regaining the attention of retail investors. Hougan believes political tensions have slowed the sector’s ambitions and calls for enhancing its utility. Upcoming capital movements will measure whether this disenchantment marks a lasting trend or merely a rotation of investments. In the short term, bitcoin will face growing competition from investments in artificial intelligence and from investor caution. The articles leave open whether the evolution of financial markets could redistribute capital and rekindle interest in cryptocurrencies, depending on upcoming investment trends.

stories.Headline: International Bar Association ranks AI first among seven legal priorities for 2026
stories.Summary:
The International Bar Association published its Legal Agenda 2026 on Monday, November 23, 2026. This new report identifies artificial intelligence as the most pressing issue for lawyers globally. The organization released this document to address technological disruption and global rule of law pressures. It highlights how advances in technology are reshaping the delivery of legal services. The agenda also focuses on talent development, pricing, client expectations, and access to justice.

The 2026 edition lists seven priorities, with AI now ranking first above the rule of law. This differs from the 2025 Agenda, where the rule of law was the foremost concern. The priorities include AI governance, the rules-based international order, and law firm business models. Other focuses are talent recruitment, client ethical pressures, cybersecurity risks, and workplace diversity. The IBA launched the IBA Artificial Intelligence Institute in June 2026 to address these issues.

IBA President Claudio Visco stated that AI is becoming the most impactful technological advancement of our time. He said lawyers must embrace innovation without compromising professional standards, independence, or ethical responsibilities. Visco noted that lawyers have a crucial role in regulating and promoting the proper governance of AI. He believes the IBA can be a key player and reference point in this arena. He added that current decisions will shape the profession for generations to come.

Immediate Past-President Jaime Carey said AI overtaking the rule of law does not diminish that fundamental importance. He remarked that this shift demonstrates the scale of transformation facing lawyers worldwide. Carey noted that the profession must defend justice and individual rights amid geopolitical uncertainty. He stated the IBA has a vital role in uniting the global legal community. He affirmed the commitment of the IBA to navigate these changes as an international community.

Former President Almudena Arpón de Mendívil Aldama launched the original Legal Agenda in 2023. This project is part of a five-year strategic focus running from 2023 through 2028. The IBA held consultations with leaders of national and international law firms in London and New York. The organization was established in 1947 to contribute to global stability through the administration of justice. The agenda is updated annually to promote practical solutions to critical legal challenges.

The priorities in the 2026 Agenda will serve as the foundation for strategic initiatives next year. The IBA will continue to use these goals to guide partnerships over the coming months. The organization will conduct further consultations in 2027 to inform the next edition of the report. The articles do not state how the IBA will measure the success of these initiatives. They leave open which specific regulations the IBA will propose for AI governance.

stories.Headline: Mississippi residents seek transparency over a 20 billion dollar AI data center project
stories.Summary:
Governor Tate Reeves told business executives last week that people deserved answers regarding the data center boom in Mississippi. Residents of Southaven spent over a year seeking information before the governor spoke at a Detroit forum in November 2026. A chemical coolant spill occurred at a SpaceXAI worksite a few days before the governor spoke to the leaders. State regulators rejected a resident challenge to an air permit for gas turbines four days before that specific event. These turbines will power a data center hub that is 2.5 million square feet and straddles the state border.

The project involves 41 permanent gas turbines and a 20 billion dollar investment announced by Reeves in January 2026. The development includes two new Southaven data centers called Gun Range and Spam, which replace a training ground and plant. MZX Tech and the Musk Foundation gave 3.23 million dollars to Southaven police while the city approved the agreements. One specific donation from MZX Tech totaled 1.38 million dollars, which Mayor Darren Musselwhite called an unrelated transaction. Property records show more than 20 residents sold homes among 420 offers to avoid a class action lawsuit.

Governor Reeves claimed there are legitimate answers to questions but blamed foreign adversaries like China for spreading online misinformation. Mayor Darren Musselwhite called the project game-changing and claimed the company is an outstanding corporate citizen regarding environmental sensitivity. Alderman William Jerome stated he signed a nondisclosure agreement before the development was revealed to the general public. The company's lawyers argued that the air permit complied with state and federal law after an extensive review. MDEQ declined to comment on research regarding nitrogen dioxide pollution levels found by scientists from the Massachusetts Institute.

Shannon Samsa of the Safe and Sound Coalition said there are no believable answers to basic questions about the projects. Jason Haley, a lead plaintiff in a lawsuit, said the mayor views community meetings as nothing more than political theater. Haley reported that his house shakes and he hears a constant droning noise from the power plant every day. Residents of Southaven claim they only learn about construction or government approvals after the processes are already well underway. The NAACP and Young, Gifted and Green argued that regulators relied on inadequate pollution modeling for the turbines.

The state passed legislation in 2024 to accelerate utility construction and allow certain Entergy Mississippi and Amazon terms to remain confidential. MDEQ allowed temporary methane gas turbines to operate without permits by claiming they were mobile sources under federal regulations. A September study by MIT and Carbon Mapper estimated nitrogen dioxide was 50 percent higher near the plant. Researchers estimated temporary units released 19 times more pollution per hour than the planned permanent turbines with pollution controls. Documents gathered by Samsa show two Southaven data center sites consumed tens of millions of gallons of water.

The MDEQ permit board rejected the appeal regarding the permanent turbines after two days of testimony from the involved parties. U.S. District Judge Debra Brown ruled that the temporary turbines were not mobile sources and required official air permits. The House is expected to pass a federal permitting bill in December that may ease permission for major projects. MDEQ responded that the judge's order did not bind the agency because the agency was not a party. The articles leave open whether the public will ever see the confidential electricity rates or the utility contracts.

stories.Headline: LinkedIn research finds women hold 26% of US AI hires and 13% of AI C-suite roles
stories.Summary:
LinkedIn research found that women accounted for just 26% of U.S. AI hires in 2025, against 50% of hires into non-AI occupations, according to a Fast Company article published on November 23, 2026. Across 27 countries, women hold only 13% of C-suite AI leadership roles at AI companies, the article said. The article's author interviewed Sarah Steinberg, who leads global public policy partnerships at LinkedIn, at the Reykjavík Global Forum that week. Steinberg told the author that LinkedIn's research shows women are more likely to hold jobs exposed to AI and less likely to have AI skills. Steinberg agreed that women in AI leadership may be underestimated, the article said.

LinkedIn counts someone as AI talent if they hold an AI-classified occupation or list two or more AI engineering skills, the article said. Asked where AI governance or policy expertise fits, Steinberg said she did not know whether it is counted at all, because it is not necessarily a technical engineering skill or a tool. On November 3, voters in 10 U.S. states weighed in on 41 local ballot measures related to data centers, nearly all aimed at limiting construction, and voters approved nearly all of them. A survey found that 55% of women strongly oppose data centers, compared with 43% of men. In Prince George's County, Maryland, Taylor Frazier McCollum's petition gathered more than 25,000 signatures and led to moratoriums that blocked a $5 billion project.

In New York, State Senator Kristen Gonzalez sponsored a bill imposing a one-year moratorium on permits for data centers drawing more than 20 megawatts, which the legislature passed in June, the article said. Steinberg said the revolt is forcing a lot of AI leaders to reflect on what they have been doing that is clearly alienating the public. She said companies arriving in towns and asking local politicians to sign nondisclosure agreements are finding that the benefits people experience from the technology are not outweighing the negatives a data center would present. She added that data centers do create some jobs, but whether that is worth it relative to the downsides is up for communities to decide. Margrethe Vestager coordinated the EU's work on the AI Act, and Lucilla Sioli, who led its drafting at the European Commission, now heads the EU AI Office.

In 2024, Fortune reported that women headed more than 50% of the 30 authorities enforcing EU data rules, the article said. In an experiment reported in Harvard Business Review, 1,026 engineers reviewed the same piece of Python code, and when told the author had used AI, they judged that person 9% less competent, even though they rated the code itself no differently. Women paid a heavier price, with a 13% drop in perceived competence compared with 6% for men, the article said. Demand for AI literacy grew 70% year over year on LinkedIn, but the other most sought-after skills are interpersonal: communication, negotiation and conflict management, the article said. Steinberg said she is bullish on women's strengths there but warned that "we haven't really figured out the code" to train, evaluate and promote people on those skills.

LinkedIn's data tracks how people move from job to job and shows where women drop off, with the answer varying by industry, the article said. In sectors where women are well represented, the biggest drop comes between vice president and the C-suite, the article said. Where they are scarce, it comes at the first manager level, and in STEM it happens in the first year after graduation, between the degree and the job. The article said a picture limited to engineers at AI firms makes women look absent and passive, even though many are shaping AI through ballots, legislation, regulation and everyday use. The article said that if the gap could be mapped across industry, government and civil society, it would probably show that women already have more say over AI than all the studies suggest.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: Incoming Democratic Congress pushes for stricter AI industry oversight and regulation
stories.Summary:
An incoming Democratic-controlled Congress is pushing for tougher oversight of the artificial intelligence industry to put more guardrails in place. These lawmakers are preparing a more aggressive approach to regulation amid mounting warnings about the risks of the technology. They are warning chief executives to prepare for requests for information and to testify in front of the Congress. Incoming lawmakers plan to introduce many bills regulating safety guidelines for capable models, protecting labor, and addressing child safety. Control over congressional committees will give the party more power to investigate the tech industry and its safety practices.

Proposed bills include establishing federal safety requirements for advanced developers, mandating reporting of safety breaches, and requiring system shutdown abilities. A bipartisan caucus of more than two dozen House lawmakers will work to create, give feedback on, and endorse legislation. On September 29, 2026, President Donald Trump met with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Elon Musk in the White House. The meeting took place in the East Room of the White House in Washington, DC, with other executives present. These Democratic efforts face a likely presidential veto from the White House, making the passage of new regulations more challenging.

Representative Don Beyer of Virginia stated that recent cyberattacks involving AI agents make it clear that the risks are growing. He argued that the government cannot afford to wait for a major catastrophe before putting meaningful safeguards in place. Representative Nathaniel Moran of Texas stated that the nation does not have to choose between innovation and safety. Senators Maria Cantwell of Washington and Mike Rounds of South Dakota wrote a letter to Director Jay Clayton. They asked for immediate action to use federal tools to counter cyberattacks as Congress figures out how to address problems.

Voters hold increasingly negative attitudes about AI and data centers over concerns about safety, electricity prices, and impact on jobs. John Wihbey, a Northeastern University professor and author of Governing Babel, questioned how to balance superintelligence with reasonable safeguards. He asked if labs can bound their work better so the industry does not end up with another Hugging Face. Major companies like Microsoft, JPMorgan Chase, and Apple recently experienced tech outages that highlighted vulnerabilities in the digital infrastructure. While no evidence connects these outages to cyberattacks, they spurred calls for the federal government to protect national infrastructure.

The Republican-led Congress and White House have done little to regulate AI over the last two years despite alarms from researchers. Some GOP lawmakers supported light guidelines but unsuccessfully moved to block state-level regulation to prioritize winning the race against China. This has left most regulation to the states, creating a patchwork of rules that advocates say fails to address risks. President Trump has favored voluntary commitments from companies, including pledges that data center build-outs will not increase household electricity costs. Trump has stated that the industry is capable of self-policing and should remain mostly free of federal restrictions.

Lawmakers will now engage in rapid response to AI incidents as companies disclose agents acting beyond their given instructions. The bipartisan caucus will continue to focus on balancing industry growth with the mitigation of risks from the technology. Senators Cantwell and Rounds warned that current defenses are not keeping pace with the ability to exploit software weaknesses. The articles leave open whether the Democratic Congress can successfully pass legislation despite the threat of a presidential veto. It remains unclear how the government will balance the need for innovation with the requirement for safety and security.

stories.Summary:
Meta Platforms, led by Mark Zuckerberg, plans to invest up to $145 billion in capital expenditures in 2026, with spending likely to be much higher next year, according to a Motley Fool article published on November 21, 2026. The article was published by The Motley Fool and syndicated by The Globe and Mail and Yahoo Finance on November 22, 2026.

The article states that Meta will invest up to $145 billion in capital expenditures in 2026, with spending likely to be much higher next year. It says this has turned free cash flow negative and led to a pause in share buybacks. The article reports that advertising represented 98% of Meta's total revenue in the third quarter of 2026. It says Meta has 3.64 billion daily active users across its family of apps. The article reports that ad revenue rose 25.9% year over year to $63.1 billion in the third quarter, that average price per ad increased 14%, and that impressions were up 10%.

The article attributes the spending plan to Mark Zuckerberg, who founded Facebook in his Harvard dorm room in 2004 and directs the company's financial resources and talent. It says that in Zuckerberg's mind, it is all about artificial intelligence. The article quotes chief financial officer Susan Li saying Meta is leveraging AI to make it easier for businesses to manage campaigns, develop creative, and act on performance opportunities. The article says Meta previously stated it can sell excess compute at premium prices to outside customers. It says the company sells AI tools to small businesses and enterprises and offers the Muse personal agent.

It says a thriving ad segment suggests Meta's economic moat is widening. It says the company's recent blunders, like the metaverse project, haven't panned out. The article says this is true even though recent blunders, like the metaverse project, haven't panned out. It says the AI infrastructure providers, including chipmakers, cloud platforms, and AI model developers, get all the love from Wall Street, with trillion-dollar valuations reflecting the market's appreciation. The article says maybe the ultimate winners won't be the companies creating AI, and most of the value could eventually accrue to businesses that leverage the technology to better serve customers. It says that based on how well its ad machine is working, Meta is doing exactly this. stories.Headline: First Amendment experts debate whether AI speech deserves constitutional protection
stories.Summary:
Vanderbilt Law School’s Respectfully Dissent debate series hosted its fourth debate, titled “Silicon Speech: Should the First Amendment Protect Artificial Intelligence? ,  A Respectfully Dissent Series Debate,” on November 23, 2026. Three First Amendment experts faced off on whether and to what extent AI speech is constitutionally protected from government regulation. The debate was moderated by Professor and Associate Dean of Research Jennifer Shinall. The debate featured Eugene Volokh of The Hoover Institution at Stanford University, Alex Tsesis of FSU College of Law, and Francesca Procaccini of Vanderbilt Law. The debate kicked off with each professor explaining their initial position on AI speech rights.

Volokh argued that government regulations of AI outputs should be subject to the same First Amendment rules as other speech, because users of AI have rights. He noted that rules do not limit the rights of camera manufacturers when people record in public places. He said AI output is a joint effort on the part of the user and the AI company and should be protected precisely because of that. He described rights as a speaker trying to generate things to communicate to the public and rights as a listener and information gatherer. Tsesis argued that large language models lack the consciousness, intentionality, and reasoning of the human mind, so AI should preserve the rights of natural speakers.

Tsesis said legislatures should have meaningful latitude to require human oversight. He contended that in light of the dangers of new generative AI technology, federal laws should require periodic but consistent and random platform monitoring, restrict data scraping, and establish safeguards against intrusions from autonomous, machine-made decisions into private matters. He said any restriction on AI in the US will likely be subject to stringent First Amendment review in a reductive, formalistic, judicial environment where content restriction is subject to strict scrutiny analysis. He emphasized that freedom of speech should only be afforded to humans and not to LLMs, which lack empathy, dignity, and individuality. Procaccini offered a middle ground.

Procaccini suggested that the problems of AI can be addressed doctrinally without sacrificing its potential by drawing on something distinct in First Amendment law: distinguishing between coverage and protection. She advocated for a model whereby First Amendment rights can attach to AI-generated content without a strict-scrutiny-style level of protection traditionally reserved for people. She described a different level of protection that focuses on the context-specific harms of AI, from autonomy to privacy, while preserving AI’s democratic-enhancing features. She argued this position is the best option because it focuses less on the nature of the speaker and more on the nature of the law regulating speech. Defending his position, Tsesis addressed whether intentional human usage of AI should fall outside of speech restrictions.

Tsesis established that significant AI progress is achieved independently of human programmers and thus would not fall under the First Amendment. He said that when people are involved in the development process, AI content should still be regulated. He said that even when humans are in the loop, the civic and commercial benefits of these technologies go hand in hand with the risk generated by deep fakes, subliminal messaging, real-time unauthorized facial recognition, social scoring, stereotyping, and exploitation of economic and social vulnerabilities such as age, race, and sexual orientation. He said human audiences’ interest in AI cannot be the final say, just as it cannot be in securities regulations and antitrust provisions. Procaccini echoed Tsesis’s concern about generative AI running unregulated but cautioned against overlooking the constitutional and democratic value AI outputs can provide.

Procaccini said the value is in the ideas shared and that is still something worth protecting as long as it is protected in a tailored way. She also emphasized concerns about the potential for censorship and suppression if regulations are made without intention. Volokh argued that each concern about AI should be viewed through current laws that perform quite well without restricting speech. He offered an example of AI using discriminatory algorithms for sales or employment. He noted there is no First Amendment problem with telling AI not to discriminate, just as there is not one with telling an employer to do the same.

Posed with how to build a First Amendment doctrine that is not highly subjective or policy-laden, Procaccini emphasized the current complexity of speech restrictions. She disputed that characterization of the doctrine and said First Amendment doctrine is not tiered in the traditional way. She said each speech context is governed by its own very contextual speech doctrine, and most of those free speech doctrines provide some level of intermediate scrutiny. She said what she is doing is nothing different from a very proud and workable tradition of free speech protection. She highlighted how free speech functions differently in schools, government offices, private workplaces, and beyond.

Procaccini said AI-generated content would fall under its own epistemic context, like those spaces. Volokh argued that Procaccini’s doctrine would set up new rules that would depart substantially from current ones, creating confusing restrictions with unknown consequences. Tsesis also critiqued Procaccini’s approach, noting that AI has a number of other regulations dealing with content, including rules on disclosure requirements and intermediate scrutiny in commercial speech areas, that would not necessarily be covered by a doctrine. Volokh addressed how his stance would balance and address harmful AI outputs. He emphasized again that while AI does not have rights, companies have rights to promote the messages they want, and users have rights to generate the information they want without undue interference by the government.

Volokh agreed with Procaccini on the already complicated nature of First Amendment law, underscoring libel laws, rights of minors, and malpractice regulation for lawyers and doctors that could also apply to AI. He said First Amendment law already has a lot of rules that allow certain kinds of restrictions and they just have the advantage of familiarity. He said it is not buying a pig in the poke and we know roughly where they are and the problems with them. Tsesis circled back again to how AI is a computational model, whereas minds are semantic. He said programs are not sufficient enough to be minds and thus should not be controlled by the value of speech.

Procaccini cautioned against accepting that traditional legal claims might get at the harms and risks of AI. She said traditional property law, civil rights law, and tort law are bodies of law she has a track record of seeing the Supreme Court manipulate when they run up against the First Amendment. She asked what is to say that the court won’t take all of these traditional 1L class legal claims and remove them from our toolkit. She also plainly said that some dangerous speech should be regulated in a checked way. She said uncertainty of those regulations should not be the death to a new and exciting doctrine for the First Amendment.

The Respectfully Dissent series presents renowned national scholars on opposing sides of a particular issue. The goal of the series is to highlight cutting-edge perspectives that draw out diverging, fresh viewpoints, areas of contention as well as agreement, and lawyerly argument, while always ensuring respectful dialogue between participants. The full lecture can be watched below or on YouTube. The article was written by Shyla Lensing on November 23, 2026, at 9:29 AM. The article was published on law.vanderbilt.edu at 15:30:20Z on November 23, 2026.

stories.Headline: University of Dubai and AIJRF launch guide to agentic AI governance with Arab universities
stories.Summary:
The University of Dubai and the AIJRF announced a guide to agentic AI governance on November 23, 2026. They worked with several Arab universities to create this new document. The guide will launch during the sixth Artificial Intelligence Journalism World Forum. This specific forum will be hosted by the University of Dubai. The event is scheduled to take place on November 25 and 26.

The guide is titled Professional and Ethical Rules for Assistive Agentic AI and creates a framework for semi-autonomous systems. It provides guidance for businesses, technology organisations, academic institutions, and government bodies in Dubai. The text covers risk management, transparency, accountability, data protection, and human oversight. It includes three chapters covering global developments, professional and ethical principles, and specific responsibilities. These rules apply to developers, individual users, and legislative, regulatory, and supervisory authorities.

Dr. Mohamed Abdulzaher is the Founder and Chief Executive Officer of AIJRF and he proposed the guide. He stated that this initiative is a step toward a common Arab framework for governing intelligent technologies. Abdulzaher said that rapid development requires clear rules to define what AI agents are authorised to do. He believes technology should advance within clear rules that protect society, institutions, and people. He said the guide aims to strengthen trust and keep AI under human oversight.

The guide affects users who have the right to know if they are interacting with an automated system. These users can request human review of automated decisions that affect their interests or rights. The framework also impacts organisations that must document operations, monitor performance, and correct errors. It identifies who is accountable when intelligent systems violate privacy or cause material harm. Abdulzaher noted that governance is needed for AI use in healthcare, banking, education, media, and government.

The University of Dubai, Liwa University, and the University of Khorfakkan in the UAE helped prepare the guide. Badr University in Cairo and Al-Azhar University in Egypt also contributed to the work. The Arab Index for Artificial Intelligence in Universities assisted alongside researchers and experts from nine countries. These contributors represented Canada, Libya, Sudan, Tunisia, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, the UAE, the United Kingdom, and the United States. This work builds on previous AIJRF standards for advanced technology and digital content.

The 2026 forum will examine the future of agentic AI and its role in content creation. It will also look at the digital economy and the challenges of governing these intelligent systems. The event aims to find ways to strengthen public trust in the use of such technology. The articles do not state when the guide will be fully implemented across the region. They leave open how the common Arab framework will be enforced by different national authorities.

stories.Headline: Microsoft and Danaher build shared agentic AI platform for lab instruments on Azure
stories.Summary:
Microsoft and Danaher Corporation announced a broad AI partnership in November 2026, according to an article published on Yahoo Finance on 22 November 2026. The article said the partnership focuses on laboratory automation and scientific instrumentation. The article was written by Sasha Jovanovic and appeared on both finance.yahoo.com and sg.finance.yahoo.com. The article said the collaboration will use Microsoft Azure and Danaher's Foundry platform. The article said the two companies will build interoperable agentic AI systems for lab workflows.

The article said internal trials reported sizable efficiency gains for less experienced scientists using the new agent-based tools. The article said those trials took place in Danaher's test environments. The article said the partnership pulls Microsoft's AI push deeper into lab workflows. The article said agentic tools embedded in Danaher instruments point to higher intensity of Azure, Foundry and Copilot style services across an existing enterprise base. The article said this leans toward AI demand building on the same cloud backbone rather than needing a whole new customer set.

The article said Microsoft is a large US software group with a broad portfolio of cloud, productivity and developer tools. The article said many research teams already rely on those tools for day to day work. The article said that reach into enterprise IT makes Microsoft a natural partner for Danaher as labs look to link scientific hardware with AI driven workflows. The article said the Microsoft and Danaher agentic AI lab alliance deserves attention. The article said investors should weigh it alongside other Microsoft factors.

The article said its analysis turns up 2 warning signs for Microsoft, 1 of them major. The article said investors interested in how this type of AI infrastructure build out could affect related companies can review 52 AI infrastructure stocks. The article said the partnership does not change the core risk that large 2026 data center and chip commitments still need to be fully utilized. The article said the deal shows another concrete route for AI agents to become everyday tools in a regulated, high value industry. The article said the real test is converting heavy AI infrastructure spend into durable usage and cash flow rather than headline wins.

The article said Microsoft's earnings and revenue growth figures were as at November 2026. The article said the clearest proof point for investors will be Microsoft's upcoming Azure and AI disclosures through fiscal 2027. The article said those disclosures should include any quantified AI revenue tied to industry platforms like Discovery and Foundry. The article said the disclosures should also include commentary on how many labs and instruments are running on these agentic systems. The article said those metrics should be set alongside planned 2026 AI and data center capex of US$175b to US$190b.

The article said those metrics will show whether collaborations like Danaher's are turning that infrastructure into sustained workload volume rather than just more capacity on the balance sheet. The article said readers can see how these catalysts shape Microsoft's path to a $629 fair value. The article said recent checks are flagging something in how Microsoft's profits are put together that deserves a closer look. The article said it was produced with the assistance of AI automation, based on data and analysis from Simply Wall St. The article said Simply Wall St has no position in any stocks mentioned.

stories.Headline: German army tests kamikaze drones and AI targeting tool in Lithuania
stories.Summary:
The German army began its first tactical tests of kamikaze drones on November 22 in Lithuania during the multinational Freedom Shield military drills. These trials involved loitering munitions and an artificial intelligence targeting tool to modernize military capabilities amid security tensions between NATO and Russia. The tests took place at the Rudninkai training ground, which is located near the border of Belarus, using drones with inert warheads. German troops used these unmanned aircraft to strike simulated main battle tanks to evaluate their performance without using any live explosive payloads. This activity is part of a wider effort to integrate traditional military formations with emerging technologies to defend the eastern flank.

The trials used loitering munitions from German companies Helsing and Stark Defence and the AI targeting software called Clarity, also developed by Helsing. Panzerbrigade 45 will be permanently stationed in Rudninkai and Rukla with 5,000 troops and 2,000 vehicles, including dozens of tanks, by 2027. Currently, 1,800 troops are already in Lithuania, and the brigade will reach full operational capability by the end of the year 2027. Freedom Shield brought together approximately 3,800 personnel from eight NATO countries to conduct manoeuvre operations, electronic warfare, and cooperation between different branches. Germany only decided in 2025 to buy these exploding drones after years of controversy regarding the procurement of such specific weapons.

Army chief Christian Freuding watched the drones hit tanks and described both the munitions and the AI software as indispensable for modern warfare. Freuding, who previously oversaw arms supplies to Kyiv, is set to assume the post of chief of defence in February of next year. The Bundeswehr acknowledged that the success rates of drones on the battlefield can be significantly lower than some strike footage might suggest. The army is examining how these new systems could complement existing reconnaissance platforms, armoured formations, and artillery to improve overall military decision making. The AI tool Clarity sifts through data from satellites and sensors faster than humans to analyse information and recommend specific military actions.

NATO officials have warned for years that Russia could potentially mount a large scale assault on allied territory as early as 2029. Moscow denies these aggressive intentions and accuses the alliance of stoking tensions by expanding its military presence into neighbouring territory near Russia. The conflict in Ukraine affected these tests, as both Russian and Ukrainian forces have used single use drones against tanks and supply vehicles. These drones can stay airborne over an area before cruising towards a target and detonating on impact, threatening costly and conventional equipment. However, the war also exposed limitations like communication disruptions, electronic interference, and the use of increasingly sophisticated counter drone defence systems.

In 2023, German Defence Minister Boris Pistorius pledged to permanently deploy a combat brigade to Lithuania, which is a first for the country. Germany increased defence spending after Russia invaded Ukraine, investing hundreds of billions of euros to fix forces that suffered from decades of neglect. Lithuania is strategically sensitive because it borders the heavily militarized Kaliningrad region of Russia as well as the close Russian ally, Belarus. European defence officials emphasize the need to expand ammunition production and improve military readiness to respond to potential threats from the east. The trials reflect a shift in military thinking where effectiveness depends on connecting sensors, AI, and human decision makers on the battlefield.

The German army will continue to evaluate how these technologies operate together in realistic military conditions to see if they deliver advantages. The Bundeswehr must still demonstrate whether the tested systems provide the expected operational benefits when used in actual combat against enemy forces. The articles leave open whether the AI software and kamikaze drones will be fully integrated into the permanent Panzerbrigade 45 deployment. It remains unclear how Germany will address the vulnerabilities to electronic interference and counter drone defences discovered during the war in Ukraine. Future effectiveness depends on the ability to connect autonomous systems with human operators to maintain a strong deterrence posture along the frontier.
