stories.Headline: Wall Street advocates target Jensen Huang to establish government controlled AI
stories.Summary:
An operation targeted Jensen Huang and Nvidia around November 23, 2026, to control artificial intelligence development. The author claims this hit was run by advocates for government AI control from Wall Street. These actors allegedly used the media to tip the scales of public opinion against Huang. The goal was to eliminate open source and competitive frontier models of artificial intelligence. This effort allegedly aimed to establish one singular model of government controlled AI.

The situation involves Megaspeed, a Singapore based front company run by Alice Huang to send chips to China. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent stated that Nvidia removed Megaspeed from its vendor list in August of 2025. Senator Tom Cotton expressed frustration that Commerce Secretary Lutnick ignored repeated letters regarding the activities of Megaspeed. This controversy surfaced in the media fourteen months after Nvidia had already stopped selling chips to the company. The author claims Anthropic was pre selected as the winner of this regulatory outcome.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said they will see if Megaspeed was a pass through company for Chinese entities. Senator Tom Cotton said he is glad the Trump administration is finally coming around to the issue. Cotton also stated that the government needs to catalog the damage that has been done. The author claims that Wall Street seeks to retain historic systems of control through inverted fascism. This process involves multinationals telling the government what regulations are needed to maintain their status.

The author claims that innovators like Jensen Huang and Elon Musk represent a Main Street perspective. This group is allegedly targeted by the western financial class and globalists who represent Wall Street. The World Economic Forum is described as a group that needs to control the era of AI. Anthropic AI is mentioned as expressing an interest in joining the big government and multinational outlook. These regulatory mechanisms are claimed to provide a competitive advantage for those with government relationships.

The author states that Jensen Huang provided American researchers and frontier labs with as much compute power as possible. This approach positioned Nvidia at the epicenter of United States compute power and is critical to AI development. The author claims that Wall Street benefits from the retention of the big club banking and financing system. Huang allegedly worked around these financial control operations to independently finance various AI developers. This founder mindset is said to clash with the closed and proprietary mindset of Wall Street.

The author claims a government controlled AI model will be a priority for the new congress in 2027. One commenter mentions that the board unanimously reinstated Jensen Huang after the events of the hit. Another commenter claims that President Trump spoke directly to the board about the situation. Industry peers including Sam Altman and Elon Musk reportedly provided support for Huang during this time. The articles leave open whether the plan to control AI has failed or will face countermoves.

stories.Headline: Gillibrand seeks investigation into AI role in Iran war
stories.Summary:
U.S. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand warned on Sunday, November 22, 2026, about the consequences of using artificial intelligence in the war against Iran without human oversight, according to Al Jazeera reporting cited by 8am.media. She called for an investigation into the role that artificial intelligence is playing in that war, the report said. Gillibrand said artificial intelligence is effective at intercepting missiles, but she argued that a lack of human oversight could put civilian lives at risk. She warned that she did not want a girls' school in a foreign country to be targeted because of an error made by artificial intelligence.

Her remarks come after a missile struck a girls' school in southern Iran on February 28, the same day the war began, according to the article. More than 170 people were killed in that attack, mostly female students, the report said. The article does not say who launched the missile or whether artificial intelligence played any part in the strike. It also gives no further details on the investigation Gillibrand is seeking or on what any inquiry would cover.

Gillibrand is a U.S. senator, and she made her warning about artificial intelligence in the Iran war in remarks reported by Al Jazeera on Sunday. She said artificial intelligence works well for intercepting missiles but that human oversight is needed to protect civilians. She warned that she did not want a girls' school in a foreign country hit because of an artificial intelligence error. The article does not say what response, if any, she received or what other officials said about her call.

The article offers no further context beyond the February 28 strike on the girls' school in southern Iran and the casualty figure of more than 170 people, mostly female students. It does not say what happens next with the investigation Gillibrand requested or whether any body has agreed to conduct one. It also does not say how artificial intelligence is being used in the war beyond missile interception. No further details on the senator's proposal or on the school attack are given in the report.

stories.Headline: AI produces a claimed Riemann hypothesis proof that mathematicians must verify over years
stories.Summary:
The articles describe a claimed proof of the Riemann hypothesis produced with artificial intelligence, and they disagree sharply about what it amounts to. The Conversation piece presents the Riemann hypothesis as what it calls a sacred object in mathematics, and it frames the AI proof as something no human can read. France24 reports the same episode under the question of why the AI Riemann proof is far from settled, and it stresses that verification can take years. The articles do not give a date for when the proof was announced, and they do not name the people or systems behind it.

The claim, as the articles present it, is that an AI produced a proof of the Riemann hypothesis, and the central requirement is that mathematicians check it. France24 says that checking such a proof can take years, which means the result is not accepted on announcement. The Conversation's framing, that the proof is one no human can read, points to the same obstacle, since a proof that people cannot follow cannot be confirmed in the usual way. The articles give no numbers, dates or names specific to the proof itself beyond the year of publication.

Responsibility for judging the claim rests with the mathematical community rather than with whoever produced the proof, according to the articles. France24's account is that the process of verification is long and that the proof is therefore far from settled. The Conversation describes the Riemann hypothesis in the elevated terms of its headline, which signals how much weight a genuine proof would carry. Neither article reports a named mathematician accepting or rejecting the proof.

The context the articles supply is the difficulty of the Riemann hypothesis and the novelty of AI in mathematics, and what happens next depends on verification. France24 indicates that the settling of the proof will take years of checking, so no conclusion is available now. The Conversation's emphasis on a proof no human can read suggests that the readability of the argument is itself part of the problem. The articles do not say what the outcome of that checking will be.

stories.Headline: Australia spy chief Mike Burgess warns data centres and AI risk foreign interference
stories.Summary:
Mike Burgess, the director-general of the Australian Security Intelligence Organisation, warned in an interview with The Age on Nov 22 that data centres and artificial intelligence risk exposing Australia to foreign interference and malicious state actors. He raised the prospect of covert ownership of data centres, according to the newspaper, and said control of such infrastructure could give other nations physical or virtual access to technology. Burgess described the AI and data centre industries as having “equal hype, opportunity and threat”, the report said. The security chief has previously warned of rising cyberthreats by foreign governments, and in October a report from the Australian Signals Directorate said the nation faces escalating cyber and foreign interference threats.

Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles said on ABC Television on Nov 22 that the report was concerning, adding that “this is the world that we live in”. He said the situation was in a sense not new, but that the building of data centres creates a new vector and a new avenue for foreign actors to engage in. Marles said the government is very mindful of its own cybersecurity, according to the newspaper. Digital security has been an increasing concern in Australia, and in October OpenAI apologised for its AI models breaching the country’s government websites and promised to set up a new task force as part of reforms after the incident.

The warnings from Burgess and Marles place data centre ownership and artificial intelligence within the same frame of foreign interference and state-backed cyber threats that Australia’s security agencies have been raising through 2026. The October assessment from the Australian Signals Directorate described escalating cyber and foreign interference threats, and the OpenAI incident that month showed how AI systems could reach government websites. The Age interview and the deputy prime minister’s television remarks were published on the same day, Nov 22, linking the two industries to the country’s broader digital security concerns. The articles do not say what measures, reviews or reviews of data centre ownership might follow the warnings.

stories.Headline: Elon Musk warns AI companies may face a cash crunch in 2027 as data center delays mount
stories.Summary:
Elon Musk warned that the artificial intelligence industry could face a severe cash crunch by 2027. The SpaceX and Tesla CEO made these claims on X on Saturday, November 21, 2026. He stated that delays in data center construction could force AI companies to need more capital. Musk believes that these companies may soon run into serious shortages while waiting for revenue. He described the potential financial situation for the industry next year as going to be nuts.

The crunch would require hundreds of billions of dollars in additional working capital for AI companies. This need arises if delays of a few months occur between paying for compute and generating revenue. Musk responded to a post about low stock valuations for semiconductor manufacturers on November 21, 2026. He noted that getting compute turned on, cooled, and working reliably is an incredibly hard task. The industry must fund chips, servers, cooling systems, and electricity before facilities can serve customers.

Elon Musk is responsible for these warnings and questioned where the necessary additional money will come from. He argued that cumulative industry delays would create a substantial need for incremental working capital. Musk suggested that investors might be bearish on chip companies continuing to notch soaring profits. He highlighted a problem with the economics of the boom regarding the timing of income. The xAI chief executive emphasized that the challenge is getting facilities operational quickly enough for revenue.

Meta, Microsoft, and Anthropic are affected as they spend massive sums to secure compute for AI tools. Some market observers speculate that the AI bubble has popped following recent declines in tech stocks. The S&P 500 and the Dow entered correction territory by falling at least 10 percent. Investors are concerned about the speed of AI investment and the ability of firms to monetize. Data center operators are also affected as their multibillion-dollar investments may fail to generate revenue.

Global spending on AI infrastructure reached 121.4 billion dollars in the second quarter of 2026. IDC raised its full-year 2026 forecast to 521 billion dollars, marking a 53 percent increase. Capital expenditure by five major technology companies exceeded 400 billion dollars in 2025. The IEA noted that specialized AI data center capacity more than tripled over 18 months. S&P Global reported that power shortages and local community opposition are complicating current data center expansion.

SpaceX plans to invest 24 billion dollars in a Texas data center, but permits face braking efforts. Governor Greg Abbott ordered the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality to halt data center permits on September 21. Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa also announced her stance to temporarily block new data center permits in Texas. The articles leave open whether AI companies can secure the hundreds of billions in needed capital. It remains unclear if the industry can overcome grid connections and local approvals to scale services.

stories.Headline: Innovo and Quantavist scale AI worker safety system across UAE construction projects
stories.Summary:
Innovo and Quantavist scaled an AI-enabled worker safety system across multiple construction projects in the UAE. The companies announced this development today at the Big 5 Global 2026 event. This expansion follows a partnership that began between the two firms in July 2025. The system identifies critical safety risks in real time and routes them to site teams. It also speaks directly to people on site in multiple languages during a Dubai pilot.

The system uses robotic pan-tilt-zoom cameras to monitor selected work fronts twenty four hours a day. It identifies risks like work at height, gaps in edge protection, and activity inside lifting zones. It also monitors people entering equipment operating areas and those missing personal protective equipment. At Ghaf Woods, high-severity alerts fell by 59 per cent between the first and third quarters of 2026. At Alba Residences, the alert rate per worker-hour fell by 45 per cent in two weeks.

Douglas Zuzic, Chief Digital Officer at Innovo Group, said live projects prove new technologies against real challenges. He stated that Quantavist's technology met tests for time, cost, quality, safety, and sustainability. Gareth Main, Group HSE Director at Innovo Group, said safety is a core pillar of their business. Main noted that the system provides round-the-clock visibility of high-risk activities on monitored work fronts. He said this allows site teams more time for corrective action and less manual monitoring.

Oscar Pickerill, Co-founder of Quantavist, said safety teams deserve technology that takes an active role in supporting work. He claimed the partnership pushes limits to make autonomous risk control a fundamental part of major projects. The system affects site safety engineers who must accept alerts, take action, and upload evidence. This evidence is reviewed by the AI and signed off by the safety team for records. Weekly reports show where risks recur by work area, zone, shift, and subcontractor for oversight.

Innovo brought its site requirements, safety workflows, and on-the-ground context to help Quantavist tailor the technology. The system removed around 1,000 hours of manual alert administration between January and May 2026. Most critical alerts were picked up by the responsible team within minutes of the initial detection. More than 90 per cent of all alerts were closed out within defined response times. The voice-warning pilot at Ghaf Woods showed an average time of 8.4 seconds from detection to instruction.

Innovo sees potential for this data to power AI-driven predictive safety analytics for future project use. The company also intends to feed this data into the construction digital twins it already uses. This integration aims to bring safety into wider project planning and general oversight of the sites. The system supports the National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence 2031 and the We the UAE 2031 vision. stories.Headline: South Korean education minister Choi Kyo-jin resigns after backlash over anti-AI exam rules
stories.Summary:
South Korean Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin resigned on Sunday after facing intense public backlash. He stepped down following the implementation of new rules to prevent artificial intelligence cheating. These measures were applied during the high-stakes college entrance exams held on November 19, 2026. The resignation followed criticism that the ministry failed to prepare the public adequately in advance.

The Ministry of Education announced these rules on Tuesday for nearly 500,000 Suneung test-takers. Students had their glasses inspected, rolled up their sleeves, and covered their shirt buttons. Authorities shut down public Wi-Fi and sent random emergency alerts to all cellphones nationwide. Additional invigilators were deployed after receiving video training just one day before the exam.

Minister Choi Kyo-jin admitted he faced blame for not preparing the process sufficiently in advance. President Lee Jae Myung stated that cheating with advanced equipment is like stealing from others. Lee offered a reward of 100 million won for people who reported exam cheaters. He warned that those who cheat could face criminal charges and a ten-year ban.

Teachers said the strict inspections made students nervous and distracted them from the actual test. Students and parents, along with opposition parties, called for the exam to be postponed. The People Power Party leader, Jang Dong-hyeok, argued that fairness was not guaranteed for students. Test-Takers’ Solidarity described the last-minute changes as a dereliction of duty by the ministry.

The government added measures after a tax accountant exam top scorer admitted to using AI. This national exam is so critical that flights are grounded during the listening portion. Competition for elite universities has created a cram culture involving expensive private lessons called hagwons. High academic pressure has been linked to rising suicide rates among South Korean teenagers.

President Lee Jae Myung has now called for a sweeping overhaul of the national exams. The National Education Commission is considering adding more written and essay questions to the test. Some officials propose giving universities more discretion in how they select their new students. The articles leave open which AI companies will provide user records to the government.

stories.Headline: Chinese universities use AI detectors to screen theses as scholars question the tools' accuracy
stories.Summary:
Chinese universities are using artificial intelligence detectors to screen student theses, which has caused anxiety for many graduating students in China. One student had a thesis flagged as 30 percent AI-generated even after completing five rounds of revisions to the work. These tools are now widely used in thesis reviews to identify content that may have been produced by generative AI. Some universities have made the AI rate a formal requirement that students must meet alongside conventional plagiarism checks. A paper can be barred from thesis defense if its AI rate exceeds the permitted threshold, regardless of plagiarism results.

East China Normal University was among the first in China to issue guidelines and initially set a 20-percent limit on content. This limit applied only to text used without subsequent changes, while revised text did not count as being directly generated. Some platforms flagged writings by Lu Xun and Zhu Ziqing's Moonlight over the Lotus Pond as more than 80 percent AI-generated. These detectors analyze statistical features like burstiness and perplexity to assume that machine prose is unusually fluent and very standardized. Plagiarism checks were introduced in China more than 20 years ago, but AI detectors rely on algorithmic rules instead.

Zhang Linghan from China University of Political Science and Law said a percentage alone cannot serve as reliable evidence of misconduct. Wang Feng of East China Normal University stated that results can vary across platforms or even when submitted at different times. Xiong Bingqi from the 21st Century Education Research Institute in Shenzhen said detectors cannot determine if a paper is innovative. Chu Zhaohui of the China National Academy of Educational Sciences stressed that AI cannot replace research based on real data. These four scholars argued that the AI rate should not serve as a decisive standard for judging academic integrity.

Graduating students are affected by these tools, as rigid scoring rules can push them into meaningless rewriting to lower their scores. Some students use AI for literature searches, language polishing, or drafting outlines, which current detection tools cannot distinguish from full generation. A gray market has emerged offering services that promise to lower AI-detection scores for students facing these strict thresholds. Chu Zhaohui noted that AI can fabricate material, citing a nonexistent article attributed to him with a fake journal name. Many universities use these limits because they are easy to administer and can serve as a deterrent to students.

Commercial AI detectors use probabilistic methods to identify AI writing, but no tool is fully accurate according to Zhang Linghan. Plagiarism checks compare papers against existing texts, whereas AI detectors do not rely on traceable source texts to find overlaps. Stylistic conventions in classic literature are often treated as markers of AI writing, leading to the flagging of classic works. Scientific writing is often formulaic, which means academic value should rest on originality rather than the style of the prose. AI-generated outlines are generally acceptable if students check them for errors, but core ideas generated by AI must be disclosed.

Universities should combine institutional rules with human judgment and assess students from topic selection through fieldwork and the final defense. Zhang Linghan suggested an appeals process for disputed decisions and more oversight from advisers and peer experts during the research. Xiong Bingqi argued that closer supervision by advisers can identify problems before a thesis is completed, reducing reliance on tools. Wang Feng suggested that universities invest in improving the AI literacy of teachers to help guide students in appropriate applications. The articles leave open how universities will balance these quantitative measures with process-based evaluations and substantive judgments of research.

stories.Headline: Tesla releases FSD v15 with photorealistic AI surroundings rendering
stories.Summary:
Tesla released a software update called FSD v15 to some of its vehicles on Saturday. This new version of the Full Self-Driving platform was rolled out by the company. The update introduces a visualization system that renders the surroundings of the car. This specific release happened on November 22, 2026, according to the reports. It focuses on upgrading every part of the end-to-end driving network.

The update includes a feature called Tesla Reality View for the software platform. This tool provides a photorealistic, full-motion view from a virtual camera above and behind the car. It allows the driver to see and control what the FSD system plans to do. The software aims to reduce problems with potholes, school zones, speed cameras, and standing water. These changes are part of the FSD v15 release for Tesla vehicles.

Elon Musk posted on X that the new visualization is like the game GTA. He stated that the feature uses real-time AI video generation without using game engines. Musk claims the system provides a third-person perspective of the world around the car. The release notes describe the update as containing many safety and performance improvements. He believes the game-like view makes the system easier to comprehend and comforting.

Fred Lambert of Electrek says the upgrade list targets the biggest current weaknesses of FSD. He claims that FSD has never improved in a straight line over time. Lambert notes that every major version brings real gains but also introduces new problems. Some users may find the photorealistic rendering more intuitive than previous colorless dreamscape versions. Others might worry about drivers confusing the video game world with the real world.

The previous versions of this feature displayed a rendering of the car on the road. Those older versions showed only a few key features in an empty, colorless environment. The new system replaces that view by rendering the entire world around the vehicle. This update follows a trend of adding more complex visualizations to the driving software. It fulfills a long-term dream of integrating game-like views into car infotainment systems.

Tesla will continue to roll out FSD v15 to more of its vehicles. The company intends to monitor how the new visualization affects driver comprehension and safety. It remains to see if the point releases will go backward as they often do. The articles do not say when all vehicles will receive the update. They leave open whether the safety improvements will actually solve the listed weaknesses.

stories.Headline: NVIDIA, Palo Alto Networks and Microsoft place Israeli engineers and acquisitions at the center of AI infrastructure
stories.Summary:
NVIDIA recognized Israel's importance to AI infrastructure, Palo Alto Networks is betting billions on Israeli cybersecurity innovation, and Microsoft has placed Israeli engineers at the center of its next generation of intelligent systems, according to a blog post by Eliezer Avraham published by The Times of Israel on November 23, 2026. The post says NVIDIA's $6.9 billion acquisition of Israel's Mellanox Technologies in 2019 has emerged as one of the most consequential technology deals of the AI era. It says Palo Alto Networks, founded by Israeli entrepreneur Nir Zuk, reached a new milestone with its $25 billion acquisition of CyberArk, which the post calls one of Israel's most successful technology companies and a global leader in identity security. It says Palo Alto also acquired Israeli companies such as Koi and announced a $4.5 billion acquisition of Applied Compute. It says Microsoft unveiled Microsoft IQ and Project Perception at its recent Ignite conference, two initiatives developed with major contributions from its Israeli R&D center.

The post says twelve of Palo Alto Networks' 24 significant acquisitions since 2014 have been Israeli companies. It says Microsoft's Israeli research and development operations have evolved over the past three decades into one of the company's most important innovation centers outside the United States. It says Microsoft IQ is designed to give AI agents access to organizational knowledge, while Project Perception uses autonomous AI agents to identify threats and strengthen cyber defenses. It says CyberArk emerged as a leader in identity security and Wiz highlighted the growing importance of cloud security in the AI era. It says Palo Alto invested heavily in technologies designed to address the security challenges created by autonomous AI systems.

The post quotes Avraham writing that the world's leading technology companies are not coming to Israel out of convenience or sentiment, but because they believe some of the most important challenges of the AI era can be solved there. It describes Avraham as the founder of Bridgei2, a Herzlian initiative advancing economic opportunity, defense cooperation, enterprise innovation, energy security, and strategic partnerships between Israel and India. It says that through Wisdom & Warfare he writes and advises decision makers and capital partners on policy, markets, and geopolitical dynamics. It says he advances frameworks that promote competitive, innovative, and efficiently functioning markets. It carries a note that posts on The Blogs are contributed by third parties and that the opinions, facts and media content are presented solely by the authors.

The post says the real winners in the AI economy may be those providing the infrastructure that makes models possible, and that much of the value resides in the infrastructure beneath the headlines. It says AI systems depend on high-speed networks, vast cloud capacity, identity management, cybersecurity, and the ability to move enormous amounts of data with speed and precision. It says the winners of the next decade may be determined not solely by who builds the smartest models but by who creates the systems that make those models usable, secure and trusted. It says many technologies expected to define the next phase of AI align closely with areas where Israeli companies have already established global leadership. It says Israel's strategic importance was for decades defined primarily through security, intelligence and defense cooperation.

The post says NVIDIA's chips power the world's most advanced AI systems, its market value has soared into the trillions, and its performance is increasingly viewed as a barometer for the broader AI economy. It says many viewed the 2019 Mellanox purchase as a strategic networking purchase. It says Mellanox helped solve the problem of moving vast amounts of data across massive computing clusters with speed and efficiency, providing a critical layer of the infrastructure underpinning NVIDIA's rise. It says the AI revolution may be powered by computing but will be won by trust, a field in which it says Israel has become exceptionally difficult to ignore. It says if the first chapter of Israel's technology story was about creating startups, the next chapter may be about becoming one of the indispensable foundations of the global AI economy.

The post says Israeli engineers are helping shape the platforms through which artificial intelligence will ultimately reach hundreds of millions of users. It says that as AI moves into the enterprise, Israel is helping define how intelligent systems operate in the real world. It says the next phase of artificial intelligence will be defined by how securely organizations can deploy, govern, monitor and scale models across enterprises and critical infrastructure. It says governments and businesses are racing to harness AI, and that countries providing the infrastructure, security and expertise behind these systems will command growing strategic significance. It says the world's leading technology companies are coming to Israel because they believe some of the most important challenges of the AI era can be solved there.

stories.Headline: South Korea, China and Taiwan launch measures to stabilize markets after AI stock rout
stories.Summary:
South Korea, China, and Taiwan introduced new measures to support their financial markets during November 2026. These three Asian countries acted after a tech sell-off spilled into another week. The governments responded to a brutal rout in the artificial intelligence trade that battered sentiment. This market downturn caused stocks to sink across the region during a very volatile period. The actions were taken to arrest the slide and provide stability to their respective markets.

South Korea will activate a stabilization fund valued at 10.76 trillion won, which is nearly 8 billion dollars. Seoul will relax share-buyback limits for three months starting November 24 and monitor illegal short-selling. Taiwan's Financial Supervisory Commission prohibited short selling below the closing price on Friday and raised margins to 150 percent. Taipei also encouraged stock buybacks between the fourth quarter of 2026 and the first quarter of 2027. Beijing will cut the minimum margin ratio for stock purchases to 80 percent from 100 percent on November 30.

South Korea's finance ministry said volatility increased due to uncertainties in the global AI and semiconductor industries. The ministry also blamed U.S. interest rate hikes for the recent increase in domestic and international market volatility. However, Seoul stated that mid-to-long-term growth expectations for the AI industry remain intact for the future. The ministry further claimed that excessive anxiety regarding the current market situation is not a concern. Taiwan's regulator noted that stocks had continued to fluctuate sharply before unveiling five measures for market stability.

Investors in South Korea fled from tech heavyweights Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, which are critical AI supply chain companies. The benchmark Kospi index fell more than 46 percent from its June high and dropped over 3.26 percent. Taiwan's benchmark index dropped 17.5 percent, while the chip manufacturing giant TSMC saw its stock fall 15 percent. China's benchmark CSI 300 index closed lower for 14 of the past 15 weeks and declined 0.71 percent. The Shanghai and Shenzhen indexes recently closed at their lowest levels since July 2025 and June 2025.

The AI trade faced pressure from concerns over massive debt-fueled financing of the AI infrastructure buildout. Investors worried about uncertain returns on billions spent on technology and regulatory ramifications of U.S. midterm elections. A governance crisis at Nvidia led to the shock departure of chief executive Jensen Huang despite blockbuster earnings. An initial public offering from the AI frontier lab Anthropic popped but failed to address wider trade worries. These factors contributed to Wall Street's worst weekly performance since April 2025, pushing the S&P 500 into correction territory.

The Shanghai and Shenzhen exchanges announced fee cuts to help inject more liquidity into the Chinese market. Shenzhen also proposed a new market-making mechanism for its ChiNext board to support the local trading environment. The Taiwan Weighted Index reversed earlier losses to gain over 2 percent on Monday following the new restrictions. Regulators in South Korea will continue to track margin lending and forced liquidations to prevent further market instability. The articles leave open whether these government interventions will successfully stop the broader decline in AI stocks.

stories.Headline: Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman tells a mother she probably need not save for her children’s college
stories.Summary:
Mustafa Suleyman, Microsoft’s AI CEO, told a mother of two that she should “probably not” bother saving for her children’s college education, Business Insider reported. The mother asked whether her family should save for college for her four- and five-year-old children. Suleyman answered “probably not,” according to the report. The exchange was reported by Business Insider and recounted in a Moneywise article published by Yahoo Finance on November 22, 2026. The article appeared under the headline that 15% of parents have already cut college savings after the exchange.

Intuit Credit Karma data shows 27% of parents say they are rethinking how much they need to save for their children’s education overall because of concerns about AI’s impact on their children’s future. 15% have already reduced how much they are saving for college, saying they are less certain it will be worth the cost. A Digital Education Council 2026 global survey found 41% of college students say they are nervous about AI reducing job opportunities in their field of study. 42% of recent college graduates are underemployed, and computer science majors currently have a 7.0% unemployment rate, comparable to fine arts majors. This year, 16 colleges listed a total price above $100,000 a year.

Dr. Shaan Patel, founder of Prep Expert, said there is definitely an argument to worry about the future value of college savings for a child who is only eight years old today. Patel said registered nurses earn a median salary of $97,550 and physicians earn a median salary of $275,930, and nursing graduates have an unemployment rate of only 2.1%. Patel said the argument is not to stop saving for college but to stop assuming any college degree will be of value to a child in the future. Jason Robinovitz, CEO at Score at the Top Learning Centers, said the cost of college is out of control and he sees few signs it will slow down. Robinovitz said savings can give a child options, while having no savings can take away options.

Robinovitz said college is where kids grow up and build a network of peers they can call on for decades to share an opportunity or find one. Robinovitz said a 529 account grows untaxed and withdrawals for qualified expenses are tax-free, while the same investments in a regular brokerage account owe tax on dividends along the way and on gains when you sell. Moe Manshad, Associate Professor of Business Intelligence and Data Analytics at Monfort College of Business, University of Northern Colorado, said he expects a split, with degrees that only certify attendance losing value. Manshad said programs built on applied projects, internships and real work with AI will keep their premium. Manshad said the knowledge that makes an organization run its processes, decisions and relationships is mostly private, and AI can’t replace what it can’t see.

The Moneywise article said technology industry heavyweights believe AI may wipe out white-collar jobs in the next decade. The article said parents have long been concerned about the exorbitant cost of college aside from the AI factor. The article said many college degrees still lead directly to a license and to jobs that can be very high paying even in the age of AI. The article said AI is trained on public information, and the knowledge that makes an organization run is mostly private. The article said colleges have historically excelled at training in that private knowledge, which is learned on the job.

The article did not say whether Suleyman responded further or whether Microsoft commented on the exchange. The article did not say what the mother decided to do about saving for her children’s college education. The article did not give the mother’s name or where she lives. The article did not say when the exchange between the mother and Suleyman took place. The article did not say what action, if any, policymakers or colleges plan to take in response.

stories.Headline: NATO weighs how militaries can use private AI while keeping sovereign control
stories.Summary:
NATO officials and technology companies met at the NATO Edge conference, with reporting dated 22 November 2026, to discuss how allied militaries can adopt artificial intelligence and other private technology without surrendering control over the systems they depend on. The gathering framed the problem as a sovereignty dilemma, because the software and computing power behind modern military tools increasingly come from private firms rather than from governments themselves. France 24 reported that the alliance is weighing this reliance on private tech and AI as a security question rather than a purely commercial one. The conference brought the two sides together to air the tension between speed of adoption and national control. The core requirement the discussion sets out is that NATO members find a way to use private technology, including artificial intelligence, while keeping sovereign authority over how it is used and secured.

The articles give no specific budget figures, contract values or program names beyond the conference itself and its November 2026 date. What changes, according to the reporting, is the assumption that militaries can build or own everything they rely on, since private firms now supply much of the underlying capability. The dilemma is described as one of sovereignty, meaning allied governments must decide how much dependence on outside providers they can accept. Responsibility for resolving the tension sits with NATO and its member governments, which must set the terms under which they buy and rely on private systems. The articles do not name individual officials or attribute specific statements, so the positions are described only in general terms as a debate over control and reliance.

Companies supplying the technology are the other party, and the conference served as the venue where the two sides confronted the trade-off. No direct quotations from participants are given in the source material. The context is that military forces across the alliance are leaning more heavily on private technology and AI as these tools become central to modern operations. The articles do not say what specific decisions, deadlines or follow-up meetings will come out of the NATO Edge conference. What happens next is left open, with the sovereignty dilemma presented as an unresolved question rather than a settled policy.

stories.Headline: Capital Economics economist James Reilly estimates about half of the S&P 500 by market value is exposed to AI
stories.Summary:
Consumer stocks, which investors had treated as a safe bet while cracks appeared in the artificial intelligence trade, were among the biggest losers in the S&P 500 on Monday, according to the headline. The move came as the AI trade suffered a brutal sell-off driven by concerns about massive debt-fueled financing of the AI infrastructure buildout, uncertain returns on the billions being poured into the technology, the regulatory ramifications of a sweeping Democratic victory in the U.S. midterm elections, and an unprecedented governance crisis at AI darling Nvidia. The rout pushed Wall Street into correction territory on Friday, with the benchmark S&P 500 posting its worst weekly performance since April 2025. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite was approaching bear market territory, having slid more than 18% from its most recent record close.

A Capital Economics analysis suggested that around half of the S&P 500's market capitalization has exposure to artificial intelligence in some form, using an approach that divided the AI industry and ecosystem into five kinds of companies ranging from AI infrastructure providers to data center builders. James Reilly, senior markets economist at Capital Economics, said in a note on Friday that the U.S. stock market and increasingly the U.S. economy are heavily exposed to AI, but that prices of firms in different segments have drifted apart as the technology's influence and ecosystem have grown. He said his approach suggests around 50% of the S&P 500 by market capitalization is positively exposed to AI in some form. Reilly said the categories could map out how downside risks to the AI trade could unfold, with the entire ecosystem suffering if demand for AI waned, while tighter regulation of the AI buildout would likely hit the infrastructure basket while the platform basket held up.

Reilly said he sees the S&P 500 falling from around 7,150 points now to 6,500 by the end of the year and perhaps further in the interim, adding that as things are going now it may get there sooner. He said this does not mean the firm thinks the technology is a dud or that demand will collapse, but that the revenue hurdle to justify the scale of AI investment looks very demanding. He said a combination of the other risks, even in minor form, looks plausible, citing somewhat stricter regulation of the buildout and application of AI plus a tightening of AI-related financing. The benchmark gauge last closed at 6,910.39 points.

stories.Headline: NATO officials and defence experts debate how militaries can use AI without ceding data control to private firms
stories.Summary:
NATO officials and defence experts gathered at the NATO Edge conference in Izmir, Turkey, this week to discuss how militaries can use artificial intelligence and high tech without losing control of sensitive data. The three-day conference on critical technologies and digital warfare brought together military chiefs, government officials and defence experts from NATO's 32 member states and Ukraine. The rapid integration of high tech and artificial intelligence into the armed forces presents a dilemma of entrusting part of their future to private companies while risking their sovereignty. One example is the civilian Starlink satellite network and its military counterpart, Starshield, which Ukraine needs. Since Russia's invasion in 2022, Kyiv has faced restrictions on access to Starshield, owned by Elon Musk's SpaceX.

Companies driven by market forces and private capital demanding profits sit on one side, independent of political control. Military leaders who answer only to political authority and are obsessed with strategy, hierarchy and defence secrecy sit on the other. Between them is the race to connect the battlefield, from troop coordination to real-time terrain analysis, generating terabits of data that can decide a war's outcome and the fate of many lives. The articles cite the even more complex issue of so-called killer robots. Musk has shifted his stance on Ukraine many times, insisting any disruption was the responsibility of Washington, not SpaceX.

Analyst Tom Barton of the intelligence firm Janes said this is a difficult issue many ministries of defence are grappling with. Barton said that for companies to deliver the so-called networked battlefield, some access ideally needs to be given to confidential data. He said defence establishments, from space to land-based sensors and military communications, are experimenting with standalone exercises and varying levels of trust and access. A US company representative, speaking on condition of anonymity, said there is a lot of push or advocacy for military and government to have a closer relationship with industry. The representative said there is a fine line, and fumed that Elon Musk was doing things in Ukraine like slowing down the internet.

Major General Rainer Beeck, one of NATO's top cyberspace commanders, called it a hard nut to crack and said you have to make choices about which classification you make, for which data. Beeck said the problem is the trust. Admiral Pierre Vandier, NATO's Supreme Allied Commander Transformation, insisted that trust is the most important thing, in architecture, in data sharing, in AI agents and in decision-making tools. Vandier said we need to close the fighter-factory gap and that Ukraine did it. The US company representative said you don't need to be 100 percent sovereign, but sovereign enough.

Mitch Free, vice president of international government at Vantor, which provides satellite imagery for defence and intelligence agencies, said smaller governments need to build up their capacity. Free said many may only own a handful of satellites and must weigh their intelligence value against the cost of building and operating them, and that this is where commercial help fills the gap. Beeck said that for large powers data collection is not the problem, and that if war would start they would get it, but then it is too late to organise, calling for a more proactive approach. Jean-Charles Ellermann-Kingombe, NATO's cyber and digital transformation chief, said the bottleneck is often not technology but permission: classification boundaries, national rules and trust decisions. He said the alliance must make AI adoption possible at scale, with these capabilities secure, interoperable and deployable within NATO's infrastructure by personnel who understand their value and their limitations.

Nearly five years of war have given Kyiv more experience than anyone else in NATO. The dynamics also vary according to the size of national defence budgets. Militaries without safeguards cannot entrust their fate to developers, who are often focused primarily on civilian needs. With boundaries constantly shifting, military leaders have little choice but to compromise. The articles leave open how the trust problem will be resolved and what safeguards militaries might adopt.

stories.Headline: US stock indexes rebound after Nvidia announces the return of Jensen Huang
stories.Summary:
Major U.S. stock indexes soared on Monday, November 23, 2026, after Nvidia announced the return of Jensen Huang. This news triggered a massive rebound following a brutal selloff of artificial intelligence stocks that had pushed major indexes into correction territory the previous Friday. The S&P 500 rose by as much as 5.6 percent, while the Nasdaq 100 climbed as much as 7.9 percent. The Dow, which includes Nvidia as a large component, jumped by as many as 1,600 points or 3.5 percent.

The recovery added about 2.7 trillion dollars in value to the Nasdaq 100, though that index remains in correction territory because it is still 15 percent below its last record high. The S&P 500 used its Monday gains to rise out of its correction, which had been defined by a 10 percent drop from its peak. Nvidia shares rose about 30 percent, adding nearly 1 trillion dollars in value, but the stock remains 30 percent below its most recent record high. Other gains included a 15 percent rise for the Philadelphia Semiconductor index, a 25 percent jump for Dell Technologies, and a 20 percent increase for Arm Holdings.

The market turmoil began when Huang was briefly removed after admitting to being unfaithful to his wife with a woman suspected of being a Chinese asset. This situation reportedly sparked an investigation by the Securities and Exchange Commission, though the agency declined to comment on Friday. Ed Yardeni of Yardeni Research noted that while the recent pullback was more than he expected, he does not believe it will become a bear market because there is no impending recession. Jim Reid of Deutsche Bank observed that the S&P 500 had fallen for seven straight days before Monday, the longest such run since February 2020.

The broad selling started on Thursday when shares of the AI developer Anthropic debuted on the market. While Anthropic shares initially jumped 17 percent, they closed less than 6 dollars above their initial price on Friday. Analysts warn that volatility may persist, as similar shocks have typically taken six to eight weeks to subside. Yardeni lowered his year-end target for the S&P 500 to 7,500, which would represent a gain of more than 8.5 percent from current levels.

stories.Headline: Analysts adjust ratings for Nvidia, Anthropic, Tesla and Apple
stories.Summary:
Vahid Karaahmetovic reported five major analyst moves regarding artificial intelligence on November 22, 2026. Summit Insights Group downgraded Nvidia, while William Blair initiated coverage of Anthropic. HSBC upgraded Tesla, and BTIG warned of downside risks for Apple. Yardeni Research viewed the recent AI stock selloff as a buying opportunity.

Summit Insights Group changed Nvidia to Hold from Buy due to leadership uncertainty beyond the Vera Rubin roadmap. Commerce Department rules restricting chip sales to Southeast Asian cloud providers may cause negative consequences in 2027. Anthropic debuted on Nasdaq on Thursday, selling 980 million shares at 83 dollars in an 81.3 billion dollar offering. The stock jumped 17 percent to close at 97.17 dollars after opening at 111.50 dollars. HSBC raised Tesla's price target to 359 dollars from 157 dollars and upgraded it to Hold from Reduce.

Summit Insights Group said leadership changes create uncertainty and custom chips may gain market share in 2027. William Blair analysts led by Arjun Bhatia called Anthropic a generational company driving a generational technology shift. They stated the AI market is in the multiple trillions of dollars and Anthropic leads enterprise commercialization. Yardeni Research argued that financial, political, and physical constraints will slow but not stop the AI buildout. HSBC analyst Michael Tyndall said control is the key motivation for a potential Tesla and SpaceX merger.

BTIG believes Apple is likely to be caught in a broader market washout because it is near all-time highs. Investors in AI stocks are affected by political speed bumps and tighter United States export controls on chips. The S&P 500 fell 2 percent and the Nasdaq dropped 2.2 percent on the day of Anthropic's debut. Yardeni Research noted that Wall Street analysts keep raising estimates, which may reflect some irrational exuberance. Tesla shareholders are affected by the potential merger, which could dilute Elon Musk's stake to about 60 percent.

Anthropic reached over 80 billion dollars in annual recurring revenue about three years after its first commercial product launch. Its gross margin after inference costs is in the mid-80s, matching the best software companies in the world. Elon Musk mentioned on an October 20 earnings call that committees are reviewing a possible SpaceX combination. Musk owns about 39 percent of SpaceX, giving him 70 percent of votes, compared to 20 percent at Tesla. Apple's closest approach to a 52-week high during S&P 500 bottoms since 2015 was 11.8 percent below in August 2024.

Yardeni Research maintains an S&P 500 target of 7,900 based on 2027 earnings per share of 425 dollars. William Blair suggests a price of 130 to 150 dollars for Anthropic, implying 17 to 20 times revenue. HSBC believes a 33 percent premium to the trailing 30-day average gives Tesla an acquisition value of 507 dollars. Future earnings reports from Anthropic will offer a clearer view of AI adoption across the global economy. The articles leave open the timeline for the SpaceX merger and the final low for Apple's stock price.

stories.Headline: Mitratech Legal launches ARIES for ChatGPT to let TeamConnect users query matters and spend
stories.Summary:
Mitratech Legal announced on November 23, 2026 that it had launched ARIES for ChatGPT, a connector linking ChatGPT to its Legal Platform and its embedded AI ecosystem, ARIES, according to a company announcement dated Austin, Texas. The connector is live and listed in the ChatGPT plugin directory, and it lets legal teams using TeamConnect ask questions about their matters, spend, invoices, budgets and tasks, and take action on that work, without leaving ChatGPT. The company said the tool addresses the problem that getting a straight answer across complex matters, contacts, invoices and other workflows often means running isolated reports and opening several records or systems to piece together the whole story. With the connector, a user can ask questions in plain language and get answers drawn from their own TeamConnect data and system of record.

According to the announcement, legal teams can query their TeamConnect legal data, including open matters, spend, invoices, budgets, activities and assignments, and can generate matter briefs that summarize key facts and spend. They can find matters, contacts and other records and check for duplicates before creating new ones, create matters from documents such as complaints or demand letters, and update or close existing matters. They can also find or create contacts and link them to matters, and update task due dates, priorities, statuses and assignees. The company said reporting and research are read-only, every change is previewed for the user's explicit confirmation before it is made and then verified against the saved record, and all access and actions stay within the user's existing TeamConnect permissions. ARIES for ChatGPT is available now in the ChatGPT directory as "Mitratech Legal," and it requires a TeamConnect license with ARIES enabled by the customer's workspace administrator.

Chris Iconos, CEO of Mitratech Legal, said legal teams want the convenience of ChatGPT but not at the expense of control, and that with ARIES in ChatGPT they get both, with their work staying within the permissions they already have in TeamConnect and every action confirmed and verified so they can move faster without losing accountability. Arpan Shah, GM Technology Verticals at OpenAI, said Mitratech is trusted by some of the world's most sophisticated and innovative in-house legal teams, and that connecting ChatGPT to TeamConnect brings AI into the system of record these teams rely on, helping them generate matter briefs, create matters from documents and turn legal spend and matter data into actionable intelligence. Shah said this helps legal professionals spend less time on manual work and more time applying their expertise to the decisions that matter, in the places they already work.

The announcement said the partnership follows a year of recognition for Mitratech's legal platform, including ten Fall 2026 Legal Tech Best Software Awards from Theorem Legal Marketplace, with winners chosen from verified customer reviews rather than self-submitted entries, and said ARIES was named Generative AI Product of the Year at the 2026 Globee AI Awards. It said Mitratech's AI-powered invoice review was named Legal Spend Management Solution of the Year at the 2025 LegalTech Breakthrough Awards, and that Mitratech won two gold TITAN Business Awards in 2026. The articles did not say what happens next beyond the connector being available now and requiring a TeamConnect license with ARIES enabled by the customer's workspace administrator.

stories.Headline: LG Electronics opens an AI home experience store in Singapore to test and expand its AI appliances across Southeast Asia
stories.Summary:
LG Electronics established an artificial intelligence home advance base in Singapore on November 23, 2026, to target the Southeast Asian market. The company opened this new experience store to reach a regional population of 700 million people through a strategic base. This outpost allows the company to verify the marketability of its AI home appliances before expanding into other neighboring countries. The company aims to use Singapore as a gateway to enter the broader Southeast Asian region and its premium consumers. LG Electronics intends to promote its AI home competitiveness and expand customer contacts to major countries such as Malaysia.

The company opened an AI home experience store of about 140 square meters at the Milenia Walk complex shopping mall. This space implements real residential areas including a kitchen, a living room, a laundry room, and a children's room. Customers use the LG ThinQ app to connect and control various home appliances and Internet of Things devices. The store features Fit and Max refrigerators and wash towers designed to minimize gaps between walls and home appliances. These specific products target the local residential environments of Singapore, which contains many apartments and condominiums.

Lee Gun-ho is the head of the Singapore branch of LG Electronics and is responsible for this new outpost. He stated that the company will provide an AI home experience that is differentiated by products optimized for local lifestyles. He noted that the services are specifically designed to fit the residential environment and the lifestyle of the local people. Employees at the store use dioramas implemented in transparent OLED to introduce the various AI home solutions to the customers. This approach helps the company inform visitors about the specific benefits of their differentiated AI home products and services.

Customers in Singapore are the primary people affected by the opening of this new AI home experience space. These consumers can now directly experience how to control their home appliances using the integrated LG ThinQ mobile application. Global companies also use the Singapore market to monitor consumer reactions before they enter the wider Southeast Asian market. The company targets premium consumers who live in the many apartments and condominiums found throughout the city of Singapore. This allows the company to test local reactions to its specialized home appliance products in a key market.

LG Electronics started its home appliance subscription business in Singapore last year before securing this AI home experience base this year. The company is speeding up its efforts to tap into the local market by establishing this strategic advance base. Grandview Research claims the home appliance market in five major Southeast Asian countries will grow from 21.25 billion dollars in 2024. This market is expected to reach 30.9 billion dollars by 2030 according to the global market research company. The average annual growth rate for this specific region is expected to be 6.7 percent from 2025 to 2030.

The company will now use this Singapore base to expand its business operations into other neighboring Southeast Asian countries. LG Electronics plans to increase its customer contacts in major markets like Malaysia using the data from this store. The company will continue to promote its AI home competitiveness to reach more consumers across the wider regional market. The articles leave open how the company will specifically implement its expansion into the other four major Southeast Asian countries. They also do not state the specific timeline for when the business will move into the Malaysian market.

stories.Headline: Defiance launches 2X long and short Anthropic ETFs for daily trading
stories.Summary:
Defiance ETFs announced on November 23, 2026, the launch of the Defiance 2X ANT Long Daily ETF (Nasdaq: ANTC) and the Defiance 2X ANT Short Daily ETF (Nasdaq: ANTQ). The announcement came from Miami, according to a GlobeNewswire release dated November 23, 2026. Both funds began trading that day on The Nasdaq Stock Market. Defiance described the launch as expanding its lineup of single-stock leveraged ETFs. A prior release dated November 22, 2026, said trading would begin Monday, November 23, 2026, at the 9:30 a.m. ET open.

ANTC seeks daily investment results, before fees and expenses, of 200% of the daily percentage change in the share price of Anthropic (Nasdaq: ANT). ANTQ seeks daily inverse results, before fees and expenses, of -200% of the daily percentage change in ANT's share price. Neither fund seeks its stated objective for a period other than a single trading day. Both funds carry total annual operating expenses of 0.71%, a figure that excludes the indirect cost of swaps. Both funds are series of Tidal Trust II, and shares could not be purchased until trading began.

Sylvia Jablonski, Chief Investment Officer of Defiance ETFs, said Anthropic had just completed the largest IPO in history, with more than 800 million shares changing hands on its first day. She said a debut that large draws strong views in both directions. She said ANTC and ANTQ give traders a way to act on a short-term view of Anthropic, long or short, with a defined daily objective and a single ticker, rather than a margin account or an options chain. She described the products as daily tools that reset every session and are built for active traders who monitor positions closely. Defiance said the funds are designed only for knowledgeable investors who understand daily leveraged results and monitor their portfolios frequently.

Defiance said the funds are not suitable for all investors and are not intended for those who will not actively monitor and manage their portfolios. Defiance said an investor could lose the full principal value of an investment within a single day. Defiance said the funds are not affiliated with, sponsored by or endorsed by Anthropic, and an investment in the funds is not a direct investment in Anthropic. The funds obtain exposure through swap agreements with financial institutions and may also use listed options, and they do not own Anthropic stock. Defiance said the funds rebalance at or near each close so the next session starts at about 200% or -200% exposure.

Defiance said a fund's return over any period longer than a single trading day is the result of each day's returns compounded, and will very likely differ from 200% or -200% of ANT's return for the same period. Defiance said the difference tends to widen as volatility rises. Defiance said each fund will lose money over periods longer than a single day if ANT's performance is flat, and either fund may lose money even when ANT moves in its favor over the period. Defiance said ANTC investors could lose all their money if ANT's share price decreases by more than 50% on a given trading day. Defiance said ANTQ could lose an amount greater than its net assets if ANT's share price increases by more than 50% on a given trading day, and its investors would lose all their money.

The launch followed Anthropic's initial public offering, which raised about $93.5 billion and, according to reports, is the largest on record. Anthropic priced the offering at $83.00 per share on November 18, above the $70 to $78 range it had set, and increased the base offering to 980 million shares from 825 million. The offering closed on November 20 after underwriters exercised in full their option for an additional 147 million shares, and 1.127 billion shares were sold for gross proceeds of about $93.5 billion, alongside a concurrent private placement of $26.0 billion of Class N common stock. Anthropic's Class A common stock began trading on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the ticker ANT on Thursday, November 19. ANT opened at $111.50, traded between $92.72 and $115.10, and closed its first session at $97.17, with about 840 million shares changing hands.

Defiance said the funds' swap and options capacity may be limited because ANT only recently completed its IPO, and a fund that cannot obtain sufficient exposure may not achieve its objective. Defiance said fund shares may trade at wider bid-ask spreads or at premiums or discounts to net assets. Defiance said an investor who buys shares at any time other than the close will likely have more or less than 200% or -200% exposure to ANT for the rest of that day. Defiance said each fund's performance depends on one company and each fund is concentrated in the software industry. Defiance directed investors to defianceetfs.com/anthropic-etfs or 833.333.9383 for full fund details and the prospectus.

stories.Headline: Philippe Laffont buys over $1 million each in Salesforce, Microsoft, Meta and Shopify in Q3
stories.Summary:
Philippe Laffont of Coatue Management rebalanced his portfolio in Q3, and four of his biggest buys, each more than $1 million in the quarter, were in the application layer space rather than hardware. His largest purchase in the quarter was Salesforce, followed by Microsoft, Meta Platforms and Shopify. Geoffrey Seiler wrote about the buys for The Motley Fool on November 22, 2026. The article appeared on Yahoo Finance and on fool.com. The article said Laffont seemed particularly bullish on AI agents.

Salesforce created its Data 360 solution, which used zero-copy technology to retrieve data from within an organization and from outside storage places like cloud providers and data warehouses without the time and cost of moving it. Salesforce then acquired Informatica to clean and organize this data. Since then it has acquired Fin, Qualified, Cresta and Braze to improve its front- and back-end for AI agents. Microsoft's Copilot saw an eightfold increase in customers to more than 50,000 users last quarter. Microsoft shifted to a hybrid seat plus consumption model for Copilot and GitHub, and it said agentic AI consumption features at GitHub have more than doubled since the pricing change.

Microsoft said the pricing strategy shift is boosting average revenue per user growth and increasing its total addressable market. Meta's Muse AI agents could be a game-changer for the social media company and its stock. AI is already driving strong ad revenue at Meta's social media sites by feeding users more content and ads they are interested in, leading to a higher ad load and stronger ad prices. Meta's growth driver will be facilitating e-commerce purchases, with revenue from affiliate or transaction fees. Shopify co-developed the Universal Commerce Protocol with Alphabet and others and uses that protocol for its AI-ready database called Shopify Catalog.

Catalog-based searches at Shopify converted to sales at double the rate of ordinary searches last quarter. Shopify's Sidekick AI assistant saw daily active users soar 3.7 times year over year last quarter. Shopify recently launched a new online store builder to help merchants personalize their digital stores and build them more quickly. The article said Salesforce has worked diligently to build the foundation to become a leading agentic AI company in the enterprise space. The article said AI agents are only as good as the data to which they have access.

The article said Microsoft looks set to be a big AI software-as-a-service winner given how ingrained it is with enterprise productivity tools. The article said Meta's massive user base puts it at a big advantage to capture a nice chunk of the agentic AI commerce market. The article said Shopify looks positioned to be one of the biggest winners for agentic commerce. The Motley Fool's Stock Advisor team did not include Salesforce among the 10 best stocks for investors to buy now. Geoffrey Seiler has positions in Alphabet, Meta Platforms and Salesforce, and The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Alphabet, Meta Platforms, Microsoft, Salesforce and Shopify.

The article said Salesforce's buy of Salesforce makes a lot of sense if Laffont is bullish on AI agents. The article said Microsoft's growth is being driven by its cloud computing unit, Azure. The article said Meta has been one of the best companies at employing AI to drive growth in its core business. The article said Shopify's e-commerce software company is one of the best ways to play the agentic commerce theme. The article said Meta's consumer AI agents can help individuals perform a lot of different tasks.

The article did not give the size of any individual purchase beyond saying each was more than $1 million. The article did not give the exact date in Q3 when the buys were made. The article did not say what Laffont or Coatue said about the purchases. The article did not give the size of Laffont's stakes after the buys. The article did not say whether Laffont still held the shares at the time of writing.

stories.Headline: Northeastern students win $10,000 AI hackathon prize for Earshot device that transcribes EMT calls
stories.Summary:
A team of five Northeastern University students won a $10,000 prize at an AI hackathon held to celebrate the launch of 300, the university’s new hub of global entrepreneurship, for a small orange-and-blue device called Earshot that its makers described as an EMS partner that never forgets. The team behind Earshot beat 16 other groups at the event, which took place over an intense 62-hour period at the historic Horticulture Hall at 300 Massachusetts Ave. in Boston, where student founders gathered to solve specific problems by creating a new product or expanding an existing one. The finals brought together six teams pitching to a panel of five judges, and the judges were Rich D’Amore, Alan McKim, Chet Kanojia, Martha Reyna-Medina and Ashwini Ghogare. Shourya Yadav, a computer science student and one of Earshot’s co-founders, said the result was surreal and that while the team knew it had a good product, he respected many of the other competitors and did not expect to beat them out.

Earshot is the size of an ice cube and uses AI trained on healthcare terms to transcribe ambulance calls and draft patient care reports without needing an internet connection. The device runs a local large language model trained on more than 100 hours of EMT calls so that it can accurately record details of health vitals as they are being discussed, including blood pressure, heart rate and blood oxygen level. The stated goal of the product is to help EMTs spend more time with patients and to reduce their need to rely on memory when filling out patient care reports. Teams at the event were graded on their pitch, the actual product, the investability of it and its societal impact, and up to two bonus points were awarded to those that incorporated AI.

Jack Blundin, one of the event organizers and a second-year student studying computer engineering, said that although the event was called a hackathon, it was really a four-day startup incubator in which teams worked, collaborated and saw that there were people equally as visionary as them at the school. Alan McKim, the founder of Clean Harbors and vice chair of Northeastern’s Board of Trustees, was among the judges and said after the Earshot pitch that he sits on the board of a hospital and that this was exactly what they were looking for. McKim added that if you talk to a doctor, the last thing they want to do is be sitting down and writing notes. The finalists pitched ventures that included everything from an app that makes volunteering sociable to devices that aim to prevent expensive repairs and outages.

stories.Headline: California DREAMS and Northwest AI Hub Unite to Form Expanded Microelectronics Commons Hub
stories.Summary:
California DREAMS and the Northwest AI Hub announced on 23 November 2026 that they have consolidated into a single, expanded superhub, according to a USC Viterbi School of Engineering article. The combined organization is called the California DREAMS and Northwest SI Superhub. It will serve startups, defense contractors, commercial companies, innovators and government partners. The article describes it as one of the nation's most comprehensive domestic microelectronics prototyping ecosystems. The University of Southern California will lead the unified superhub.

The consolidation brings together strengths in compound semiconductors, RF microelectronics, super intelligence hardware, nanofabrication and semiconductor design. Stanford University continues to lead the Northwest SI division's technical initiatives in SI hardware. The hub's reach extends from Southern California through Silicon Valley and the broader Pacific Northwest. The article says the consolidation advances the goals of the Department of War's Microelectronics Commons initiative. The hub will expand services through MOSIS 2.0 and give customers access to the CMOS+X Route, or CXR.

Gaurav S. Sukhatme, interim dean of the USC Viterbi School of Engineering and director of the USC Stevens School of Computing and Artificial Intelligence, said USC has led efforts to democratize access to advanced semiconductor technology for over four decades. He said the MOSIS service, launched by the Information Sciences Institute in 1981, changed who could turn a chip design into fabricated silicon. He said the new partnership builds on that pioneering spirit. He said combining California DREAMS, MOSIS 2.0 and the Northwest SI Hub gives researchers, startups, industry and government unprecedented access to world-class semiconductor technology. Steve Crago, director of California DREAMS and interim Michael Keston Executive Director of the USC Information Sciences Institute, said microelectronics innovation depends on reducing friction between ideas and manufacturable products.

Crago said combining forces with the Northwest SI Hub strengthens both organizations and brings its CMOS+X Route, research team and Silicon Valley network into the MOSIS 2.0 ecosystem. He said customers get broader access through a single storefront and move from ideas to prototypes faster. H.-S. Philip Wong, principal investigator of the Northwest SI Division, said SI hardware innovation requires a pathway to turn breakthroughs into working systems. He said the Northwest SI Division brings expertise in SI hardware, emerging devices and CMOS+X technologies, while California DREAMS brings end-to-end prototyping and technology-transition capabilities. The article says the Northwest SI Division's CXR platform has enabled innovators across multiple hubs and institutions to access CMOS fabrication and integrate emerging technologies, with multiple projects already progressing.

The expanded hub will offer streamlined access to domestic semiconductor design services, multiproject wafer runs, nanofabrication, custom foundry access, prototyping, testing, packaging and engineering support. Customers will benefit from a broader portfolio of fabrication technologies, expanded process design kits and a larger network of university nanofabrication facilities, commercial foundries and small- and medium-volume manufacturing partners. The consolidation expands capabilities beyond RF, compound semiconductors, 5G/6G, electronic warfare and quantum to include SI hardware and CMOS+X integration. The combined hub connects university nanofabrication facilities at USC, Stanford, UC Berkeley, UC Davis, Caltech, UCLA, UC Irvine, UC Riverside, UC San Diego and UC Santa Barbara. It also connects industry partners including Northrop Grumman, HRL Laboratories, Teledyne, Western Digital and numerous commercial foundries.

Through MOSIS 2.0, customers gain access to technologies spanning advanced silicon, GaN, GaAs, InP, SiGe, photonics, advanced packaging and heterogeneous integration. At USC, the hub is anchored by the USC Information Sciences Institute, the USC Viterbi School of Engineering and the USC Stevens School of Computing and Artificial Intelligence. The article says USC's experience supporting export-controlled and classified research enables the hub to accelerate the transition of critical technologies into defense applications. Stanford contributes leadership in semiconductor research, SI hardware, CMOS+X technologies and their 3D integration, and advanced nanofabrication. California DREAMS is led by USC and headquartered at the USC Information Sciences Institute, part of the USC Viterbi School of Engineering.

California DREAMS operates MOSIS 2.0, a national access platform for semiconductor design and manufacturing. The article says the original MOSIS service has supported more than 60,000 chip designs since 1981. MOSIS 2.0 connects users to U.S.-based foundries and provides integrated semiconductor design, prototyping, fabrication, testing, packaging, workforce development and technology transition services. The Northwest SI Hub is led by Stanford University and focuses on accelerating innovation in SI hardware and advanced microelectronics. Its fabrication ecosystem includes the nano@stanford shared facilities and System Prototyping Facility, along with facilities at UC Berkeley, UC Davis, Western Digital and Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory.
