stories.Headline: Mona Lew applies statecraft training to AI governance and privacy engineering
stories.Summary:
Mona Lew transitioned from data privacy work to a career in AI governance. She achieved this shift after graduating from the Institute of World Politics in 2020. Her academic journey began when she attended an open house for prospective students. She first enrolled in a certificate program before pursuing a full master's degree. This educational path allowed her to move into global consulting and financial services.

She earned a Master of Arts in Statecraft and International Affairs from the Institute of World Politics. Her studies focused on India and the perspectives of people in China and Russia. She previously worked for the District of Columbia Office of the State Superintendent of Education. Now, she works at a multinational financial services company focusing on privacy engineering. Her role involves enterprise architecture, privacy, enterprise risk, and global regulations.

Mona Lew stated that the rigor of her education provided a foundation for complex environments. She said that AI governance is a human problem rather than a technical one. She noted that disagreement across borders is usually about history and institutional fear. Lew claimed that her training prepared her for ambiguous projects with disconnected information. She also said that Professor Marek Jan Chodakiewicz taught her how to think.

The work affects cross-functional teams from around the world who manage emerging technology risk. Lew interacts with regions like China, which has specific requirements for cross-border data transfers. She also deals with European privacy and AI rules that emphasize individual rights and accountability. Her clients benefit from her cultural insights and her ability to interpret regulatory expectations. She helps these organizations assess and govern how technologies are responsibly introduced.

Lew originally prepared for paralegal work during her undergraduate studies in law. She realized that this specific career direction was not what she wanted to pursue. Dr. John Lenczowski challenged her to serve a cause higher than herself during her recruitment. She took a propaganda class with Dr. Glancy that increased her discernment of information. This background in statecraft helped her apply classroom learning to real-time privacy problems.

Lew now evaluates how new applications use data and integrate with existing systems. She identifies potential issues early to examine implications for regulatory obligations and architecture. She encourages current students to seek out mentors and learn from experienced practitioners. The articles do not state which multinational financial services company currently employs her. They leave open the specific future projects she will undertake in AI governance.

stories.Headline: Economists and officials at a Stanford forum debate policies to manage AI's uncertain effect on U.S. jobs and growth
stories.Summary:
The Stanford Institute for Economic Policy Research held its Fall Policy Forum on AI's economic and political effects on Nov. 12, 2026, gathering leaders in business, government and academia. The forum, titled "Economic Policy in the Age of AI," focused on what is happening today and how policies can handle the expected and the unexpected. Mary C. Daly, president and CEO of the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco, delivered the opening keynote. Neale Mahoney, the Trione Director at SIEPR and the TG Wijaya Professor of Economics at Stanford, kicked off the event and moderated a Q&A with Daly. Speakers included Anton Korinek of the Anthropic Institute, Jennifer Duff of Mesa, Ariz.'s city council, Scott Strand of Google, David Deming of Harvard College, Josh Zoffer of CIV, Erika McEntarfer of SIEPR, Ioana Marinescu of the University of Pennsylvania, Ben Hyman of UCLA's California Policy Lab, Elena Patel of the Urban-Brookings Tax Policy Center and Ezra Kagan of RAISE US.

Prompted to estimate AI's contribution to U.S. economic growth in the next three years, economists' predictions ranged from 1.5% to 30%, Korinek said. Strand said AI adoption is "broad yet shallow," with automating tasks accounting for just 10% of current usage. Deming described three potential outcomes: a white-collar jobs apocalypse, a broken career ladder for young workers, and AI as "a normal technology" akin to the internet or personal computer. Patel noted that individual incomes make up 85% of federal tax revenues, and she said there is talk of imposing an AI usage tax and a "windfall" tax on companies profiting from AI. Duff said Mesa, a city of 530,000, now has rules around water and power use and restrictions on the location and height of data centers.

Mahoney said, "We do too much predicting, and not enough planning, around AI," and said policymakers face pressure to act and need evidence-based advice. Daly said she is "extremely bullish" about what AI will ultimately mean for the economy but is keenly aware of the need for policymakers to be proactive. "The transition dynamic matters," Daly said, and if the AI economy hasn't worked as wanted in 10 years, "it won't be the technology's fault. This is ours to decide." Korinek said the range of predictions "tells you how large the span of uncertainty is."

Zoffer said "the right has said, 'We want reindustrialization' and the left has said, 'We want electrification,'" and said he would love to see trillions of dollars expected to pour into data-center development used to create jobs in the United States, finance clean energy infrastructure and help the U.S. reindustrialize. McEntarfer said "Our social safety net here in the U.S. is pretty rickety," and said an obvious place to start is unemployment benefit programs run by states. Marinescu and Hyman suggested "wage insurance" to subsidize workers transitioning to lower-paying jobs, and said employers could be given tax breaks to train workers for new roles or to allow job sharing to minimize layoffs. Hyman said that if there are a lot of correlated layoffs across many different firms, that kind of minimizes the crowd-out across job seekers when they are searching for fewer and fewer jobs. Kagan said it is imperative, in getting ready for this disruption, to start building the muscle at the state level, within educational institutions and within the federal government to deliver new programs and new policies if a policy window opens.

Duff said she would like to see a policy framework that smaller municipalities, which don't always have the money to hire outside advisers, could use to broker more advantageous deals with developers. Mahoney said in kicking off the event that in a labor market meltdown, workers wouldn't be the only ones to suffer, because a falloff in income tax revenues could cripple government programs like Medicare and Social Security. The articles say the widespread layoffs many anticipated would strike fast haven't happened, and the same goes for the widely expected productivity surge key to economic growth and improved living standards. The articles say AI isn't infiltrating white-collar work with zero impact on blue-collar jobs, and that mechanics are using the technology to inspect worn engine parts and farmers to plant crops.

Duff said Mesa is learning from mistakes made when data-center developers demanded non-disclosure agreements preventing local officials from talking publicly about the terms of proposed projects while also expecting hefty tax subsidies. Duff said, "We went from one extreme and not even knowing what a data center is to it affecting an entire election in our nation in just five years." Duff said she wants data-center developers to disclose publicly their emissions and to commit to sustainable practices, and said Mesa is trying now to be ahead of this and to anticipate what it needs to prepare for and negotiate instead of being empty-handed and just stumbling. McEntarfer recounted her own brief but agonizing attempt to apply for unemployment after she lost her BLS job in what has been widely viewed as a political move by President Trump.

Zoffer recently authored a SIEPR Policy Brief examining job growth at U.S. factories given the demand for data-center components. The articles leave open which, if any, of the discussed policies, including wage insurance, tax breaks, an AI usage tax, a windfall tax, a consumption tax or a value-added tax, will be adopted. The articles also leave open what the forum's discussions will lead to and whether a policy window will open. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Nebius shares drop as the company raises projected investment to 27 billion dollars
stories.Summary:
Nebius shares fell 16 percent on Friday during a broad selloff of artificial intelligence equities. This retreat affected infrastructure providers and headline names in the sector. The decline followed a sharp rally tied to NVIDIA earnings and the Anthropic initial public offering. Investors began reassessing whether huge sums spent on infrastructure can earn adequate returns. This market shift occurred as S&P 500 futures dropped 0.9 percent.

The company reported third quarter 2026 revenue of 980.8 million dollars, which is up 571 percent. Nebius narrowed its 2026 revenue outlook to the low end of 3.0 billion to 3.4 billion dollars. Projected investment rose from a 20 billion to 25 billion dollar range to roughly 27 billion dollars. Third party data center capacity is arriving later than planned, shifting some revenue into 2027. These changes occurred while the stock traded at 91.52 dollars on Friday.

Nebius reported that delays from third party providers caused the narrowed revenue outlook for 2026. Evercore senior managing director Amit Daryanani said neocloud providers face constraints around financing and capacity. He stated that NVIDIA described the demand environment as extraordinarily strong for these providers. Daryanani noted that neoclouds need more funding and infrastructure to serve this high demand. He also mentioned that NVIDIA neocloud financing totals roughly 32 billion dollars.

Analysts are affected by the tension between long term confidence and cautious valuations for the company. Baird analyst Rob Oliver kept an Outperform rating but cut his price target to 200 dollars. Gil Luria of D.A. Davidson reaffirmed a neutral rating and halved his target to 125 dollars. Tyler Radke of Citi stayed bullish but lowered his target to 215 dollars on November 16. Two other houses set targets between 200 and 245 dollars on November 13.

The market grew more critical of the case for the build out and sector spending. Anthropic priced its initial public offering at 83 dollars per share, above the 70 to 78 range. NVIDIA reported quarterly results that were above expectations, which reinforced optimism about infrastructure demand. CoreWeave discussed revenue of 11 million dollars per megawatt, compared to 20 million for long term contracts. Restrictions on Chinese companies accessing cloud infrastructure in Asia may increase Western capacity.

Nebius is pressing ahead by giving compute credits worth 150,000 dollars to Physical AI Awards winners. These winners include Chef Robotics and Archetype AI, who also receive mentoring and technical support. The company must now align its investment needs with available infrastructure and growth. Articles leave open whether current demand conditions will persist over the longer term. It remains uncertain if the business model can convert growth into an economically viable business.

stories.Headline: AI finds software flaws faster, prompting rushed patches that disrupt banks and airlines
stories.Summary:
In the span of one week, Microsoft services went down, flights were grounded nationwide, some banks' services briefly stopped working and an internal platform for the National Security Agency went dark. The outages occurred around Nov. 16 and Nov. 17, 2026, and left people wondering whether artificial intelligence was the culprit. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin discussed the outages in a Fox News interview and said he asked someone in the tech industry what could be causing them. National Intelligence Director Jay Clayton pointed to flaws that AI detected in a programming language used in systems across the world. Senate Intelligence Committee Vice Chairman Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., said some of the recent outages were "AI-related."

Mullin said the person he asked believed it is "super intelligence," the Trump administration's preferred term for AI, and said on Nov. 17 he could tell with 98% certainty "we're not seeing the cyberattack." Clayton said in a separate Nov. 17 Fox Business interview that "the patching that has gone on following that has caused some of these systems to not come back up when you patch them as expected." Warner said in a Nov. 18 CNBC interview that AI tools "spot vulnerabilities in all of our existing systems" and companies are in "this mad rush to create patches." On Nov. 17, a cybersecurity start-up using an OpenAI model found a critical software flaw in a programming language used by government agencies, banks, hospitals and the majority of Fortune 500 companies. Qualys reported that Microsoft addressed 1,235 vulnerabilities in November, compared to 68 in November 2025.

Bryan Ward, a Vanderbilt University computer science assistant professor, said "vulnerabilities are being discovered and exploited faster than ever before, especially with increasingly capable AI models." Stuart Madnick, an MIT Sloan School of Management information technology professor, said AI is often able to find flaws 10 to 100 times faster than humans. Madnick said an organization that previously found four or five flaws in a year would now be aware of 40 to 400. Nicholas Leiserson, president of the Center for Advancing Cybersecurity at the Institute for Security Technology, said unintended consequences such as services becoming unavailable can be a trade-off when companies update their systems. Ward said recent events should be "a wake-up call" and the public should improve its cybersecurity posture.

Microsoft said it had a technical issue unrelated to AI or AI agents, and the problem stemmed from a "network capacity upgrade." The nationwide ground stop happened after a router upgrade disrupted the FAA telecommunications infrastructure, government officials said, and investigators have ruled out an AI system the FAA recently rolled out. JPMorganChase attributed its outage to a "temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems." Mayank Morya, CTO at Mitigata, told India Today Tech that the underlying vulnerability across these incidents is a "concentration of technology dependencies." Saakar S Yadav, founder of Lexlegis.ai, added that reliance on a few cloud, identity, and payment providers increases disruption risk.

Major US banks experienced disruptions on November 16, with JPMorgan Chase confirming a software bug in its systems caused the issue, and the bug affected Chase and other banks making transactions with it. Microsoft's 365 suite of apps, including Outlook, faced a global outage for millions of users for nearly 36 hours after a server update. The US Federal Aviation Administration cancelled over 10,000 flights following a router update, though a US Transport Secretary confirmed no AI link. Microsoft's 365 outage affected users in 74 countries, including Indian airlines IndiGo and SpiceJet. Mandar Patil, executive VP at Cyble, warned that AI may enable hackers to conduct autonomous attacks by interacting with APIs and enterprise applications.

Paulos Yibelo, who recently founded a company called PWN AI, discovered a vulnerability in document and image processing software that is ubiquitous across the internet. The bug, called Upload2Shell, would enable a hacker to break into Google, Zoom and potentially thousands of other companies' software just by uploading a file. Yibelo found that Ghostscript, software initially created 38 years ago to convert images to different formats, could be exploited by uploading files containing a custom font to execute malicious computer code. Yibelo reported the flaw to Artifex, the Ghostscript developer, and affected companies, which issued patches. Google's Threat Intelligence Group reported hackers created an AI framework to scan security patches for flaws in older software versions and execute attacks.

Patil said companies need to implement gradual rollouts, innovative deployments, operational tests, and versioning of changes. Sunil Peter, VP at Maveric Systems, recommended developing and testing independent fallback mechanisms so operations continue even if primary systems fail. Peter also highlighted the need for crisis management communication, with IT, incident response, and executive leadership teams coordinating through independent encrypted messaging tools. Professor Himanshu Joshi from IMI Delhi noted that while technical failures are not new, their impact is greater due to interconnected systems. Ward said more secure software systems must be built in the future, but there is an immediate need to fix problems now.

stories.Headline: CrowdStrike schedules virtual event on fighting AI-powered threats with AI
stories.Summary:
CrowdStrike announced a virtual event titled "The Next Era of Cyber Defense: Fighting AI-Powered Threats with AI," dated November 20, 2026, on its website. The event is scheduled for the Americas on December 9 and for JAPAC and Europe on December 10. CrowdStrike leaders will give a special update on the latest AI threats, frontier AI readiness, and the shift to the agentic SOC. Adam Meyers, CrowdStrike Senior Vice President of Counter Adversary Operations, will give a special AI threat briefing on the latest AI-enabled adversary activity. The briefing includes real-world examples of attackers putting agentic AI to work.

The event covers AI detection and response, which secures AI adoption and development from agents to models to prompts across endpoints, cloud, and SaaS. It also covers AI observability, which evaluates agents pre-deployment and then observes their behavior and enforces accountability in production. CrowdStrike offers a Frontier AI Readiness and Resilience Service to reduce exploitable risk with ongoing scans, expert prioritization, and guided remediation. It also offers a Shadow AI Visibility Service to discover hidden AI tools, activity, and agents across endpoint, cloud, and SaaS. Project QuiltWorks is described as an industry coalition mobilizing to close the frontier AI vulnerability gap at scale.

CrowdStrike states that AI is changing the speed and scale of cyberattacks and that defenders need to keep pace. The company says the event will feature CrowdStrike leaders and a briefing from Adam Meyers on AI-enabled adversary activity. CrowdStrike describes its Falcon Complete as elite 24/7 managed detection and response across the entire attack surface. It describes Charlotte AI as autonomous intelligence fueled by world-class expertise that accelerates outcomes. CrowdStrike says its Next-Gen SIEM is the world's only AI-native SOC platform.

CrowdStrike says its Agentic SOAR orchestrates agents, workflows, and automation across a security ecosystem. It says its Agentic SOC Transformation unlocks machine-speed responses with unified data and agentic workflows. CrowdStrike says its Frontier AI Readiness and Resilience service addresses risk as the time between patch and exploit continues to collapse. It says its Agentic Adversary Emulation red teams an environment to simulate real-world attacks and validate defenses. CrowdStrike lists customers by industry including small business, federal government, Department of War, state and local government, financial services, healthcare, election security, education, retail, and manufacturing.

CrowdStrike's resources include the 2026 Global Threat Report, the 2026 Threat Hunting Report, a New Adversary Hub, and an AI Security Hub. Its training and education offerings include CrowdStrike University, Cybersecurity 101, and Hands-On Workshops. Its events include Fal.Con Europe, Fal.Con Las Vegas, and CrowdTour. CrowdStrike's pricing tiers are Falcon Go, Falcon Pro, and Falcon Enterprise. CrowdStrike advertises a Black Friday and Cyber Monday sale from November 23 to December 4 on Falcon Go, Pro, or Enterprise.

CrowdStrike's site promotes guidance on Java4Shell and NGINX2Root to find exposures, monitor post-exploit activity, and remediate faster. It invites those who experienced a breach to contact the company. The article text ends mid-sentence at "Cyber Superintell," leaving the full description of the Cyber Superintelligence Lab incomplete. The articles give no further details on the event's speakers beyond Adam Meyers or on registration terms. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Clinicians must critically assess AI outputs at each decision stage to ensure safe care
stories.Summary:
A perspective published in Discover Artificial Intelligence on the safe clinical use of artificial intelligence argues that safety may depend less on how well a model performs and more on whether clinicians can evaluate what it produces. The authors are Ryan W. Hunton, Tama The and Jonathan Ilgen, and the article is titled The arc of uncertainty across clinicians' interactions with AI, published in volume 6, issue 1, as Article 1936, with DOI 10.1007/s44163-026-02851-3. The piece was reported by Blake Davidson on November 21, 2026, through Scienmag, and carried by bioengineer.org the same day. The authors describe large language models as increasingly used across clinical settings to support clinical reasoning and decision-making.

The analysis holds that AI-assisted reasoning should be examined as an unfolding sequence of decisions rather than a single isolated moment, beginning with the choice of whether to consult AI for a given clinical question. The process then moves through deciding how to engage with the tool, how to interpret its output, and finally whether to act on the guidance in a clinical case. Each stage, the authors say, introduces distinct points of vulnerability and potential failure, including inappropriate tool selection, incomplete or biased inputs, overconfidence in fluent responses, and failure to recognize underlying errors or appreciate clinical nuance. They add that these vulnerabilities are shaped by the same clinician factors that govern clinical reasoning more broadly, such as medical experience, clinical workload and how providers handle uncertainty. Early studies suggest strong performance on medical knowledge and reasoning tasks with the potential to reduce medical errors, but emerging evidence also highlights safety concerns, since outputs can contain clinically significant management errors that are not readily apparent to users.

The authors conclude that safe clinical implementation depends not merely on advancing model quality but on cultivating the clinician's ability to critically assess model responses. They say preparing clinicians to identify when algorithmic outputs must be questioned, verified or entirely set aside will be crucial as automated reasoning tools become more deeply embedded in routine patient care. Recognizing that AI-clinician collaboration is a continuous process, they argue, reveals key opportunities for targeted medical training. The article leaves open the central question of how to integrate these tools into practice to consistently improve patient outcomes.

stories.Headline: HHS Secretary Kennedy finalizes HIPAA rule cutting patient record response time to 15 days
stories.Summary:
The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services' Office for Civil Rights finalized a 363-page HIPAA Privacy Rule overhaul, released late Monday, November 16, 2026, and slated for Federal Register publication Thursday, November 19, 2026. HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. announced the final rule, which cuts patient record response time to 15 days. The rule is titled HIPAA Privacy Rule: Changes to Support Coordinated Care and Individual Engagement and Reduce Regulatory Burdens. HHS OCR issued the proposed modifications in January 2021, during the final days of President Donald Trump's first term. The proposal remained on the back burner during the Biden administration.

The rule becomes effective 60 days after publication, on January 18, 2027, and HIPAA-regulated organizations must comply 180 days after the effective date, or July 17, 2027. Business associate agreements must be updated by January 18, 2028, at the latest, and existing BAAs not renewed or modified before the compliance date are deemed compliant until renewed or modified, subject to transition provisions. The rule cuts the response deadline for patient access requests from 30 calendar days to 15 days, with a one-time extension of up to 30 additional days under specific circumstances. It clarifies patients' rights to obtain electronic health information through personal health apps, including consumer apps not subject to HIPAA, and prohibits refusing transmission solely because an app lacks encryption at rest. It bars unreasonable identity verification measures, stating organizations in the Trusted Exchange Framework and Common Agreement generally should not refuse requests through personal health apps when conditions are met, including a cryptographically signed token from a credential service provider certified consistent with NIST Identity Assurance Level 2 and Authentication Assurance Level 2, and matching demographic information.

Kennedy said Americans should never have to fight for access to their own health records. He said the rule modernizes HIPAA to serve patients and helps providers spend more time delivering care and less time navigating bureaucracy. HHS OCR dropped a proposal that would have relaxed the minimum necessary standard for certain disclosures of sensitive health information. The rule clarifies that health plans may use and disclose PHI for individual-level care coordination and case management, and expressly permits disclosures to social services agencies, community-based organizations and similar third parties for care coordination and case management. HHS retained the minimum necessary standard for applicable healthcare operations disclosures rather than adopting a proposed exception for certain care-coordination activities.

Privacy attorney Adam Greene of Davis Wright Tremaine said he appreciated deletion of the requirement to obtain acknowledgments of receipt of the notice of privacy practices, which he said was founded on good intentions but led to administrative burden and confusion with minimal corresponding benefit. Privacy attorney Kirk Nahra of WilmerHale said he would have liked an additional stage to obtain new comments on issues that changed significantly since the proposal five years ago. Nahra said HHS chose coordination over individual privacy, a complicated decision that essentially allows disclosure over the objection or lack of permission from the consumer. Privacy attorney Iliana Peters of Polsinelli said her biggest concerns involve administrative burdens, including the 15-day access deadline, which she called a very short amount of time. Several healthcare industry groups, including the College of Healthcare Information Management Executives, signed a letter to HHS last week warning that loosening identity verification for third-party apps could expose providers to security threats and regulatory scrutiny.

The final rule eliminates the requirement for covered healthcare providers to make a good-faith effort to obtain patients' written acknowledgment of receiving a Notice of Privacy Practices. It abandons a requirement that would have obligated covered organizations to exercise individuals' right of access on their behalf by requesting designated record sets from other covered entities. Greene said that proposal would have led to a substantial unfunded mandate taxing covered entities' already limited resources. Greene said the final rule includes helpful changes but nothing earth-shattering, and he does not expect compliance to be difficult, though changes to notices and right-of-access policies will take significant time and resources. Peters said organizations must still update, redistribute and post their notices, update websites with required fee information and revise applicable business associate agreements.

Greene said the most significant gains for patients will likely come in quicker access to their protected health information and fewer obstacles to exercising this access. Nahra said companies should remain cautious about these disclosures even if permitted, and should be cognizant of security risks and ensure appropriate steps beyond the identity confirmation limitations. The signatories of the letter did not immediately respond to ISMG's request for comment on the final rule. The rule also defines electronic health record and revises permissible access fees, specifying which fees apply. The articles leave open how covered entities will implement the shortened deadline and what further guidance HHS may issue.

stories.Headline: Sarvam AI launches Token Factory platform to provide AI inference services in India
stories.Summary:
The Bengaluru-based startup Sarvam AI launched its Token Factory platform on November 16. This commercial platform provides developers and enterprises access to multiple AI models through computing infrastructure. The launch focuses on the emerging inference-as-a-service market within India. It allows users to access various AI models via a common API. This initiative brings the artificial intelligence infrastructure ecosystem of India into focus.

The platform hosts the proprietary Sarvam 105B model, Google's Gemma 4 31B, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, Kimi K3.1 Pro, and GLM 5.3. Billing is in Indian rupee, with introductory rates for Sarvam 105B at ten rupees per million input and twenty-five per million output tokens. Other model prices range from fourteen to nine hundred fifty rupees per million tokens, while cached input costs zero point twenty-five rupees. The service offers ISO 27001 and SOC 2 Type II certifications and promises ninety-nine point ninety-five per cent uptime. It operates on privately procured GPUs and does not use capacity subsidised under the IndiaAI Mission.

Sarvam AI stated that its access to government-supported GPU capacity ended in March 2026. The company clarified there are no commercial arrangements involving royalties, data sharing, or licensing fees with the developers of hosted models. It explained that these are open-weight models that can be downloaded and deployed on privately owned infrastructure. The company also noted that it serves more than four hundred fifty billion tokens daily through DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. Sarvam stated that zero data retention is provided only upon explicit request from the user.

Sanchit Vir Gogia of Greyhound Research said the platform keeps the B200 cluster busy and provides income while a trillion-parameter model is built. Manoj Dhanda of Utho Cloud called the development positive, stating that demand for tokens will outgrow any single entity's capability. Businesses handling sensitive information may have concerns because user data is used for training or fine-tuning by default. Other affected players include L&T through Vyoma.AI, E2E Networks via Jarvislabs and Blaze, Utho Cloud, and Mirror Security. Mirror Security offers an encrypted token factory using homomorphic encryption for enhanced data security.

The company was selected under the IndiaAI Mission to develop homegrown foundation models and received access to four thousand ninety-six Nvidia H100 GPUs. This six-month computing allocation was worth around two hundred forty-seven crore rupees, including a government subsidy of ninety-eight point sixty-eight crore rupees. Indian infrastructure players are moving beyond GPU rentals to monetise computing capacity through managed services for domestic and global workloads. The process of AI inference allows trained models to generate responses to user prompts. Many previous infrastructure investments in India focused on setting up data centres and procuring GPUs.

Introductory pricing for the Token Factory services will run until the end of 2026. Sanchit Vir Gogia suggested that founders should show by the end of 2027 that customers stayed for Sarvam after arriving for DeepSeek. Utho Cloud is looking to enter the domestic inference space by early 2027. The articles leave open whether the service is a revenue play or a data play. They also leave open the specific number of GPUs Sarvam runs, the utilisation rates, and the amount of full-price traffic.

stories.Headline: CrowdStrike acquires Zscaler for 43.9 billion dollars to bolster AI security
stories.Summary:
CrowdStrike agreed to acquire the network security provider Zscaler in a massive deal on Monday, November 23, 2026. This all-stock transaction is valued at 43.9 billion dollars to combine two significant security businesses. The acquisition comes as artificial intelligence is supercharging cyberattacks and increasing the sophistication of threats. This move marks the biggest acquisition to date for the company known as CrowdStrike. The deal is expected to close during the second half of CrowdStrike's fiscal year 2028.

Zscaler shareholders will receive 1.135 CrowdStrike shares for each share they own under the terms of the agreement. The deal pushes the Austin, Texas-based vendor into the network security market to better defend corporate networks. Zscaler is based in Santa Clara, California, and operates in more than 185 countries globally. The combined market value of these two companies exceeded 265 billion dollars as of Friday's close. This transaction follows a year of high-profile hacks, including one involving the company known as Hugging Face.

CrowdStrike CEO George Kurtz stated that the company is building a single control plane to deploy and control AI. He said this operating system will enable any agentic application to run safely for their customers. Kurtz claimed that the company sees a path to become the largest AI safety and security company ever. Analysts at JPMorgan wrote that the addition of Zscaler could bring more breadth during an era of consolidation. They noted that network security positions the company more effectively for the rising demand for AI Sovereignty.

Shares of CrowdStrike dropped 10 percent on Monday, while Zscaler shares surged more than 15 percent. The deal affects Zscaler's 11,000 global customers, which include more than half of the Fortune 500 companies. Businesses are accelerating software patching and upgrades to prevent bad actors from exploiting vulnerabilities with AI tools. Recent outages affecting Microsoft, JPMorgan Chase, and the Federal Aviation Administration have sparked anxiety for many businesses. Other affected entities mentioned include United Airlines and the National Security Agency during recent technology disruptions.

CrowdStrike has seen shares soar about 80 percent this year due to skyrocketing demand for AI security. Zscaler reported record revenue of 3.35 billion dollars in fiscal 2026 but has not turned an annual profit. The security market is valued at 244 billion dollars, with spending projected to grow nearly 12 percent. Zscaler's cloud-based products replace traditional virtual private networks that were targeted by suspected Chinese and state-sponsored hackers. CrowdStrike's flagship Falcon product previously caused a global IT meltdown during a botched software update in 2024.

CrowdStrike reported fiscal third-quarter earnings of 34 cents per share on 1.58 billion dollars in total revenue. Zscaler's fiscal first-quarter earnings also surpassed estimates, though the company faced fears of a potential SaaSpocalypse. The articles leave open whether the combined entity can close the gap with market leader Palo Alto Networks. It remains unclear how the new company will distinguish legitimate automated activity from malicious AI agent traffic. The reports do not state when the final regulatory approvals for the 43.9 billion dollar deal occur.

stories.Headline: Large law firms weigh AI fluency in hiring and attorney pay
stories.Summary:
Large law firms have started to change how they recruit and evaluate their lawyers as of November 23, 2026. These organizations are now weighing the artificial intelligence fluency of their staff during the hiring process. This shift occurs as these firms increase their overall investment in various artificial intelligence tools. The ability to use these technologies is becoming a standard requirement for many legal professionals.

This new approach to management requires both partners and associates to demonstrate a high level of AI innovation. The firms are now using these technical skills to determine how they compensate their attorneys. Being open to these technological changes is no longer considered a niche skill for a small group. Instead, it has become a necessary qualification for those seeking to advance within these organizations.

Andrew Maloney reported that these rapid changes in evaluation are transforming the legal employment landscape. He noted that AI fluency is increasingly becoming a requisite for lawyers at some of these firms. The reporting suggests that the ability to integrate these tools is now a key metric for success. This evolution reflects a broader trend of integrating advanced technology into the core of legal practice.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: Jay Clayton links NSA outage to AI-assisted PHP patching as experts debate change risk
stories.Summary:
A series of major technology outages hit the United States, disrupting email, air travel, banking and government operations, according to SecurityWeek. The incidents included a nearly day-long Microsoft 365 outage, a nationwide FAA ground stop, a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase that slowed transactions at other banks, and an outage affecting the NSA's classified internal network. United Airlines and Apple also experienced disruptions. Officials said there was no evidence of a cyberattack or a link between the incidents. Microsoft traced its outage to a months-old software defect, the FAA blamed a newly installed router, and the NSA cited routine maintenance.

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton linked the NSA disruption to patching for a PHP vulnerability found with the help of AI. Sen. Mark Warner said AI-driven vulnerability discovery is pushing organizations to patch many systems at once, putting strain on infrastructure that wasn't built for that pace of change. Industry professionals commented on whether AI-accelerated patching played a role, the need for tested rollback plans, and the fragility of interconnected systems. One professional said there is strong reason to believe AI-accelerated patch velocity is already causing major operational incidents, based on direct experience with customers deploying large OpenJDK updates. That person said the Java community has had to absorb four update events in the past four weeks, including three separate critical vulnerability events, and that security-only updates minimize risk by limiting change to what is necessary.

Another professional said AI plays a part but should not be made the whole story, and that the outages look less like an AI problem than a change problem, with updates pushed onto systems that can't take much change. That person said a fix that takes the service down is a security failure too, and asked who owns the choice between leaving a flaw open a few more days and risking the service by closing it tonight. A third professional said AI is finding vulnerabilities faster than many remediation processes were built to handle, noting that Microsoft fixed more than 1,400 vulnerabilities in its October security release, a monthly record, and 1,094 in November. That person said nothing published so far links this pressure to the recent Microsoft 365 outage, but Microsoft's own explanation shows how easily planned work can take a service down.

stories.Headline: mEinstein outlines Human Context Contracts to define revocable human authorization for AI agents
stories.Summary:
mEinstein is outlining a framework called Human Context Contracts, which the company says is meant to address how human authorization can be represented and applied when AI agents interact with personal information and external systems, according to an article published by aithority.com on November 23, 2026. The company describes the framework as a way to translate human consent into defined, enforceable and revocable authority over autonomous actions. The article says existing consent mechanisms were largely developed for websites and digital services, while autonomous agents introduce requirements involving delegated authority, task limitations and accountability. Prithwi Thakuria, Founder and CEO of mEinstein, said a checkbox records consent but an autonomous system needs permission it can actually execute.

The framework is designed to represent distinctions between kinds of permission through structured requests that specify the purpose, required information and permitted action, and its architecture includes authorization conditions covering the requesting entity, scope, duration, value, revocation and audit records. The article gives the example of a request to find a flight, which may authorize an AI assistant to search and compare available options, while purchasing a ticket, selecting a payment method, accepting a connecting flight or disclosing travel information to external services may require separate authorization. It also says a healthcare system may be authorized to assess clinical-trial eligibility without automatically receiving permission to disclose patient information to a research sponsor, and a financial assistant may evaluate mortgage readiness without having authority to share an individual's complete financial information or submit an application. Thakuria said permission to know something is not permission to share it, and permission to share it is not permission to act on it. The framework forms part of the company's broader Human Intelligence Infrastructure concept, which addresses the relationship between enterprise AI systems and an individual's private, user-controlled information, and the company summarizes the operating principle as AI interprets, rules govern, device executes.

The article says the issue is receiving attention across the AI industry, noting that the National Institute of Standards and Technology has been examining AI-agent identity and authorization, including how agents establish authority, operate under delegated permissions and maintain evidence connecting their actions to human authorization. It also says Microsoft has outlined a Dynamic Permissions approach in which AI agents receive permissions appropriate to specific tasks rather than relying on unrestricted standing access, with permissions limited by task and duration and additional verification for actions requiring human approval. OpenAI's computer-use guidance similarly distinguishes direct user instructions from information encountered by an agent during operation and recommends confirmation before certain consequential actions, including financial transactions and the transmission of sensitive information. The article says Mastercard's Verifiable Intent initiative focuses on establishing evidence of consumer authorization when AI agents conduct purchases, and its Agent Pay Trust Framework incorporates identity, intent, controls, execution and intelligence into the management of agent-led transactions.

The article says the framework also addresses the operational limitations of repeated approval requests, because rather than requiring confirmation for every individual action, permission boundaries can define which activities an agent may perform independently and which require renewed authorization, and changes in circumstances or actions outside the approved scope may trigger additional verification. It says that as AI agents take on more responsibilities across digital services and commercial transactions, the distinction between consent, delegated authority and executable permission is becoming an important consideration for system developers and organizations. The article describes Human Context Contracts as mEinstein's approach to structuring that authorization layer, with the aim of maintaining defined human authority as autonomous systems perform increasingly complex tasks. The article does not say when the framework will be available or how it will be adopted.

stories.Headline: US Senate passes permitting reform bill to accelerate energy construction for AI power demand
stories.Summary:
Financial markets suffered major losses this week as concerns over an artificial intelligence bubble grew. The US Senate passed a bipartisan permitting reform bill on Thursday to speed up energy construction. Confusion is also growing over new Medicaid work requirement rules that are set to begin in January. Investors feared the AI boom could bust despite a record initial public offering from Anthropic on Thursday. The entire stock market was pummeled on Friday during one of the worst weeks in years.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 passed the Senate with a 62-33 vote. It rewrites the Clean Water Act, the Endangered Species Act, and the National Environmental Policy Act. The bill changes the National Historic Preservation Act of 1966 and shortens timelines for getting most permits. It requires data centers to pay for energy usage and exempts some projects from environmental review. These changes aim to lower energy costs and speed up oil, gas, solar, and hydropower projects.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and Senator Ruben Gallego supported the bill to bring down carbon emissions. Senator Martin Heinrich said the legislation provides a real opportunity to make electricity more affordable for families. Republican Senator Shelley Moore Capito stated that Americans deserve bipartisan solutions that make life more affordable. These authors argued that cutting red tape allows more energy production and lowers prices for the public. They believe working people cannot afford to wait years for these necessary infrastructure improvements to happen.

The Sierra Club and Natural Resource Defense Council opposed the bill because it weakens bedrock environmental protections. Executive Director Loren Blackford said the bill is deeply flawed and threatens endangered species and tribal sovereignty. Nearly a dozen tribal organizations warned that the changes limit Indigenous input on sites with important cultural significance. Labor unions, oil and gas companies, and most clean energy industry groups expressed their support for the measure. Many voters in recent elections prioritized cost of living and affordability issues over these environmental concerns.

The NASDAQ dropped 10 percent this week, marking its worst performance since the pandemic year of 2020. The S&P and Dow Jones indices both ended the week in a correction after dropping 10 percent. In September, the Federal Reserve raised interest rates for the first time in over three years, increasing borrowing costs. NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang resigned this month following suspicions of an affair with a woman spying for China. Democrats are set to take over Congress and many state governments in January and promise to slow AI.

The permitting bill must now clear the House before it reaches the desk of President Donald Trump. The House is out of session next week for Thanksgiving and must extend government funding by December 11. Republicans may need Democratic votes in a narrowly divided chamber to pass the bill before January. It remains unclear if the House will pass the bill or if Democrats will wait until January. The articles leave open whether the AI market is a bubble or just a temporary readjustment.

stories.Headline: Romanian lenders must align credit scoring models with GDPR and EU AI Act rules by 2026
stories.Summary:
The EU AI Act is being applied in phases and treats credit scoring and automated lending decisions as high-risk artificial intelligence, according to a guide published by Global Advisory Experts on November 22, 2026. The same guide states that the General Data Protection Regulation already governs profiling and automated decision-making. It says Romanian banks, non-bank financial institutions and credit servicers using scoring models answer to two overlapping regimes. Each regime has its own documentation, governance and enforcement expectations, the guide states. The guide is written for compliance officers, data protection officers, in-house counsel, risk and model owners, and vendors that supply banks, non-bank financial institutions and credit servicers in Romania.

The GDPR is Regulation (EU) 2016/679, and its Article 22 gives individuals the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing, including profiling, where that decision has legal effects or similarly significantly affects them. The guide cites a refusal of credit as a frequently cited example, and it states that Article 35 requires a Data Protection Impact Assessment where processing is likely to create a high risk for individuals. Articles 13 and 14 set transparency duties, and the recitals add that where Article 22 applies, people must be able to obtain human intervention, state their point of view and contest the decision. The EU AI Act is Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, and it classifies AI systems used to assess the creditworthiness of natural persons, or to establish their credit score, as high-risk. The guide states that the model file a bank keeps for prudential and data protection purposes needs to be able to support AI Act conformity as well.

The Romanian Data Protection Authority, ANSPDCP, supervises GDPR compliance, handles complaints and enforces national practice, including on profiling and automated decisions, the guide states. The National Bank of Romania, BNR, supervises credit institutions and non-bank financial institutions prudentially and sets expectations on model risk, internal governance and outsourcing. At EU level, the European Banking Authority issues guidelines on outsourcing and the use of innovative technologies, and the European Data Protection Board and the European Data Protection Supervisor publish guidance on applying data protection principles to AI. Consumer protection law, overseen by the National Authority for Consumer Protection, ANPC, adds rules on the fairness, clarity and timing of communications to borrowers. The guide states that these bodies together define the enforcement environment a programme has to satisfy.

The guide states that the AI Act contains limited carve-outs, such as systems used to detect financial fraud, and that fraud-detection tools are treated differently but the boundary should be documented carefully instead of assuming an exemption. It states that a model need not take the final decision alone, and that if it materially drives the creditworthiness assessment it may fall within scope. It states that ANSPDCP has published a list of processing operations that require a DPIA, and that this list should be checked. The guide states that for a single significant model, three to four months from start to go-live is a realistic expectation, with monitoring continuing indefinitely afterwards. It states that supervisors expect a dated audit trail, and that missing or inconsistent papers are among the most reliable triggers for escalation.

The guide sets out ten steps, including mapping the use case and data flows, classifying the model's risk, completing or updating the DPIA, setting up model governance, building explainability and transparency, designing human oversight, running vendor due diligence and contracting, setting up recordkeeping, building redress and adverse-action processes, and operating ongoing audit and reporting. It assigns owners for each step, including the model owner with the DPO, Legal, Compliance and Risk, the DPO with Risk, Legal and the model owner, Risk/Model Validation and IT, Compliance, Legal and Communications, Credit Operations and Compliance, Procurement and Legal, Compliance and IT, Legal and Customer Operations, and Compliance and Internal Audit. It states that if a high residual risk cannot be mitigated, prior consultation with ANSPDCP may be required. It states that explanations must make sense to a borrower, not be a technical data dump, and that reviewers should be trained so oversight is real and not a rubber stamp. It states that a validation report describing a superseded version is worse than none.

The guide states that an inspection, whether by ANSPDCP on data protection or by BNR on prudential grounds, will test whether a coherent, dated set of documents can be produced. It states that the minimum file for automated credit scoring in Romania is listed in the guide with the internal owner of each item, and that everything should be kept under version control and aligned with the live production model. It states that the ten steps form a defensible path and that some can run in parallel. It states that for every step the owner should be confirmed, the minimum documentation captured and sign-off dates recorded. It states that the durations in the guide's table should be treated as minimums for one model of moderate complexity, and that portfolios of models scale accordingly.

stories.Headline: Big Law firms launch AI spinouts and special units as they adapt to AI native workflows
stories.Summary:
Weil Gotshal planned to launch an AI native spinout called Kepler, headed by Arnie Fridhandler, a partner in Weil’s private equity practice who previously oversaw DealVision360, the firm’s AI-enabled deal engine, before the firm atomized. The supposed plan was to spin Kepler out, gain external investment and focus on transactional work, and Artificial Lawyer believes this may still happen, although clearly via a new launchpad. Freshfields accidentally leaked that it was, and perhaps still is, planning to spin out a heavily AI-focused part of the business centred around its Lab group. Kirkland has been working with Palantir to build its own AI-focused offering around private equity and funds work, which feels like a distinct project rather than the entire firm moving into very deep deployment of AI. Goodwin is building proprietary AI-based tools for various needs such as venture financing, and Wilson Sonsini has long had Neuron, a separate group focused on more automated workflows, often for more routine startup needs, with genAI feeding into that more recently.

Cooley has launched GO Public, a proprietary AI-based tool that leverages ChatGPT Enterprise to support Form S-1 drafting, and there is also a project with Legora for its GO Lab, which will help with needs such as NDAs and contractor agreements for Y Combinator startups. The article says there are many more such moves, with several clustering around either routine contract needs or funds work, two of the key areas the fully AI native, New Model law firms are focused on. The article asks why the AI business unit has to spin out, and gives one answer as Bar rules if a firm is going to get outside investment, though it notes there are MSO structures that can handle that. It also asks why an AI-driven workflow becomes a separate business unit or offering within the firm, often with a new brand name so clients and the firm’s lawyers know it is not part of the main organisation. The article says true AI native workflows, where the goal is to reduce human input to the necessary minimum, feel alien to Big Law’s traditional business model.

The article says the Big Law model is primarily based on leveraging human intellectual labour, not the labour of GPUs sitting in data centres, with that human labour measured in time inputs converted into money. It says that in the New Model human labour is there to guide, fine-tune and quality check the work of the AI, rather like a partner does today in Big Law with their team of associates. It says it is therefore only natural that when a Big Law firm really goes deep into AI, applying the methodology fully to a workflow, it then separates this out from the main work of that firm. It says partners, despite what some may think, can be very entrepreneurial and may seize the opportunity to make extra money via an AI spin-off. It adds that one could argue the instinct to make money from AI by externalising it, rather than applying it deeply in a way that changes the firm’s DNA, is part of the challenge.

The article says the New Model AI native law firms have come into existence mostly via lawyers from Big Law moving into open spaces to create firms that are not in conflict with the model they were trained within. It says Baker McKenzie has said it no longer wants to use the hour as its default billing mechanism, which Artificial Lawyer understands is a direct result of the New Model law firms proliferating around the world. It says moving off the hour allows a firm to really use AI as it was intended to be used, as fully as possible, and that this move differs from the spinouts and special units because it is a whole firm strategy, not a separation strategy. It says the current manual model makes a ton of money and places all the risk on the buyer, as matters are open-ended and sold on time taken. It says all you have to do is stay busy and work and work and work, and the money rolls in, and asks why change what works.

The article says Artificial Lawyer uses the term AI native as a loose term meaning you are using a lot of AI from start to finish of a matter, with how native you are, how deeply AI is used, really on a spectrum. It says Big Law firms can therefore claim to be AI native but appear radically different to many new AI native firms in the market, which is why AL tends to use the term New Model for legal businesses that have really changed how they do things. It says the New Model approach is not about where in a process you use AI, or how much you use on each task, but that the strategy is always to focus on getting the work done as quickly and as efficiently as possible, not using increasing time as a measure of increasing value, and staffing client needs with the clear intention that any work will have AI at its heart. It says AI makes the New Model possible, and that if you are truly AI native in spirit then you evolve into the New Model, while if you are not, those deep AI activities end up as spinouts and special units, so you are still operating the Old Model. It says this evolutionary step towards the New Model is causing the separation at present within Big Law.

The article says Artificial Lawyer believes Big Law oil and AI Native water can mix, comparing it to car companies moving from petrol to electric vehicles, oil companies moving into green energy at scale if they wanted to, newspapers going digital and law libraries going digital. It says for this site there is a way forward, and that Big Law’s many special AI units and spinout plans are just symptoms of one model trying to synthesize a new model into how it operates. It says the result is not perfect but is a step in the right direction, at least mostly, and shows Big Law can be very creative and adaptive when it wants to be. It says it is clear we are not there yet, and that these moves are an intermediate step, a get around, oil and water trying hard to mix but not quite getting there. It says eventually that will change, and asks whether Big Law oil and AI Native water can mix.

stories.Headline: Akkodis launches a global AI Factory and uses itself as client zero to scale enterprise AI
stories.Summary:
Akkodis, a digital engineering consulting company that is part of the Adecco Group and is headquartered in Switzerland, announced on November 23, 2026 the launch of its AI Factory, which it describes as a global model designed to accelerate the development, adoption and scaling of enterprise AI. The company said it is operating the model within its own business, applying the same principles it offers to clients that are moving from AI experimentation to enterprise-scale value. Akkodis said the AI Factory is already connecting AI solutions and reusable capabilities across the company globally, with the first global AI Factory solutions now in production through common pathways for intake, governance and deployment. The company said the model is not a single centralized technology platform but an enablement ecosystem that connects countries, engineers, business teams and specialists with reusable capabilities, development resources and expertise. The AI Factory brings together four core functions, which Akkodis lists as Design, Build, Run and Govern, covering the operating model and architecture, the development of solutions and reusable components, the move into production and lifecycle support, and the security, compliance and decision frameworks needed to manage AI responsibly.

Akkodis said the model helps teams decide whether to reuse or adapt existing capabilities, combine expertise across countries or develop something new, rather than assuming every AI requirement demands a new solution. The company said its AI use case intake agent, a common entry point that structures AI opportunities and identifies governance and duplication risks, is now live across Akkodis. Through AI Factory as a Service, Akkodis said it brings that experience, engineering expertise and reusable capabilities to clients seeking to move from fragmented AI initiatives toward scalable enterprise capability. Jo Debecker, President and CEO of Akkodis, said that scaling AI is not simply a technology challenge and that it requires organizations to connect innovation with the systems, expertise and operating models needed to turn it into repeatable value.

He said the company sees that challenge with its clients and experiences it itself, and that the AI Factory helps Akkodis learn by doing while putting Akkodis Intelligence into practice by combining human expertise and technology. Akkodis said it serves as "client zero," testing and refining the model in a complex global enterprise environment, and that applying and refining the AI Factory internally and with clients creates a continuous feedback loop that improves both internal execution and customer delivery. Akkodis cited its 2026 What CTOs Think research, which found that while AI ambition continues to grow, organizations often struggle to turn experimentation into repeatable, scalable execution, widening the divide between enterprise-wide AI orchestration and fragmented efforts across functions, systems and skills. Among the AI solutions Akkodis said it is developing and integrating with clients are a multi-agent AI coworker that it says can reduce B2B sales proposal preparation from three days to approximately five minutes, a supplier communications agent designed to save 45 to 55 hours per user each month, a contract review agent designed to reduce review time by at least 30%, and an executive office assistant that reduces administrative effort while improving decision and action traceability.

stories.Headline: Huckleberry.ai files 8-K after Delaware court ruling on asset distribution
stories.Summary:
Huckleberry.ai Inc. filed SEC Form 8-K on November 23, 2026, covering Regulation FD Disclosure and Financial Statements and Exhibits, according to Quantisnow. The filing followed a press release the company issued the same day about a Delaware Court of Chancery decision dated November 10, 2026. The decision concerned the potential distribution of assets to stockholders after the company's completed transaction with Progress Software Corporation. Huckleberry.ai, formerly Domo, Inc., trades on Nasdaq under the symbol HUCK. The report's date of earliest event reported was November 23, 2026.

The filing's Item 7.01 attaches the press release as Exhibit 99.1 and incorporates it by reference. Item 9.01 lists Exhibit 99.1, the press release dated November 23, 2026, and Exhibit 104, a Cover Page Interactive Data File embedded within the Inline XBRL document. The cover page gives the company's address as 3300 N Triumph Boulevard, Suite 100, Lehi, UT 84043, and its telephone number as (385) 338-5608. It lists Class B Common Stock, par value $0.001 per share, on The Nasdaq Global Market, with commission file number 001-38553 and IRS Employer Identification No. 27-3687433. The report was signed by Tod Crane, Chief Financial Officer, on November 23, 2026.

Huckleberry said it does not agree with the Court's ruling and is evaluating its options. The Board, the company said, takes seriously its fiduciary duties to all stockholders, and its evaluation includes an assessment of the Court's ruling, the Company's assets that would be legally available for distribution to stockholders, the Company's obligations to third parties, and applicable law. The company said it will provide updates as appropriate. The press release states that the amount and timing of any distribution to stockholders is uncertain while the company evaluates its options. Tod Crane, Chief Financial Officer, is listed as media and investor contact at ir@huckleberry.ai.

Quantisnow's AI-written summary rated the news negative for shareholders, saying the company disagrees with the court ruling on potential asset distribution. The summary states that no outcome or distribution is confirmed. Quantisnow listed the stock at $3.05 at news time and described the company's sector as Technology and its industry as Computer Software: Prepackaged Software, listed since 2018. Quantisnow's page defines Regulation FD as an SEC rule requiring public companies to share material information with all investors at the same time, and describes the Court of Chancery as Delaware's court for corporate disputes, including disputes between companies and their stockholders.

The press release carries forward-looking statements under Section 27A of the Securities Act of 1933, Section 21E of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995. These include statements about the company's evaluation of options relating to the Court's decision and its plan for future updates. The release cites risks and uncertainties included under the caption "Risk Factors" and elsewhere in the company's SEC filings, including its Annual Report on Form 10-K filed with the SEC on April 16, 2026, and subsequent filings. It states that all information in the release and attachments is as of the date hereof and that the company undertakes no duty to update it unless required by law. The 8-K states that information in Item 7.01 shall not be deemed "filed" for purposes of Section 18 of the Exchange Act or otherwise subject to the liabilities of that section.

The company said it will provide updates as appropriate, without specifying a date. The filing leaves open the outcome of the company's evaluation of its options and whether any distribution to stockholders will occur. The amount and timing of any distribution remain uncertain. The filing does not state what the Court's November 10, 2026 decision requires or what specific options the company is weighing. The filing does not state when the transaction with Progress Software Corporation was completed.

stories.Headline: Judge Chung bars Colorado from enforcing its AI law until 14 days after an xAI injunction ruling
stories.Summary:
A federal magistrate judge in Denver, Cyrus Y. Chung, entered a two-page minute order on April 27, 2026, barring Colorado Attorney General Philip J. Weiser from enforcing the state's artificial intelligence law. The order was docketed as ECF No. 24 in Civil Action No. 26-cv-01515-DDD-CYC in the U.S. District Court for the District of Colorado. It granted the parties' Revised Joint Motion to Vacate Scheduling Conference and Suspend Case Deadlines and Stipulation to Temporarily Stay Enforcement, filed as ECF No. 22. The caption lists X. AI LLC as plaintiff, the United States of America as plaintiff-intervenor, and Weiser as defendant. The order followed the United States' motion to intervene, which the court granted shortly before April 24, 2026.

The order bars enforcement, including the initiation of an investigation, for alleged violations of SB24-205 or any legislation replacing or amending it enacted during this legislative session. The bar covers violations that occurred or may occur on or before 14 days after the court rules on xAI's forthcoming motion for a preliminary injunction. xAI must submit that motion, and if necessary an amended complaint, within 28 days after final adoption of rulemaking implementing SB24-205 or any replacement or amendment. The order vacated the Scheduling Conference set for June 16, 2026 and stayed all case management and other deadlines pending resolution of the motion. It denied as moot an earlier version of the motion, ECF No. 18, which xAI and the Attorney General had filed without the United States.

The court weighed the factors from String Cheese Incident, LLC v. Stylus Shows, Inc., a 2006 District of Colorado decision, and said in a single sentence that a stay would not prejudice the plaintiff, who does not oppose the motion. The order said the stay would avoid burdening the parties with the costs of litigating, promote judicial economy and efficiency, not negatively impact nonparties, and serve the public interest. According to the revised joint motion, the Attorney General has exclusive authority to enforce SB 24-205 under section 6-1-1706(1) of the Colorado Revised Statutes. The revised motion said the Colorado AI Policy Working Group convened by Governor Jared Polis published a draft bill to repeal and replace SB 24-205 on March 17, 2026.

The motion said the Attorney General did not intend to issue rules until the 2026 Regular Session of the General Assembly ended and did not intend to enforce SB 24-205 or any replacement until rulemaking concluded. The revised motion described SB 24-205 as becoming effective June 30, 2026. The first version of the joint motion, filed April 24, 2026, applied the Attorney General's promise not to enforce or investigate only to xAI, and all three parties filed the revised motion the same day asking the court to replace it. Chief Judge Daniel D. Domenico, to whom the case was reassigned on April 14 after the parties did not all consent to a magistrate judge, referred the revised motion to Magistrate Judge Chung on April 27. The revised motion's signature blocks list Wheeler Trigg O'Donnell and in-house counsel for xAI, lawyers from the Justice Department's Civil Division and Civil Rights Division including Assistant Attorney General Harmeet K. Dhillon, and First Assistant Attorney General Heather Kelly and Senior Assistant Attorney General Kate Field for Colorado.

The order protects every company covered by the law, not only xAI. The Colorado House passed SB 26-189 by 57 votes to 6 on May 9, 2026, repealing and replacing SB 24-205 with a narrower law on automated decision-making technology used in consequential decisions. According to the General Assembly's record, Governor Polis signed it on May 14, 2026, its substantive obligations begin on January 1, 2027, and it required the Attorney General to complete rulemaking by the same date. On July 1, 2026, the Federal Trade Commission released a proposed policy statement naming Colorado's law as amended by SB 26-189 and arguing that conflicting state requirements are impliedly preempted, a statement that remains a proposal.

Proposed rules were published on August 11, an interim draft followed on October 6, and a public hearing took place on October 26. According to the Colorado Department of Law, the Department adopted the rules on November 19, 2026, covering both SB 26-189 and HB 26-1263, the Conversational Artificial Intelligence Services Act, which the Department calls the Chatbot Safety Act. The adopted rules prevent chatbot operators from relying on government identification alone for age assurance, and the Department has asked the Attorney General for a formal opinion on them. Once that opinion arrives, the rules and the opinion go to the Secretary of State, and the rules become final twenty days after publication, according to the Department.

According to the court docket, the only filings since April 27 are two motions by counsel to withdraw, filed on October 2 as ECF No. 25 and November 16, 2026 as ECF No. 28, each followed by an order, and no motion for a preliminary injunction and no amended complaint appear as of the November 16 entry. If the November 19 adoption counts as final adoption, xAI's motion is due on December 17, 2026, by PPC Land's calculation, while the Department's description reserves "final" for twenty days after publication by the Secretary of State, and no publication date has been set. Because the bar covers violations through the 14th day after the ruling, conduct on January 1, 2027 would be open to enforcement only if the court rules on or before a date the articles leave unstated. Which reading the parties apply is not stated anywhere on the docket.

stories.Headline: Huckleberry.ai disputes Delaware court ruling on stockholder asset distribution and weighs its options
stories.Summary:
Huckleberry.ai, the company formerly known as Domo, said on Monday that it does not agree with a Nov. 10 decision of the Delaware Court of Chancery concerning a potential distribution of assets to its stockholders after its sale to Progress Software. The company said in a statement furnished with an 8-K that it is evaluating its options following that ruling. The board's evaluation covers the court's ruling, the company's assets that would be legally available for distribution to stockholders, its obligations to third parties and applicable law. Huckleberry.ai did not describe what the court ordered and said it will provide updates as appropriate. The Nov. 23 statement is the company's first public response to the ruling.

Domo completed the sale of substantially all of its assets and employees to Progress on Sept. 22, 2026, excluding its net operating loss carryforwards, and Progress assumed certain liabilities, according to the company's 8-K from that day. Domo's AI and data platform became part of Progress. After purchase price adjustments, a warrant repurchase and other closing items, the remaining company started with about $221 million in cash, equal to about $4.46 a share, and kept more than $900 million in net operating loss carryforwards along with other assets and liabilities not included in the sale. It renamed itself Huckleberry.ai and began trading on Nasdaq under the symbol HUCK on Sept. 24, replacing DOMO. How that cash is used, whether paid out to stockholders or kept to use the tax losses, is what the court dispute bears on.

The board is assessing the ruling, the assets legally available for distribution, its obligations to third parties and applicable law, the company said in its statement. Huckleberry.ai said it does not agree with the Delaware Court of Chancery's Nov. 10 decision on a potential distribution of assets to stockholders. The company, which trades on Nasdaq under the symbol HUCK, said it is evaluating its options and will provide updates as appropriate. The articles do not say what happens next beyond that evaluation and the promised updates.

stories.Headline: Pennsylvania representatives introduce four bills to regulate AI use in schools
stories.Summary:
Lawmakers in the Pennsylvania House of Representatives recently introduced four separate bills to regulate how artificial intelligence is used within schools. These legislative proposals aim to address critical issues such as student privacy, academic integrity, teacher training, and mental health services. Each of the four bills successfully passed through the committee stage but was subsequently tabled in the House. None of these measures have received a final vote from the representatives at this time.

House Bill 2785, introduced by Rep. Peter Schweyer, would stop vendors from selling or using student and employee data to train AI models. Rep. Brandon Dukes introduced House Bill 2786, which would require all public and nonpublic schools to adopt AI policies by the 2027-28 school year. This specific bill would also ban AI from making final decisions regarding student grading, discipline, graduation, promotion, placement, and special education. House Bill 2787, from Rep. Melissa Shusterman, would prohibit schools from using AI to provide behavioral and mental health services. Finally, House Bill 2788, introduced by Rep. Chris Pielli, would establish a professional development grant program to train employees on AI literacy and cybersecurity.

Rep. Peter Schweyer, who serves as the chair of the House Education Committee, is responsible for leading the effort to create a clear approach to this technology. He stated that the commonwealth must provide students with age-appropriate AI tools taught by human teachers while protecting them from bad actors. Schweyer suggested that while AI could be as transformative as the internet, it could also be as destructive as the atom bomb. He believes the actual impact of the technology will likely fall somewhere between those two extremes.

The proposed rules come as teachers struggle to determine if student assignments are original work or the product of a bot. Lawmakers are attempting to balance the benefits of preparing students for a technological future with the need to maintain safety and privacy. If these bills move forward, they would fundamentally change how school districts contract with outside technology companies and manage classroom policies. The current status of the legislation remains stalled in the House after the initial committee approvals.
