stories.Headline: SpaceX plans 74 billion dollar AI sites as Texas governor-elect Hinojosa pledges data center moratorium
stories.Summary:
SpaceX announced on November 12 that it will spend over 74 billion dollars on two AI supercomputing sites in Arizona and Texas. Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa pledged a moratorium on new data center construction in Texas after winning the gubernatorial race on November 3. This policy puts the 24 billion dollar Starbase plan at risk as she takes office in January. The Democratic Party also won a landslide victory in both chambers of Congress during the November 3 midterm elections. These political shifts create a new regulatory environment for massive AI infrastructure investments across the United States.

The Arizona campus near Willcox Playa covers 747 acres and requires 6,000 MW of power, costing about 50 billion dollars. In Texas, the 444.45 acre Starbase site near the Port of Brownsville involves a 24 billion dollar investment. The Texas project includes 35 gas turbines producing 750 MW, which received a state air permit on November 16. Cameron County commissioners voted 3-2 on November 17 against a 10-year, 100% property tax abatement for 13 billion dollars. The Starbase city commission will consider its own tax abatement on December 9, the same day as the Arizona vote.

Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa told FOX News she does not dislike data centers but dislikes how they exploit Texas residents. She stated she will freeze new permits until the state legislature passes new protections for the interests of residents. Attorney General Kris Mayes asked the Cochise County commission on November 19 to postpone its December 9 vote. Mayes said the people of Cochise County deserve answers before officials approve a project of this magnitude. She has planned a town hall for December 3 at Cochise Elementary School to address these concerns.

Arizona Corporation Commissioner Kevin Thompson said data centers should pay for new generation built specifically for their own use. He suggested that upgrades improving general grid reliability should be shared, like spreading peanut butter across a piece of bread. Residents are affected by APS seeking a 14% to 16% rate increase for customers serving 1.5 million homes. Senator Ruben Gallego and Representative Yassamin Ansari indicated that congressional investigations into Elon Musk could take place next year. Elon Musk expressed regret over spending over 400 million dollars on political donations, calling himself quite foolish.

The Arizona project would draw nearly two-thirds of the all-time system peak hit by Arizona Public Service this summer. The permit application for the Arizona site lists 3.6 billion dollars in grid upgrades to support the campus. In Texas, SpaceX offered 220 million dollars for water projects tied to a de-annexation before Starbase annexed the land. Brownsville implemented a 90-day data center moratorium in early November, but officials say the Starbase project falls outside it. The Arizona campus would use dry cooling and an existing well for drinking water and maintenance.

The Cochise County Planning and Zoning Commission will vote on the Arizona project on December 9, 2026. The Starbase city commission will also hold its vote on tax abatements on that same day in December. SpaceX has expressed interest in building data centers in Bulgaria this month as it looks beyond the United States. The articles leave open whether the Texas governor will cooperate with Musk once she takes office in January. It remains uncertain if federal regulations will replace state laws if Democrats formally control Congress in January.

stories.Headline: Peter Wildeford puts 60% odds on Congress banning recursive self-improvement by late 2027
stories.Summary:
Peter Wildeford estimates a 60 percent chance Congress bans recursive self-improvement by late 2027. He believes there is a 98 percent chance a bill is introduced. Wildeford is the head of policy at the AI Policy Network. He shared these forecasts while speaking on the MTS podcast. He notes that political views on AI shifted rapidly during 2026.

The Safe and Accountable Federal Evaluations Artificial Intelligence Act proposes binding safety and security standards. It would station government examiners inside labs like OpenAI and Anthropic to provide real scrutiny. This framework is supported by Representatives Jacobs, Beyer, and Malloy. The AI Safety and Innovation Caucus, led by George Whitesides, Don Beyer, and Nathaniel Moran, shapes this agenda. It replaces voluntary company reviews with mandatory government notifications of safety incidents.

Wildeford says current safety evaluations are flawed because companies control what evaluators see. He argues that people maximizing profit should not make all safety and security decisions. He believes resident examiners would prevent labs from unilaterally deciding what to disclose. Wildeford suggests the banking industry serves as a successful model for this type of scrutiny. He claims this structural change increases the cost and friction of operating frontier labs.

Lawmakers are affected by recent rogue AI attacks and a Hugging Face incident. Governor Gavin Newsom's expert panel recommends emergency shutdown authority and capping recursive self-improvement. This approach is tougher than the transparency rules found in SB 53. Wildeford notes that SpaceX and other firms have complex headquarters in Texas and California. He argues that California has the right to preempt dangerous practices due to its technology nexus.

In January 2026, federal evaluation of AI for national security was considered unthinkably aggressive. By May 2026, President Trump signed an executive order for pre-deployment evaluations after the Mythos model. Wildeford attributes recent outages at Apple, Chase, and the FAA to AI-driven patching accidents. He sees a one-in-three to 50/50 chance of a 10 billion dollar cyber incident within one year. He believes AI is discovering vulnerabilities faster than providers can safely patch them.

Wildeford predicts AI will fully replace an AI research and development researcher by March 2028. This timeline follows reports that Anthropic engineers moved 12 times faster using internal AI models. He notes that Anthropic uses a five-level breakdown of automation for its internal reports. The articles leave open whether Anthropic has surpassed OpenAI or is simply experiencing catch-up growth. They also leave open which specific forms of recursive self-improvement the government will ban.

stories.Headline: Alpha School in Palm Beach Gardens uses an AI app as primary teacher for morning lessons
stories.Summary:
The Alpha School in Palm Beach Gardens, a private school where the primary teacher is an artificial intelligence app rather than a person, was the subject of a CBS12 report broadcast on November 23, 2026, and the school is part of a network that now claims 50 campuses across the country, with two of them in Palm Beach County. For two to three hours every morning, students learn math, reading, science and other subjects from an app that senses when they have mastered a subject and then moves them on to the next one. The adults in the building are called guides, and they help students through morning frustrations with the app but usually do no actual teaching. Kirsten Berg, the Dean of Parents, who is basically like the principal, said the school has a lounge area with a lot of books, which she called one of her favorite areas because it is something you probably would not expect to see there.

The school claims it can teach kids twice as much in half the time, and Scott Dangerfield, a reading specialist who worked for years in public schools, said every student learns at their own level and pace, with one student in his class working on 8th-grade subjects while in 2nd grade. He said that in prior schools he taught to the middle, so some students were bored because the material was too easy and others were left behind because it was too difficult, and he said he now feels he is teaching what used to take a full school day in just two hours, adding that he is not teaching because the app is their teacher. Sean McKenna, the school's head guide, said the school is taking everything legacy schooling has done and essentially flipping it on its head, and instead of babysitting and busy work it is actively teaching children to learn in two hours and then helping them become better people and teaching them life skills. Annual tuition is $50,000, and Berg said one of the biggest things she has talked with parents and folks in Palm Beach County about is trying something different because the traditional education system they were coming from was not working.

With the fundamentals over before lunchtime, the school gets creative for the rest of the day with interactive workshops that could include visiting a gym, holding a puppet show or doing a nature walk, and students Lily and Laila described a workshop as an activity or experience where they learn new life skills. Lily said they learned the thriller dance with a professional dance coach, learned receiving feedback and applying it, and did a flash mob at the mall on Saturday, and the girls' mothers said that since starting at the school they have seen major changes, with one daughter who used to beg not to go to school now saying she cannot wait to go tomorrow. A New York Times expose, according to the report, uncovered that many students are not learning twice as much in half the time at Alpha Schools and that some kids struggling in public school needed all day to keep up in the app, while many students who actually attend are already high achievers when they arrive. The report said the school's software platform is being pushed out to public schools across the country according to The New York Times, and McKenna said it will change society, how we teach and raise our children to be better adults and human beings, and that it will be something that is going to change the world.

stories.Headline: Natalie Buda Smith leads the Library of Congress in using AI to manage its collections and explore synthetic DNA storage
stories.Summary:
Natalie Buda Smith, the first leader of AI innovation at the Library of Congress, is currently guiding the institution in using artificial intelligence to manage its vast collections. The library maintains more than 181 million physical items and approximately 200 million gigabytes of digital data. Staff members are increasingly employing AI to analyze agricultural trends for the Congressional Research Service and to translate documents into English for public use. The institution has experimented with machine learning for nearly a decade to digitize manuscripts and identify images, but current technology is now far more accurate.

These new tools allow the library to re-upload old items because the computer vision no longer makes basic historical errors, such as mistaking a book for a cellphone. However, the library must now spend more resources to manage third-party bots that scrape the database and slow down the systems. Smith believes that blocking these companies is not an option because many people now use AI tools instead of web browsers to find information. She is also exploring a project to store data in synthetic DNA, which she claims could last thousands of years without using energy.

Natalie Buda Smith is responsible for these initiatives and explains that all AI produced work is still reviewed by human staff. She refuses to force the technology on resistant employees because she believes they must feel comfortable to use the tools effectively. Smith is currently hesitant to launch a public chatbot for the library because she has not yet found a system that is sufficiently authoritative and trustworthy. She views these efforts as part of a meaningful job to ensure the institution continues moving forward into the future.

stories.Headline: MiniMax AI model turns theoretical cryptographic attacks into practical breaks
stories.Summary:
MiniMax announced that its internal AI model developed practical attacks on academic cryptographic designs. The company used this model to break research cryptography and past competition candidates. These events were reported on November 22, 2026, by various sources. The internal AI turned theoretical cryptographic attacks into working breaks. This model was tested on the CryptanalysisBench benchmark co-created by Anthropic.

The model, called MIM, recovered LOCKER shared secrets in two seconds and reduced its solver matrix from 42 petabytes to 58 megabytes. It solved 55 previously unsolved TII McEliece challenge instances, bringing the total solved from 41 to 96. MIM found a missing ampersand in DRS signature code and forged messages for COLM, a CAESAR competition winner. It also attacked the Waterfall-256 hash in 0.045 seconds and the NSA ARADI cipher for 8 rounds. These attacks targeted academic designs, public challenge parameters, and past NIST post-quantum cryptography candidates.

MiniMax is responsible for these findings and released technical reports and proof-of-concept code on GitHub. The company stated that these results do not affect currently deployed cryptographic standards. They noted that they shared the findings with the authors of each scheme in advance. MiniMax explained that the model is internal-only but available to qualified researchers who apply. They wrote that evaluating security margins still depends on review by human cryptographers.

The results affect the perceived security of academic designs and past competition candidates. Anthropic is mentioned as the creator of the benchmark and a previous record holder for cryptanalysis. MIM outperformed Anthropic's multi-GPU solver by 6,180 to 43,400 times on a single 64-core server. It also beat a 96-core HAWK attack in 30 minutes using only one core. These speedups compare selected challenge instances across different hardware rather than overall model performance.

The articles provide background on other MiniMax products like the M3.1 Flash 428B model and H3-Image. The M3.1 Flash API costs 0.15 dollars per million input tokens and 0.60 dollars per million output tokens. NVIDIA's Vera Rubin offers Day 0 support for this model with throughput up to 200K TPS/GPU. Artificial Analysis ranked H3-Image first among open-weight models for editing and generation. The M3.1 Flash model is reported to run three times as fast as M3.

Qualified researchers and developers can now apply for testing access to the internal MIM model. The company has already provided the recovered keys and a TII checker script for public verification. Human cryptographers must now assess how secure the targeted cryptographic designs remain. The articles do not state if the model will ever be released to the general public. It remains unclear if these methods can break production-strength Classic McEliece.

stories.Headline: Bank of Portugal governor warns Europe lags US in AI investment
stories.Summary:
Bank of Portugal Governor Álvaro Santos Pereira warned on Friday, November 20, 2026, that Europe risks falling further behind the United States in artificial intelligence investment. He spoke at the ninth Future of Banking conference in Lisbon, organised by Jornal de Negócios at the SANA Marquês hotel. The governor said Portugal's banks enjoy stronger balance sheets and improved credit quality. He set out an agenda spanning energy risks, regulatory reform, cybersecurity and financing of technological transformation. The central bank expects growth of around 2.3% in 2026, easing to 1.8% in 2027.

The governor put the non-performing loan ratio at 2.1%, a marked contrast with double-digit levels of earlier years. He said the proportion of euro-area banks adopting generative AI rose from 46% in 2024 to 86% more recently. Around 43% of US workers were using AI at work, compared with 32% in Europe, he said. The share of companies using AI in production was approximately 7% in the United States and 4% in Europe. Six reporting requirements have already been discontinued, with another two scheduled to disappear by the end of 2026.

Santos Pereira said growth of the Portuguese economy remains "reasonable, not spectacular, but reasonable." He said, "We have to ask ourselves whether it is sustainable to continue along this path of not increasing public capital decisively." He said, "If we have a very cold winter, that will put more pressure on natural gas prices and, obviously, on electricity prices as well." He said, "I think there is clearly room for us to continue raising deposit interest rates closer to those in the euro area." He said, "The big question is who will capture the financial gains associated with this: the banks, the customers or the technology suppliers."

He said interest paid on deposits by Portuguese banks remains significantly below the euro-area average. He said public debt remains historically high and the downward trajectory must continue. He said European gas storage levels in some northern markets were below their averages of the previous decade. He cited competition with Asia, disruption in the Middle East and uncertainty around the Strait of Hormuz as added risks. He said the European Central Bank would continue to safeguard price stability.

He described AI as a general-purpose technology comparable to steam power, electricity, computers and the internet. He said AI is spreading more quickly than earlier general-purpose technologies. He singled out cybersecurity as a top systemic concern for the financial sector. He said the Bank of Portugal has begun work on post-quantum encryption and signed a memorandum of understanding with the Bank of Spain. He said stronger supervision introduced over the past 15 years should be preserved but unnecessary complexity can be removed.

He said the objective is to establish a single point of contact for bank reporting during the first quarter of 2027. He reported the elimination of 465 Bank of Portugal regulatory provisions in connection with the IMF's Financial Sector Assessment Program, with a further reduction of around 100 envisaged for 2027. He said the bank intends to assemble its applicable rules in a single rulebook. He said simplifying regulation will be a top priority in the coming years. He said the central bank would discuss the reporting arrangements with banks.

stories.Headline: Nvidia and IBM launch joint research to correct quantum errors using GPUs and AI
stories.Summary:
Nvidia and IBM, joined by the U.S. Department of Energy's Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory, announced they will launch full-scale joint research to correct quantum computer calculation errors using GPUs and AI. The two companies disclosed the research plan to coincide with SC26, an international supercomputing conference held in Chicago. In the joint research, a quantum computer equipped with IBM's Nighthawk quantum processor and Nvidia's AI computing system DGX B200 will be placed side by side in the same facility and linked to each other. Nvidia also unveiled TCBP-JOBS, an algorithm for quantum error correction research. A research team from IBM, the Institute of Physical and Chemical Research, and Nvidia combined a quantum computer with GPUs to calculate the molecular structure of iron and sulfur contained in proteins and other substances in living organisms.

In the company's tests, error decoding speed improved by up to 13,000x compared with major existing methods, and the time required to study the design of a new quantum computer can be shortened from 12 weeks to 45 minutes. According to IBM, calculation accuracy improved 79-fold compared with conventional experiments of the same kind. In separate research, the binding structure of a drug-discovery-related protein and a candidate compound was modeled at a scale of up to 12,635 atoms, and the work was selected as a finalist for the 2026 ACM Gordon Bell Prize. The two companies will also advance efforts to connect quantum processors to Slurm, the open-source software widely used for supercomputer job management. Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory will leverage knowledge cultivated in high-energy and nuclear physics research to participate in error correction and the design of next-generation computers.

Krista Svore, Nvidia's vice president of quantum computing application research, said that to make quantum computers useful for science, progress is needed in everything, including error correction, application fields, and the systems that connect quantum processors with high-speed computing. Ian Buck, Nvidia's vice president, noted that scientific simulation requires CPUs that can maintain performance while continuously moving large amounts of data, explaining that Vera eliminates the bottleneck between computation and data transfer. The company said this is performance in a specific error-correction task and does not mean the quantum computer itself became 13,000x faster at computation. The company stated that all figures are test results under specific conditions announced by each company and do not guarantee the performance of the products as a whole. The articles state that the timing for general-purpose quantum computers to reach practical use remains unclear.

Terray Therapeutics further trained the model to extract chemical reaction information from scientific figures and diagrams, identifying about 76% of the reactions described in test data. Biotech company Therna applied the model to the design of messenger RNA medicines, and the accuracy of predicting the range of protein expression levels reportedly nearly doubled compared with existing state-of-the-art models. The U.S. Argonne National Laboratory is incorporating Nemotron into multiple AI agents that design and evaluate protein candidates for treating cancer and other diseases. The German Climate Computing Center will adopt Vera for its next-generation supercomputer HLRE-5, targeted to begin operation in early 2028. Vera-equipped racks are scheduled to ship from early 2027 through Dell, HPE, Lenovo, and Supermicro.

Quantum computers use qubits, basic units that can handle 0 and 1 simultaneously, and hold the potential to solve problems that conventional machines cannot solve in realistic time. However, errors arise easily from slight changes in the external environment, making quantum error correction, distributing information across multiple physical qubits to detect and fix errors, indispensable. This correction computation is enormous, and high-speed processing via GPUs is key. According to estimates published by the International Energy Agency on November 19, 2026, data centers worldwide consumed just under 500 terawatt-hours of electricity in 2025, accounting for 1.7% of global power demand. If current policies continue, data center power demand is projected to roughly double 2025 levels by 2030.

Nvidia simultaneously announced a suite of AI models for scientific researchers, Nemotron for Science, and the foundation for its high-performance computing CPU Vera. Nemotron 3.5 Super VL was combined with chemical data and additional training methods, enabling it to read chemical reactions described in papers and draft experimental procedures, as well as support the design of proteins and drug candidate substances. A dataset containing about 50,000 questions for evaluating and training chemical reasoning, LitmusBench v0.2, was also released, and the models and data are available on Hugging Face. The company unveiled a Vera rack system equipped with 192 of its own designed CPUs, featuring about 300 terabytes of memory and 1 petabyte of storage, with 88 cores and 176 threads per CPU, memory bandwidth of 1.2 terabytes per second, and more than 200 terabytes per second across the entire system. In the company's tests, fluid simulation performance was 1.9x that of x86-based systems and 2.4x in performance per watt, and for weather forecasting models it expects 1.6x performance and 2x energy efficiency.

stories.Headline: AI-native biotechs advance 45% of Phase II drugs versus 29% industry-wide, Oliver Wyman finds
stories.Summary:
Drugs from AI-native biotechs, companies built around artificial intelligence platforms, advanced from Phase II trials at a rate of 45%, compared with 29% for the industry overall, according to an Oliver Wyman analysis reported on November 23, 2026. The firm said early-trial success for these developers runs more than 40% higher than the industry rate, based on limited clinical data. In Phase II, the tests of whether a drug works, 45% of the programs advanced. The analysis covers 46 Phase II programs, and roughly half of them are still running. AI-discovered molecules make up only about 1% to 2% of the clinical pipeline.

Investment in AI drug discovery and licensing deals reached $46 billion in the first half of 2026, after $43 billion in 2025 and $12 billion in 2024. Oliver Wyman says roughly 90% of drug candidates fail and development averages $2.67 billion per asset. Because more drugs are clearing early trials, someone has to pay for the larger trials that follow, and the firm says the limit on drug development shifts from science to capital. Smaller developers that cannot fund every program will need partners, which could put more late-stage drugs up for licensing. A Nature Medicine paper reports that an AI-built pill, rentosertib, helped patients with a lung disease gain lung capacity, with the trial following 71 patients for 12 weeks; patients on the highest dose gained 98.4 ml of lung capacity while placebo patients lost 20.3 ml, and side effects were similar across groups.

The authors say AI found the drug's target and designed the molecule, and they say larger, longer trials are needed. The FDA and the European Medicines Agency introduced 10 guiding principles for AI drug development, and the FDA says drugmakers and product developers can consider them but they are not rules. The first five are human-centric design, a risk-based approach, adherence to standards, a clear context of use and multidisciplinary expertise, and the last five are data governance and documentation, model design and development practices, risk-based performance assessment, life cycle management and clear, essential information. Gabriel Innes, an assistant director at the FDA's drug center, told a RAPS panel that the center has received more than 1,500 AI-related submissions, which have grown exponentially since 2016, mostly applications to begin human trials followed by new drug applications and biologics license applications. Innes said AI is becoming quite routine and called the principles a starting point for future standards.

stories.Headline: Nous Research's Hermes Agent leads a comparison of seven personal AI agents on memory, security and cost
stories.Summary:
A comparison of personal AI agents published by MarkTechPost on November 22, 2026, rated seven products on memory, security and cost, with prices given as US list prices as of November 21, 2026. The article describes a personal AI agent as software that runs continuously, keeps memory across sessions and acts inside a user's apps, reached by chat, email or voice. It says the category began in November 2025 when OpenClaw started as Clawdbot, a weekend project by Peter Steinberger, and that twelve months later Google, OpenAI, Meta and Perplexity all ship their own versions. The products are split into two camps, self-hosted agents that run on a user's machine or server with any chosen model, and managed agents that run on a vendor's cloud VM and come bundled with a subscription. The ranking placed Hermes Agent from Nous Research first, OpenClaw from the OpenClaw Foundation second and Gemini Spark from Google third, followed by OpenAI dots, Meta Muse, Perplexity Personal Computer and the open-source NanoClaw, IronClaw and ZeroClaw projects.

Hermes Agent was listed as free under the MIT licence plus model tokens, running on a user's machine or server with Docker, Modal and Daytona backends, and keeping MEMORY.md and USER.md files plus SQLite FTS5 session search. The article says its defaults fail closed, with an unanswered approval prompt denied after 300 seconds and a hardline denylist, and that it can turn completed complex tasks into reusable skills. OpenClaw was listed as free under the MIT licence plus tokens, or about $12 to $49 a month on managed hosts, with full host access unless its opt-in sandbox is enabled, and was rated best for widest chat-channel reach. Gemini Spark from Google was listed at $19.99 a month on AI Pro in the US, running on dedicated Google Cloud VMs, using Google account context through connected apps and asking before spending money or sending email. OpenAI dots was described as included in eligible ChatGPT Pro and Business Premium plans, running on an OpenAI cloud computer, with proactive research read-only and passwords hidden from the model.

Meta Muse was listed as free with $20 and $100 tiers, running in a secure VM in Meta's cloud, learning preferences and forgetting on request, with a Sentinel agent gating internet access and approvals for email and purchases. Perplexity Personal Computer was listed at a Pro or Max subscription, running on a user's Mac plus Perplexity cloud, with on-device authorization, two-factor authentication and an audit trail, and its memory was not detailed publicly. The article says the scoring covered memory, meaning what persists, where it is stored and whether a user can read, edit or delete it, security, meaning default permissions, the isolation boundary, approval gates and the public incident record, and cost, meaning the subscription price or token spend plus hosting for self-hosted options. It says the facts come from vendor documentation, launch posts and independent security research, and that the ranking reflects overall fit for an individual user rather than raw capability. It gives no further details on what happens next for any of the products.

stories.Headline: Andrew Law sells Nvidia shares to invest 123 million dollars in Palantir
stories.Summary:
Billionaire Andrew Law traded two major AI stocks before a recent market crash that occurred around November 2026. Law managed his investments through Caxton Associates, where he serves as the chairman, CEO, and a leading shareholder. He sold a massive amount of Nvidia shares while simultaneously placing a large bet on Palantir. These moves happened ahead of the worst week for Wall Street since April 2025. The market crash saw the S&P 500 plunge 8.6 percent and the Nasdaq suffer a 10 percent loss.

Law slashed his Nvidia position by 99 percent by unloading 1,008,726 NVDA shares during the third quarter. He initiated a new position in Palantir by purchasing 856,221 PLTR shares worth about 123 million dollars. Nvidia lost 47 percent of its value since October, while Palantir fell 31 percent from its October high. The crash followed a Blue Wave election victory and a scandal involving Nvidia founder Jensen Huang. Anthropic shares also tumbled 8.5 percent on Friday, just one day after its highly anticipated IPO.

Chairman Harvey Jones confirmed the board will not reinstate Jensen Huang and refused to discuss the ongoing investigation. Interim CEO Colette Kress raised the fiscal 2028 sales growth projection to 75 percent from a previous 70 percent. Law believes in the longer term prospects of Palantir despite the risks surrounding the current valuation of the stock. Gregory Jensen of Bridgewater Associates claimed he was the first check to Anthropic and saw promise in OpenAI. Jensen mentioned talking with Dario Amodei about scaling laws and the evolutionary process used to create intelligence.

Evercore analyst Mark Lipacis believes Nvidia could become cheaper and expects a derate to as low as 8x P/E. Most other analysts remain bullish, with a Moderate Buy consensus and an average price target of 232.59 dollars. Goldman Sachs analyst Gabriela Borges maintains a Buy rating for Palantir with a price target of 235 dollars. Borges believes Palantir is well positioned for Sovereign AI, which she expects to be a transformation phase in 2027. Investors are affected by persistent inflation and hawkish Federal Reserve commentary pointing toward higher interest rates.

Nvidia reported third quarter revenue of 115.84 billion dollars, which was a 103 percent increase year over year. The company generated 43.77 billion dollars in free cash flow and has 227.3 billion dollars for share repurchases. Palantir reported third quarter revenue of 2.31 billion dollars, with U.S. commercial revenue surging 148 percent to 984 million. Palantir's U.S. commercial revenue surpassed its U.S. government sales of 953 million dollars for the first time ever. These results occurred amid regulatory tensions with China and fears of tougher AI regulations and data center restrictions.

Nvidia forecasts fourth quarter revenue of 130 billion dollars, plus or minus 3 percent, beating the 125.3 billion estimate. Palantir expects fourth quarter revenue between 2.649 billion and 2.653 billion dollars, exceeding the 2.46 billion analyst forecast. Palantir raised its full year sales outlook to between 8.53 billion and 8.534 billion dollars, above the 8.2 billion estimate. The articles leave open whether the CEO vacuum and investigations will continue to cap the upside for Nvidia. It remains uncertain if Palantir can sustain its rapid expansion following signs of slower U.S. commercial bookings.

stories.Headline: Congressional researchers propose marijuana tax rules as model for taxing AI data centers
stories.Summary:
A report from the Congressional Research Service released on November 18 identifies the federal tax treatment of marijuana businesses under Section 280E as a possible model for taxing artificial intelligence companies and data centers, according to The Marijuana Herald. The report, titled Taxing AI: Alternative Approaches, examines several methods Congress could use to tax the growing artificial intelligence industry. Among the options discussed is applying restrictions similar to those that have long prevented marijuana businesses from deducting ordinary operating expenses on their federal tax returns. Under Section 280E of the Internal Revenue Code, businesses trafficking in Schedule I or II controlled substances are generally prohibited from deducting standard business expenses, even when operating legally under state law. They can subtract the cost of goods sold from their revenue when calculating gross income, but generally cannot deduct expenses such as rent, employee wages, utilities and depreciation.

The CRS report dedicates an entire section to marijuana tax treatment, explaining that the restrictions make the resulting tax resemble a value-added tax. Researchers discuss whether comparable limitations on business expense deductions could be applied to participants in the artificial intelligence market, although they acknowledge uncertainty about the feasibility of such an approach. The report returns to marijuana taxation in a separate discussion of potential gross receipts taxes on AI data centers, describing an alternative that would apply the same general tax treatment as marijuana businesses. Under this approach, companies would be taxed on receipts minus the cost of goods sold, without the full range of ordinary operating expense deductions available to most businesses. CRS notes that because data centers generally do not manufacture or sell physical inventory, applying this approach would effectively function as a gross receipts tax, subjecting nearly all their revenue to taxation rather than just their profits.

The analysis comes as members of Congress consider multiple proposals to increase taxes on AI-related businesses. Senator Ron Wyden (D-OR), for example, has separately proposed a gross receipts tax on data centers, along with restrictions on depreciation deductions and other tax benefits. CRS identifies the marijuana-style tax treatment as a closely related alternative to the gross receipts approach. Other proposals discussed in the report include taxes on electricity consumption, computer processing power, digital advertising revenue and AI-related services.

The report also examines arguments against additional AI taxes, including concerns about reduced investment, economic productivity and international competition. The comparison comes as Section 280E remains a major financial issue for marijuana companies. An April federal order moved certain qualifying medical marijuana activities to Schedule III, generally removing those activities from Section 280E's restrictions. However, marijuana activities that remain classified under Schedule I continue to face the deduction limitations, and federal tax guidance addressing businesses with multiple activities remains pending.

stories.Headline: Nvidia and AI chip stocks lose over $4 trillion as bubble warnings mount
stories.Summary:
The articles report that global stock markets weakened in lockstep recently, with tech stocks under particular pressure, and that US stocks ushered in a "Black Friday" on Friday with all three major indices suffering sharp losses. The articles state that the market value of tech stocks evaporated by more than 4 trillion US dollars this week. They state that the Dow Jones Industrial Average and the S&P 500 fell by nearly 10% from their highs, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq plunged nearly 18% from its peak, erasing all gains so far this year and hitting the threshold of a bear market. The articles state that the CBOE Volatility Index, known as the "fear index", once hit 40, the highest level since the tariff turmoil in April 2025.

The articles state that emerging cloud computing and chip companies related to AI, such as NVIDIA, Philadelphia Semiconductor Index constituent enterprises, SanDisk, Micron Technology, Broadcom, and Marvell Technology, generally posted double-digit declines. They state that NVIDIA's share price almost halved compared to early October. They state that Anthropic, described as an AI star company, went public this week, and that after a short period of rise its share price once fell by more than 10%. The articles state that the declines were caused by the interweaving of a series of unfavorable factors: growing market doubts about AI investment returns, NVIDIA facing strong regulation, the Federal Reserve continuously sending interest rate hike signals, and the Democratic Party, which advocates slowing down AI development, winning a big victory in the midterm elections. The articles state that the recently released minutes of the Federal Reserve meeting show that almost every Fed official is worried about what will happen to the financial system if the AI boom disappoints investors.

The articles state that European Central Bank policymakers pointed out in a recently released report that the global debt-driven artificial intelligence investment boom has "similarities" with the subprime mortgage bubble that triggered the global financial crisis nearly 20 years ago. They state that Ray Dalio, founder of Bridgewater Associates, warned that a large amount of debt funds is currently being used to support investments in the AI field, and that as interest rates continue to rise and financing costs keep increasing, the market will gradually approach the critical moment when the bubble begins to burst. The articles state that Gary Gensler, former chairman of the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, warned that the AI boom has formed a bubble that could burst before the U.S. presidential election in November 2028 and trigger an economic recession. The articles state that Howard Marks, co-founder of Oaktree Capital, said in a recent interview that an AI investor must, to a certain extent, accurately predict at least the evolution of technology, computing power demand, competition landscape, technology beneficiaries, financing availability, and the exact time points when all the above events occur. The articles state that evaluating these key elements is extremely difficult.

The articles state that warnings about the AI boom have become more numerous since the second half of this year. They state that the birth of each round of disruptive technology does not necessarily bring returns to investors, and that most people suffer heavy losses in technology bubbles. The articles state that technologies will eventually be implemented, but most investors cannot escape the bubble. They state that every major disruptive innovation is almost inevitably accompanied by bubbles and crashes, with the technology a great success but investors' assets vanished. The articles state that in the steam age there were the canal bubble and the railway bubble, and that in the electrical age investment booms in aviation, automobiles and power facilities triggered local crises.

The articles state that after the railway boom, railway lines were laid everywhere, including remote poor areas with no commercial capacity to support them, and that the income generated was only a quarter of the builders' expectations. They state that in the early automotive stage three power routes formed, including improved steam engines, electric motors and gasoline engines, and that at its peak there were hundreds of automobile manufacturing enterprises in the United States, more than half of which could not survive for 6 years. The articles state that General Motors was on the verge of bankruptcy twice in the early 20th century, and that during the Great Depression auto stocks including General Motors plummeted sharply again. They state that after the information age bubble burst around 2000, most stock markets took at least more than ten years to get out of the haze of losses.

The articles state that on March 10, 2000, the Nasdaq hit its all-time high, and that a few days later the financial reports of major Internet companies were released, all falling short of expectations. They state that a report at that time pointed out that 71% of the more than 200 Internet companies had negative profits, and that 51 of them would burn out their cash within a year, in a report titled "Burned Out". The articles state that the Federal Reserve began to raise interest rates and some star companies lacking profit models were ordered to delist, and that by October 2002 the Nasdaq index had fallen to only a quarter of its peak level. They state that the media at the time predicted that 5 trillion US dollars of wealth vanished into thin air in this bubble burst. The articles state that the burst of tech bubbles is essentially caused by the split between financial capital and productive capital, and that the degree of harm caused by the three tech bubbles depends on the degree of separation between financial capital and productive capital.

stories.Headline: David Tepper sells Broadcom and AMD stakes to buy Nvidia and Micron shares
stories.Summary:
Billionaire David Tepper of Appaloosa Management reshuffled his artificial intelligence semiconductor positions during the third quarter. The owner of the Carolina Panthers exited his positions in Broadcom and Advanced Micro Devices. He used this rotation to buy shares of Micron and Nvidia. Tepper also reduced his stake in Alphabet by nearly half. These moves occurred as he managed his estimated net worth of 28.5 billion dollars.

The rotation involves selling Broadcom and Advanced Micro Devices to buy Nvidia and Micron. Tepper cut his Alphabet stake nearly in half during the third quarter of 2026. He bought Nvidia shares before Jensen Huang stepped down as the company chief executive. Alphabet co-developed Tensor Processing Units with Broadcom to deliver better performance per dollar. These TPUs are used in Alphabet's new TPU 8tx AI system.

Geoffrey Seiler from The Motley Fool believes Tepper made a mistake with these specific trades. Seiler prefers the three stocks Tepper sold over the shares of Nvidia. He argues that Nvidia could face margin compression and a loss of market share. Seiler notes that memory tends to be a commodity with big boom and bust cycles. He warns that Micron is highly exposed to changes in conventional memory prices.

Counterpoint Research projects that custom AI chip shipments will surpass data center GPU shipments in 2028. Bloomberg Intelligence believes TPU sales outside Google Cloud could grow to 135 billion dollars by 2028. Anthropic revealed that its Claude Mythos model can run on AMD GPUs in two to three days. This development affects Nvidia by narrowing its CUDA moat and opening doors for ASICs. Large customers, except Space Exploration Technologies, are developing their own custom chips.

Alphabet developed its TPUs more than a decade ago to create a comprehensive ecosystem. Anthropic is now using these solutions, as is the company known as OpenAI. Advanced Micro Devices recently started shipping Helios systems that combine GPUs, CPUs, and networking. These systems are significantly cheaper than the end to end server racks sold by Nvidia. GF Securities expects the NAND flash memory market to become oversupplied as soon as next year.

Nvidia may face lower profitability even if the company manages to grow its total revenue. The market is moving from the research phase into a global rollout called Act 2. It remains open whether Tepper's rotation into Nvidia and Micron will actually pay off. The articles do not state if Tepper will change his positions again soon. They leave the future performance of the Helios systems and TPU sales as projections.

stories.Headline: Amazon sells second generation Ray-Ban Meta glasses for $284
stories.Summary:
Meta and Ray-Ban released the second generation of their camera-equipped Wayfarer smart glasses, and on November 22, 2026, Gizmodo reported that Amazon was selling the Matte Black model with clear lenses for $284 instead of $379, the lowest price the second generation had reached. The glasses carry a 12 MP camera in the corner of the frame that captures photos and records video in 3K Ultra HD, and recording starts with a tap on the frame or a voice command. Meta AI is built in, so wearers can ask about what is in front of them or have a conversation translated while traveling without reaching for a phone. Open-ear speakers sit near the ears without blocking them, and five microphones in the frame pick up the voice for calls and Meta AI requests, even outdoors in the wind.

Battery life is rated at up to 8 hours of moderate use, and the charging case holds another 48 hours, so a long weekend away does not require a separate charger for the glasses. Meta and Ray-Ban offer the Gen 2 with a wide range of lenses, including Transitions lenses that darken outdoors and clear up inside, along with Standard and Large frame sizes to fit different faces. A separate Fox News deals article from November 19, 2026, said shoppers could save up to 25 percent on select styles from Ray-Ban and Oakley, with Meta glasses starting at $249 for up to 15 percent off and Ray-Ban Meta glasses starting at $379 for up to 25 percent off. That article said buyers could save up to $115 on Ray-Ban Meta Gen 2 glasses, including Wayfarers with matte-black frames and clear, transition or tinted graphite lenses, and that the Oakley Meta line started at $399 with up to 25 percent off, including the Vanguard model in lens colors such as pink, blue, red and yellow.

Ray-Ban Meta is the best-selling line of AI glasses on the market, according to IDC sales data cited by Gizmodo, and the Gen 2 refines what made the first pair popular. Gizmodo described the translation feature as the most impressive part, because it makes the glasses genuinely helpful on a trip abroad rather than just fun to wear, and said the open-ear speakers let you hear your playlist and the traffic around you at the same time, which feels safer on a bike or a city sidewalk. The Fox News article said the glasses let people take calls, snap photos and more, all hands-free, and that the Oakley Meta glasses can connect with Garmin smartwatches to provide real-time insights and alerts while you move. The Fox News piece was written by Caitlyn Martyn, an editor who primarily writes and edits commerce content for the Deals section, and both articles state that the publishers may earn a commission when readers buy through links on their sites.

Gizmodo framed the appeal around moments like filming a child's first bike ride without training wheels, since pulling out a phone usually means watching through a screen instead of with your own eyes, while the glasses put the camera on your face. It said the 12 MP camera changes the kind of footage you get, whether it is a cooking session filmed while both hands are busy or a concert where you would rather not hold your phone above the crowd. The Fox News article presented the glasses as a gift idea for the tech lover on a list, noting that the Adventurer model has a classic tortoiseshell frame, brown lenses and standard or high-bridge fit options. Neither article says what happens next beyond the current deals, which the articles describe as available now at the prices given.

stories.Headline: Sony and Warner sue Anthropic over pirated lyrics used to train Claude
stories.Summary:
Sony Music and Warner Music's publishing arms sued Anthropic in California federal court on August 28, 2026, a filing reported September 1, accusing the company of pirating song lyrics and sheet music to train its Claude AI chatbot. The suit claims Anthropic misused copyrighted song compositions, including hundreds of lyrics and sheet music from The Beatles, Taylor Swift, Michael Jackson and hundreds of other artists. The labels say Anthropic downloaded millions of pirated books from LibGen and PiLiMi, including books containing copyrighted lyrics and sheet music. The case names CEO Dario Amodei and co-founder Benjamin Mann individually. It was filed in the U.S. District Court, Northern District of California.

The labels seek damages of up to $150,000 for each infringed copyright, covering tens of thousands of compositions, and a court order barring Anthropic from using their works. Universal Music Group and Sony Music filed a second copyright lawsuit against Suno on September 18, 2026, in the U.S. District Court, District of Massachusetts, a 45-page complaint targeting Suno's v6 model. The labels claim v6, which Suno said is trained exclusively on licensed music, actually uses their recordings without consent, and that because the new models are partly built on users' outputs derived from former models, they remain in violation. Jason Isbell filed a proposed class action against Suno on August 31, 2026, with David Lowery, Guy Forsyth and Eduardo Calle, on behalf of musicians whose names Suno has accepted as prompts. SOCAN, the Society of Composers, Authors and Music Publishers of Canada, filed a statement of claim reported September 15, 2026, citing 150 Suno songs it says are identical or nearly identical to works by Joni Mitchell, The Weeknd, The Tragically Hip and others, seeking $20,000 per work and $10,000,000 total.

Universal Music Group sued DistroKid, in a filing reported September 15, 2026, accusing the distributor of flooding streaming platforms with AI-generated slop and of violating federal copyright laws and Delaware's Deceptive Trade Practices Act. Germany's Federal Court of Justice issued its Metall auf Metall VI decision on September 3, 2026, ruling the disputed use permissible under the pastiche exception for the period from June 7, 2021, when the relevant German provision came into force. The US Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit heard arguments on September 25, 2026, in SoundExchange's appeal against Music Choice, and has not yet ruled. SoundExchange says SiriusXM's alleged underpayment now exceeds USD $400 million, a claim SiriusXM denies, and the complaint claimed Music Choice invented its own formula for allocating BES receipts, which the CRB's regulations do not permit. The appeal has put SoundExchange's $3.4 million lawsuit against Sonos on hold.

Music Choice has denied underpaying, arguing that under the rule it owes royalties only on revenue from music it provides exclusively to business customers. Suno is asking a federal judge to dismiss the Isbell lawsuit, arguing that using an artist's name to describe a musical style is protected speech, comparing its technology to a producer asking musicians to create something with more of a Jason Isbell vibe. District Judge Angel Kelley has not ruled on Suno's dismissal request, and the musicians are scheduled to respond by December 1, with Suno's reply due December 15. Putting Jason Isbell into Suno created a song called Paper Bell, described by the AI software as a contemporary Americana singer-songwriter track with fingerpicked acoustic guitar, featuring a male voice imitating Isbell's vocal elements. Warner broke away from the $500-million joint copyright lawsuit originally launched by Warner, Sony and Universal against Suno and has since signed a licensing deal with Suno.

Universal Music Group sued Anthropic in 2023 and earlier this year over the alleged use of copyrighted song lyrics in AI training, and Anthropic already paid $1.5 billion to resolve a class action from a group of authors. Suno launched v6, its first model trained on licensed music, weeks before the second suit, after partnering with Warner Music Group, BMG and Believe. The original label suit against Suno was filed over two years earlier. The Kraftwerk case is the legal ancestor of basically every sampling lawsuit filed in the United States since, including early cases like Bridgeport Music v. Dimension Films.

The SoundExchange dispute with Music Choice is more than seven years old, originally filed years ago. The second UMG and Sony suit against Suno is still in early stages, so no settlement talk yet. Suno has responded to each suit differently, settling with some labels while fighting others in court. SOCAN's lawsuit raises questions about the place of Canadian artists in a music industry increasingly shaped by American tech companies. The articles leave open how Judge Kelley will rule on Suno's dismissal request, how the Second Circuit will decide the SoundExchange appeal, and how the Anthropic, DistroKid and SOCAN cases will proceed.

stories.Headline: SAP CFO Dominik Asam reports a 70 basis point fall in cloud gross margin
stories.Summary:
SAP shares closed Friday at €181.10, down 2.1%, as a wave of selling in AI and technology names rolled from Wall Street and Asia into European markets. The retreat came even as Anthropic made its market debut, an event that, according to Reuters, failed to restore investor confidence in the AI sector. Questions over whether hefty AI spending will eventually translate into durable returns continued to hang over software stocks. The selling pressure hit SAP alongside other technology names despite the company's own AI announcements during the week.

Speaking Thursday at Morgan Stanley's technology conference, CFO Dominik Asam said SAP's cloud gross margin fell 70 basis points year on year on a currency-adjusted basis. He pointed to the product mix and introductory offers for AI products as contributing factors, Reuters reported. The disclosure landed as a reminder that SAP's AI build-out carries a near-term cost. To give investors a clearer read on that business, Asam said SAP will introduce a new metric in January covering revenue from its Business AI Platform. The gauge targets a specifically defined slice of SAP's AI operations, while his margin commentary addressed the cloud segment as a whole.

On the corporate front, SAP has completed its acquisition of TechWolf, a provider of an AI platform for work intelligence. SAP expects the business to become the intelligent core of its SuccessFactors portfolio, supporting AI-driven personnel and workforce planning. The company's retail ambitions were on display as well: on 11 November, SAP and VF Corporation opened the S.Fashion innovation space at SAP headquarters in Walldorf, where the partners will test AI-powered processes for the fashion trade, including a smart fashion store. These moves extend SAP's AI reach into workforce planning and retail processes beyond its core software business.

Separately, board member and Chief Customer Officer Thomas Saueressig has announced he will leave to take a role outside the company. He will remain in his post until the end of March 2027, with Emmanuel Raptopoulos set to take over his duties on an interim basis from January. IONOS has appointed Saueressig as its CEO effective 1 April 2027, and Achim Weiß will step down from that role on 31 March 2027. The articles do not say what happens next beyond these dates and appointments.

stories.Headline: US appeals court rules 2022 spending law unconstitutional due to proxy voting
stories.Summary:
The en banc US Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit ruled on Friday, November 20, 2026, that a major spending law was passed unconstitutionally. The court found that the House of Representatives failed to meet the required quorum during the passage of the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2023 on December 23, 2022. This occurred because the House relied on a pandemic era rule that allowed members to record their presence through proxies. Out of 431 total votes, only 205 members were physically present, which fell short of the 218 members needed for a legal quorum.

The ruling specifically blocks the federal government from enforcing the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act against the state of Texas. This $1.7 trillion funding law also included roughly $45 billion for NATO allies and Ukraine, $40 billion for disaster relief, and the Electoral Count Reform Act. It further established a ban on using TikTok on government devices and funded various federal agencies. While the current relief is narrow, law professor Jonathan Adler noted that the court's reasoning could potentially invalidate every other provision within the omnibus bill.

Judge Cory Wilson wrote for the 9-8 majority that the Constitution's Quorum Clause cannot be bypassed by congressional rules or fiat. He stated that proxy presence does not count toward the legal requirement for members to be physically present. In a dissent, Judge James Graves argued that the majority was improperly inserting a larger requirement into the Constitution by demanding physical presence. Judge Haynes also issued a separate dissent against the majority opinion.

Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton initiated the legal challenge in 2023 to prevent the enforcement of the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act. Inimai Chettiar of A Better Balance suggested that judges in Mississippi, Louisiana, and Texas might cite this ruling in future worker lawsuits. The federal government has not yet announced if it will seek a review from the Supreme Court. Professor Adler expressed doubt that the decision will stand and suggested a petition for certiorari is likely.

stories.Headline: Warsh says AI could speed innovation and growth while warning of job losses and market risks
stories.Summary:
Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh said Monday that artificial intelligence could accelerate innovation and usher in an era of faster economic growth, in remarks that also acknowledged risks from the technology. Warsh said the adoption of AI could also lead to widespread job loss or a steep drop in the stock market if the healthy returns expected from the huge investments in AI infrastructure don't materialize. Warsh's remarks kicked off a one-day conference on AI and productivity at the Fed's San Francisco branch. Warsh did not mention inflation, even though many of his colleagues blame the buildout of data centers for accelerating price increases. Warsh did not comment on what the Fed's next steps would be on interest rates, nor did he say anything about recent government data showing that inflation accelerated last month.

That data led many of Warsh's colleagues on the Fed's rate-setting committee to signal their support for additional interest rate hikes, including at the Fed's next meeting in December. The Fed refers to AI as "super intelligence" following an executive order issued by President Donald Trump requiring federal agencies to use the term. Warsh appointed five different task forces soon after taking the helm at the Fed, and the conference Monday was part of a task force Warsh set up to evaluate AI and its impact on the economy's efficiency. Fed staff has begun evaluating different scenarios for how AI's impact may play out, Warsh added. Warsh has long said, including before his nomination as Fed chair, that AI could significantly boost the economy's efficiency, which would enable it to grow without worsening inflation.

"What might set SI apart, as an economic influence, is that it could supercharge idea generation," Warsh said. "It appears to be changing the method ,  and, at least as important, the speed ,  of innovation. If idea generation broadens, growth could be sustained at a level substantially higher than the long-run average." "As policymakers, we have to be mindful that great opportunities rarely come risk free," Warsh said. "And the risks in this case, if overlooked, can be highly disruptive and economically costly."

Warsh said that "after significant capital investment and stock market gains, expected returns could turn down and equity valuations could fall, leading to an economic slowdown and a more notable rise in unemployment." Warsh spent more time in his remarks considering the downsides of AI than he has in previous speeches. Other Fed officials have increasingly voiced concern that AI is fanning inflation because the buildout of AI infrastructure has sharply raised demand for computer chips, electronic components, electricity and copper. Those increases, in turn, have lifted the cost of smartphones, computers and other consumer electronics. Smartphone prices rose last month at the fastest pace on record, the government said last week.

Fed Vice Chair Philip Jefferson said Friday that if AI does accelerate economic growth, it could lead to higher interest rates over time, even if inflation declines. "If the new technology leads to permanently higher levels of productivity growth, it may increase firms' desire to invest and, hence, their demand for funding, raising the level of interest rates," Jefferson said. Warsh's generally optimistic outlook on the new technology is a view at odds with many of his colleagues. Warsh has previously touted AI as a technology that could significantly boost the economy's efficiency, which would enable it to grow without worsening inflation.

In turn, the Fed could potentially lower interest rates under that scenario. The conference Monday was part of a task force Warsh set up to evaluate AI and its impact on the economy's efficiency. Warsh appointed five different task forces soon after taking the helm at the Fed. Fed staff has begun evaluating different scenarios for how AI's impact may play out, Warsh added.

Warsh did not address AI's impact on inflation, a top concern of many of his Fed colleagues. Last week, several policymakers expressed concern that AI is fanning inflation because the buildout of AI infrastructure has sharply raised demand for computer chips, electronic components, electricity and copper. Smartphone prices rose last month at the fastest pace on record, the government said last week. Warsh did not comment on what the Fed's next steps would be on interest rates.

Many of Warsh's colleagues on the Fed's rate-setting committee signaled their support for additional interest rate hikes, including at the Fed's next meeting in December. Fed Vice Chair Philip Jefferson said Friday that if AI does accelerate economic growth, it could lead to higher interest rates over time, even if inflation declines. The articles do not say what the Fed decided about interest rates at its December meeting. The articles do not say how Warsh's task forces other than the AI and productivity task force will report their findings.

stories.Headline: Lenovo and Microsoft expand Hybrid AI Factory to help small businesses run AI locally
stories.Summary:
Lenovo has enhanced its Hybrid AI Factory portfolio in collaboration with Microsoft, according to an article published by Small Business Trends on November 22, 2026. The offering combines Lenovo’s integrated infrastructure solutions, specifically the ThinkAgile series, with Microsoft’s Azure Local and Foundry Local. This partnership is intended to let businesses use AI closer to their operational data, which the article says supports faster insights and improved decision-making without compromising security and sovereignty. The article frames the announcement around small businesses seeking to deploy artificial intelligence while keeping control over their data and workloads.

The Hybrid AI Factory supports local inference, conversational RAG, agentic AI, and vision AI in environments businesses operate and trust, a Lenovo representative said, according to the article. The infrastructure includes the Lenovo ThinkAgile MX650a V4 systems, which feature NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs, and the article says NVIDIA RTX PRO 4500 GPUs are included for those with different capacity needs to balance performance and cost. Lenovo Top Choice Express and Lenovo AI Express are named as programs meant to provide quicker access to necessary infrastructure and accelerate the move from AI pilot projects to full production. The article says the offering lets small businesses use familiar Azure tools to manage workloads across hybrid cloud environments.

Data protection is another focal point, and the article says businesses can choose from various hyperconverged or disaggregated architectures so they can scale compute and storage needs independently. Lenovo’s introduction of confidential computing with Azure Local is described as protecting sensitive data during processing, and a Lenovo spokesperson said confidential VMs and confidential GPUs give organizations greater confidence to bring AI models into environments where privacy, resiliency, regulation, and operational control matter most. The article notes that implementing a sovereign AI framework requires careful planning and governance as organizational needs, regulatory landscapes, and technology requirements evolve, and it says Lenovo’s advisory services offer tailored assessments and roadmaps for aligning AI initiatives with business goals. It adds that the offering extends to broader business IT needs through Azure Virtual Desktop Hybrid features, which the article says may appeal to businesses with remote or decentralized operations.

The article says small business owners should consider potential challenges, including the planning and governance that a sovereign AI framework requires. It directs interested businesses to Lenovo’s Premier Solutions and ThinkAgile series and to the original press release for more information. The article presents the Hybrid AI Factory as setting the stage for a controlled and efficient deployment of technology capable of driving growth. It does not say when the offering becomes available or what it costs.

stories.Headline: OpenAI claims its AI agents produced a 166-page proof of the Navier, Stokes problem
stories.Summary:
On September 8, 2026, OpenAI announced on the social media site X that its internal system had found a solution to the Navier, Stokes problem, a claim the articles describe as a claimed attainment of superintelligence in mathematics. The company said a decentralized swarm of roughly 10,000 autonomous AI agents, using a not-yet-released frontier model, worked for about 88 hours and produced a 166-page proof and Lean formalization. The announcement did not name Tristan Buckmaster, a professor at New York University’s Courant Institute of Mathematical Sciences, or his friend Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic. On September 7, 2026, Buckmaster and Alpöge had formally announced forced-Euler results they had been developing, work that did not solve Navier, Stokes but was an important step toward a possible solution. The omission ignited a priority dispute, and many people, including Buckmaster, do not believe OpenAI’s denial that its agents saw the unpublished work.

The problem concerns whether the description of smooth three-dimensional fluid motion modeled by the Navier, Stokes equations can break down, and it has remained unresolved for roughly 90 years. Mathematicians tried for almost a century, and in 2000 the Clay Mathematics Institute promised a $1 million prize to anyone who solved it. The announced solution used a smooth external force and a vortex, a spinning swirl of fluid, that spirals inward and gets increasingly elongated, like spaghetti. OpenAI said the proof was produced by a group of agents using a next-generation model significantly more capable than GPT-6 Astra, and that the group produced an analytical proof and Lean formalization showing a fluid can develop a singularity in finite time. On October 6, 2026, OpenAI released 722 mathematical manuscripts at once, a GitHub repository ranging from number theory and geometry to mathematical physics and computer science, with proofs, supporting artifacts, and many plain-English explanations.

OpenAI’s README said the collection includes results at different stages of verification, that not all have accompanying Lean formalizations, that it will continue to update the repository as it obtains them, that some unformalized results could have issues, that it will endeavor to fix any such issues quickly, and that it is exploring community-hosted repositories. OpenAI said its agents did not see Buckmaster and Alpöge’s unpublished work and that its proofs differ significantly. OpenAI said it will not claim the million-dollar prize, and its stated goal was to demonstrate the progress of its AI models. The Clay Mathematics Institute has said the problem “apparently” has been settled, but its established process for evaluating the proof and assigning credit is deliberately unhurried. Buckmaster expects the proof to survive that review.

Buckmaster said of the AI-generated proof, “It was the worst mathematics I’ve ever seen in my life, but it was actually correct!” In an October 2, 2026, World Science Festival video interview conducted by physicist Brian Greene, Buckmaster explained that the proof was almost incomprehensible, containing irrelevant calculations, unnecessary complications, and passages that seemed to make little sense. Asked whether he had personally checked the entire proof, Buckmaster answered, “No,” and the answer involved other AI agents and Lean, a computer program that checks mathematical proofs according to precisely defined rules of logic. Buckmaster denies that the supervising mathematicians at OpenAI correctly understand the meaning of their agents’ work. Two days after the 722-manuscript release, Buckmaster said, “We’ve had whole research programs wiped out on Tuesday by their dump.”

Expert mathematician Martin Bridson of Oxford described the release as “breathtaking,” but other reactions ranged from astonishment and excitement to intense anger and opposition, and some mathematicians called OpenAI’s action “carpet bombing” or “the mathocalypse.” On October 7, 2026, a newly formed advocacy group calling itself the Association for Human Mathematics published a response. Buckmaster was among the first outside experts invited by OpenAI to publicly examine the AI-generated proof, and at the time he was working informally with mathematicians connected to both OpenAI and Anthropic on related problems. Buckmaster believes mathematics has reached a moment comparable to IBM’s Deep Blue defeating world chess champion Garry Kasparov in 1997, and that the implications go well beyond mathematics. Evaluating the collection could take months or years, and the historic figure was 722 manuscripts, not 722 separate and independently confirmed breakthroughs.

In a September 29, 2026, Numberphile interview, Brady Haran asked Buckmaster how he was feeling after the preceding weeks, and the professor began laughing when asked if he was ready to start. Media outlets all over the world were seeking interviews and trying to stir up controversy between him and OpenAI, while Buckmaster’s real interests were in mathematics and computer science. During the week of the breakthroughs and controversies, he was also helping to care for a two-month-old baby at home and estimated he had averaged approximately two hours of sleep per night. Colleagues would come to his university office and find him asleep at his desk, and Haran jokingly asked whether Buckmaster felt as though he had been mugged by 10,000 AI agents. OpenAI organized the papers into families of related results, and several manuscripts might concern one discovery, supply alternative proofs, or extend an earlier result.

A successful Lean check establishes that the encoded statement follows from its stated assumptions, but it does not by itself prove that the formalization perfectly captures every claim in a long prose manuscript, and humans must still examine that correspondence. The articles leave open whether the proof will survive the Clay Mathematics Institute’s deliberately unhurried review and how credit will be assigned. They leave open how the priority dispute between OpenAI and Buckmaster and Alpöge will be resolved. They leave open what the Association for Human Mathematics published on October 7, 2026, and how the 722 manuscripts will fare as verification continues. They leave open how long evaluation of the collection will take and which of the unformalized results may have issues.

stories.Headline: Seoul education chief Chung Keun-sik pushes vocational high schools and essay-based grading as AI reshapes work
stories.Summary:
Superintendent Chung Keun-sik of the Seoul Metropolitan Office of Education recently proposed a plan to strengthen career education. He discussed these goals during an interview this month at the National Assembly in Yeouido, Seoul. The plan focuses on nurturing vocational high schools as artificial intelligence reshapes industry work and job structures. Chung argues that students must learn hands-on skills because AI is taking over knowledge processing. He believes direct experience and skill acquisition are becoming more important as AI technology advances.

The office will expand essay-based assessments, raising their share in semester grades to 35 percent by 2027. By 2030, more than 50 percent of regular exams will be converted to the essay format. The office will support teacher training and specialized graders by 2032 and use Chaeum AI for grading. A new five-tier school grading system will apply to the 2028 college admissions cycle for current high school sophomores. This system expands the top tier of students from 4 percent to 10 percent.

Superintendent Chung stated that the perception of college entrance as the ultimate goal of education must change. He argued that getting into Seoul National University does not guarantee a life for a student. Chung believes a child who tests well is different from a smart or fine child. He said the current admissions structure prioritizes university rankings over the actual aptitudes of the students. He noted that students often choose majors to match their scores rather than the work they want.

Parents and students are facing excessive anxiety regarding the new five-tier grading system and admission prospects. Universities are also affected because they must find new ways to distinguish among applicants in the top tier. Chung believes this anxiety is largely a psychological problem and urges a focus on everyday learning. He expressed concern that elementary students relying on digital devices may lack basic reading and writing skills. He suggested a balance between digital education and traditional methods like discussion and reading.

The articles state that a gap exists between college studies and the work people actually do in Korea. The government wants to change local education grants from 20.79 percent of domestic tax revenue to economic growth rates. Superintendents proposed a compromise to keep the tax link but use excess increases for future national investment. The state would cover one-third of the excess decrease if grants fall more than 5 percent. The Seoul office could not accommodate 965.7 billion won in requests, including 676.6 billion won for environments.

The office will continue implementing the phased transition toward essay-based assessments and the new grading system. Chung seeks social consensus before introducing the Alpha Phone to curb student overdependence on smartphones. He continues to push for stable education finances to maintain and improve conditions in schools. The articles leave open how the government will respond to the superintendents' proposed grant funding compromise. They also leave open how the office will define specific Alpha Phone regulations for different grade levels.
