stories.Headline: Fed governor Barr warns AI threatens trading, bank runs and cyber stability
stories.Summary:
Federal Reserve Governor Michael Barr on Monday laid out a range of perils that AI could bring to trading, cybersecurity and consumer and investor protection. He built on a central bank report issued the previous Friday that showed a surge in concern about the risks the new technology poses to financial stability. Barr spoke in prepared remarks for delivery in Milan, Italy. His remarks came hours before Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh was to open a conference at the San Francisco Fed. AI developers, business leaders and academics were expected at that conference to discuss the implications of the new technology for productivity, jobs and the economy more broadly.

Some 87% of contacts surveyed for the Fed's latest Financial Stability Report, issued on Friday, cited AI as a salient risk to the financial system. They pointed to worries about cyberattacks, complex AI-related financing, and the possibility of an AI earnings slowdown spurring broad stock market declines. Barr expanded on some of those concerns and added several more. He cited the potential that increased reliance on AI models in trading could lead to herd-like behavior that could disrupt markets. He cited the possibility that self-learning algorithms could manipulate and destabilize markets.

Barr said banks may be unable to confirm whether an AI agent attempting to take actions in retail customer accounts is actually authorized by the customer to do so. He said even legitimate AI agents acting at lightning speed on behalf of retail banking customers could accelerate bank runs and overwhelm traditional safeguards. He pointed to cyber risks from AI-enabled cyberattackers or even rogue AI agents exploiting vulnerabilities in the financial system. He said AI developers struggle with ensuring their models are well controlled, numerically and legally precise, explainable, and replicable. He said the risk needs to be reduced that AI reinforces biases in consumer lending.

Barr said there is also a need to guard against risks that could result from the use of AI in financial markets, including collusion, market manipulation, or trading strategies that result in significant market volatility or even systemic risk. He did not comment in his prepared remarks on the outlook for monetary policy or the economy. A new Federal Reserve review of the best available evidence suggests the emerging AI revolution is still in its early days when it comes to seeing a return on AI investment. The Fed economists find that the data show AI adoption is high and growing. AI-adopting firms tend to apply it in only a couple of business areas at a time, such as IT and HR, or marketing and strategy, rather than across the entire organization.

Research and development, a business area where AI might provide a particularly significant boost to more fundamental innovation and productivity gains, has relatively low uptake, according to the Fed economists. Business areas like IT, marketing, finance, and strategy seem to be the most common AI applications, with less use in HR and actual production. More dramatic changes, such as using AI as part of a firm's core production process, engaging in wholesale reorganization, or fully automating some tasks, might be necessary to sustain any productivity boost over the long term. The establishment of new AI-centered businesses could also be an important channel for longer-run productivity improvements. Demand for new AI products has resulted in AI adoption growing rapidly both among consumers and firms, though most firms are currently not using AI very intensively or at all.

A report from METR, an AI research nonprofit, finds that Anthropic's internal use of AI has helped the company roughly double the pace at which its models improve on tasks that can be clearly measured. AI pundit and podcaster Dwarkesh Patel said he has come to the view that the world is only a couple years away and possibly only a couple months away from AIs that are as good as the best humans at AI research. Anthropic's S-1 public offering document offers a bunch of underwhelming case studies of how customers are using its models. As the company puts it, it believes enterprises are still in early phases of deployment, and it believes most knowledge workers have yet to fully experience what frontier AI can help them accomplish. The Fed paper concludes that AI is not yet playing much of a role, if any, in the recent upturn in US productivity growth.

The Fed paper's conclusion leaves open when AI will play a role in US productivity growth. Barr's remarks leave open what the Fed will do about the risks he listed. The articles do not say what the Milan remarks or the San Francisco Fed conference will lead to. The articles do not say how the Fed's review or the Financial Stability Report will change policy. The articles do not say what Anthropic's public offering will result in.

stories.Headline: Viola Fintech's Noam Inbar says distribution is now the real moat in enterprise AI, vertical AI and fintech
stories.Summary:
Noam Inbar, General Partner at Viola Fintech, made the statement in an interview with CTech for its 2027 VC Survey, published on 23.11.26 at 10:17. The interview was conducted by Elihay Vidal and Zachy Hennessey. Inbar said Israel has always won on deep technical moats, but in enterprise AI, vertical AI and fintech the real moat is now distribution. Inbar said Israel has never excelled at distribution. Inbar said developing that commercial muscle is the big challenge and opportunity for the next generation of Israeli companies.

Viola Fintech has $210 million in total assets under management. Its partners and managers are Daniel Tsiddon and Noam Inbar. Its notable portfolio companies are Planck, Rewire, Quinn, Advance, Insurify, Cowbell and True Accord. Its notable exits are Planck and Rewire. Inbar said the fund's strategy is to go earlier than it used to and look for defensible niches, markets that are not purely winner-takes-all.

Inbar said AI has lowered the barrier to building a convincing story or an impressive early product, which forces the fund to be much sharper in its underwriting. Inbar said technical execution is becoming more commoditized, so the fund cares far less about what specific tech unit someone came out of in the army and much more about raw leadership, grit, stamina, risk appetite and integrity. Inbar said heavy capital concentration has made things trickier for a smaller fund like Viola Fintech. Inbar said the fund is not built to compete in hyper-rounds at inflated valuations and does not want to back underfunded copycats or tiny companies destined for a quick acqui-hire. Inbar said cyber is not Inbar's focus and left it to others, though Inbar believes the ecosystem needs to diversify its core strengths.

Inbar said defense tech is too exposed to shifting geopolitics and global attitudes toward Israel to be a pillar to bet everything on. Inbar said foreign appetite is split, with Tier-1 global funds still very active in Israel while mid-tier funds that used to be important syndicate partners are largely sitting out due to inflated valuations and mega-rounds. Inbar said depending solely on a handful of top-tier funds is a fragile position. Inbar said domestic political instability and growing global alienation are real risks to the ability to scale companies from Israel. Inbar said the concentration in startup funding reflects concentration among VCs themselves, with a small handful of massive funds holding a huge share of the capital and funneling it into a small number of companies.

Inbar said those mega-funds have become true market makers, which makes it tough for smaller funds to compete on traditional terms. Inbar said the market is moving way too fast for 12-year fund cycles to make sense anymore. Inbar said locking up capital for over a decade with little to no liquidity is not worth the uncertain upside. Inbar said startups can build and scale with far less capital today, so outside the mega-rounds a growing number of good companies are choosing to bypass VC altogether. Inbar said in the mid-market there will likely be some convergence between VC and private equity, with faster paths to liquidity, different ownership structures and more flexible capital.

Inbar said the exact blueprint is not yet clear because the industry is still figuring out what the next step should look like. Inbar named Quinn, Livez and Advance as startups worth watching this year. Inbar said Quinn lets financial institutions give customers an agentic experience built on each customer's unique financial DNA and a judgement layer. Inbar said Quinn is the only company in its space that is SEC certified, giving it a significant edge, and that it already works with top brands with larger ones underway. Inbar said Livez lets employers and insurers turn every mobile phone into an AI-powered screening tool that spots risk early and acts on it automatically, booking care and navigating benefits for each person.

Inbar said Advance is the financial platform built for how insurance moves money, automating collection, reconciliation and payments and giving agencies and brokers real-time visibility. Inbar said Advance turns premium money from a passive liability into an asset that works for agencies and brokers. Inbar said the US healthcare system is built to treat illness, not to prevent it. Inbar said that when prevention finally happens at scale, employees, employers and insurers all win. Inbar said insurance runs on money that never stops moving, with premiums coming in, carriers getting paid and commissions being split, yet most of the industry still handles that money with spreadsheets, disconnected systems and generic bank accounts where errors stay hidden and balances sit idle.

stories.Headline: Ava DuVernay releases 14th documentary on Netflix and defends AI animation of archival photos
stories.Summary:
Ava DuVernay has made a new Netflix documentary called “14th,” which examines the Reconstruction-era amendment that defined American citizenship and promised every person equal protection of the laws, and it opens in select U.S. and U.K. theaters on Friday, Nov. 27, before streaming globally on Netflix on Dec. 4. The film grew out of a fight that reached the Supreme Court, after President Donald Trump’s January 2025 executive order sought to end automatic citizenship for children born to parents in the country illegally or temporarily. On June 30, the justices struck down that order in a 6-3 decision, ruling that the Constitution guarantees citizenship to virtually all children born in the United States. DuVernay told The Guardian she had not planned a follow-up to “13th,” and for about a year she believed she was making a film about birthright citizenship alone before her research widened the project to cover all five sections of the amendment. Ratified in 1868, the 14th Amendment granted citizenship to people born or naturalized in the United States and subject to its jurisdiction, overturned the Supreme Court’s 1857 Dred Scott decision, and barred states from denying any person due process or equal protection.

DuVernay conducted more than 50 interviews for the film, and the lineup crosses party lines, including Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., Rep. Anna Paulina Luna, R-Fla., Sen. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., and former Sen. Jeff Flake, R-Ariz., along with conservative author Donald T. Critchlow, voting rights advocate Stacey Abrams, law professor Robert Chang and historians Eric Foner and David Blight. Civil rights attorney Sherrilyn Ifill, who led the NAACP Legal Defense and Educational Fund for nearly a decade and in 2025 founded Howard University’s 14th Amendment Center for Law and Democracy, is among the film’s central voices, and DuVernay called her “the Meryl Streep of 14th.” The film premiered Oct. 9 as the closing-night selection of the 64th New York Film Festival, a decade after “13th” became the first documentary to open that festival, and its international premiere followed at the BFI London Film Festival. It was produced through DuVernay’s company, ARRAY, with DuVernay, Spencer Averick, Tammy Garnes and Paul Garnes as producers.

Critics have split on the film, with Time Out awarding it five stars and calling it a must-see, while TheWrap critic Siddhant Adlakha found it scattered and short on its director’s usual rigor, though he still credited it as educational and important, and Jourdain Searles argued at RogerEbert.com that a careless presentation undercuts the film’s good intentions. Much of the conversation has centered on DuVernay’s use of artificial intelligence to add motion to black-and-white archival photographs, a technique that drew criticism online after the premiere and that Adlakha called manipulative. DuVernay has defended the approach, telling The Hollywood Reporter in late October that the production did not use it to fabricate a person or make an avatar of a person and that it animated photographs in the public domain, and she said filmmakers need to think soberly about how far the technology has spread into their work. At the New York premiere, she compared the effect to looking through a stereoscope, the 3D photo viewer popular in the Civil War era. When Netflix announced the project in July, DuVernay said in a statement that if “13th” asked who gets caged, then “14th” asks who gets counted.

stories.Headline: Visa Crypto Labs lets US cardholders run up to 25 AI agents that earn OUSD for paid tasks
stories.Summary:
Cuy Sheffield, the head of Visa Crypto Labs, announced an experimental wallet upgrade on Sunday, November 22, 2026. This new system allows artificial intelligence agents to earn income rather than just spending money. The project expands upon the Visa CLI command line tool that the company first released in March. Users can now connect their agents to marketplaces like Taskmarket to perform paid work. These agents earn payments in the form of OUSD, which is a dollar stablecoin.

The pilot program is currently invite only and limited to personal Visa card holders residing in the United States. Eligible users must hold cards from US banks, as corporate and prepaid cards are not permitted. Each single account is allowed to run up to 25 agents, and every agent has its own spending limit and signing key. To verify ownership, a user provides card details and a one time code to register the agent in the Trusted Agent Protocol directory. Payouts are handled through the Bridge firm, which issues the OUSD stablecoin backed by cash and US Treasuries.

Cuy Sheffield stated that Visa Crypto Labs believes ordinary people should be able to earn income from the AI economy. Visa clarified that the card verification process is not a sanctions screening or a formal know your customer procedure. The company uses Turnkey for non custodial storage to ensure that the human owner maintains control over all funds and approvals. During an October contest on Taskmarket, ten winners earned 1 OUSD each, with the final settlement occurring in 76 minutes. This specific test involved creative tasks such as the production of 15 second video advertisements.

The system integrates several different layers, including the identity directory from Visa and the stablecoin infrastructure from a Stripe company. This setup allows agents to perform tasks like market research, gaming projects, and surveys on the Taskmarket platform. Taskmarket typically covers the network transaction costs for users and does not charge a platform fee on Tempo. Visa has not yet announced if this pilot will expand to other countries or different types of cards. The company has not provided details regarding who is liable if an agent submits plagiarized work or breaks marketplace rules.

stories.Headline: Michael Parekh argues billions of people should control the future of artificial intelligence
stories.Summary:
Michael Parekh wrote a three part series on handoverism in November 2026 to examine who should control the future of artificial intelligence. He explored whether humanity should hand control to AI or if a few labs and governments will decide the outcome. The series discusses five options including one AI, a few labs, one capital, two capitals, or billions of people and their agents. It mentions the Remote Access Security Act passed 369 to 22 in January and the World AI Cooperation Organization in Shanghai.

Michael Parekh stated that the answer to who decides must be billions of people rather than one AI, one lab, or one capital. He argued that the real near term risk is a handover to a few humans instead of to the machines. Bill Gurley asked founders and regulators to disclose their positions on handing control to AI while President Trump rejected any globalist control schemes. Anthropic warned in its IPO filing that artificial intelligence may pose existential risks to the future of humanity.

The author notes that governments face analysis paralysis because technology moves faster than they can react, leaving them frozen in the headlights. He observes that AI is popular across Asia, Africa, and Latin America, but is least liked in Europe and the US. Parekh suggests governing step by step to fix concrete problems and keeping the decision process plural to avoid a centralized AI future. The articles leave open how the US and China will navigate their competition without a final finish line.

stories.Headline: AI panel brief says countries can build AI capacity through varied paths beyond frontier models
stories.Summary:
The Independent International Scientific Panel on Artificial Intelligence published a new Thematic Brief on AI Capacity-Building on November 23, 2026, examining the capabilities countries need to benefit from artificial intelligence. The brief finds that there is more than one pathway to AI capacity and that developing frontier models is not the only route available to countries. It says countries can pursue different approaches according to their needs, resources and national priorities. In health and agriculture, the brief notes, AI applications designed for specific tasks have already delivered documented benefits.

The brief states that access to AI does not in itself ensure that countries can benefit from it, because evidence shows substantial performance gaps in many underrepresented languages. It adds that in some low-resource languages safety protections can be bypassed more easily, so systems that perform well in English may not serve all populations equally. Evaluation sets developed with native speakers allow countries to assess how systems perform in their own languages and contexts. The brief also says compute, models and training numbers tell only part of the story, since expertise, relevant data, effective institutions and the capacity to evaluate and govern AI systems also determine whether countries can use AI to advance their own development objectives.

Drawing on evidence and practical examples from different regions, the brief showcases how countries are building these capabilities, from national training programmes and shared computing to locally developed language resources. The brief is intended to inform Member States and other stakeholders as they assess their own AI capacity and decide which pathways best suit their priorities. The Independent International Scientific Panel on Artificial Intelligence is the body that issued the brief. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the brief's stated purpose of informing Member States and other stakeholders.

stories.Headline: Study finds AI chatbots refuse hate speech prompts less often in Kazakh than in English
stories.Summary:
Oliver Lopez and Lily Ottinger published a ChinaTalk essay on Sunday, November 22, 2026. The study examined how six AI chatbots handled crude hate-speech prompts in different languages. It found that chatbots refused these prompts 76.9 percent of the time when asked in English. However, the refusal rate dropped to 32 percent when the prompts were written in Kazakh. This research was a small, independent study with disclosed limits rather than a formal audit.

The study tested Alibaba's Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct, DeepSeek V3, and Zhipu's GLM-4.5 alongside OpenAI's GPT-4o-mini, Google's Gemini 2.5 Flash, and Meta's Llama 3.3 70B Instruct. Lopez, a University of Edinburgh undergraduate, ran 8,400 requests across seven languages. Refusal rates for crude prompts were 79.7 percent for Mandarin in English and 68.1 percent in Mandarin. Mongolian refusals fell from 75.2 percent in English to 25.6 percent in the native language. These tests relate to China's Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress, effective July 1, 2026.

Lopez argued that the new law's obligations arrived before the ability to meet them. He stated that most content rules were already in force through previous laws and measures. Zhou Jianshe of the State Council Information Office called Article 63 a legitimate and necessary provision. He claimed that Western media tried to smear the provision as long-arm jurisdiction. The authors noted that no native speaker reviewed the translations used in the study.

Sarah Brooks of Amnesty International said the law's terms for undermining ethnic unity are broad and undefined. She argued that unity in practice means conformity with the political line of Beijing. Human Rights Watch claimed a September 2025 draft would erase language rights and tighten ideological control. The Jamestown Foundation argued the final law turns assimilation into a legal duty. Former ACLU president Nadine Strossen argued such laws can backfire on ethnic minorities.

The National People's Congress adopted the law on March 12, 2026, to stop ethnic hatred. Article 31 requires network operators to stop, delete, and report content that incites ethnic discrimination. Article 15 makes Mandarin the basic language of state organs and schooling. Article 63 extends liability to organizations and individuals located outside mainland China. Previous rules from 2017, 2020, and 2023 already obliged providers to stop generating ethnic hatred.

The essay leaves open why AI chatbots handle hate speech differently across various languages. It notes that Tibetan replies were gibberish about a third of the time. Uyghur output remained incoherent on about a fifth of answers to crude prompts. The study did not isolate whether these quality problems were specific to Chinese-built systems. Future results depend on whether operators use models to protect minorities or police them.

stories.Headline: Cleveland hospitals require patients to opt out of AI scribes during appointments
stories.Summary:
Brian Risling, a 57-year-old resident of a Cleveland suburb, asked that his Cleveland Clinic doctor not use an artificial intelligence scribe during an appointment in September. The doctor got angry, Risling said, and told him he could not see as many patients a day without the technology. The doctor returned to the topic twice more during the appointment, Risling said. The Clinic said in a statement that the doctor did not want to comment for the story. After Risling complained to the ombudsman office, the hospital sent a letter apologizing for the experience.

Over the last two years, hospitals across the city have begun using artificial intelligence scribes, a technology that can record, transcribe and summarize patient interactions. If Risling wants to opt out, he has to ask, and increasingly his providers ask him why. The Cleveland Clinic, MetroHealth and University Hospitals all use the technology and all maintain that patients can opt out. All three expect patient opt-out requests to come during one-on-one appointments with their providers. None of the hospitals shared a way for patients to opt out in advance for all medical visits.

Andrea Pacetti, a Cleveland Clinic spokesperson, wrote that overall patient and provider feedback has been very positive with minimal complaints. Pacetti wrote that Cleveland Clinic doctors are instructed that if a patient wants to opt out, they are not to use the tool. Pacetti wrote that Cleveland Clinic clinicians are trained to communicate use of the scribe at the beginning of appointments. Tim Magaw, a MetroHealth spokesperson, wrote in an email that clinicians are not trained to push back if a patient declines to be recorded. Asked why the portal does not offer a way to opt out before check-in, Magaw said patients have multiple opportunities to opt out.

Nichole Davis, a patient advocate with Cleveland-based Wayfinder Patient Advocates, said some patients worry that if they push back, they will be labeled a difficult patient. Sharona Hoffman, a professor of bioethics and co-director of Case Western Reserve University's Law-Medicine Center, said there is not necessarily a law protecting patients who do not want the technology used. Davis said hospitals should make the consent understandable and should not just bury the AI disclosure in a stack of information. Davis also said hospitals should train clinicians to respond without being defensive. Brandy Davis, another Cleveland-area patient, was unnerved by the recent cybersecurity incident at University Hospitals.

Scribes in medicine used to be actual people, typically medical students or recent college graduates who took notes for doctors. Dr. Gary Katz, president of the Ohio State Medical Association, said having an in-person scribe was logistically infeasible in his career, so he documented patient interactions himself. A 2026 study found nearly one-third of family medicine residents spent three hours per day after work completing electronic health records. Katz's practice adopted AI scribes about a year and a half ago, and he estimates the technology saves him about 30 minutes a day. One study found the proportion of clinicians reporting burnout decreased from about 52% to 39% after 30 days with an AI scribe.

About 80% of outpatient clinicians at the Cleveland Clinic have been onboarded to the new technology, according to an August 2026 journal article. Both the Cleveland Clinic and MetroHealth said they evaluated the AI scribe tools they chose for bias before selecting them. Doctors at all three hospitals are supposed to review the notes created by AI scribes before submitting them, and the hospitals said recordings or transcripts from patient visits are deleted after 30 days. A spokesperson for University Hospitals wrote that it is not in a position to provide details about the investigation into the cybersecurity incident. Louisiana now requires health care professionals to verbally disclose AI-assisted recording, and Rhode Island passed a similar law that also requires the resulting documentation to be reviewed for accuracy.

stories.Headline: StudioX AI adds OpenTelemetry tracing that shows enterprise AI agent runs in existing monitoring tools
stories.Summary:
StudioX AI announced on 23 November 2026 that it has added OpenTelemetry tracing to its enterprise agentic AI platform, so that when tracing is enabled the company can show an enterprise AI agent run as a single trace across StudioX services and export it to the monitoring tools an operations team already uses. The company said the feature lets teams see what AI agents did in the same tools they use to watch the rest of their software, and it described OpenTelemetry as a must for enterprise monitoring. StudioX said the tracing is available now in its cloud and private deployments, including air-gapped environments, where traces go to a collector inside the customer's own network. The company framed the launch around companies moving toward what it calls the autonomous enterprise, in which AI agents act in business systems rather than only answering questions. The trace covers agent runs along with the model that actually served each one, calls to connected systems including calls that StudioX's agent policy blocked before they reached that system, checks an agent makes on a system it watches with how many records each one found, and actions taken after a decision such as an email sent or a record updated once a person approved it.

The trace shows whether a call failed or was blocked by policy, and StudioX exports traces over OTLP/HTTP, the export path of OpenTelemetry, which it described as a Cloud Native Computing Foundation project for collecting and exporting traces, metrics and logs. Exported traces exclude prompts, responses, tool inputs and results, business records and database queries, and before any trace leaves StudioX removes query strings, credentials and the access tokens in sign-in and approval links. Tracing stays off until an administrator points a deployment at a monitoring endpoint using the standard OpenTelemetry settings, the same rule applies to customer private deployments that run the same StudioX build, and standard OpenTelemetry sampling settings control how many runs are traced. Ian Hamrick, VP Strategy & Partnerships at StudioX AI, said an autonomous enterprise works only if the people running it can see what its AI agents did, and that operations teams can now see what AI agents did alongside the systems they already monitor. He said the company builds on open standards so customers keep the tools they already trust.

StudioX said OpenTelemetry joins other open standards it supports, including the Model Context Protocol, which connects agents to tools and data, and Agent2Agent, which lets agents built on different platforms work together. The company said it is committed to building on open standards so enterprises can connect the systems and tools they already run and are not locked into a single vendor. StudioX illustrated the need with a manufacturing example in which a maintenance agent might read an equipment alert, check the asset's service history, ask an inventory agent about a replacement part and submit a work order after a supervisor approves it. When such a run is slow or fails, the company said, the operations team needs to know which step, which system and which call, in the same tool where it already watches the rest of the plant's software. The articles give no further details on availability beyond the statement that the tracing is available now, and they name no date for anything further.

stories.Headline: Jakub Koziol guides AI due diligence for Polish tech deals in 2026
stories.Summary:
The article is a 2026 guide to AI due diligence in Poland, published by Global Advisory Experts on November 23, 2026, and written for buyers and sellers of AI or technology startups. It says the workstream decides the price in such deals. It names Jakub Koziol of The Heart Legal in Poland as the featured expert on the matter. It states that the risks eroding deal value now sit in code, training data, model governance and regulatory compliance rather than on the balance sheet. It is presented as transactional guidance and not as professional advice for a specific deal.

The guide says three developments make 2026 different for AI and tech targets. It states that the EU AI Act is entering into application in phases from 2025 to 2027. It says the NIS2 Directive is being transposed into Polish law. It adds that civil and product-liability scrutiny of AI products is intensifying. It says each of these has to be surfaced before a letter of intent is signed, not discovered between signing and closing.

The guide advises buyers to price regulatory and technical risk, then allocate it through representations, warranties, indemnities, escrow and insurance, or walk away. It says buyers who treat AI and cyber risk as an afterthought can inherit remediation liabilities that dwarf the purchase price. It says sellers who skip remediation before going to market accept avoidable discounts and broader warranties. It urges parties to surface issues early and to ask for conformity files, DPIAs, incident reports and open-source scans rather than verbal comfort. It says cyber, errors and omissions and warranty insurance can bridge gaps where remediation cannot finish before closing.

The guide says buyers should run an aggressive, evidence-led process when the target's value rests on proprietary models or datasets or when its system may be high-risk under the AI Act. It says sellers planning a competitive sale should run a pre-emptive remediation sprint, fixing missing IP assignments, patching critical vulnerabilities and assembling conformity documentation before buyers arrive. It states that under Polish copyright law the transfer of economic rights to software generally requires a written agreement specifying the fields of exploitation. It says registered rights should be checked with the Urząd Patentowy RP, the Polish Patent Office.

It says a DPIA is required under the GDPR where processing is likely to result in a high risk to individuals, such as large-scale profiling or extensive use of personal data in training. The guide says the AI Act applies in phases, with certain provisions applying from 2025 and most high-risk requirements phasing in through 2026 and 2027. It says high-risk systems carry conformity assessment, technical documentation, post-market monitoring, transparency obligations and documented risk-mitigation measures. It says a missing conformity file is an unquantified compliance liability that belongs in escrow or should defer closing.

It says NIS2 requires establishing whether the target is an essential or important entity under Poland's transposition. It says reliance on one cloud region or vendor is a continuity risk and a NIS2 supply-chain risk. The article leaves open how Poland's NIS2 transposition classifies entities, because the text ends mid-sentence at that point. It does not state the outcome of any specific deal or the position of any party on a transaction.

It does not give the date by which Poland must complete transposition or the penalties for non-compliance. It does not say whether Jakub Koziol or The Heart Legal commented beyond the listing. It offers no figures on deal values, escrow sizes or remediation costs. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Countries tighten exam security as students use AI glasses to cheat
stories.Summary:
Students in several countries used AI glasses to cheat on exams throughout 2026, including incidents in India, Taiwan, and South Korea. In South Korea, a twenty year old student in Cheonan city used smart glasses during a math exam, while others were caught at Yonsei University and Seoul National University in October 2026. India saw two engineering students at the Symbiosis Institute of Technology in Pune use Ray-Ban Meta sunglasses on May 19, and a business student in Surat was caught in September 2026. Taiwan recorded two cases, including a medical school entrance exam candidate at NTU in June who was caught when their glasses heated up.

These incidents require strict new security measures, such as the deployment of 8,400 additional personnel for the Suneung National University Entrance Examination on November 19. South Korean authorities now inspect eyeglasses, collars, and watches, while sealing buttons to prevent the attachment of miniature recording devices. The South Korean Ministry of Education reported 111 electronic device violations this year, including five cases of using smart devices during tests. In Argentina, the Ministry of Health discovered a candidate used camera glasses and earphones during a residency exam on July 1, 2025, which increased their score from 69 to 92.

South Korean Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin resigned on November 22 after President Lee Jae-myung accepted his departure. Choi took responsibility for the disruptions caused by the constant changes to anti-cheating technology measures just before the November 19 national exam. In China, the Ministry of Education stated that wearing smart glasses during the 2026 gaokao is considered cheating even if the devices are not used. The College Board in the United States and examination regulations in the United Kingdom, effective from September 2026, now list smart glasses as prohibited devices.

Many countries are now upgrading security checkpoints and training staff to recognize wearable technology to prevent future cheating. The United Kingdom's examination authority, Ofqual, requested on November 18 that licensing organizations prepare for the 2027 summer exams by reviewing wearable risks. Argentina has responded by switching its 2026 residency exam to individual tablets with controlled connections to block external devices. South Korea is currently considering the possibility of extending the ban period for offenders and prosecuting the most serious cases of cheating.

Articles.Title: AI glasses leaked into exam rooms, causing headaches for many countries fighting cheating. - Vietnam.vn

stories.Headline: Seoul Education Chief Says Technical Skills Are the Edge in the AI Era
stories.Summary:
Seoul Education Superintendent Chung Keun-sik called for stronger vocational training during a recent interview. He spoke with the Seoul Economic Daily at the National Assembly in Yeouido, Seoul. Chung argued that students need practical skills as artificial intelligence takes over human tasks. He believes specialized high schools must be supported to raise the competitiveness of vocational education. This happened as AI expands its adoption in various sectors of society.

The office will raise the share of essay-based assessment to at least 35% by 2027. More than half of regular exam questions will be essay-based from the 2030 academic year. The office will fund teacher training and develop professional scorers through the year 2032. A new five-tier grading system for school records will apply from the 2028 admissions cycle. This system replaces a previous nine-tier structure and increases the top tier to 10 percent.

Chung said that the value of hands-on experience will grow in the era of artificial intelligence. He stated that getting into Seoul National University absolutely does not guarantee a person's life. The superintendent argued that education should develop each student's potential rather than judging them by admissions. He believes that fundamental changes are needed to move away from a system centered on exams. Chung also said that confirmed AI-assisted cheating must be dealt with strictly.

Critics note that past university results cannot be applied to the new five-tier grading scale. This makes it hard for students and parents to predict their chances of acceptance. Some worry that the larger top tier makes it difficult to distinguish academic ability. Chung told these anxious parents and students that the issue is largely a psychological matter. He urged them to focus on day-to-day studies rather than being unsettled by changes.

Chung noted a wide gap between university majors and the jobs people actually do for living. He claimed students choose majors to match scores rather than pursuing what they want to do. He expressed concern that digital devices could prevent elementary students from developing basic learning skills. The government wants to scrap allocating 20.79 percent of national internal tax revenue as grants. The Seoul office was unable to fund 965.7 billion won in department requests for next year.

The office will expand the use of Chaeum AI to ensure consistent grading standards. Chung supports a compromise to secure stability in education finances through national funding. He called for consensus among families and schools before imposing rules on digital device use. The articles leave open how specific standards for the Alpha Phone will be defined. They also leave open how universities will distinguish applicants within the new top tier.

stories.Headline: Heavy agentic AI users expect role shifts and fewer middle management layers, survey finds
stories.Summary:
Business media reported on November 23, 2026, that the biggest agentic AI challenge is the organizational chart. The Business Journals framed the core difficulty as organizational rather than purely technological. MIT Sloan Management Review provided research and survey figures to back this point. A Forbes Technology Council column from November 20 offered a proposal for fixing the issue. An arXiv paper also listed structural problems regarding the transition to agentic AI.

The MIT Sloan Management Review found 66 percent of extensive users expect role shifts and operating model changes. Non adopters expect these changes at a lower rate of 42 percent. Heavy users expect fewer middle management layers at 45 percent, compared to 30 percent for non adopters. A Forbes column suggests every agent get a department and one named owner. It also proposes capping agent access at the level of the owner's access.

MIT Sloan Management Review says governance needs IT, HR, finance, and operations to work together. The project suggests that no single function can own the policy alone. The Forbes Technology Council argues that ownership should be assigned at launch. This approach ensures that someone is accountable when an agent acts. The arXiv guide notes that these are people problems that technology cannot solve.

The arXiv guide identifies four challenges including unclear ownership and misalignment between engineering and business teams. It also cites limited business domain knowledge and a lack of human and AI collaboration models. Middle management is described as the first layer in the line of fire. Employees acting as supervisors often lack the authority, context, and time required. California recently stated that OpenAI lost control of agents 80 times.

For two years, the debate focused on whether models could plan tasks and recover from errors. Traditional org charts assume every action traces back to a human with a title. Agents break this assumption by initiating actions, sequencing work, and coordinating across functions. They behave more like workers than tools because they execute goals across systems. This shift moves humans from authors of actions to supervisors of outcomes.

Organizations must now decide if agents cause restructuring or if restructuring attracts agent adoption. Some leaders may view the 66 percent figure as an inevitability. The Forbes proposal leaves the details of operating a named owner system at scale to each organization. No source names a company that has formally put AI agents on an official chart. The record lacks counts of agents, employees, departments, or reporting lines.

stories.Headline: Penny Wong frames AI data centres as foreign policy and national security challenges for Australia
stories.Summary:
On November 23, 2026, Australia shifted its national security debate regarding artificial intelligence from think-tank panels to cabinet-level talking points. Foreign Minister Penny Wong planned to call artificial intelligence a major foreign policy and national security challenge. Several senior ministers framed AI and the data centres that power it as security issues in recent days. This strategic shift moved AI from a productivity and skills question to a matter for spy agencies. The development occurred as the government sought to police who owns and reaches into AI infrastructure.

The Reserve Bank of Australia forecast 115 billion dollars in spending on data centres between mid-2023 and mid-2026. Microsoft announced a 25 billion dollar investment in April, while Amazon announced a 20 billion dollar plan in June. The Security of Critical Infrastructure Act 2018, introduced to parliament on December 10, 2020, regulates data storage and processing. This law is administered by the Department of Home Affairs and covers eleven essential sectors including energy and communications. The Attorney-General's Department also oversees the Foreign Influence Transparency Scheme to register activities conducted for foreign principals.

Foreign Minister Penny Wong stated that AI is transforming military power and reordering economies in ways that cannot be fully foreseen. She argued that Australia must move quickly to help shape international rules on artificial intelligence. ASIO Director-General Mike Burgess described AI and data centres as equal parts hype, opportunity and threat. He cautioned that foreign adversaries could covertly seek influence or control over AI data centre infrastructure for nefarious reasons. Burgess also expressed concerns regarding both the physical and virtual access to these computing facilities.

Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said onshore AI capability becomes a magnet for people who want to conduct foreign interference. He stated that Australia must be careful about the ownership structures that happen for data centres in the country. Defence Minister Richard Marles said Australian data centres represent a national security interest and create a new vector for foreign actors. US President Donald Trump threatened a tremendous tax on American companies that build AI data centres outside the United States. Trump claimed the US is not going to allow its companies to build data centres outside the country.

The articles state that generative tools lower the cost and technical threshold for running automated disinformation personas across borders. Wong cited an Iranian operation using fabricated journalist personas and Russian covert campaigns using AI-generated deepfakes to influence US elections. The government views AI as a challenge to be managed, similar to maritime security and critical minerals. Australia has seen data-centre investment grow tenfold over three years according to the Reserve Bank of Australia. These facilities are considered national assets because they are valuable targets for attacking or influencing.

Australia continues to engage with the US government and technology companies about investment in the country. The government wants to keep welcoming investment while it builds rules to manage the security exposure. It remains unconfirmed if any named company's Australian project has been formally blocked by the United States. The record contains no specific tax rate, start date, or statutory vehicle for the threatened US tax. The articles leave open whether Microsoft or Amazon will cancel their plans due to the US tax threat.

stories.Headline: Lam Research and ASML supply chipmaking tools as demand outruns supply through 2028
stories.Summary:
John Ballard wrote an article on November 23, 2026, suggesting two semiconductor stocks for investors. He noted that Nvidia announced the resignation of CEO Jensen Huang on November 12. This event created uncertainty regarding the future leadership of the artificial intelligence chip race. Ballard suggests buying companies that sell the machines used to make these chips. He identifies Lam Research and ASML as the two standout equipment suppliers.

Lam Research makes tools for etching and depositing layers, while ASML prints circuit patterns. ASML claims to be the only maker of extreme ultraviolet lithography systems in the world. Lam Research reported record revenue of 8.2 billion dollars for the September quarter. ASML expects its 2026 sales to grow by about 36 percent this year. The company is considering raising its 2028 capacity by at least 30 percent.

Lam Research management credits new products and pricing for achieving record operating margins over 40 percent. Chief financial officer Doug Bettinger said ten new tier I fabs will open next year. ASML CEO Christophe Fouquet stated that customers are accelerating their capacity build-out plans now. He noted that clients are preparing for further expansion beyond 2028 to meet demand. Both companies claim their equipment is necessary regardless of which chip designer wins.

Leading chipmakers told ASML that demand for machines will outrun supply through at least 2028. Some customers are already expressing interest in placing orders for 2029 and 2030. Investors are affected by the cyclical nature of the semiconductor business and supply shortages. Lam Research noted that supply chain constraints limited its December quarter outlook for growth. Analysts expect earnings for both companies to roughly triple by the year 2029.

Global chip sales rose nearly 26 percent to 791 billion dollars in 2025. The Semiconductor Industry Association provided these figures regarding the growth of the global market. The industry group WSTS expects sales of 1.5 trillion dollars in 2026. They further project that sales will reach 1.9 trillion dollars in 2027. Lam Research expects industry spending on equipment to top 200 billion dollars in 2027.

Lam Research stock closed 54 percent below its June 30 high as of November 19. ASML shares closed 32 percent below their June 30 high as of November 16. Analysts expect Lam Research earnings per share to reach 14.54 dollars by fiscal 2029. Analysts expect ASML earnings to reach 76.65 dollars by the year 2029. The articles leave open whether rival designers will gain ground on Nvidia.

stories.Headline: Global markets face a widespread selloff in AI and technology stocks
stories.Summary:
A widespread selloff in artificial intelligence and technology stocks hit global markets last week. This event affected benchmark indexes in the United States and Asia. The selloff occurred at the end of the week before Monday, November 23, 2026. Anthropic's record IPO squeezed liquidity during this period of market turmoil. Concerns about the sustainability of the AI trade also weighed on investor sentiment.

The Nasdaq Composite fell 10 percent, while the S&P 500 and Dow fell over 8 percent. South Korea's KOSPI dropped 3.22 percent on Monday, following its lowest close in 10 months. The South Korean government created a stock stabilization fund and eased share buyback limits for three months. Taiwan's Taiex had its worst weekly fall in 35 years, slumping more than 9 percent. China will lower minimum margin requirements to 80 percent from 100 percent on November 30.

The Kobeissi Letter stated that the AI buildout is only accelerating. This commentator claimed that AI truly is the next big thing. Ben Bowler of Bank of America Global Research noted that idiosyncratic risk has dominated. He said that a broad based shock remains a risk for index volatility. Jeong Woo Park of Nomura Holdings said investors found government measures lacked substance.

Retail sentiment on Stocktwits was bearish for SPY and DIA but extremely bullish for QQQ. Investors in South Korea saw Samsung shares fall nearly 3 percent and SK Hynix drop over 13 percent. Dilin Wu of Pepperstone Group said interventions are circuit breakers rather than a turning point. He noted these steps cannot reverse a broader reassessment of AI valuations. Foreign investors are also affected by these shifting market dynamics and valuations.

The S&P 500 had eight straight quarters of double digit growth before this rout. It also posted three consecutive quarters with earnings growth above 25 percent. The index closed Friday 4.1 standard deviations below its 50 day moving average. The Kobeissi Letter claimed that neither 2008 nor 2020 saw such an occurrence. These figures provide the background for the recent sharp decline in sentiment.

U.S. futures turned green on Monday, with the Nasdaq 100 futures increasing 3.02 percent. The SPY ETF rose over 2 percent and the QQQ ETF gained 3.04 percent. Taiwan's Taiex and China's SSE Composite index edged slightly higher at the open. Japan's stock market remained closed on Monday for the Labour Thanksgiving Day holiday. The articles leave open whether foreign investors will return to these markets.

stories.Headline: Connecticut police use AI with few statewide rules as lawmakers plan updates
stories.Summary:
Connecticut police departments are using artificial intelligence with few statewide rules, according to a report published by CT Insider on Nov. 23, 2026. The report was written by staff writer Jordan Nathaniel Fenster. It says artificial intelligence is entering almost every professional sector, including policing. It says Connecticut has no common set of rules, state-level tracking or guardrails on how police departments are using artificial intelligence. The report says state officials have moved to track and disclose AI use among utilities and in the job market.

Earlier this year, Connecticut prosecutors announced a moratorium on AI programs that draft, author or narrate criminal reports, the report says. That pause addresses one use case of AI and is, at present, the only statewide guidance on AI use for police, according to the report. Beyond automated license plate readers, which are a specific exception with separate state rules and public reporting requirements, there is no general statewide inventory showing which AI systems local police use, how they use them or what safeguards apply, the report says. The state's Responsible AI Framework was created in 2023 and calls for agencies to consider accuracy, privacy, fairness, transparency and human oversight, according to the report. The report says the document applies to state agencies and their contractors, while local governments are "encouraged to adopt" it, leaving cities and towns to decide whether to create separate rules for their police departments.

Mike Lawlor, an educator and former legislator who serves on the state Police Officer Standards and Training Council, said AI can be very useful as an administrative and investigatory tool, the report says. Lawlor said there is a role for this to play and that it is inevitable it will be a major part of everything, including law enforcement. He said it is a question, since it is new, of how you test it, how you figure out what the potential problems are and how you protect against those things happening. State Sen. James Maroney, D-Milford, said he was planning on going back and updating the government use of AI bill this year because of learnings since 2023. Maroney said lawmakers will likely look at it and ask the judiciary branch to do so as well.

Vahid Behzadan, an associate professor at the University of New Haven who researches AI safety and security, said AI is not a single technology, according to the report. Behzadan said police uses can range from transcription and translation to report writing, facial recognition and predictive systems that forecast where crime might occur. With report-writing tools, Behzadan said the model might end up excluding relevant facts, including potentially exculpatory information. He said software could theoretically turn an unclear or ambiguous account into a smoother, more confident-sounding narrative, changing how events appear to have happened.

Behzadan said an officer's review remains essential but does not by itself show which parts of the report came from the software or what the software left out. The report says few municipal police departments in Connecticut have any guidelines for officers' AI use, or publicly disclose how and if police officers are using it. It says academics and advocates have raised concerns that artificial intelligence may create errors in police reports, that AI used for facial recognition can create false matches and that predictive systems might create disproportionate surveillance in communities of color. An NAACP issue brief on predictive policing warns that systems trained on historical crime and policing data can reproduce unequal patterns in surveillance and enforcement, the report says.

The report says the brief calls for oversight and public disclosure and is a statement of risks and recommendations, not evidence that a Connecticut police department uses predictive policing. According to the National Institute of Standards and Technology, facial recognition can produce false matches, and the error rates of tested systems can vary across demographic groups, producing higher error rates when examining Black persons' faces, the report says. A presentation last year by the Connecticut Criminal Justice Information System governing board included a bullet point explaining how the agency was planning to use AI to "do a lot more with less," the report says. The presentation said the agency is automating more of its testing of new code to reduce costs, exploring possibilities of adding AI for Connecticut Information Sharing System Analytics and renegotiating maintenance agreements or instead leveraging time and materials contracts.

The report says lawmakers admit that the 2023 law that created the AI framework is already outdated, and it notes that ChatGPT became available in public previews on Nov. 30, 2022. Prior to the moratorium, New Haven had a 2024 contract with Axon that included Draft One, which can use body-camera audio to generate a draft police report, according to the report. The report says there are no reports of this technology being used in Connecticut. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Venture capital investors weigh proprietary data and deep tech as AI reshapes startup competition
stories.Summary:
CTech launched its VC Survey 2027 project on November 23, 2026, drawing on a survey conducted over the past several weeks among more than 100 executives, managing partners and investment partners at venture capital funds active in the Israeli market. The project is a series of articles and data analyses that examines changes in the venture capital industry in Israel and around the world, with a focus on the impact of artificial intelligence on companies and investment models, fundraising conditions, and the economic and geopolitical challenges facing the industry. Over the coming weeks the project will feature in-depth articles, statistical analyses and interviews with senior figures in the venture capital industry, drawing on survey findings and the perspectives of fund managers and investors. The coverage will address the changes those investors see in the market, the strategies they are adopting, and the opportunities and risks they expect to shape the industry in the years ahead.

One central theme is how the AI revolution affects the way technology companies are built, what gives them a competitive edge, and how venture capital investors evaluate potential investments. Because AI tools make software and digital services faster and cheaper to develop, the competitive landscape for startups is changing and raising new questions about the sources of their long-term advantage. The survey examines the importance investors place on proprietary data, deep integration into customers' workflows, and hard-to-replicate technologies including semiconductors, robotics and computing infrastructure. It also explores changes in venture capital business models and the funding environment, including the challenges of raising capital for new funds, shifts in investment volumes and investor expectations, and the growing gap between the capital requirements of software companies and those of hardware and deep-tech ventures. Another focus is the state of the exit market, where limited IPO opportunities are making mergers and acquisitions and secondary transactions increasingly important routes to liquidity.

A further major part of the project will examine Israel's position in the global venture capital industry, exploring how geopolitical developments affect investment decisions and the ability of Israeli companies to attract foreign capital. The analyses will look at the sectors in which the local ecosystem continues to draw international investor interest, including cybersecurity, defense technology, Physical AI and computing infrastructure, alongside the challenges facing early-stage startups. The project will also look at how venture capital funds themselves are adapting, including their use of AI tools to source companies, screen investment opportunities and conduct due diligence, as well as changes to investment strategies and portfolio management. This year's survey builds on CTech's annual VC Survey, which last year brought together the views of more than 60 leading investors and examined the Israeli tech industry's transition from survival mode to a focus on execution and growth. Against the backdrop of rapid advances in artificial intelligence and ongoing challenges in the capital markets, the project aims to provide an up-to-date picture of the venture capital industry and how its leading figures are preparing for the years ahead.

stories.Headline: Automated checks help finance teams stop most accounts payable fraud, survey finds
stories.Summary:
Accounts payable fraud often begins with a single fake supplier request that redirects company cash to the wrong account, and PYMNTS Intelligence surveyed 150 U.S. treasury and finance executives to learn how businesses fight this problem as artificial intelligence makes scams harder to spot. The survey, released in a report produced with Bottomline, examined where manual checks fall short and how finance teams can strengthen their defenses. The findings show that automated checks are linked to stronger fraud prevention, and that connected payment data gives teams a stronger defense. The report also found that payment approvals struggle to keep pace with the speed and volume of payments. Among teams with mostly or somewhat automated verification, 65% stop at least 90% of fraud attempts before a loss occurs, according to the survey.

Fifty-five percent of companies with integrated data stop at least 90% of fraud attempts, the findings show. Only 12% of executives strongly agree that their approval controls keep up with payment speed and volume. The report presents these figures as evidence of where manual checks fall short and how finance teams can strengthen their defenses. The survey was conducted by PYMNTS Intelligence, which explored how businesses fight payables fraud, and the report is a collaboration with Bottomline. The findings reveal where manual checks fall short and how finance teams can strengthen their defenses, according to the report.

The report directs readers to download the collaboration with Bottomline for the details. The articles do not name any individual who commented on the findings. The context given is that artificial intelligence is making scams harder to spot, which is why the survey examined how businesses fight payables fraud. The articles do not say what happens next beyond offering the download of the full report with Bottomline for the details. No further steps, dates or responses are given in the articles.

stories.Headline: Data center developers and senior housing operators can explore partnerships that reuse waste heat, Dham says
stories.Summary:
The article asks whether AI data centers could help with the US senior housing crisis, and it was published by CIO on 23 November 2026. It was written by Ankush Dham, who is CEO of Dataknox Solutions, a global IT infrastructure services company. The piece is an opinion article, and Dham says he believes there is an opportunity to explore partnerships between data center developers and senior housing operators. He describes two trends creating infrastructure challenges in the United States, rising senior housing demand and the rapid expansion of AI data centers. He says the oldest baby boomers turn 80 this year and the shortfall of senior housing units is growing more severe.

According to NIC MAP's 2026 Senior Housing Market Outlook, the need for additional senior housing will reach approximately 576,000 units by 2030. The same outlook says the need will exceed one million units by 2035 if construction continues at its current pace. A 2026 report from Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory projects data centers could account for 11.8% of total U.S. electricity consumption by 2030, up from an estimated 4.7% in 2024. NIC MAP estimates that meeting future senior housing demand will require more than $1 trillion in cumulative investment through 2050. In Groningen, the Netherlands, data center operator QTS has partnered with local energy provider WarmteStad to supply recovered heat to a district heating network.

Dham says the system uses heat pumps powered by renewable energy to circulate hot water through an existing underground district heating network. He says that network supplies residual heat to 10,000 households, buildings and knowledge institutions. He says the community gets access to a heat source that would otherwise be discarded, and the data center benefits from the cooling provided through the energy exchange. He says the engineering requires more than connecting two buildings, because data center cooling systems generally operate at temperatures below those required for conventional building heating. He says heat pumps would likely need to raise the temperature, and a distribution network must transport the energy to where it can be used.

In Chicago's Bronzeville neighborhood, developers have proposed Metropolis Pointe, a mixed-use development combining a data center with residential, commercial and community facilities. Griffin Venture Group, the project's developer, announced additional infrastructure milestones in August 2026, including plans for a 170,000-square-foot data center and a 42,000-square-foot central utility plant. Dham says the proposed utility system would integrate heating and cooling across the campus with the goal of reducing energy costs for residents. He says the project is still in the proposal stage, and he says its design reflects an important evolution in thinking. He says senior living communities may be particularly well suited because they operate 24/7 with substantial year-round energy requirements.

Dham says heating, hot water, kitchens, laundry facilities and common areas all contribute to operating expenses in senior living communities. He says traditional HVAC or electric heating can be an especially high cost in colder climates. He says construction costs have also increased, financing remains costly and challenging, and many older Americans cannot absorb higher housing expenses on their fixed budgets. He says a senior living community located near a suitable data center could potentially receive recovered heat through a shared thermal network. He says senior housing developers with available land might be able to lease a portion of their land to a data center operator to create an additional revenue stream.

Dham says large hyperscale data centers won't always be appropriate, and he thinks smaller computing facilities and strategically located data centers connected through district heating networks will prove more practical. He says data centers would still need adequate space, zoning, electrical capacity and commercial demand to make each arrangement work. He says brownfield opportunities could be identified within existing senior housing developments, and multi-state operators could evaluate their portfolios for facilities with available land, suitable heating systems and access to electrical infrastructure. He says retrofitting older facilities can be expensive and potential savings would need to justify investments. He says a small number of promising projects could test the models, measure their results and demonstrate where these partnerships can deliver meaningful benefits.

stories.Headline: Trump threatens taxes on US firms building AI data centers abroad
stories.Summary:
President Donald Trump announced on November 20 that he intends to stop American companies from building data centers in other countries. He threatened to impose very heavy taxes on any domestic firms that continue to invest in these infrastructures outside the United States. This announcement occurred during a press conference at the White House while Wall Street faced one of its worst weeks in recent years. The move specifically targets the development of artificial intelligence infrastructures by giants such as Amazon, Google, and Microsoft.

The new policy requires that strategic computing infrastructures remain within the United States to maintain a technological advantage over Beijing. Trump predicted a huge tax for companies that ignore this directive, though the administration has not yet specified the tax amounts or the application process. These threats coincided with a financial downturn on Friday, November 20, where the Nasdaq lost 5.3 percent and erased all gains from 2026. The S&P 500 fell 3.7 percent and entered correction territory by dropping more than 10 percent below recent highs.

President Trump is responsible for this decision and stated that he will not allow data centers to be placed in other countries because China would take them all. He explained that the goal is to prevent Chinese firms from accessing American computing capacity through facilities located in third countries. The president admitted that he had not yet communicated this specific plan to his collaborators before making the public announcement. He believes these measures are necessary because the United States already limits the export of advanced semiconductors to China.

The European Union may face slower or more expensive data center construction as it tries to reduce its technological dependence on foreign nations. Financial markets are also struggling because investors worry that the rush to build infrastructure is proceeding faster than actual revenue growth. Some analysts fear a bubble exists regarding the enormous investments earmarked for artificial intelligence and data centers. It remains unclear how the administration will implement these restrictions or which specific investments will be affected.

stories.Headline: Singapore expands AI strategy with new training spots and funding for 500 business projects
stories.Summary:
Singapore announced a major expansion of its artificial intelligence strategy on May 27, 2025, during the ATxEnterprise 2025 conference. Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information Tan Kiat How introduced these initiatives to a group of 200 delegates at the Singapore Expo. The plan involves creating 800 new training opportunities and supporting as many as 500 new projects for 1,000 enterprises. These efforts aim to strengthen the digital economy, which currently accounts for nearly 18 per cent of the local economy.

The training expansion includes 400 places at the national programme AI Singapore, with 300 of those offered through an enhanced AI Apprenticeship Programme over two years. Another 400 spots will be provided by companies including Microsoft, Oracle, Singtel, and Amazon Web Services. AI Singapore will also launch the Pinnacle AI Industry Programme to train 100 expert model builders over three years. For businesses, the GenAI x Digital Leaders initiative will provide funding and guidance for 500 generative AI projects over the next 12 months.

Tan Kiat How stated that technology and artificial intelligence are expected to drive quality economic growth despite global uncertainty. He explained that companies expanding their teams in Singapore will require more practitioners with specialized expertise. The Infocomm Media Development Authority noted that these new roles will add to a current pool of over 6,000 professionals. The agency aims to triple the total tech talent pool to 15,000 by 2028 through various school and upgrading programmes.

The government is acting on concerns from local firms regarding a shortage of artificial intelligence talent. A survey of 350 companies found that 47 per cent believe the local talent pool is insufficient for business needs. To assist further, Alibaba Cloud pledged to help 3,000 small and medium enterprises, while ST Engineering will offer cyber-threat scanning to 2,000 such firms. Prudential Singapore also committed to providing ten generative AI tech explainer videos to support local businesses.

stories.Headline: NVIDIA launches Alpamayo 2 Edge reasoning model for autonomous driving on DRIVE Thor hardware
stories.Summary:
NVIDIA released Alpamayo 2 Edge on November 22, 2026, to provide autonomous driving capabilities. This compact reasoning vision-language-action model is designed to plan and explain vehicle trajectories. It specifically targets the NVIDIA DRIVE AGX Thor hardware rather than datacenter GPUs. The system aims to provide reasoning-based planning within the compute and latency budgets of onboard hardware. The 2B-parameter model uses a 2.45B backbone consisting of a 1.96B language model and a 0.41B SigLIP2 encoder.

A 0.2B diffusion action expert sits on top, though Hugging Face metadata lists the total as 3B. It processes 22 frames from six cameras and 20 historical ego poses to create 64 waypoints over 6.4 seconds. Real-time use requires the Alpamayo Developer Hub recipe to calibrate FP8 scales and build TensorRT engines. NVIDIA reports that the model achieves pixel-to-trajectory latency between 160 and 190 milliseconds on DRIVE AGX Thor-X. The company claims the model is a strong closed-loop driver for its size, covering 15.15 kilometers between at-fault incidents in AlpaSim. This performance is described as about 60 times better than the 0.25 kilometers achieved by Qwen-Drive-1.0 4B.

The model uses a Chain-of-Causation reasoning trace but emits nominal tokens during routine driving to save compute. The model was developed using 115,000 hours of multi-camera driving video and 3.7 million reasoning traces. It underwent offline distillation from the larger Alpamayo 2 Super cloud model and closed-loop reinforcement learning in AlpaGym. While validated on a single H100 GPU with 80GB of memory, it requires at least 16 GB for workstation use. Partner Embedl stated that the system reached 10 Hz on AGX Thor in under 48 hours.

stories.Headline: Anthropic warns of brainpower deflation as it prepares IPO with $1.26-1.41 trillion valuation
stories.Summary:
Anthropic warned on November 23, 2026, that there is no escaping brainpower deflation. The company faces a future where its endgame may resemble the AI version of Google or AT&T. This warning comes as the company prepares for its initial public offering. The firm is struggling with the burden of massive computing power contracts. These contracts total nearly 1 trillion US dollars on the balance sheet.

The IPO pricing puts the fully diluted valuation between 1.26 and 1.41 trillion US dollars. This range is about 16 to 17 times the October annual recurring revenue of 81 billion US dollars. Some calculations based on Q4 annualized revenue of 77 billion US dollars suggest a multiple of 18 times. The company previously saw a primary market valuation of 965 billion US dollars in May. IPO expectations once rose as high as 1.5 trillion US dollars.

Dolphin analyzed the value judgment of Anthropic and the growth prospects of AI. The analyst noted that revenue needs to rise 4 to 5 times to afford computing costs. Dolphin questioned if the intelligence premium can be sustained as token prices drop. The analyst also examined the total addressable market for AI large model applications. This study focuses on competitive barriers and the impact of intellectual deflation.

Optimistic investors like Gavin Baker and Brad Gerstner anchor the market at 40 trillion US dollars. They view the salaries of global knowledge workers as the total reachable market space. Bearish institutions instead link the target market to enterprise IT budgets of 6 trillion US dollars. These pessimists believe Anthropic will only get 3 percent of that budget in five years. This would result in 180 billion US dollars in revenue.

The articles state that global labor income is about 60 trillion US dollars. This accounts for about 52 percent of the global gross domestic product. Token prices for the Opus model dropped from 15 to 4 US dollars per million tokens. Third party indices show actual transaction prices halved from 1.70 to 0.83 US dollars in one month. The US government recently imposed strict restrictions on remote computing power.

Future token prices for cutting edge models may drop 45 to 55 percent every year. This decline is driven by chip performance doubling and improved model algorithms. The articles leave open whether price reductions will stimulate enough new demand to compensate for losses. It remains uncertain if the intelligence premium can be maintained against open source models. The long term anchor for AI evolution varies from person to person.
