stories.Headline: Optima Arch's AI-made Slotbound sells 100,000 copies in three days on Steam
stories.Summary:
On November 13, 2026, the indie game Slotbound launched on Steam and sold 100,000 copies within three days, according to eu.36kr.com. South Korean individual developer Optima Arch made the game, which combines 3×3 slot machine gameplay with Roguelike and auto-battle mechanisms. Sales revenue reached 356,000 US dollars in the first 48 hours, and sales exceeded 50,000 copies in that same period. The game's peak concurrent player count exceeded 30,000. By contrast, other AI-made games drew almost no attention one month after release, with some earning less than 10 US dollars.

Mobilegamer.biz interviewed multiple individual developers who used AI tools to make games, asking about actual download volumes and revenues. Ahmed Alshuail's Sprout: Cozy Idle Garden landed on Google Play on August 30, 2026, and on the App Store on September 30. As of October 28, it had 121 downloads and about 6 US dollars in revenue, with 4 US dollars from IAP and about 2 US dollars from advertising. Marc Fienberg's Zen Ten Match, built with Claude Code, React Native and Supabase plus RevenueCat and AdMob, had 74 real players across iOS, Android and web as of October 13, with about 3 US dollars in advertising revenue in its first three weeks. Arin Agrawal's Calc Quest, made with Flutter, accumulated more than 25,000 players but only about 120 US dollars from advertising and IAP.

Iain Atkinson's Tennis Tycoon, made with Claude, sold about 3,000 US dollars, but AI Tokens during development cost thousands of US dollars. Ivan Soyer, developer of Dusk Climber, said he invested about 1,500 US dollars in AI tools and Tokens, and the game got about 1,000 downloads one month after launch but has not generated any revenue yet. Optima Arch said that in 2025, introduced by his family, he first came into contact with AI game development. He did not even know how to get started, so he first asked AI to make a square that can move via WASD keys. When that simple program ran successfully, he gradually began to try to make a complete game.

Before the official launch, Optima Arch had released the Demo on itch.io and Steam and continuously shared development progress on social platforms. In September 2026, the number of Steam wishlists for Slotbound had exceeded 100,000. Deniz Sancar's 38-0-0, a football draft game made with Claude Code, topped the free game list on iOS in the UK in the summer of 2026. It has accumulated about 300,000 downloads on iOS and more than 700,000 on Android, and Sancar said revenue from advertising and IAP is enough to support full-time game development. Ken Law's Harpagia, a text-based idle RPG for iOS and Android, has accumulated about 155,000 US dollars in revenue over the past year, averaging about 13,000 US dollars a month, with total downloads above 50,000.

Ken Law previously worked in technical roles at Amazon and Meta, with about 12 years of experience in the technology industry. After getting in touch with AI tools, he began to try to use Cursor and ChatGPT to assist in game development. According to an interview with Starter Story in September 2026, Harpagia has not launched paid advertising campaigns and mainly acquires users through organic traffic, with daily operating costs of about 500 US dollars per month. Law has an educational background in computer science and has long been engaged in software engineering and technical management work. Sancar has a background in the marketing industry, and his own marketing company runs alongside his game work.

The articles leave open the specific revenue of 38-0-0, which the developer has not announced. They leave open how Slotbound's sales and revenue developed after the third day and after the first 48 hours. They leave open whether the developers whose games earned little will change their products or marketing. They leave open what share of the games' downloads or revenue came from AI-assisted work versus other factors. They leave open how the interviewed developers' figures were verified.

stories.Headline: CertiK and Columbia University researchers formally verify production AI operators from DeepSeek and FlashAttention
stories.Summary:
CertiK and Columbia University researchers announced TensorLean on November 20, 2026. This project achieved the first formal verification of multiple production-grade AI operators. The verified operators include those from DeepSeek and the FlashAttention library. This process uses mathematical proof to ensure that GPU code meets expectations. The team focused on verifying compiled PTX instructions rather than source code.

The project evaluated 149 compiled GPU kernel instances across different hardware generations. It covered DeepSeek's DeepGEMM and the FlashAttention operator library from versions two to four. The team found 38 correctness issues across six libraries, including 23 from FlashAttention. Two defects were found in DeepGEMM, and 66 total instances failed verification. These instances spanned the Ampere, Hopper, and Blackwell GPU architectures.

The researchers stated that traditional testing cannot find all possible errors in complex GPU kernels. They explained that TensorLean handles concurrency by using role-based classification and representative threads. To manage dynamicity, the team used loop invariant technology to cover all parameter combinations. They addressed floating-point precision by calculating the upper bound of accumulated rounding errors. The team also decoupled mathematical logic from memory layout to reduce specification costs.

The researchers noted that defects in FlashAttention could affect every model using it. This library is widely deployed in frameworks like PyTorch, vLLM, and SGLang. The team found a specific error in FlashAttention-4 that 17,760 tests on an H100 missed. This highlights how underlying computational errors can cause chaotic and unpredictable model outputs. Such failures could endanger safety in critical systems like autonomous driving.

The articles mention a previous reliability crisis involving the Claude large language model. In August 2025, some Claude users saw Thai text and syntax errors in English prompts. Anthropic explained that a runtime optimization for TPU servers caused these computational errors. This anomaly emerged on August 25 and was rolled back by September 2, 2025. These errors disrupted the model's normal probability distribution and undermined the user experience.

The team completed formal verification for 27 kernels related to DeepSeek. They also inspected 37 source code kernels from FlashAttention, totaling 102 compiled instances. The team wrote specifications for 72 open-source kernels using 10,278 lines of code. The articles do not state if the discovered defects have been fixed. It remains open whether this method will be applied to other AI operators.

stories.Headline: MiniMax releases MIM model that solves Millennium Prize Problems and breaks cryptographic records
stories.Summary:
MiniMax released an internal model called MIM that broke global records in automated cryptanalysis on November 20, 2026. This AI system cracked multiple cryptographic puzzles and solved two Millennium Prize Problems. The model proved the Riemann Hypothesis and the Navier-Stokes equations. These achievements occurred on the same day. The Lean official team confirmed the verification of the Riemann Hypothesis proof.

The MIM model used a 64-core server to solve the TII McEliece challenge in 1.8 to 5.36 seconds. This speed was 6,180 to 43,400 times faster than a multi-GPU cluster used by Anthropic. For a lattice isomorphism problem, MIM used a single-core CPU to find a key in 30.9 minutes. Anthropic previously used a 96-core server for nearly four hours on this task. MIM also cracked the Waterfall-256 algorithm in 0.045 seconds.

MiniMax stated that Chinese teams are now competing in the AI for Science battlefield. The company released eight analysis reports with runnable code to prove these results. They claimed that cryptanalysis is a brutal testing ground for large models. The company highlighted that MIM converted high-order mathematical derivations into practical attack codes. This process demonstrated the ability of AI to carry out scientific exploration.

Anthropic engineers responded by reposting and liking the results of the MiniMax model. The AI affected the security boundaries of post-quantum cryptography candidate schemes like LOCKER-I and ROLLO-I. It also impacted the COLM algorithm, which had been published in the Journal of Cryptology. A known expert noted that cryptography tests are brutal because scripts either recover the key or they do not. The model also found a human error in the DRS signature verification logic.

The articles state that the TII McEliece challenge previously had an academic record of 9.2 hours. The NIST standardization competition serves as a primary benchmark for the cryptography community. ETH Zurich and Anthropic created CryptanalysisBench to test if models memorize training data. The LOCKER-I scheme previously required 42 PB of memory to construct a specific matrix. The COLM algorithm had won the CAESAR authenticated encryption competition after five years of selection.

MIM compressed the LOCKER-I matrix from 42 PB down to 58 MB. The model used a mod 2 sublattice to reduce a search from 118 dimensions to 80 dimensions. It forged a legitimate ciphertext for COLM0 using only two queries. The articles leave open how long other mathematical fortresses can resist such AI. They also leave open the future of algorithms that previously had no known practical attacks.

stories.Headline: Netizens use AI to develop custom desktop pet software
stories.Summary:
Netizens have started developing custom desktop pet software using AI as these gadgets gain popularity again. This trend emerged recently and was reported by the author Guozi on November 23, 2026. Users are creating these tools to kill boredom rather than to improve their production efficiency. Many people are sharing their self-made cases on social media platforms like Douyin and Xiaohongshu. These creations allow people who do not understand code to get in touch with software development.

The process requires a desktop Agent like WorkBuddy to customize functions according to specific user needs. Guozi used this tool to package a minimalist workday motivator as a desktop plugin for Mac. Some users create pets using photos of their own animals or favorite cute anime girls. Others make pets from images of roommates or bosses to crawl on the desktop for fun. One user developed a tool called RememberPal to record solar and lunar calendar birthdays for Mac.

Guozi stated that the era of building tool applications from scratch has finally arrived for everyone. The author claimed that numbers can save those who are oppressed by numbers like KPI or OKR. Guozi noted that people are not afraid of hardship when they are doing things that are fun. The author mentioned that AI makes the world feel different for a code novice like himself. He explained that WorkBuddy provides 100 free points daily for users who log in every day.

Overworked office workers are affected by this trend and use these tools to motivate their daily work. Some users include fitness plans in their motivators because they are trained by bosses and clients. Others use animations of donkeys pulling mills to express the feeling of spinning in the same place. Some netizens make their tools look like antivirus software to hide how they are making money. People with trypophobia are advised to stay away from pets that look like crawling cockroaches.

The articles state that vibe coding desktop pets were popular for a while before the workday motivators. Independent developers previously focused on a three-piece set consisting of bookkeeping, diary, and to-do list tools. Google announced at the Google I/O 2026 conference that Google AI Studio now supports Android applications. Users can now input natural language to generate an Android APK installation package for mobile devices. This shift means that almost anyone can now customize their own basic bookkeeping or diary tools.

Users can now make simple application tools without downloading software or paying for expensive memberships. The articles leave open whether users have the motivation to spend time and energy using Agents. Complex apps that require servers or high concurrency still have very high thresholds for AI development. Guozi offered to share a dmg file for Mac users or an HTML file for Windows users. It remains to be seen how many people will move from funny tools to useful ones.

stories.Headline: A translator and technical writer lists eight AI terms for readers beyond tokens and prompts
stories.Summary:
The article lists eight AI terms it says are worth knowing beyond tokens, prompts and hallucinations, and it was published by eu.36kr.com on 2026-11-22 at 06:00:00Z. It was written by Shenyi Translation, a translation and compilation team under 36Kr that covers technology, business, workplace and life and introduces foreign technologies, perspectives and trends. The author says they are an AI enthusiast and technical writer who has created AI-related content for more than 5 years. They say they recently read an article titled “Master These 5 AI Terms and You Will Outperform 90% of People” and were familiar with all five terms in it. They say they wrote this article to share 8 more terms in plain language without piling up obscure technical jargon.

The article says a native large language model is like a brain in a jar that cannot open Slack, send emails or know when to stop on its own. It says the Harness is software wrapped around the model that lets it call tools, read information, manage permissions, control retry logic and termination conditions, and ask for help when needed. It says code agents are an example, with the Harness providing tools to read files, edit code and run tests while managing instructions and feedback to the model. It says two applications using the same base large model can perform very differently because their Harness opens different tools, instructions and result verification methods. It says Agents can perform operations step by step, call tools and complete a task independently, giving a refund example in which the agent finds the order, checks the refund policy, drafts the application and asks for approval before submission.

The article says the basic agent workflow is to plan actions, perform operations, verify results and decide what to do next. It says an agent is like an assistant with a to-do list authorized to use specific software, and that the upper limit of tasks depends on available tools and permissions. It says an agent that can only browse web pages is completely different from one connected to your email, files and calendar. It says you must confirm what content an agent can access, what information it can modify and when it needs your approval. It says MCP can basically be understood as the USB-C interface in the AI field, providing a unified standard for AI applications to connect to tools and data sources.

The article says that without a unified standard developers often need separate docking programs for each AI application, but with MCP one set of connections can be reused by multiple compatible applications. It says the MCP server opens specific tools or data to AI applications, for example letting AI assistants retrieve internal company documents or create new work orders in project management tools. It says configuration is still required, the AI application itself must support the protocol and you must grant corresponding access permissions. It says if a product claims to support MCP you can pay attention to what services it can connect to and what operations the assistant can perform through the protocol. It says most agent work follows a loop pattern of selecting an action, performing it, checking the result and retrying if it fails, and that a code agent may modify files, run tests, read error messages and adjust the code.

The article says this loop may go wrong, with the agent repeatedly performing invalid operations or stopping early before the task is completed. It says Loop engineering refers to designing the operation rules of this loop, including how the agent receives feedback and judges whether to continue, and that it is an emerging direction in agent development. It lists questions the loop must answer, including to what extent a task is considered completed, the maximum number of retries, the maximum time and cost, when the agent should ask humans for help and who or what mechanism verifies results. It says you can require a code agent to pass specified tests before success or set it to stop after three consecutive failures and explain the cause. It says a Skill is a pre-saved execution process the agent can call directly when it encounters a matching task, with a reimbursement form example specifying which fields to fill in, how expenses are classified and what to do when receipts are missing.

The article says that in Anthropic's skill specification instructions are written in the SKILL.md file and the supporting package can include scripts, templates and reference documents. It says that in Claude you can add custom skills or template skills on the skills page, and that ChatGPT adds skills on the customization page. It says the agent at first only sees the name and introduction of a skill and loads the full detailed instructions when it judges the skill is needed. It says MCP opens up access to tools and data for agents while skills tell them how to use these tools to complete specific work, with a monthly sales report example. It says GEO relates to how your content can be retrieved and cited by AI agents, and that people now ask ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity or Google AI Summaries for answers and click links far less often.

The article says GEO, Generation Engine Optimization, aims to get your brand mentioned, your content cited and your products recommended when AI generates responses. It says AEO, Answer Engine Optimization, aims to make your content suitable for direct answer generation, including answer cards on search engines and Q&A content from AI assistants. It says the two concepts overlap and different companies do not have completely consistent classification standards for them. It says clear descriptions, accurate product information and reliable sources increase the probability of your content being cited, but even doing all these well does not guarantee the AI will mention you.

It says Computer Use refers to an AI system's ability to interact with the screen by clicking, typing, scrolling pages and selecting content, following a process of taking a screenshot, determining the next action, clicking or typing and reading the screen again. The article says ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity and Grok all support Computer Use, and that ChatGPT can enable this function in the integration menu under Settings. It says Computer Use is useful when an application does not open a suitable API interface, which is the channel for software to exchange information and execute instructions directly. It says that even if a booking service does not open a docking interface, the agent can still enter information in the booking form.

It says Computer Use carries risks, as the agent may click the wrong button, misread the page or get stuck at a certain step, and that important operations such as order placement, submission and account information modification must be manually reviewed. It says AGI generally refers to AI that can reach the same level as humans in a wide range of intellectual tasks, including learning knowledge in unfamiliar fields, solving various different problems and transferring learned knowledge across domains. The article says researchers have not yet reached a consensus on AGI's exact definition and evaluation criteria, and that Google DeepMind has a paper proposing judgment ideas from two dimensions, the breadth of system capabilities and task performance. It says Superintelligence goes a step further, with capabilities that significantly surpass humans in the vast majority of intellectual tasks.

It says AI that is only good at a single task cannot be counted as either, and that even a model that writes excellent code and solves complex math problems may perform very poorly in other things. It says when companies mention these two terms in their promotions you should check their specific definitions and what capabilities the system has verified instead of only looking at the labels. It says that next time a vendor says their product is equipped with agents you can ask what specific tasks it can complete, and if it supports MCP you can check what applications it can connect to. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Canadian Chamber of Commerce publishes article on making AI count for business
stories.Summary:
The Canadian Chamber of Commerce published an article titled The Case for Canada: Making AI Count on November 19, 2026, on its website. The article appears under the chamber's business, economic and policy insights, which the chamber describes as powerful tools and insights on Canadian business conditions and trends. The chamber presents itself as the national voice of business, saying it unites over 400 chambers of commerce and boards of trade representing more than 200,000 organizations across every region of Canada. The article's page also sets out the chamber's membership offer, saying members gain influence no single business can achieve alone and that its councils and committees are platforms for members to collaborate on policy solutions.

The chamber says it unites businesses of all sizes, sectors and regions, giving them a platform to shape economic policy, expand their influence and ensure their voice is heard where decisions are made. It invites businesses to add their voice to the public policy conversations that are shaping the country's economic future. It also says membership opens doors to real impact, advocacy and opportunity, and that joining its advocacy efforts brings influence beyond what one business can achieve alone. The page describes its events, webinars and gatherings as places where members connect, learn and discover as a network.

The chamber frames its work as running from local main streets to global markets, and it says it is at its best as a network when members connect through the events it hosts. It lists tools to boost productivity, save money and achieve goals, alongside insights on Canadian business conditions and trends. The article itself gives no further details on what making AI count involves, and the page carries no figures, dates or names beyond those above. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Anthropic shares fall 9.1% as AI trade selloff hits global markets
stories.Summary:
Shares in Anthropic plunged 9.1 per cent on Friday, November 20, 2026, as a broad selloff hit Asia and the United States. The company behind the Claude chatbot saw its stock price drop almost to the initial public offering price during the day. Trading eventually closed at US$88.30 per share after the company pared some of its losses. This decline followed a first day jump on Thursday that had previously boosted the company's valuation. The event occurred as the wider artificial intelligence and technology trade began to unravel across global markets.

The listing gave Anthropic a market value of about US$1.6 trillion, ranking it among the fifteen biggest publicly traded companies. The company raised US$119.5 billion total, including US$93.5 billion from the IPO and US$26 billion from a private placement. Underwriting banks, including Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, exercised a greenshoe over-allotment option to sell additional shares to the public. These twenty-two banks earned a record US$550 million in fees, with the two lead firms collecting about US$113 million each. The offering pushed the combined wealth of the seven founders to US$166 billion.

Emmanuel Valavanis of Forte Securities said there is a buyers strike for Anthropic and the wider artificial intelligence and tech trade. He noted that many clients without allocations are not prepared to pick up the pieces from the market hangover. Raphael Thuin of Tikehau Capital said he was impressed by the wealth creation and the company's reasonable cash flow burn. However, Thuin added that he would prefer more diversified businesses and wants post IPO volatility to fade before engaging. Ravi Mhatre of Lightspeed Venture Partners said the public listing shows there is a viable business model.

The selloff affected the Nasdaq 100 Index, which fell 5.6 per cent, and the S&P 500 Index, which sank 3.7 per cent. Ann Miletti of Allspring Global Investments said demand was positive, but investors still worry about the actual returns of AI. Fund manager Olivier David of Vega IS stated he would consider buying if the stock gets close to the IPO price. The volatility index spiked to over 29, a level where companies typically do not find the market welcoming for IPOs. Employees were able to sell holdings immediately, with some 2024 options potentially worth US$66 million.

Anthropic is the first frontier AI model maker to go public and its IPO eclipsed the June SpaceX record of US$86.2 billion. The company has more than 11,900 customers delivering US$100,000 of revenue each on a trailing twelve month basis as of September. Its run-rate revenue reached US$81 billion by October 31, which was US$10 billion higher than at the end of September. The company's coding agent, Claude Code, is used by software developers and engineers at Nasa. First time stock sales raised US$258 billion this year, beating the US$195 billion haul seen in 2021.

Investors are now testing whether there is an appetite for companies pioneering AI technology rather than those making chips and data centres. The market is waiting to see if the current volatility fades and if the stock price drops below the IPO level. This debut sets the stage for rival OpenAI, which does not plan to go public before the year 2027. Spark Capital holds a stake valued at US$17.1 billion after investing US$75 million in the company during 2023. The articles leave open whether the AI trade can revive or if investors will remain on the sidelines.

stories.Headline: Global AI sell-down pushes Straits Times Index below 5,000 level
stories.Summary:
The Straits Times Index fell below the 5,000 threshold on Friday, November 20, 2026. This decline happened during a global sell-down of artificial intelligence trades. Market players are proceeding with caution after the index dropped 2.1 per cent. The slide occurred as Asian markets experienced their worst sell-off in seven months. Some investors are taking a wait-and-see stance regarding the current market volatility.

The index hit an intraday low of 4,968.35 before closing at 4,975.17. Taiwan's Taiex plummeted 6.2 per cent and South Korea's Kospi fell 5.2 per cent. Japan's Nikkei 225 was down 5.1 per cent and Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index shed 3.7 per cent. The FTSE Bursa Malaysia KLCI fell 0.6 per cent during the same period. The S&P 500 and Nasdaq fell 2 per cent and 2.3 per cent, respectively.

Kenneth Goh of UOB Kay Hian said it is hard to call a bottom. He noted the index fell in eight of the last nine sessions. Dan Chang of PhillipCapital called the 5,000 level crucial for technical support. Ritesh Ganeriwal of Syfe described the current slowdown as a reset rather than a retreat. Charu Chanana of Saxo said the Anthropic IPO showed investors remain keen on AI.

Investors who are worried point to forced selling abroad that has not finished. Margin calls increased at brokerages and private banks, according to sources and Moomoo Singapore. Asian markets are vulnerable due to heavy exposure to semiconductor and infrastructure supply chains. Three local banks came off all-time highs, while chip plays lost their footing. Many domestic plays are now trying to find their feet again.

The STI has extended its losses by more than 10 per cent since early October. The index lost about 4 per cent over the past two weeks. An AI unwind began in the US and affected broader market sentiment. AI giant Anthropic debuted on the Nasdaq on Thursday with a 17.1 per cent gain. This gain was viewed as underwhelming by some market participants.

Investors are now getting choosier about which businesses to back and at what price. Some wait to see if Taiwan and Korea steady before judging the STI. It remains unclear if enormous AI spending can translate into sustainable profits. The market is still facing concerns about valuations and elevated bond yields. Analysts are unsure if the current slump is definitive or a correction.

stories.Headline: AidFinder uses AI to match disaster survivors with aid programs as founder seeks first state customer
stories.Summary:
When the Palisades fire tore through Jonathon Nostrant’s Los Angeles neighborhood in January 2025, his house was damaged but still standing, while many of his neighbors’ homes were destroyed. After the fire, Nostrant found a tangle of federal, state and local assistance programs, each with its own forms, eligibility rules and deadlines. Survivors with insurance must also report their payouts to every agency they apply to, because FEMA cannot pay for losses an insurer already covers. Insurance was already a sore subject in the Palisades, and a year before the fire State Farm dropped roughly 1,600 policies in the neighborhood, Fortune reported as the fire burned. Nostrant said in an interview that his own insurance claim was fighting with him.

That experience led to AidFinder, a Miami-based startup Nostrant co-founded that uses AI to match disaster survivors with programs they may qualify for, explain eligibility rules and prepare applications, with survivors reviewing everything before submission. The intended customers are states, which would offer the platform to residents under their own banner. For now it is a pitch: AidFinder has not signed its first state customer and survivors have yet to use the platform, Refresh Miami reported on Nov. 17. Nostrant told the outlet the company is in talks with 30 states, including Florida, and that Craig Fugate, who ran FEMA under President Barack Obama, has accepted a seat on its board.

Nostrant has spent much of his career teaching machines to listen, launching the voice-activated alarm clock Moshi at the University of Southern California in 2008 and later founding Ivee, an early AI-powered home assistant. AidFinder applies the same idea to turning a survivor’s account of what happened into the right applications for the right agencies. The pitch arrives as Washington pushes more of the recovery burden onto states, and FEMA Administrator Cameron Hamilton has told state emergency managers to prepare to handle more of the work themselves. Recounting Hamilton’s remarks at a National Emergency Management Association gathering, Nostrant described the federal message as wanting to empower states, counties and cities to be equipped not just to respond to the disaster but to help people recover.

AidFinder’s answer is a branded front door, and Nostrant said the company is giving states the ability to launch a landing page powered by AidFinder that matches residents with recovery programs. FEMA advises survivors to photograph or film damage inside and outside their homes before cleanup and to list damaged belongings, records that support both an insurance claim and a federal aid application. AidFinder is built around the same principle, letting residents store identification, tax records and photos of their homes in a secure digital vault before disaster strikes. The question now is whether a state will pay to offer it.

stories.Headline: China and Singapore agree to deepen cooperation in artificial intelligence and green development
stories.Summary:
Chinese Vice Premier Ding Xuexiang met with Singaporean Prime Minister Lawrence Wong in Singapore on Sunday, November 22. During this meeting, Ding expressed that China is willing to work with Singapore to deepen mutually beneficial cooperation. The focus of this partnership includes artificial intelligence and green development through the use of the bilateral cooperation mechanism. Ding is currently visiting Singapore to co-chair these mechanism meetings alongside Singaporean Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong.

This initiative requires both nations to fully utilize their existing bilateral cooperation mechanism to expand their partnership. The two countries aim to sustain a strong momentum of close exchanges in science, technology, education, and culture. These efforts are intended to consolidate the public foundation for the growth of their all-round high-quality future-oriented partnership. Prime Minister Lawrence Wong specifically noted that Singapore looks forward to strengthening cooperation in the digital economy and artificial intelligence.

Vice Premier Ding stated that the bilateral cooperation mechanism meetings have continuously enriched their dimensions and yielded new achievements. Prime Minister Wong expressed his belief that these meetings will consolidate and expand the all-round cooperation between the two sides. He also suggested that both nations should further enhance people-to-people exchanges to boost mutual understanding. Wong added that Singapore is ready to advance cooperation between ASEAN and China across various fields.

This diplomatic effort occurs as Singapore prepares to assume the rotating chairmanship of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations next year. Prime Minister Wong intends to use this upcoming leadership opportunity to further the relationship between ASEAN and China. The two leaders believe that these strategic steps will build upon the foundation laid by the guidance of their respective national leaders. Both officials emphasized the importance of maintaining these high-level exchanges to ensure continued regional stability and growth.

Articles.Title: Chinese vice premier says China ready to strengthen AI, green development cooperation with Singapore - Xinhua

stories.Headline: Anthropic employee claims to solve Riemann Hypothesis using Claude AI
stories.Summary:
Levent Alpoge, an employee at Anthropic, claims to have solved the Riemann Hypothesis with the help of the Claude artificial intelligence model. This mathematical puzzle concerning the distribution of prime numbers has remained unsolved since Bernhard Riemann first formulated it in 1859. The proposed proof consists of approximately 17 million lines of Lean code and an AI-generated explanation exceeding 250,000 pages. While the code has passed formal verification checks, the Clay Mathematics Institute still lists the hypothesis as unsolved.

The achievement requires a shift in how researchers approach discovery, as Alpoge admits he does not fully grasp the underlying mathematics. Shing-Tung Yau, a Fields Medalist, describes the development as a great contribution that could start an era where answers are found before they are understood. James Maynard from the University of Oxford expressed confidence in the proof but noted that it requires further scrutiny. Conversely, Terence Tao of the University of California warned of proof indigestion, where machine arguments exceed the human capacity for comprehension.

Anthropic announced this discovery immediately after its stock-market debut, leading some to question the role of corporate publicity in science. Twenty-five Fields Medalists have warned that treating mathematics as a race could distort the discipline and prioritize speed over knowledge. Alex Kontorovich of Rutgers argued that computer approval cannot replace the intellectual process of following reasoning to develop deeper logic. These experts suggest that human supervision remains indispensable because software errors or translation mistakes could lead to flawed conclusions.

The mathematical community now faces the risk of cognitive outsourcing if people accept conclusions without retracing the intellectual journey. Future mathematicians may need to focus on formulating questions and evaluating machine reasoning rather than just solving established problems. There is a concern that students might become mere operators of systems if they abandon the fundamentals that develop intuition and resilience. The current debate centers on whether progress should be measured by the number of problems solved or by the expansion of human understanding.

stories.Headline: China Unicom launches GridTong AI platform to automate workloads for community grid workers
stories.Summary:
China Unicom launched an intelligent solution called GridTong to reduce the repetitive manual workloads of grassroots community grid workers. This platform uses Ascend computing infrastructure, large language models, and AI agents to automate data logging and reporting tasks. The system has been deployed in more than ten provincial-level regions, including Beijing, Shanghai, Jilin, Hebei, and Guizhou. It currently serves over 100,000 frontline workers and has processed more than 10 million resident demand records.

The solution requires no hardware renovation or additional equipment investment because it supports instant access through existing mobile applications. It integrates the Yunxi Open Communication Platform and Yuanjing MaaS Platform to provide AI voice reception, on-site inspection, group message comprehension, and report generation. In Beijing, the system reportedly shortened average incident submission times from three minutes to 30 seconds with a 99 percent classification accuracy rate. In Jilin city, the platform serves nearly 2,000 workers and has achieved a 99 percent closed-loop resolution rate for resident demands.

China Unicom stated that the platform was developed to empower grassroots work with inclusive AI and bridge the digital divide. The company claims the tool lowers the threshold for digital application and allows staff of all technical levels to operate efficiently. By converting unstructured data from calls and photos into standardized work orders, the company says it frees staff for more resident visits. Workers in the Huaguoyuan community of Guiyang described the system as a portable intelligent assistant that reduces reporting burdens.

stories.Headline: Global leaders and educators call for collaboration to use AI to close learning and economic divides
stories.Summary:
John Lee Chi-kin chaired a high-level session on AI ethics and social responsibility in Hong Kong on October 27 and 28, 2026. This event occurred during the Global University Presidents and Leaders Summit 2026 to discuss high-tech innovation and the future of education. China also hosted APEC 2026, which focused on the three pillars of openness, innovation, and cooperation for the Asia-Pacific community. Participants at the 2026 Global South Modernization Forum in Cairo, Egypt, also called for the effective use of artificial intelligence. These leaders aim to use technology to close divides in learning, information, and economic opportunities across different global societies.

The mission requires collaboration between governments, academia, the technology sector, and the business community to dismantle barriers to accessibility. Hong Kong serves as a bridge to ASEAN and Belt and Road Initiative countries, supported by the Chinese mainland. The Education University of Hong Kong, or EdUHK, is ranked within the top seven globally in education by QS. Since 2017, EdUHK has served as a core consultant for World Bank education initiatives in Vietnam to foster digital transformation. The university also promotes policy dialogue and talent development in the United Arab Emirates, Kazakhstan, and various ASEAN countries.

John Lee Chi-kin and other leaders believe that education is central to harnessing AI for productivity and human development. Shannon Kane, an assistant clinical professor at the University of Maryland, says candidates must be prepared to judge AI outputs. Jennifer Kidd from Old Dominion University believes teachers must understand how AI works and its different impacts on learning. Justin Reich of MIT's Teaching Systems Lab argues that domain knowledge is necessary to tell if AI output is useless. Tracy Rock from the University of North Carolina at Charlotte says faculty should be critical rather than just AI cheerleaders.

Novice educators are affected by these changes, as over half of teachers now use AI for parts of their jobs. A 2023 ISTE report found that 56 percent of new teachers lack confidence in using technology in the classroom. K-12 school districts are affected by inconsistent policies, with some districts banning AI while others embrace the new technology. Students at George Mason University in Fairfax, Virginia, are now studying the benefits and drawbacks of AI in instruction. Many teacher candidates are also affected, though nearly a quarter of them do not want AI preparation in programs.

Teacher preparation has long struggled to effectively prepare aspiring teachers to integrate technology into their classroom instruction. An EdWeek Research Center survey of 268 teacher educators in August and September 2026 revealed various hurdles in AI integration. About 60 percent of faculty members decide individually whether to include an AI focus in their specific university courses. Many programs struggle to offer AI instruction because other priorities and national accreditation standards take precedence over new technology. Faculty professional development is limited, with only 14 percent of respondents reporting that they receive ongoing professional development.

Next, programs must navigate the rapid development of AI, which 57 percent of respondents cited as a major hurdle. Faculty at the University of North Carolina at Charlotte are using communities of practice to learn about tools like Gemini. Some instructors, like Jennifer Kidd, must revamp their course materials every single semester because the technology changes so quickly. The articles leave open whether K-12 school district leaders will actually prize AI skills when hiring new teacher candidates. It remains unclear if high-quality research will soon prove whether AI tools can actually improve student learning outcomes.

stories.Headline: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO amid chip supply allegations and personal scandal
stories.Summary:
Jensen Huang resigned as president, chief executive and director of Nvidia on November 12, 2026. He stepped down four days after he publicly apologized for having an extramarital affair. Huang had spent 33 years building the company into the engine of the AI boom. His departure followed allegations regarding his relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Megaspeed. He also faced claims that restricted chips were improperly supplied to businesses she controlled.

The crisis involves Megaspeed, a Singapore data center company transferred in March 2023 to Alice Huang. Speedmatrix, a Malaysian subsidiary, bought between 4.13 and 4.81 billion dollars of chips from May 2024 to February 2026. New U.S. rules on November 16 designate Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand as high-risk transshipment destinations. These rules target data centers with roughly 750 Nvidia H200 chips providing remote access to American technology. Nvidia's China revenue for fiscal 2025 was about 25 billion dollars.

Jensen Huang stated he would be willing to return to his leadership role at the company. The board of directors rejected that prospect despite a petition with 204,000 signatures calling for his return. CFO Colette Kress is now the interim CEO while the company faces intense regulatory pressure. California's attorney general served Nvidia with a subpoena on November 19 regarding these various allegations. Huang is required to appear at a House hearing on December 1.

Tencent and Alibaba executives said restrictions would delay products and accelerate reliance on domestic Chinese chips. Martin Lau of Tencent noted the next Hunyuan model could take longer to release due to these rules. A senior Chinese cloud executive claimed the policy would effectively wipe out overseas computing support in one stroke. ByteDance is seeking computing capacity in North America to reduce its exposure to disruptions in Southeast Asia. Alibaba CEO Eddie Wu said the rules would affect services planned for next year.

Megaspeed was originally a subsidiary of Chinese gaming company 7Road before its assets rose to nearly 3 billion dollars. The U.S. Commerce Department began investigating in 2024, and the Justice Department took over on November 17. Nvidia's off-balance-sheet commitments and guarantee exposure total about 550 billion dollars, with potential losses of 118 billion dollars. The company's third-quarter revenue was 115.8 billion dollars, which represented a 103 percent increase year-over-year. Huang and his wife held only 3.58 percent of shares under a one-share, one-vote structure.

Morgan Stanley warned that development and execution risks could rise over the next 12 to 18 months. Republicans moved to tighten chip controls before January after Democrats won midterm majorities in the government. President Trump said he might allow sales of the latest Nvidia chips in two or three years. The articles leave open whether the Justice Department investigation will lead to formal findings of guilt. It remains uncertain if the AI buildout will be shaped by governments or by corporate speed.

stories.Headline: Zurich and St Gallen warn shared AI logic keeps client risks correlated
stories.Summary:
New research from Zurich Insurance Group and the University of St. Gallen warns that a client can switch AI vendors or deploy multiple systems and still carry the same underlying risk as a competitor using a single provider. The report, titled The AI Resilience Challenge, draws on 50 expert interviews that University of St. Gallen researchers conducted between July and September 2026. It identifies two ways AI-related losses can spread, the first being concentration risk, which arises when many organizations depend on the same provider, model or infrastructure and a single failure causes simultaneous losses across unrelated businesses. The second, correlation risk, comes not from a shared provider but from shared logic, because separate AI systems may draw on similar training data, architecture or decision rules and fail in similar ways without any common outage or identifiable trigger. The report says that connection is behavioral rather than structural and may only become visible through claims, complaints, regulatory action or litigation appearing across separate organizations.

The report says the conventional assumption that using different systems or providers creates independent exposures can break down, so two clients placing their AI risk with separate insurers may still be exposed to the same underlying vulnerability if their systems share training data or decision logic. The Lloyd's Market Association, drawing on a 2025 survey of 144 managing agent respondents, 94% of them underwriters, found boards were ranking AI risk second only to geopolitical risk on their risk registers, and the survey identified a significant absence of underwriting and claims data to price AI exposures, particularly in professional indemnity. The report uses the July 2024 CrowdStrike outage as an illustration of how concentration risk propagates, when a faulty software update crashed approximately 8.5 million Windows devices globally and disrupted airlines, banks, hospitals and broadcasters, with direct losses to US Fortune 500 companies alone estimated at approximately $5.4 billion by technology downtime insurer Parametrix, though that event was not AI-related. Unlike the EU, which has adopted a risk-based legislative framework through the EU AI Act, the Financial Conduct Authority and the Prudential Regulation Authority are applying a principles-based, technology-neutral approach to AI oversight, relying on existing rules rather than introducing AI-specific legislation.

Mario Greco, group chief executive officer at Zurich Insurance Group, said companies need to know where they depend on AI, what can happen when it fails, and be prepared to respond and recover quickly. The report recommends that organizations map AI dependencies beyond direct suppliers to uncover shared points of failure, assign clear accountability for AI decisions, and test whether critical activities can continue when systems fail or need to be overridden. It frames insurability itself as a diagnostic tool, arguing that when coverage terms tighten, premiums rise or reinsurance appetite narrows, those shifts can indicate that exposure is outrunning the evidence available to price it, and that the limits of insurability reveal where broader resilience needs to be strengthened. The Zurich AI Lab, launched in October 2025 as a collaboration between Zurich, the University of St. Gallen and ETH Zurich's Agentic Systems Lab, describes this as a continuing research programme, and the report was produced as a contribution to discussion ahead of the Geneva Summit 2027.

Articles.Title: Switching AI providers does not make clients' risks independent

stories.Headline: DeepMind Institute outlines four routes from human-level AGI to superintelligence
stories.Summary:
DeepMind Institute published an essay on November 19, 2026, outlining four ways AI could move from human-level artificial general intelligence to artificial general superintelligence. The essay stressed that continued rapid progress is possible but far from assured. The four routes are continued scaling of models and data, technological paradigm shifts, coordination among large agent populations, and recursive self-improvement. In recursive self-improvement, AI systems contribute to improving later systems. Each route presents different technical bottlenecks and measurement problems.

The essay uses AGI for systems with roughly human-level capability across almost all cognitive tasks. ASI must reliably outperform large groups of human experts on work that could take those groups years, using fewer resources and less time, across virtually all tasks of human interest. Narrow superhuman performance in chess, Go or protein-structure prediction does not qualify. The essay builds on From AGI to ASI, a technical report Google DeepMind dates to June 12, 2026, and on subsequent institute discussions. The report's arXiv text illustrates the ASI bar as reliably outperforming tens of thousands of well-coordinated experts working on one problem for ten years with technology and cultural artifacts available in 2010.

The essay estimates that global effective compute, which combines hardware improvements, AI-hardware investment and algorithmic efficiency, has grown at least tenfold per year. Extrapolating that rate for a decade yields a factor of 10 billion. For each AI agent currently runnable, the scenario implies more same-quality agents than the human population, provided those trends hold. The essay's cost example applies roughly 4x lower compute demand per year from hardware and inference-efficiency gains. At that rate, a workload costing $1 billion in compute tokens would cost $1,000 after ten years.

The essay cautions that scale by itself could still fall short of full AGI if some cognitive tasks require human assistance. With broadly human-level systems available, faster and more numerous agents could help bridge the gap to a weak form of ASI. The essay says agent coordination offers a collective route, but multi-agent scaling laws are missing. Coordination inefficiencies, misinformation, manipulation and collusion can weaken large groups, requiring institutional and organizational defenses. Recursive self-improvement adds feedback loops through code and hardware designs, reusable data produced during deployment, or specialization within agent groups.

The essay identifies physical, logical and complexity constraints that would prevent arbitrarily precise predictions of real-world systems, including climates, immune systems and human societies. Human-level AI is therefore one point on a continuum, with a large and largely uncharted range between it and those limits. Continued scaling faces possible exhaustion of high-quality training data, diminishing returns as each capability step requires multiplied compute and model size, and physical or economic limits involving power generation, grids, chip fabrication and hardware interconnects. Scaling laws fitted to current architectures, data and evaluations cannot confidently predict how much scale AGI or ASI would require. Researchers are divided over whether incremental changes to the prevailing transformer paradigm can close gaps in continual learning, world modeling, decision-making and sample efficiency, or deeper shifts will be required.

The essay argues that if one pathway stalls, economic and geopolitical competition can shift effort toward the others, so restricting only training compute would not necessarily stop overall progress. Suppressing one input while others advance could also create a capability overhang, followed by steeper gains when the constraint is relaxed or circumvented. The proposed response is to model, measure, forecast and repeat through interdisciplinary work spanning frontier labs and national and global institutions. Some necessary metrics require frontier-model access, sizable evaluation compute and new benchmarking and modeling methods. Whether those pathways will produce ASI, and on what timetable, remains unresolved.

Articles.Title: DeepMind Institute Maps Four Routes From AGI to Superintelligence - Unite.AI

stories.Headline: FACT Coalition policy director urges US to end offshore tax breaks in AI supply chain
stories.Summary:
Zorka Milin, policy director at the FACT Coalition, published an article on November 23, 2026, in Bloomberg Tax arguing that the US must break the AI supply chain’s addiction to offshore tax breaks. The article says Anthropic’s record-setting initial public offering underscores enormous investor enthusiasm surrounding artificial intelligence. It says the company’s newly released financials have revived a question that has hung over the industry for years about whether companies like Anthropic and OpenAI will ever turn a profit. It says that even if Anthropic turned profitable tomorrow, it might be years before it owed any tax. It says that if the company became hugely profitable, history suggests those profits might simply be moved offshore to avoid US tax.

The article says the AI supply chain has three broad parts: hardware, cloud computing and training data, and foundation models and customer-facing applications. It says Micron reported that its operations in Singapore cut its total tax bill by nearly $6 billion, the largest savings from a tax haven yet seen in newly expanded tax disclosures. It says Micron reported only about 5% of its global profit in the US in 2026, even though nearly 70% of its revenue comes from US customers. It says Broadcom reported saving about $2.7 billion through tax incentives in Singapore and Malaysia in fiscal 2025, before accounting for US taxes on foreign income. It says Marvell, Qualcomm, and KLA reported savings of $396 million, $195 million, and $135 million, respectively, from Singapore last year.

The article says Microsoft saved $3.5 billion last year through its Irish operations, and Oracle saved more than $1 billion through Bermuda, Malta, and Switzerland. It says Dell and IBM also reported hundreds of millions of dollars in savings from tax havens, and Apple reported more than $5.2 billion in tax benefits from Ireland and Singapore. It says 10 companies deeply embedded in the AI supply chain used offshore tax havens to shave more than $20 billion off their tax bills last year. It says the US taxes the foreign income of its multinationals at 12.6%, well below the statutory 21% rate for domestic income. It says Singapore’s implementation of the global minimum tax shaved more than $9 billion off Micron’s projected savings from tax incentive arrangements in the country.

The article says the US has not adopted the OECD standard agreed to by more than 140 nations, so it collects none of the new revenue the minimum tax has unlocked. It says Broadcom’s financial statements indicate that weaker US rules for foreign income recouped only around half of the $2.7 billion the company saved from Singapore and Malaysia in 2025. It says the deduction for foreign-derived intangible income taxes income from sales abroad at a preferential rate of 14%. It says FDII saved Google nearly $4 billion last year and Nvidia more than $4.2 billion, while Qualcomm reported more than $1.6 billion in benefits across 2025 and 2026 and AMD and KLA each saved hundreds of millions last year. It says defenders of FDII say it raises revenue by drawing taxable income back to the US.

The article says recent proposals to tax AI companies directly include taxing energy consumption or compute, or denying certain corporate tax subsidies to AI data center investments. It says economist and UCLA Law School professor Kimberly Clausing proposed raising the corporate tax rate to 27%, tightening tax rules for foreign income, and repealing the FDII export subsidy, raising nearly $4 trillion over the next decade. It says international tax reforms alone could raise as much as $1 trillion, much of it from hyperscalers. It says Congress failed the same test after the internet and social media booms. It says voters are increasingly anxious about AI, opposed to new data centers, and eager to see the largest corporations finally pay their fair share.

The article says tightening US rules for foreign income by raising the rate and aligning more closely with the OECD standard could bring in hundreds of billions of dollars in revenue. It says the 15% global minimum tax is already clawing back billions in savings that many American companies once enjoyed in low-tax countries. It says the article does not necessarily reflect the opinion of Bloomberg Industry Group, Inc., the publisher of Bloomberg Law, Bloomberg Tax, and Bloomberg Government, or its owners. It says Milin leads international tax policy and other transparency priorities at the FACT Coalition. It says readers interested in writing can review author guidelines and submit pitches to Insights@bloombergindustry.com.

Articles.Title: US Must Break AI Supply Chain’s Addiction to Offshore Tax Breaks

stories.headline_source: US Must Break AI Supply Chain’s Addiction to Offshore Tax Breaks

stories.Headline: Insurers seeking more AI value need private and sovereign controls, Tim Staebler writes
stories.Summary:
Tim Staebler of NTT DATA wrote on November 13, 2026 that insurers wanting to use more AI may need more control, in an article published on nttdata.com dated November 14, 2026. He wrote that enterprise AI has become good at deploying AI in areas where it does not make a huge difference. He said productivity assistants, search and summarization are useful, citing finding an underwriting guideline on SharePoint in seconds. He wrote that these activities do not change the economics of an insurance company. He said there is more value in AI deeper in the business, such as an underwriter spotting a risk, a claims team settling a case in minutes, or thousands of routine policy changes handled without manual intervention.

Staebler wrote that deploying AI in these areas is much harder because the data is sensitive and may have to stay within a particular jurisdiction. He wrote that the decisions have financial and regulatory consequences, and the model needs answers that are both plausible and reliable. He said the insurer may need to explain exactly how the AI got there. He wrote that the closer AI gets to the heart of insurance, the less casually it can be deployed, which brings private and sovereign AI into the picture. He described two projects, one summarizing meeting discussions and producing action items, the other reviewing claims histories, medical information and proprietary underwriting data to assess a complex risk.

Staebler wrote that the first project is relatively easy to approve while the second could create far more value but raises questions about privacy, security, regulation, explainability and control. He said the lowest-impact use cases often move fastest because they are easy to govern, while those with the greatest potential can spend months between a promising business case and a nervous risk committee. He wrote that private and sovereign AI can break that deadlock by giving insurers more control over where sensitive data is processed, who can access it and how workloads are governed. He said sovereignty is not only about restricting where AI can operate but can expand where AI can safely create value. He wrote that an AI assistant drafting an email is not the same as an underwriting agent assessing a multimillion-dollar risk.

Staebler wrote that private AI and sovereign AI are often discussed as though interchangeable but are not. He said private AI is mainly about controlling the environment in which AI operates, while sovereign AI asks who ultimately controls the data, models and infrastructure, where these reside and which jurisdictions have authority. He wrote that sovereignty is not an on-off switch, and an insurer might keep customer data in-country but use a model operated elsewhere. He said smaller, specialized models can now handle tasks that once required bigger models, and you do not necessarily need a frontier model to classify a claim or extract information from a policy. He wrote that few insurers need to own every model, GPU and layer of infrastructure, and insisting on controlling everything can become an expensive solution to a problem you did not have.

Staebler wrote that an underwriting process deeply dependent on one model and its proprietary services faces risk when a better model arrives or new regulation limits that service. He said today's indispensable model could be a commodity by 2028, while the provider, pricing or regulatory environment could change just as fast. He wrote that architecture needs to survive changes in models, economics and regulation, or you risk building the next generation of legacy systems with the newest technology. He said the first phase of enterprise AI was about proving the technology worked, and now it must be trusted with something valuable. He wrote that knowing you have 137 models in production is interesting, but knowing one cut claim-processing time by 20% or reduced loss-adjustment expense is more useful.

Staebler wrote that the choice is not between public, private and sovereign AI, and insurers will need all three applied according to the value at stake, the sensitivity of the data and the consequences when something goes wrong. He said what looks like a constraint may ultimately be what allows you to use AI far more ambitiously. He directed readers to an IDC InfoBrief on AI in insurance sponsored by NTT DATA to explore how insurers can align AI architecture with value, risk and control. He described himself as Global Data and AI Practice Leader for Insurance at NTT DATA, Inc., based in Chicago, Illinois, with previous roles at NTT DATA, Slalom, Deloitte and Columbia University in New York City. The article was filed under topics AI Services and Insurance, with a copyright line of 2026 NTT DATA, Inc.

stories.Headline: OX Security finds AI agents follow unverified instructions from tools with no identifiable owner
stories.Summary:
OX Security said its research team analyzed 542,207 open-source software components between July and October 2026, using its early-warning system OX.Radar to track four ecosystems: npm, PyPI, MCP servers and Agent Skills. The company said researchers then investigated the suspicious components the system identified. According to OX Security, the findings point to a new attack path and a growing verification gap, in which instructions are becoming an attack path alongside code execution. The company said attackers can now manipulate an agent into taking actions with permissions it already has, and that security teams cannot verify what their agents connect to. OX Security said AI agents connect to MCP servers, load Agent Skills and pull packages from public registries, then act on what those components tell them, often with access to files, credentials, development tools and enterprise systems.

The company said many agents are taking orders from strangers, meaning tools with no identifiable owner that run code no one can verify before it is already in the environment. It said the attack surface is expanding from code that runs to instructions that agents follow. OX Security compared the situation to the old warning against plugging in a USB drive found somewhere, saying agents break that rule every day. Neatsun Ziv, CEO and co-founder of OX Security, said companies are giving AI agents access to critical systems while relying on trust signals built for a different era. He said the problem is not just what a tool can do, but who controls it, what code it actually runs and what instructions it can give an AI agent.

Ziv said a new model for software trust is needed. The company said it published a full report on the findings. OX Security said the research covered npm, PyPI, MCP servers and Agent Skills, and that its researchers investigated the suspicious components OX.Radar identified. The company presented the results as evidence of a growing verification gap rather than a single incident. It did not say in the article what specific malicious components were found or what happens next.

stories.Headline: Cipher Digital falls 5% as AI selloff outlasts Anthropic’s Nasdaq debut
stories.Summary:
Cipher Digital fell 5% this morning with no news of its own, as the AI selloff outlasted Anthropic’s record Nasdaq debut. Anthropic, the biggest IPO on record, fell in premarket trading a day after closing 17% above its IPO price, and the AI selloff rolled on. CoreWeave is down 7%, and IREN is off 7%, as the market sells AI data center stocks as one group. Nebius is down 7%, and it and CoreWeave build their clouds on Nvidia’s chips. After Thursday’s close, California’s attorney general subpoenaed Nvidia, CoreWeave’s key supplier and backer.

Cipher had $16.6 billion of contracted revenue across three campus leases as of Sept. 30. Analysts expect revenue to jump from $159 million in 2026 to $828 million in 2027. The stock is down 55% in 2026, and its forward price/sales multiple has fallen to 4.7x against a three-year average of 11.4x. Total debt reached $5.62 billion by Sept. 30, against $660 million of cash and short-term investments, before October’s $850 million convertible note sale. Bernstein called Cipher’s signed campuses fully funded in a Nov. 4 note, so the open question is the next lease.

Cipher has not signed a new campus lease since March, and its campuses are all in Texas. Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa campaigned on halting data centers until lawmakers pass protections. A fourth lease funded mostly with project debt would let the stock trade on its contracts. IREN’s AI cloud revenue nearly tripled from the quarter before to $200 million in the quarter to Sept. 30.

Its revenue backlog grew 22% to $20.3 billion, and its target of more than $4 billion in annualized run-rate revenue is fully contracted and funded, though the date has slipped to January. TIKR tracks 22 analysts on Cipher Digital. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Law firm leaders propose a single budget to fund junior associate training as AI takes over first drafts
stories.Summary:
A Bloomberg Law commentary published on November 23, 2026, by Kristina Bakardjiev, a former partner and current director of emerging AI at Cozen O’Connor, and Vincent R. McGuinness Jr., the firm’s president and managing partner, argues that law firms must decide who pays to build judgment in junior attorneys now that agentic AI performs the document review, summarization and first drafts that once justified billing first- and second-year associates at a multiple of cost. The authors point to Fortis Advisors LLC v. Krafton in the Delaware Court of Chancery, where a South Korean gaming company’s CEO asked ChatGPT how to avoid a $250 million earnout owed to the founders of the studio behind Subnautica, locked the founders out of the publishing platform and fired them for cause, and the court admitted records of the AI-assisted strategy as evidence of pretextual intent, reinstated the studio chief and extended the earnout. The parties settled the case this June, and the authors say a privileged call to a lawyer could have exposed the flaw in a plan that depended on the acquired company failing. The authors describe the economic exposure firms face, noting that juniors carry the lowest realization rates, that 82% of associates leave within five years and that BigHand puts the cost of each third-year departure near $1 million.

They say firms’ spending on technology tools and associate training is diffuse and duplicative, with recruiting, professional development, knowledge management, innovation and legal technology each holding separate budgets and claims on the same lawyers’ hours, and they propose a single professional advancement budget. They trace pricing history, noting that firms closed engagements with a single line for professional services rendered until hourly billing became more standard after the US Supreme Court struck down minimum fee schedules in Goldfarb v. Virginia State Bar in 1975, and they say nearly three-quarters of US law firms now offer alternative fees while AI-native entrants publish flat per-document prices for work once assigned to first-years. They suggest a transparently negotiated flat fee for associate-level work, reasonable under Model Rule 1.5 and consistent with Virginia Legal Ethics Opinion 1901, might keep AI-driven efficiency inside the firm. The authors recommend tying every approved tool to a specific use case and realistic practice problem, using AI simulators as aviation uses flight simulators, and they cite the 2026 Citi Hildebrandt Client Advisory reporting that 86% of large firms plan to grow associate ranks through 2027, only 35% intend to grow first-year classes and 25% expect AI to change their leverage model, up from 9%.

They propose making supervision a compensated bridge role for senior associates and junior partners, with billable-hour credit capped near 100 hours a year and tied to outcomes clients recognize such as satisfaction, delivery against milestones and fewer revisions. They suggest financing this from a reinvestment pool built on measured realization gains, using 24 months of billing data to baseline first- and second-year time, tracking AI use with task codes and running a control group against a test group. In their example, 20 junior associates billing $13 million and losing about $2 million to write-downs show a realization rate near 85%, and improving realization by five points returns $650,000 while reducing departures from four a year to three avoids roughly $250,000 in hard replacement costs. Against that, they say five supervisors each earning up to 100 credited supervision hours at a collected rate of nearly $600 represent roughly $300,000 in forgone collections, assuming they already meet their hourly targets, leaving a net pool of about $600,000, or $30,000 per junior associate, and even a pessimistic three-point gain recovers $390,000, leaving a pool near $340,000, or $17,000 per associate. They also urge returning some recovered time to the lawyers carrying the load, and they say a cross-functional steering group should own any AI pilot, start in two practice groups, report quarterly and expand to groups clearing realization thresholds while experimenting with fixed fees for AI-streamlined matters, restructuring toward fewer execution hours and a stronger supervisory middle tier if the pilot works and running a post-mortem if not.

stories.Headline: TensorWave signs six-year deal to supply OpenAI with 457 MW of AMD-powered AI infrastructure
stories.Summary:
TensorWave signed a multi-year partnership with OpenAI to provide 457 megawatts of AI infrastructure powered by AMD hardware, the company announced on November 17, 2026. TensorWave is the infrastructure provider supplying the capacity, OpenAI is the recipient, and AMD is the silicon supplier whose hardware powers the deployment. The announcement appeared under TensorWave's dedicated TensorWave & OpenAI partnership coverage and was reported by Ashish Joshi. The 457-megawatt figure is the total scale of the deployment covered by the partnership rather than a partial tranche. The multi-year structure indicates sustained provision of infrastructure over the life of the agreement rather than a one-time transaction.

Futurum reported on November 19, 2026 that the agreement is a six-year, 457 MW infrastructure deal to deliver dedicated AMD Instinct MI455X GPU capacity across multiple U.S. data center sites. The deployment will use AMD Instinct MI455X GPUs in infrastructure purpose-built for AMD Helios rack-scale systems, with dedicated single-tenant capacity connected through high-performance Ethernet networking. TensorWave expects to bring the first capacity online in the first half of 2027 and complete the full deployment by early 2028. The deal makes TensorWave the first publicly announced neocloud provider supporting the OpenAI-AMD strategic collaboration, which targets 6 gigawatts of AMD Instinct GPU deployments beginning with 1 gigawatt in 2026. The agreement is TensorWave's largest to date.

AMD SVP of AI Vamsi Boppana stated that the three-way combination is building the foundation to deliver AI compute at extraordinary scale and advance the broader AI ecosystem. TensorWave President Piotr Tomasik said the ability to deliver hundreds of megawatts of advanced compute reliably and at speed will separate the companies that can support frontier AI from those that cannot. TensorWave was the first public cloud to deploy AMD Instinct MI300X GPUs and has continued expanding across successive generations including MI325X and MI355X. That track record as an AMD Helios launch partner gave OpenAI confidence in TensorWave's ability to operate purpose-built Helios rack-scale systems at extreme scale. TensorWave has more than 2 gigawatts of long-term data center capacity already secured.

In January 2026, Cerebras secured a strategic multi-year $10 billion compute agreement with OpenAI, validating its hardware for the most demanding frontier AI applications. In late February 2026, Meta announced a multi-year agreement to deploy up to 6 gigawatts of AMD-based infrastructure, including the co-design of custom Instinct MI450-based GPUs. OpenAI is deliberately distributing compute commitments across multiple vendors and infrastructure models, which reduces single-source dependency and ensures redundancy for large and complex AI model training and inference workloads. Hyperscalers bring their own software, operations teams, and increasingly their own silicon, whereas neoclouds, enterprises, telcos, and sovereign AI factories need the GPU vendor to supply much of the operating stack. For AMD-centric workloads, that distinction makes a dedicated neocloud like TensorWave a more natural fit than a hyperscaler optimized around its own silicon.

The agreement illustrates how frontier AI compute demand has grown to a scale where purpose-built, long-term neocloud capacity contracts are becoming the preferred procurement model for leading AI labs. At 457 MW committed over six years, this single neocloud deal illustrates how large individual infrastructure tranches within the 6 GW program will be. Multi-year, multi-hundred-megawatt, single-tenant capacity contracts with specialized neocloud providers are displacing the on-demand hyperscaler model for the most demanding workloads. The procurement logic is built around guaranteed capacity, hardware specificity, and operational control rather than flexibility and shared tenancy. As frontier model complexity continues to grow, this template is likely to become the norm rather than the exception for labs operating at OpenAI's scale.

What to watch includes whether TensorWave brings initial AMD Helios systems online on schedule in 1H 2027 and which additional neocloud providers announce roles within the 6 GW OpenAI-AMD program in Q1-Q2 2027. Also to watch is how NVIDIA-aligned neocloud providers respond with comparable long-term capacity offerings to retain frontier AI customers. Further items are whether Meta's up to 6 GW AMD infrastructure commitment advances to named neocloud or operator announcements in early 2027 and whether additional multi-year, dedicated-capacity agreements with new vendors are announced as the broader 6 GW AMD program scales through 2027. The articles leave open which additional neocloud providers will join the program and how NVIDIA-aligned providers will respond.
