stories.Headline: Security practitioners share AI prompts that help CISOs audit policies, vet vendors and red team runbooks
stories.Summary:
The article, published by CSO Online on 23 November 2026 and written by John Edwards, sets out AI prompt ideas that security leaders can use, gathered from security practitioners. Dzmitry Romanov, cybersecurity team lead and senior security engineer at the Belarusian State University of Informatics and Radioelectronics and cybersecurity team lead with Vention, advocates a prompt that acts as a second security reviewer. Philippe Dourassov, AI pentest lead at Aikido Security, offers an adversarial agent prompt aimed at agent helpers. Brandyn Fisher, senior penetration testing technical lead at Centric Consulting, offers three prompt ideas for CISOs to deploy regularly. Kevin Surace, described as a Gen AI pioneer, offered a similar prompt idea to attendees of this year's CSO Conference and Awards in May.

Romanov says his adversarial prompt works most effectively when analyzing architecture or code, reviewing penetration test results, auditing cloud configurations, modeling threats and assessing risks. Dourassov says a second agent deployed to analyze another agent's work and correct its output can be surprisingly efficient, with the task of eliminating noise, rectifying claims and highlighting the true importance of the first agent's result. Fisher's first prompt is a vendor due diligence prompt that takes the organization's risk thresholds and the vendor, benchmarks the vendor, sweeps the Internet for security pages, breach history, customer reviews, complaints and recent news, and returns a structured report. Fisher's second is a professional writing prompt that reframes technical analysis into language a CIO or board will engage with, and his third is a tech debt reduction prompt that lists the technology stack and has AI flag underutilized tools, overlapping capabilities and consolidation opportunities. Surace's example prompt tells the model it is writing the cyber risk section of the board deck with four minutes of board time and ninety days of security operations data, producing three slides for a board that does not know what lateral movement means.

Fisher advises building each recommendation as a standing agent, project or skill, or whatever the AI platform supports, so there is a static, repeatable spot to run it instead of rewriting the prompt each time. He adds that people should not wait for a perfect first version, should get an initial prompt working even if rough, should have AI help draft the instructions, and should expect to revise it several times before it is reliable. Surace told the CSO Conference that CISOs can use AI prompts to audit policy libraries, with an example prompt casting the model as a compliance auditor given the policy library and the current text of NIST CSF 2.0, ISO 27001:2022 Annex A, SEC Form 8-K Item 1.05 and the EU AI Act, producing three lists of contradictions, gaps and stale language. He noted that this is the kind of analysis big firms do for six figures in 12 weeks. Surace also advised attendees to red team their own runbook, with an example prompt casting the model as the operations lead for Scattered Spider and giving it the incident response playbook, detection coverage matrix and on-call tree to identify the five places the runbook fails.

Olivia Brännlund, CISO at Outpost24, a cybersecurity and risk management firm, regularly uses a similar prompt that turns AI into an internal auditor and security advisor reviewing policy, processes, risk assessment, incident reports, contract clauses and specific customer requirements. Brännlund believes organizations that treat AI as an expert reviewer typically obtain more value than those that treat it as a content generator, and says the key isn't using AI to write content but using it to challenge content. Chris Hughes, who teaches in the CISO and Leading Enterprise Agentic AI Development Certificate Program at Carnegie Mellon University's Heinz College, advises asking the model what AI agents can actually do by giving it an agent's configuration, tool manifest or MCP server definitions and asking it to summarize the agent's effective permissions, the blast radius if it is compromised, and whether a human approval step exists anywhere in the workflow. Hughes says most organizations are deploying agents faster than they are documenting what those agents can reach, and that this closes the gap in minutes. Steve Tait, CTO at cloud security firm Skyhigh Security, suggests a prompt response inspection that understands both data and intent, so CISOs can determine not only whether sensitive information is entering or leaving an AI service but whether a user or agent is attempting something risky such as prompt injection, jailbreaks, policy evasion, credential exposure or unauthorized data access.

The article says that for all the talk of AI use by attackers and defenders, little attention is paid to ways CISOs and their security pros can leverage AI uniquely to expedite tasks, cut through the noise, facilitate decision-making and potentially save big on auditing. It says several specific AI prompts can help security leaders and staff handle multiple critical tasks not typically associated with AI for cyber defense, such as risk management, compliance, policy development and critical thinking. It says developing truly useful prompts isn't particularly easy, because it often requires a significant amount of research and effort, not to mention lots of fine-tuning, which can take security teams away from other critical tasks. It says the security community is here to help, with advice on unique prompt ideas that have greatly aided them in strengthening security, facilitating decision-making and saving time for hands-on defense. The article is by John Edwards, who it says has likely written more articles focusing on technology industry issues than anyone else in history.

Surace said of red teaming the runbook that it is totally worth doing and that you will have more information in an hour than you have ever had. Hughes says the model turns work that normally requires a senior architect into something an analyst can run at design review, before deployment and after every change, and that it surfaces assumptions the team stopped questioning. Hughes notes the model doesn't share your blind spots, so it tends to flag the over-permissioned tool or the missing approval gate that everyone walked past, and that once tuned the prompt becomes a control in its own right rather than a one-off exercise. Tait believes CISOs should think of prompt security as a platform control that needs to work across every major access path to AI, including Secure Web Gateway, zero trust network access, browser-based access and APIs, and says the goal should not be to plug a single gap for one AI application but to establish a consistent policy and inspection layer wherever users or agents interact with AI services. Tait adds that this means choosing an approach that can support hybrid environments, including organizations that still rely heavily on on-premises SWG infrastructure.

stories.Headline: V2 AI drives AI-powered SDLC adoption across large financial enterprises
stories.Summary:
Organisations facing higher customer expectations and volatile market conditions are turning to AI agents to speed business growth and to accelerate their software development lifecycle, according to an article on IT Brief Australia. The article says that when used strategically, AI agents let organisations release software changes two to five times more often and cut time-to-market by 30 to 60 percent. It says software is a key driver of business value, and that its real power lies in incorporating feedback to build memory for the business and evolve to meet changing needs. With AI, the article says, organisations can create faster feedback loops between customers, technology and decision-makers, creating a continuous flow from business strategy to engineering execution.

Enterprise transformation leaders call this the AI-powered Software Development Lifecycle, or AI SDLC, the article says, with AI embedded in every stage of software delivery to enhance efficiency and compound its impacts. The article says the team orchestrates a coordinated system of AI agents, with people and AI working together to deliver and run applications end-to-end. It cites Gartner estimates that AI-powered SDLC has already resulted in five to eight hours of time regained per developer, and that by 2028 teams applying AI across the SDLC will achieve 25 to 30 percent productivity and a strong competitive edge. The article says V2 AI is driving enterprise-wide AI-powered SDLC adoption across multiple large financial enterprises, and that it is witnessing firsthand the constraints of legacy software delivery models.

The article says that despite unprecedented technology investment, ideas can take months to materialise as they move through layers of analysis, development and governance, and that by the time a solution is released a critical window of market opportunity closes or the original business needs change altogether. It says the result is delays and losses in both project and opportunity costs, while organisations that deliver software significantly faster than competitors create an advantage that compounds over time. The article says the highest-performing organisations use AI to accelerate SDLC activities and elevate human decision-making, and do not use AI-powered SDLC to outsource accountability. It says humans remain responsible for approving decisions, managing risk and ensuring the resulting system meets business, regulatory and customer expectations.

The article says AI agents powered by Claude Code put AI in the driver's seat of the engineering process, with human engineers steering a team of AI agents to build out software functionality almost independently. It says AI agents can be trained for specific aspects of software development, with planning, coding and review agents operating continuously in sync, and review agents identifying high-risk paths and validating them against existing enterprise standards. Humans narrow the solution space upfront and sign off before release, the article says, and by investing effort upfront and reviewing at checkpoints, teams create the conditions for fast, accurate and scalable execution. It says the next stage is AI agents augmenting human capability throughout the lifecycle, from inception to development, quality and operations, shifting organisations from software delivery to business value delivery. The article says the future belongs to organisations that embrace AI-powered SDLC supported by governance, measurable outcomes and clear accountability.

stories.Headline: OpenText survey finds 68% of Australian firms use AI at scale despite visibility gaps
stories.Summary:
OpenText released research on 22 November 2026 showing that Australian organisations are scaling AI despite major gaps in technology visibility and operational readiness, based on a survey of 213 technology decision-makers at large organisations across six sectors. According to the research, 68% of respondents said they use AI in production or at enterprise scale, while 74% reported significant visibility gaps across hybrid IT environments. Only 19% said their IT and security endpoint data is fully aligned, which the report describes as a disconnect between AI adoption and the information needed to support it. The report covered organisations in financial services, government, manufacturing, retail, mining, and energy and utilities, representing combined revenues or budgets of about AUD $1 trillion. Legacy infrastructure remains a central issue, with 72% of respondents identifying legacy-system modernisation as a major challenge and 71% citing hybrid and multi-cloud management as a key concern.

Another 66% pointed to tool sprawl and complexity, indicating that many organisations are managing fragmented systems as they add newer platforms and services, which the report says makes it harder to maintain oversight of cloud and on-premises environments and to control operating costs. The report identified several areas requiring attention, including hybrid IT visibility, trusted operational data, infrastructure modernisation, service management links across the business, and automation with clear accountability. While 56% of respondents said their data was mostly aligned, the much smaller share reporting full alignment suggests many still lack a single reliable view across technology and security environments, and the report says fragmented or incomplete data can affect the quality of automated decisions. George Harb, Vice President for Australia and New Zealand at OpenText, said organisations need to strengthen the basics before pushing further into automation. He said AI adoption is moving quickly across Australian businesses, but the infrastructure and information needed to support it are not always keeping pace, and that many organisations are managing a complex mix of legacy systems, cloud platforms and disconnected tools.

He said that without a clear understanding of how these systems interact and support business services, adding more automation risks creating another layer of complexity. He said Australian organisations need to focus on connecting information, improving operational visibility and ensuring automated decisions are based on accurate, trusted data, and that getting these foundations right is essential to improving service delivery, managing costs and delivering meaningful returns on AI investment. The report found that IT service management is another area under review, with 76.5% of respondents saying they plan to review or are considering reviewing their IT service management platforms in the next 12 to 18 months. A further 91% agreed that a strong knowledge base improves efficiency and first-contact resolution, suggesting service management is being viewed not only as a support function for IT teams but also as a broader operational tool for managing workflows, knowledge and automation across the organisation. The survey was conducted by DataDriven and focused on large Australian organisations, and the results point to a pattern in which AI adoption is moving ahead while modernisation, systems integration and data alignment remain unfinished work for many technology leaders.

stories.Headline: Alyve CEO Mark Cameron warns Australian firms treat AI as automation rather than strategy
stories.Summary:
Mark Cameron, founder and chief executive officer of Alyve, warned that Australian businesses are adopting artificial intelligence in ways that may improve efficiency without strengthening their competitive position, according to IT Brief Australia. Cameron said many leadership teams treat AI mainly as a tool for automation and cost reduction rather than asking how it could help them enter new markets, develop new revenue streams or change the way they compete. His comments reflect a broader debate in Australian business over whether early AI spending is being directed toward operational savings rather than longer-term strategic change. Cameron, whose firm advises executive teams on AI strategy and business transformation, said that focus is becoming common in boardroom discussions. Cameron argued that the greater risk is not the direct cost of software purchases but the time lost when companies run limited trials without changing the business around them.

He said AI plans presented by senior teams often centre on making current processes faster and cheaper, which in his view risks preparing companies for an outdated model of competition while markets and customer expectations continue to shift. He said business leaders should first decide what position they want to hold in their market over the next few years, then determine where AI investment should be directed, because otherwise efficiency gains can reinforce the wrong priorities. The warning comes as organisations across sectors face pressure to show practical returns from AI spending, with back-office automation, staff productivity tools and process redesign among the easiest starting points. Cameron said that emphasis could leave boards with a misleading sense of progress, because a company focused only on internal efficiencies could still lose ground if competitors use AI to change customer experience, expand into adjacent services or rethink delivery models. He also raised concern about the use of competitors as a benchmark for AI planning, arguing that copying rival initiatives is unlikely to create meaningful differentiation.

Instead, he said, businesses should identify a small number of strengths that would make them difficult to challenge and use AI investment to build those areas, with the aim of creating difference rather than parity. He placed AI strategy closer to mainstream corporate planning than to technology deployment alone, saying leaders should link it to decisions about market direction, organisational strengths and speed of execution. Cameron also pointed to organisational learning as a factor that may increasingly separate strong performers from weaker ones, saying the value of AI lies not only in generating insights or outputs but in how quickly a business can respond to what it learns. Alyve advises executive teams on AI strategy and business transformation and has offices in Melbourne, Sydney and Brisbane.

stories.Headline: DXC and Cisco integrate AI network intelligence into DXC OASIS to speed Meraki Wi-Fi incident resolution
stories.Summary:
DXC Technology has launched a joint innovation effort with Cisco to integrate Cisco's AI network intelligence into DXC OASIS, starting with workplace Wi-Fi performance in Cisco Meraki environments, the companies said on 23 November 2026. Under the arrangement, Cisco's AI Assistant for Networking will identify likely causes of network disruption, while DXC OASIS will manage diagnostics, approvals and remediation steps under policy controls with change tracking. IT teams will retain oversight from diagnosis through to resolution, and the initial focus is on cloud-managed Meraki networks used to connect and manage workplace devices and Wi-Fi. DXC OASIS is DXC's orchestration platform for IT operations, and Cisco is contributing network intelligence, including AI Assistant, Experience Metrics and platform tools to support investigation and network actions. The effort is designed to connect network data with broader operational processes, rather than keep troubleshooting within a single management console, so an incident detected in the network can trigger coordinated checks and follow-up tasks across infrastructure, applications and service management systems.

One aim is to speed root-cause analysis by combining Cisco's network telemetry with AI-assisted diagnostics and DXC's operational processes, and another is to support a governed remediation workflow in which any action still goes through approvals, guardrails and audit tracking. A pilot cited by DXC showed incident resolution times improving from one to two hours to five to seven minutes, though DXC did not provide further details on the pilot environment and presented the result as evidence for using agentic AI with human oversight in IT operations. The first implementation centres on workplace Wi-Fi incidents in Cisco Meraki environments, connecting Cisco's AI Assistant and Model Context Protocol tools with DXC OASIS so approved actions can be taken within a structured operational process. Dan Gray, President of Global Infrastructure Services at DXC Technology, said enterprise teams do not need more alerts but faster paths to resolution, and that AI can help identify issues while realizing value requires organizations to coordinate action across people, systems and workflows. He said that by bringing Cisco's network intelligence into DXC OASIS, the companies are helping enterprises turn AI-powered insights into action, resolve issues faster, reduce operational complexity and improve the experience for IT teams and end users while maintaining human oversight and control.

Joe Vaccaro, Senior Vice President and General Manager of Network Platform and Assurance at Cisco, said enterprise networks generate massive amounts of rich operational telemetry, but turning those insights into rapid, safe remediation has traditionally required intense manual effort. He said that by integrating Cisco's AgenticOps capabilities into DXC OASIS, DXC's AI agents and engineers can collaborate across complex IT environments, delivering governed, closed-loop network automation that accelerates incident resolution while keeping human teams in control and linking back to broader enterprise context such as service management tools. The collaboration reflects a broader push by large IT suppliers to apply AI to operations management while keeping formal approval steps in place, with DXC and Cisco positioning the integration around governance and traceability as much as speed, and every action subject to policy controls and change tracking. For enterprise customers, the practical test will be whether an AI-identified network issue can move through investigation and remediation without adding operational burden, and the companies are starting with Wi-Fi performance, where user impact is immediate and the source of a problem can be difficult to isolate across devices, access points and wider IT systems. DXC described Meraki as the starting point for a repeatable model, and the companies expect to extend the same approach to other Cisco technologies over time, although they did not specify which products might come next.

Microsoft is the first company to publicly confirm its adoption of this specific Intel technology.

The implementation of EMIB requires a shift in how custom AI chips are packaged to ensure better scalability and supply. This change allows Microsoft to diversify its manufacturing sources for the high performance hardware used in Azure data centers. By utilizing Intel Foundry, the company aims to reduce its reliance on a single provider for critical semiconductor packaging. The transition focuses on the interconnect bridge technology to manage the complex requirements of multi-die chip designs.

Intel and Microsoft are responsible for this partnership and the joint announcement regarding the new packaging strategy. stories.Headline: OX Security finds prompt injection and tool poisoning in 22% of flagged MCP servers
stories.Summary:
OX Security published research on November 23, 2026, saying it had analyzed 542,207 components across npm, PyPI, MCP servers and Agent Skills between July and October 2026. The company said the research revealed two fundamental shifts, with attacks moving from execute to instruct and the traditional signals organizations use to establish trust in software no longer being enough. It said AI agents are taking instructions from third-party tools, servers and packages, and that attackers are learning how to exploit that trust. It described how prompt injection and tool poisoning exploit the instructions agents follow and the permissions they already have. The research said prompt injection and tool poisoning appeared in 22% of flagged MCP servers, compared with 16% for install or import-time execution.

It said nearly one-third of tracked MCP servers have no identifiable source owner, and just 0.4% disclose usage information. It said 82% of researcher-confirmed malicious components were already malicious in their first observed version, meaning they did not turn bad through a later update. It said one account published 2,364 servers in just 17 days, and that a handful of publishers can create common points of failure across thousands of seemingly independent tools. It also said the code you review is not necessarily the code that runs, because remote infrastructure and repository mismatches undermine traditional security reviews. OX Security is responsible for the research, and it presented the findings as its own analysis of the components it tracked.

The company said the OX Security platform is a game changer for application security teams, that it is easy to adopt and integrate into the CI/CD pipeline, and that it provides the visibility and focus needed to develop fast and secure. It said the platform supports the need for transparency and end to end traceability, giving greater control by blocking vulnerabilities and improving accuracy during the development lifecycle. It described the platform as enterprise-grade, securing applications from code to runtime and embedding real-time protection directly into AI editors and IDEs, with an autonomous security agent that connects with AI coding tools. The articles give no further context on the event and do not say what happens next.

stories.Headline: Brookings estimates $10.3 trillion in US AI infrastructure investment fuels fears of entrenched 3% inflation
stories.Summary:
The Brookings Institution estimated that U.S. AI infrastructure investment will reach 10.3 trillion dollars between 2025 and 2032. This investment boom fuels fears that 3% inflation could become entrenched as a new normal. Rising demand for electricity and semiconductors, along with construction costs, creates structural cost pressures across industry. Some warn that this shift could trigger a repricing of financial assets by lowering future cash flow values. Whether this 3% inflation level becomes entrenched remains uncertain according to the provided reports.

The Brookings Institution cited the 10.3 trillion dollar figure, which is about 13.87 quadrillion won, for the U.S. market. ABN AMRO Bank analyzed that the U.S. real neutral rate would rise 0.2 percentage point between 2026 and 2030. This occurs if annual AI investment reaches 3% of GDP in the United States. Consumer inflation reached 3.7% in the U.S. in September and 3.8% in the euro zone. The Group of Seven averaged 3.5% inflation, while OECD member countries reached an average of 4.5%.

A senior official at an economic ministry stated that inflation would be difficult to stabilize in the short term. This official noted that stabilization would remain difficult even if oil prices were to fall. ABN AMRO Bank provided the analysis regarding the rise of the U.S. real neutral rate. The Brookings Institution provided the estimates for the total U.S. AI infrastructure investment costs. These entities highlighted how data center construction increases demand for semiconductors and electricity.

Investors in financial products are advised to review bond allocations to prepare for entrenched 3% inflation. They are encouraged to diversify into inflation hedges like inflation-linked bonds and funds tied to real assets. Some warn that investors' required returns would rise if inflation stays at 3% instead of 2%. This change would affect stock, bond, and property prices currently set on 2% inflation plus a risk premium. The reports suggest that these financial assets may require a total repricing.

The reports state that data center construction increases demand for semiconductors and electricity. Costs for securing construction workers and expanding transmission networks are also rising. These factors act as structural pressure that pushes up overall industry costs. The current financial market sets prices based on a 2% inflation target plus a risk premium. This background explains why a shift to 3% inflation is viewed as a significant risk.

Investors are told to monitor the situation as the AI investment boom continues to drive costs. The reports leave open whether 3% inflation will actually become the new normal. It remains uncertain if the structural pressures from AI will permanently entrench higher inflation. Financial experts suggest reviewing portfolios to mitigate risks associated with these potential price shifts. The long-term impact on the real neutral rate depends on the scale of AI investment.

Articles.Title: AI Investment Boom Fuels Fears of 3% Inflation Becoming Entrenched - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: SK Ecoplant deploys AXen AI platform across business units to speed design work
stories.Summary:
SK Ecoplant announced on November 23, 2026, that it has fully deployed a proprietary artificial intelligence platform called AXen. This new system is now operational across the company's business units to accelerate a broad shift toward digital transformation. The platform integrates engineering and AI transformation to unify design data, work processes, and decision making into one system. It aims to reduce the time required for initial design work and the review of design changes.

The AXen platform replaces fragmented processes for regulatory checks, drawing reviews, and space layout tasks that previously required redrafting documents. It performs three core functions including the generation of equipment layout options from accumulated data and the analysis of facility interference. The system also provides an integrated search for technical information, design standards, and various regulations. Engineers can now focus on problem solving and expert judgment instead of performing simple repetitive reviews. Final results are fed back into the database to improve the precision of the artificial intelligence.

An official from SK Ecoplant stated that this platform is a concrete example of applying company wide AI transformation to design work. The representative said the company will continue to expand AI systems tailored to specific types of work to innovate operations. These efforts are intended to steadily improve project execution efficiency and the overall competitiveness of the business. The company is also developing more than 20 practical commercial projects that emerged from an internal competition called the AI Agent-thon.

This rollout is part of a larger reshaping of the business portfolio around semiconductors and artificial intelligence. SK Ecoplant is pursuing a company wide transformation that includes providing every employee with an individual AI agent. The AI Agent-thon projects cover areas such as construction cost estimate reviews and the analysis of external contracts. The company plans to expand its use of AI automation in the design process step by step starting with AXen.

stories.Headline: Hanwha General Insurance team wins financial AI contest with tool that tests product documents on simulated consumers
stories.Summary:
The 10percent team from Hanwha General Insurance won the grand prize at the 2026 Financial Artificial Intelligence Challenge. This competition was hosted by the Financial Security Institute and concluded with an awards ceremony on November 12 at the Conrad Hotel in Yeouido, Seoul. Jung Jin, who serves as a deputy general manager at the company, accepted the Financial Services Commission Chairman's Award. The winning team managed to place first among a total of 1,380 teams that entered the contest. The winning service, known as Mock Counter, uses artificial intelligence to screen financial product disclosure documents before they are released.

The system utilizes a pool of one million simulated people who are divided into 27 groups based on their age, investment experience, and financial situation. When a document is uploaded, up to 500 virtual consumers read the text and answer questions without being able to refer back to the material. This process allows the company to identify specific clauses that real consumers are likely to misunderstand before a product goes on sale. An official from Hanwha General Insurance stated that the company will pursue service innovation and financial consumer protection.

They intend to achieve this by cultivating AI talent and leveraging their existing competitiveness in digital technology. The company plans to upgrade the Mock Counter system for use in day-to-day operations to improve overall efficiency. They also intend to increase the accuracy of the tool by incorporating results from surveys conducted with actual consumers. More to follow.

stories.Headline: House committees warn Chinese AI models in US businesses pose national security risks
stories.Summary:
The House Committee on Homeland Security and the Select Committee on China released a joint report on Friday. This document warns that Chinese artificial intelligence models create national security and cybersecurity risks for American organizations. The committees launched their joint investigation in April 2026 to examine the growing use of these models. They studied how these systems are embedded in government agencies, critical infrastructure, and American businesses. The investigation lasted seven months and reviewed documents from several companies and federal agencies.

The 50-page report, titled Beijing’s AI Playbook, examines case studies of Airbnb, Anysphere, and DoorDash. It notes Chinese models accounted for 41% of downloads on the leading open-model repository over one year. The report identifies a Zhipu model capable of building cyber exploits comparable to a restricted American model. It mentions a September 2026 advisory from the NSA, CISA, and FBI regarding these security threats. The committees found that American data-labeling firms sell training data to Chinese laboratories for 500 million dollars.

Chairmen Andrew R. Garbarino and John Moolenaar stated that many Americans use AI daily without knowing it. They wrote that bringing in a model also brings in the influence of the developers in Beijing. The chairmen noted that these developers shape how information is processed and how tasks are carried out. They argued that the priorities and assumptions of the Chinese developers are embedded in the software. The report claims that these developers answer to the government of China.

The report says American firms adopt these models because they are cheap, customizable, and highly competitive. It claims the highest-ranked American open-weight model placed 10th, behind six Chinese models in one ranking. The report notes that some Chinese models generate less secure code when prompts reference U.S. government users. It mentions that South Korean banks were breached using a penetration tool powered by DeepSeek and Zhipu. These events affect any American bank, hospital, or utility that could be targeted by such tools.

The committees found that Chinese developers used proxy networks and fraudulent accounts to harvest American model outputs. This industrial-scale distillation campaign allegedly accelerated the development of competing systems with the awareness of Beijing. The State Council called for an open-source AI ecosystem with international influence to create global dependence. Developers sustain losses through state funds, state-owned shareholders, and subsidized compute to gain market share. The report claims that the assumption that Chinese models trail the U.S. by six months is wrong.

The committees recommend a national American open-weight AI initiative using public compute and federal procurement demand. They suggest NIST and CISA develop a model provenance standard and an AI bill of materials. The report proposes prohibiting PRC-developed AI models and their derivatives in federal information systems and contracts. It calls for prohibiting these models in high-risk critical infrastructure functions to protect national security. The articles leave open how the government will implement these prohibitions and manage the waiver process.

Articles.Title: House report flags Chinese AI models embedded in US businesses, cites cybersecurity and national security risks

stories.Headline: Lotte Innovate and Shinsegae I&C deploy data loss prevention tools to block leaks to outside AI
stories.Summary:
Large system integration firms are accelerating the rollout of data loss prevention solutions. Lotte Innovate and Shinsegae I&C are leading this effort to strengthen security. These companies are acting to stop confidential information from leaking to outside AI. This move happened as reported on November 23, 2026. The firms are treating security consulting and solutions as a core growth driver.

The solutions block leaks to generative AI models including ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini. These tools are considered outside AI models by the system integration firms. The measures target the transmission of company secrets, personal data, and source code. This shift requires new employees to internalize security compliance as an essential skill. The firms are building up their capabilities to provide these security services.

The Cloud Security Alliance conducted a survey of 433 IT and security professionals. These professionals identified generative AI as a major risk for data leakage. About 48 percent of the surveyed experts cited this specific security concern. However, only 22 percent of them said they strictly block sensitive information. The survey exposed a gap between AI adoption and security preparedness.

New employees are affected by these tighter guardrails and the new requirements. They must refrain from entering sensitive data into outside AI for convenience. Professional competitiveness now depends on following these baseline security rules. The articles state that employees must rethink their job skills for AI. This change makes security compliance a necessary part of their professional role.

The articles provide background on the risks associated with generative AI tools. These tools are being adopted quickly across various professional and corporate environments. Many companies are using outside AI models to increase their daily efficiency. This widespread use has created new vulnerabilities for confidential corporate information. System integration firms are responding to these risks with specialized security software.

The firms will continue to develop and deploy their data loss prevention solutions. They aim to close the gap between AI use and security readiness. The articles do not state when the full rollout will be complete. They leave open how many other firms will adopt these specific tools. It is unclear if other AI models will be added to the blocklist.

stories.Headline: LG Uplus names Kim Hong-keun to lead enterprise business in AI restructuring
stories.Summary:
LG Uplus is restructuring its enterprise business around artificial intelligence infrastructure and platforms, the company announced on Nov. 22. The reorganization for 2027 places AI data centers and fixed and wireless telecommunications networks under an AI Infrastructure Division. A separate AI Platform Division will handle AI contact centers and agent services. Kim Hong-keun, an executive vice president who previously served as chief technology officer and head of the Digital Business Division at LG CNS, will lead the enterprise business overseeing both divisions. Within the Enterprise Division, the AI Infrastructure Division will integrate AI data center operations with telecommunications infrastructure services.

The AI Platform Division will expand beyond its existing contact center and agent businesses into sovereign AI and token services. Kwon Yong-hyun, the current head of the Enterprise Division, will move to the Consumer Division. The Consumer Division will establish a Digital Business Division and reorganize its existing AI Business Group into an AI Software Division. In technology development, LG Uplus will consolidate AI research, engineering and commercialization functions previously spread across the CTO organization into a Service Development Group. The new structure will bring research and product development for proprietary technologies, including AI agents, under one organization.

Jung Sung-kwon, a senior vice president who previously headed the AI Transformation Service Development Group, will oversee the CTO organization. The Network Division will be led by Noh Sung-joo, a senior vice president who previously headed the NW Infrastructure Group, and he will oversee the transition toward AI-powered autonomous network operations. LG Uplus will also establish an AX Partnership Innovation unit and an Information Security AX unit to strengthen global partnerships and AI security. The company previously approved the promotions of Noh Sung-joo, head of the NW Infrastructure Group, and Ahn Hyung-kyun, head of the Enterprise AI Business Group, to senior vice president at a board meeting on Nov. 19. The company also appointed nine new vice presidents.

stories.Headline: UROCK showcases AI forensics tools in Oman to expand Middle East reach
stories.Summary:
UROCK said on Nov. 20 that it took part in CYSEC Oman 2026, a cybersecurity conference held in Muscat, Oman, and showed three solutions from its AI digital forensics DFAS series at the event. The lineup includes DFAS Edge, an on-device AI multimodal forensics solution, DFAS Go, a generative AI usage auditing solution, and DFAS Pro, a field-based forensics solution. DFAS Edge is scheduled for official launch in December, and it is equipped with a small language model and a neural processing unit. According to UROCK, the solution can use AI to analyze text, images, video and audio data in an integrated manner, even in closed-network and offline environments.

UROCK plans to use the exhibition to strengthen its existing partnerships with Omani government agencies while expanding its customer base into the financial, telecommunications and energy sectors. The company aims to turn contacts established at the event into commercial contracts through follow-up demonstrations and proof-of-concept projects. CEO Yoo Bong-seok took part in a national digital forensics laboratory development project and an international accreditation support initiative led by Oman's Information Technology Authority from 2014 to 2017. UROCK is currently pursuing a digital forensics laboratory development project for the Royal Oman Police and conducting a feasibility study for Oman's Cyber Defence Centre.

The Omani government has designated cybersecurity as a strategic industry and is actively promoting its development, and according to Omani government data, the country's cybersecurity market is projected to grow by approximately 8%, from $135.33 million in 2025 to $214.27 million in 2031. UROCK said demand is particularly strong for technologies capable of analyzing data in environments such as closed networks. Yoo said digital forensics is evolving into a core technology for ensuring the secure use of data and assessing information leakage risks. He said that in overseas markets it is important not simply to supply solutions but also to help local organizations develop their own capabilities to respond to cyber threats, and he added that UROCK will draw on its global business experience and AI expertise to contribute to advancing Oman's digital forensics capabilities and to establish a foundation for sustainable growth in the Middle East.

stories.Headline: Basic International launches AI SyncOps Studio for spec-driven agent development
stories.Summary:
Basic International's AI Center announced AI SyncOps Studio, an AI agent-based specification-driven development solution, the company said on November 22, 2026. The announcement follows the launch of the company's AI agent-based coding automation tool, AI SyncOps. The new solution integrates specification-driven development, in which multiple specialized AI agents collaborate around design specifications, with Agile processes in a unified studio environment. Basic International said users can monitor the status of coding automation tasks performed by AI agents in real time and control them intuitively through a single visual console. Basic International said the solution addresses problems arising from vibe coding in enterprise environments.

According to the company, vibe coding may generate code that appears to function initially but can cause data inconsistencies with complex enterprise legacy systems or introduce security vulnerabilities. The company said a more serious problem is that changes are not reflected in requirements documents or test reports, making subsequent audits and maintenance difficult or impossible. Basic International claims AI SyncOps Studio addresses these issues by systematically automating the analysis, design, development, verification and deliverable management processes of traditional systems integration projects using Agile methodologies. During the Agile-based analysis and design stages, user requirements are broken down into detailed specifications organized by epics and user stories. A Spec Agent then automatically analyzes the overall system architecture and data flows and incorporates the findings into the design, which the company said prevents uncontrolled code generation.

In the subsequent sprint-based development and verification stages, Scope Agents and Code Agents perform coding automation by writing and modifying source code within predefined areas of impact. Immediately after each task, a Quality Agent executes integration tests in accordance with the enterprise's security and quality guidelines. The solution also automatically generates project deliverables in real time. As development progresses, a Doc Agent continuously updates essential project documents, including requirements specifications, functional specifications and test reports. Basic International said this capability can significantly reduce the documentation burden associated with system implementation projects.

stories.Headline: South Korean shares fall as foreign and institutional investors sell on global chip slump
stories.Summary:
The KOSPI index plunged between 2 percent and 3 percent during early trading on November 23, sliding back to the 4,700 level. This sharp decline followed a heavy slump in major semiconductor indices and large technology stocks on the New York stock market the previous day. Foreign and institutional investors drove the sales, while retail buyers attempted to support the domestic markets. The KOSDAQ index also experienced wild fluctuations and expanded its losses from the start of the trading session.

The KOSPI opened at 4,734.90, which was a drop of 135.06 points or 2.77 percent from the previous day. Samsung Electronics fell 4.64 percent to 174,600 won, and SK Hynix dropped 3.95 percent to 1,069,000 won. Other declining stocks included Samsung Biologics at 5.39 percent, Celltrion at 4.69 percent, and KB Financial Group at 4.13 percent. The KOSDAQ started at 634.93, down 10.75 points or 1.66 percent, as growth stocks faced accelerated selling.

Market experts attributed the rout to downward pressure from the global semiconductor sector and valuation burdens on large technology stocks. An official from the financial investment industry stated that the domestic market is facing a physical endurance test as corrections in the United States deepen. This official suggested that investors maintain conservative risk management until foreign selling calms and the government stabilizes the market. The official noted that the recovery of the global semiconductor sector will likely determine the future direction of the market.

The won per dollar exchange rate rose 4.90 won to 1,341.10 as investors preferred safe assets. Foreign exchange authorities are monitoring the volatility and may implement stabilization measures to manage the currency. Market participants are also watching for the government to operate a Stock Market Stabilization Fund to strengthen defenses. Future market movements will depend on upcoming earnings announcements from major companies and the stability of large semiconductor stocks.

stories.Headline: Eugene Investment & Securities forecasts AI-driven chip equipment upcycle running through 2028
stories.Summary:
Eugene Investment & Securities said in a report released on Nov. 19 that the semiconductor equipment market's upcycle is expected to extend beyond 2027 and continue through 2028, driven by expanding investment in artificial intelligence. The brokerage forecast that equipment demand left unmet in 2027 would be carried over into 2028, laying the groundwork for a long-term upcycle extending through 2030. It said constraints on cleanroom space and supplies of certain equipment components could prevent chipmakers from fully converting their investment plans into equipment orders in 2027. According to Lam Research, the wafer fab equipment market is expected to grow from the mid-$150 billion range in 2026 to more than $200 billion in 2027, with DRAM and leading-edge foundry and logic segments forecast to post particularly strong growth that year, followed by NAND. Short-term constraints on the equipment market are therefore seen as potential sources of future growth rather than lasting obstacles, as orders delayed by limited cleanroom capacity and component shortages could be concentrated in 2028 and amplify the earnings recovery of front-end equipment makers.

Over the past three months, front-end equipment stocks posted an average return of minus 30.2%, underperforming back-end equipment stocks, which fell 14.1%, and inspection equipment stocks, which gained 5.3%, while inspection component stocks declined 2.6%. Under a bearish scenario modeled on a downturn similar to that of 2018, beginning in mid-2027, Samsung Electronics and SK hynix are projected to post operating profits of 316.2 trillion won, or approximately $237.66 billion, and 230.1 trillion won, respectively, in 2028. Those figures would represent year-on-year declines of 44% and 46%, but would still leave both companies with substantial earnings, with capital expenditure intensity ratios projected at 18.0% and 28.7%. Among individual equipment makers, TES, VM and Yesti are expected to see strong earnings growth in 2028, with Eugene Investment & Securities forecasting their operating profits will rise 33%, 57% and 57%, respectively, from the previous year.

TES is expected to benefit from deliveries of BSD equipment used in the production of base dies for foundry applications and the addition of overseas customers, while VM is projected to gain from higher average selling prices as it delivers WS equipment in 2028 and from securing overseas customers. Yesti is expected to benefit from expanded shipments of high-pressure hydrogen annealing equipment and the emergence of next-generation DRAM and NAND markets, with growth drivers including increased supplies for 1d DRAM, V11 NAND and foundry applications and the emergence of a high-pressure oxidation market for 4F² DRAM and V12 NAND. The recently raised allegations of memory price collusion involving Samsung Electronics and SK hynix are considered unlikely to be substantiated, with analyst Son In-jun saying the allegations related to memory price increases by the two chipmakers had a very low likelihood of being upheld. However, rising memory procurement costs have been cited as a factor behind weaker PC and smartphone demand and greater uncertainty over the financing of AI capital expenditure, so the resulting price burden on customers could remain a risk to market demand even if the collusion allegations are not upheld.

stories.Headline: US says it will build Super Intelligence clouds for the Philippines and Malaysia
stories.Summary:
The United States has said it will build what it calls "Super Intelligence" clouds for the Philippines and Malaysia, according to a report published by The Next Web on 23 November 2026. The report gives no further detail on the timing of the announcement, the officials involved or the sites where the clouds would be built. stories.Headline: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Microsoft join forces to set open protocols for AI agents
stories.Summary:
Rivals in the artificial intelligence industry are reportedly working together to create protocols for AI agents, according to a Sunday report by CoinDesk on the progress of the Agentic AI Foundation. The group's members include OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Microsoft, and it hopes to establish open protocols for autonomous AI agents. The goal is to prevent a fragmented internet as millions of autonomous programs prepare to conduct online transactions on behalf of users. Industry leaders caution that without unified standards, autonomous systems could quickly cause digital gridlock. The report cited an estimate from Animoca Brands Chairman Yat Siu that up to 100 billion AI agents could be transacting online within the next few years.

It also cited Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong arguing that agents will drive over 99.9% of transactions within a decade. Christopher Greenwood, CEO of Apex Fusion Foundation, told CoinDesk that without common ground rules on how people will interact and operate, it is very difficult to build something together for mutual value. Major AI companies have contributed core open-source technologies to the foundation to address the challenge. Anthropic donated its Model Context Protocol, already active across 10,000 public servers, while OpenAI contributed its AGENTS.md framework. Block added goose, and Coinbase provided its x402 payments protocol, which has already processed more than 138 million transactions.

SingularityNET CEO Ben Goertzel told CoinDesk that shared identity and security verification protocols are a positive, but dictating internal agent operations is not a good idea. He said standard protocols for agents to communicate and provide evidence of security and identity can be very good, while standardizing how agents actually operate would be bad. The news follows a warning last week by Federal Reserve Governor Michael Barr that major banks had run into AI agents attempting to act inside retail accounts without being able to determine their authenticity or customer permission. Research by PYMNTS Intelligence included in the October report "Giving AI Credit: How Far Consumers Will Let Agents Go" found that 63% would permit an AI agent to compare credit offers. It also found that 49% would allow one to complete and send in an application with their final approval.

stories.Headline: Google's Maxwell Minckler says marketers must frame why they use AI before adopting it
stories.Summary:
Maxwell Minckler, the insights lead for Europe, the Middle East and Africa at Google, wrote an article published on 22 November 2026 on Think with Google about why mindsets drive value in AI transformation in marketing. He described how a character he called “The Great Cat Detective”, invented with his eight-year-old son at bedtime, was brought to life with Gemini Omni, and how his son reacted to seeing it. He said he spends his days researching how marketers are weaving new technology into their work. He wrote that marketers at leading companies feel empowered to reimagine their workflows and roles using AI, but that the deeper question of why organisations use AI in the first place is a crucial first step. The article says there is an emerging disconnect between why many organisations push for AI and why individuals actually use it.

It says a clear organisational purpose rarely shows up on its own, and that individuals need to know why they should implement AI in their day-to-day work and why the business values that implementation. It says operating without a clear why at both the organisational and individual levels paralyses progress on AI transformation, and it explains this roadblock through the behavioural science concept of loss aversion, in which people who cannot see what a change means for them default to protecting what they already have. To overcome this, it says, leading companies turn to cognitive reframing, a technique used to challenge and replace negative thoughts with balanced, realistic ones, and it offers the reframe that AI is a revealer that commoditises what can be commoditised while revealing the parts of a job that truly matter. Minckler gave his own job as an example, saying that if he frames his job as conducting research, AI feels poised to replace him, but if he reframes his role around its real value, helping people make better decisions using research, he is empowered and can focus on the human value of his role. The article describes how leading AI companies enable this shift in practical ways, including reframe sessions, which are long-form, manager-led conversations with no slides and no training manuals, built around three honest questions about what parts of a role people want to enhance, what can be automated and what the blockers are.

It also describes AI Spotlights, unpolished, real-world before-and-after stories shared where people actually communicate, such as team newsletters or chat groups, and says these work because they model a mindset shift in action rather than showcasing a toolset or teaching a skill set in isolation. The article says mindsets matter, and that because AI toolsets and skill sets are more tangible and have clearer owners, organisations often place most of their focus on them, yet AI mindsets are equally critical in driving sustained AI adoption. It says Google's research has shown that a clear focus on maximising advantages, which it calls FOMA, is the AI framing and mindset that drives value within leading companies, and that framing the why is the crucial but often skipped first step. To help organisations move from the wow of AI to tangible business value, Minckler says Google has developed the FOCUS playbook, a five-part behavioural science framework based on multi-year research, in which marketers frame the why, own the loop, cultivate capability, uncover the unsaid and stoke the system, moving from isolated experiments to an integrated AI strategy. He says the future of marketing depends not only on adopting new technology but on how well we understand and empower the humans wielding it, and that the real magic lies in the combination of the technology and the people using it to reimagine what is possible.

stories.Headline: Dragos researchers find widespread user data leakage across AI service networks
stories.Summary:
Researchers led by HD Moore from the security firm Dragos identified significant security vulnerabilities within the artificial intelligence supply chain on November 22, 2026. The team planted 2 million digital tripwires using unique, trackable credentials to monitor how various AI services handled sensitive information. Their study revealed that AI routers and inference providers frequently expose user data to potential threats. The investigation found that at least three AI providers suffered breaches that allowed attackers to siphon prompts directly from the services.

The findings show that multiple resellers log user prompts despite privacy settings like Zero Data Retention policies. One Chinese AI lab systematically scraped secret URLs from prompts, even when those requests were routed through providers in the United States. This widespread leakage occurs because prompts are decrypted at every hop within the complex network of inference resellers. To mitigate these risks, the research suggests that users should host models on-premises or contract directly with first-tier providers to reduce intermediaries.

HD Moore stated that the current AI ecosystem has a systemic failure regarding the protection of customer data. He believes this situation poses a significant challenge for any users who rely on third-party services for sensitive tasks. The researchers used the seeding of prompts to prove that sensitive data is not being handled securely across the supply chain. This evidence highlights the danger of using intermediaries that may ignore privacy agreements or suffer from poor security.

stories.Headline: EEG study links ChatGPT essay writing to weaker brain connectivity in 54 participants
stories.Summary:
Researchers conducted a study of 54 participants who wrote essays using three different methods. One group used ChatGPT, one used a conventional search engine, and one used no tool. The researchers recorded brain activity using electroencephalography to see how participants performed. This study was reported in a segment by Deutsche Welle titled AI Cheating.

The experiment required participants to write essays under one of the three specific setups. The ChatGPT group used the chatbot, while the search group used a traditional engine. The no-tool group wrote without any external aid to isolate the tool's effect. EEG sensors on the scalp measured brain connectivity among the 54 people involved. The results are currently a preprint and have not been peer-reviewed by a journal.

Deutsche Welle asked if relying on chatbots for answers weakens knowledge and critical thinking. The broadcaster framed the issue as outsourcing brains and questioned if AI makes people think less. The reporting noted that the claim about weakening critical thinking is a paraphrase of research. It stated that the viral version of the story goes beyond what reporting supports. The segment was filed under the SHIFT banner regarding life with digital technology.

The findings affect students, parents, and employers who use chatbots instead of working things out. ChatGPT users showed the weakest brain connectivity, while the no-tool group showed the strongest. Search engine users fell in between these two extremes of reported mental engagement. ChatGPT users also reported lower ownership of their writing and had difficulty recalling text. These participants struggled to quote their own work immediately after finishing the task.

The articles describe cognitive offloading as passing a mental task to an external aid. This practice is common, such as writing a grocery list or saving a phone number. Generative AI is different because it can generate reasoning, structure, and prose for users. A separate survey from Microsoft Research and Carnegie Mellon University also looked at workplace habits. That survey associated greater confidence in AI with less self-reported use of critical thinking.

The study found an association during the task but did not prove causation. It remains unconfirmed if AI permanently weakens intelligence, memory, creativity, or critical-thinking ability. The small sample size and narrow task limit broad claims about human cognition. Future steps require replication and peer review to stress-test the methods and statistics. The articles leave open whether these findings indicate long-term changes in mental ability.

stories.Headline: Google finds an AI system that autonomously writes and launches software exploits
stories.Summary:
Google's Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant reported that they had uncovered an AI system that autonomously finds software flaws and launches exploits, according to TechGig on November 23, 2026. Investigators found an unsecured staging server that hosted a system called exploit_agent, which links to advanced cloud-based and locally run language models. This framework examines software code to identify differences related to flaws, writes working exploits, and launches them automatically. Scripts on the machine also handled later steps, including mapping internal networks, guessing passwords, planting webshells, and deleting webshells installed by rival attackers. The report describes this as a significant shift in cybercriminal operations, moving from chatbot assistance to independent attack systems.

In August 2026, attackers exploited two PaperCut print server flaws, CVE-2026-81578 and CVE-2026-82078, which allowed remote command execution without logging in when chained together. A campaign launched four days after disclosure hit hundreds of organisations through these flaws, expanding an initial foothold to domain administrator within minutes. Google also tracks open source attack frameworks such as ARTEX, CAIRN, PentAGI, CyberStrikeAI, and HexStrike AI, and the company confirmed that CAIRN and PentAGI were used against live targets. One actor ran a customised PentAGI platform that probed many Asian organisations for weaknesses from August through early October 2026.

Google recorded at least 8 zero-day exploits per month in 2025 and 11 per month in 2026, with August reaching 22. Mandiant responded to several LLMJacking incidents in 2026 where criminals drained victims' cloud computing and model quotas. Daily fraudulent bills exceeded $100,000 in these cases, with some losses reaching $1 million before cleanup. The articles do not say who is responsible beyond the actors described or what happens next.

stories.Headline: Geoff D argues that people should work with AI rather than just prompt it
stories.Summary:
The article argues that people should spend less time learning to prompt AI and more time learning to work with it, and it makes this case through two experienced creative professionals who use similar AI tools but get dramatically different results. One of them gets predictable ideas, polished presentations and the occasional useful shortcut, while the other gets sharper thinking, unexpected perspectives and work that moves forward at a completely different pace. The article says most conversations about AI still treat it like a sophisticated vending machine, where you put the right instructions in and get the right output. It acknowledges that AI can write, summarize, research, generate ideas and produce work at remarkable speed, but calls that a very limited view of what it can contribute.

The article says creative and strategic thinking rarely happens in a straight line, because ideas evolve, assumptions get challenged, perspectives shift and the first answer is rarely the best one. It says the real opportunity is moving beyond isolated requests toward something more cumulative, a way of working where context, critical thinking and intellectual exchange make the collaboration increasingly useful. It states plainly that AI does not magically become smarter with every conversation, but that the combination of human judgment, AI capabilities and relevant context can create something more effective than either working in isolation. It says much of the conversation around AI focuses on efficiency, doing more, working faster, saving time and producing more content, which it calls valuable but only half the opportunity for strategists, marketers and creatives.

The article says AI should not simply help execute an idea but should be capable of contributing to the thinking behind it, by questioning assumptions, exploring alternatives, connecting seemingly unrelated observations, making an argument stronger or explaining why it does not hold up. It says sometimes that means thinking with us and sometimes it means doing substantive thinking for us, and that the opportunity is not choosing between better thinking and faster execution but combining both. It warns that the more personalized an AI experience becomes, the easier it is to confuse familiarity with intelligence, and that an AI which consistently tells you what you want to hear could become the world's most efficient echo chamber. It calls that a serious risk for creative and strategic work, where the most valuable contribution is often the one that challenges the original thinking, and says a good collaborator should sometimes make you realize your favorite idea is not very good.

The article says that as AI becomes more powerful and accessible, the competitive advantage may increasingly come from the quality of the human-AI collaboration rather than simply the technology itself. It says the best model will still matter, and so will the skills of the person using it, but that knowing how to get an answer and knowing what to do with that answer are two very different things. It closes by suggesting the question is not whether you are good at prompting AI but whether you have developed a way of working that allows AI to tell you something you did not want to hear. The article is by Geoff D. and was updated on November 22, 2026.

Articles.Title: Stop Prompting AI. Start Working With It.

stories.Summary:
OpenAI's internal assessment found that its AI agents now complete 46 per cent of research assignments estimated to need two to four hours of human effort, according to a TechGig report published on November 23, 2026. That figure is up from 23 per cent in March 2026, the report said. Success rates for longer assignments needing four to eight hours rose from 13 per cent to 35 per cent over the same period. The report described the results as the company's latest internal assessment of how far its agents can work without help. The report gave detailed success rates across research categories between August and October 2026.

Agents reached a 79 per cent success rate in monitoring training runs but performed considerably lower when launching those runs. Writing software for inference and serving systems proved difficult, with autonomous completion at only 25 per cent. Communication tasks showed 69 per cent success and analytical assignments 58 per cent, while building research infrastructure recorded 43 per cent. Spending on coding agents rose sharply among researchers, with OpenAI estimating median daily expenditure at $2,400 in October, a 62 per cent increase from September's $1,500. At the 90th percentile, daily spending climbed to $23,000, more than doubling September's $11,000 figure.

OpenAI said human researchers remain crucial for direction, supervision and judgment. The report also said documented contributions to Safety and Alignment increased 77 per cent between January and September, attributed to recruitment and existing employees shifting their attention to safety work. Coding agents have reduced the time needed to test experimental tools from several days to just one day, according to the report. However, the report said AI systems still struggle with research judgment, software quality, experiment planning and producing reliable results, often requiring close human supervision to correct mistakes. Human oversight remains essential for software quality and experiment planning, the report said.

Articles.Title: OpenAI agents complete 46 per cent research tasks autonomously

stories.Headline: AI surveillance software creates false movement narratives by inventing journeys between camera gaps
stories.Summary:
Burak Oktenli wrote an analysis on November 23, 2026, about AI surveillance risks. He explained how multi-camera tracking can create false narratives of a person's movements. This happens when software joins authentic clips into a continuous route despite gaps. The system may invent a journey that the cameras never actually recorded. Such errors can occur when cameras lose sight of a subject.

The author mentions Hong Kong activated AI facial-recognition in its SmartView network on 16 November. The Metropolitan Police reported a 2026 pilot using live facial-recognition on existing street infrastructure. In India, AI-assisted face matching at a Delhi protest led to a legal dispute. The Metropolitan Police September 2025 report recorded 2,077 alerts and ten false classifications. Six people were approached after those false alerts, but none were arrested.

Oktenli says that high scores on existing evaluations do not prove reliability in real deployments. He argues that detection and facial recognition are different tasks from multi-camera tracking. The author claims that a strong result on one task does not establish reliability on others. He suggests that systems must flag uncertainty when they are guessing a person's path. He believes that human corrections must propagate to every downstream report before actions are taken.

The US Federal Trade Commission alleged a false match led to searching an 11-year-old girl. This 2023 Rite Aid case showed how innocent people experience consequences before corrections occur. Researchers Ergys Ristani and Carlo Tomasi noted that appearances vary with angle, light, and occlusion. They stated that similar-looking people may be joined into one route by the software. A single person may also be split into multiple tracks by the system.

The US National Institute of Standards and Technology excluded cross-camera tracking from its Face in Video Evaluation. MOTChallenge assesses tracking within a single camera and assigns fresh identifiers when people reappear. The European Union AI Act restricts certain law-enforcement uses of real-time remote biometric identification. These rules provide safeguards for exceptional uses in publicly accessible spaces. The author notes that HOTA metrics improve measurement but do not eliminate deployment testing.

Procurement should start with end-to-end trials using consenting participants and independent ground truth. Tests must count incorrect joins and broken tracks separately under ordinary working conditions. Reviewers should deliberately reject mistaken links to test if corrections reach all searchable records. Organizations must limit the retention and unnecessary dissemination of surveillance footage. The articles leave open how non-biometric tracking will be regulated under the AI Act.

Articles.Title: When AI Cameras Invent A Journey Nobody Took – Analysis

stories.Headline: Etsy lets third parties train AI on seller artwork as artists close shops in protest
stories.Summary:
Etsy updated its terms of service to allow AI training using artwork posted on its platform. This policy change caused an uproar among independent artists and small business communities. Some artists with tens of thousands of followers closed their shops in protest. These creators shared their decisions through posts on X and Instagram. The new terms of use go into effect on December 16.

The updated language appears under Section 5, titled Your Content, in the terms of use. It allows Etsy and third party partners to develop, train, test, and improve machine learning technologies. This follows clearer restrictions on AI use that the company released in October. The older terms, effective through December 15, contained no mention of artificial intelligence. The new policy grants a worldwide, royalty-free, irrevocable, and perpetual license to use content.

James Ossman, the vice president of customer operations, addressed the changes in a November 16 blog post. He stated that Etsy does not use content to train models designed to copy original work. Ossman claimed the company does not claim ownership over the creations of its sellers. He said the goal is to connect unique items with buyers. He argued that these broad rights are necessary to keep the platform going.

Some artists claim the terms allow Etsy to train generative AI on their artwork. One post with nearly 100,000 likes alleged that Etsy can resell data to third parties. Many vendors rely on the marketplace to make sales and feel their art is being scraped. These creators are affected by the potential for AI to replace their creativity. They worry that staying on the platform means their art belongs to the company.

Etsy previously stated it does not claim ownership over shop names, profile pictures, or listing photos. The company uses content to resize listings for its mobile app and translate descriptions. It also uses seller content to feature listing photos in marketing campaigns. The company trains models to identify fraudulent accounts and provide tailored recommendations to buyers. It also builds AI-powered tools to help sellers run their businesses more efficiently.

Etsy has not clarified if it uses generative AI to create advertisements from listing photos. The company has not responded to requests for further clarification on these specific practices. While the terms mention opt-out rights, the privacy policy shows no way to opt out of training. United States users can only opt out of the sale of their personal data. Courts are still deciding if it is legal to scrape copyrighted content for AI.

stories.Headline: Greg Abel says Berkshire Hathaway can fund AI power needs through its utilities and energy businesses
stories.Summary:
The article, published by The Globe and Mail on November 22, 2026, was written by Motley Fool and appeared at 6:35PM CST. It says Berkshire Hathaway's next big AI bet could be hiding in plain sight. The article states that Berkshire Hathaway is not exactly seen as an artificial intelligence play. It says the company may have more exposure to this emerging technology than you realize. The article states that the company's large utility and energy operations present opportunities for AI-related investment.

The article states that Berkshire Hathaway is usually classified as a finance business. It says the company is really a massive conglomerate with businesses including insurance, utilities, energy, manufacturing, housing, and retail. In Greg Abel's first annual letter as CEO, he reported that the company had 51 non-insurance operating businesses. In a previous letter, former CEO Warren Buffett said the company owned 189 operating businesses. The article says the definition of an operating business is probably responsible for the two different numbers.

The article states that Greg Abel is the CEO of Berkshire Hathaway. It says his acquisition of homebuilder Taylor Morrison Home for $8.5 billion suggests he is not going to suddenly shift directions. The article states that Greg Abel noted at the start of 2026 that infrastructure built for hyperscalers and data centers must be paid for by those customers. It says he said this infrastructure must reflect the risks tied to step-changes in long-term demand. The article states that former CEO Warren Buffett long focused on acquiring boring businesses that were well run and attractively priced at the time of purchase.

The article states that the company's utility operations provide the electricity that powers AI. It says the energy business helps supply the natural gas that lets utilities, and increasingly AI companies, generate electricity. The article states that Berkshire Hathaway could easily afford to buy a technology business with its cash hoard of more than $370 billion. It says Chevron, a longtime holding in Berkshire Hathaway's stock portfolio, has agreed to build a power plant that will use Chevron-produced natural gas to supply dedicated power to data centers. The article states that data center operators appear increasingly willing to pay for infrastructure built for them.

The article states that it would be exciting if Berkshire Hathaway went out and bought a giant U.S. utility such as NextEra Energy. It says it would also be exciting if the company bought a large pipeline business such as Enterprise Products Partners. The article states that Greg Abel probably would not target companies of that scale. It says the CEO could certainly afford to buy smaller players in either sector. The article states that both the utility and midstream sectors are capital intensive.

The article states that utilities own massive power plants that take years to build and require huge sums of money. It says midstream companies are no different, with their pipelines, storage, refineries, and transportation assets. The article states that it is not unusual for a utility or midstream company to have multi-billion-dollar capital investment plans extending as far as five years into the future. It says Berkshire Hathaway could make very large capital investments within its existing operations, and that this is probably the most likely outcome. The article states that Berkshire Hathaway is unlikely to start buying up AI technology businesses.
