stories.Headline: IT leaders prioritize data streaming over AI to feed real-time systems, Confluent survey finds
stories.Summary:
IT leaders are now prioritizing the infrastructure that feeds artificial intelligence over the technology itself, according to a report released on November 22, 2026. This shift indicates that enterprises are focusing on data streaming platforms to ensure information moves continuously rather than remaining locked in disconnected systems. The trend suggests that organizations are becoming more realistic about the foundational work required to make advanced technology successful. The 2026 Data Streaming Report from Confluent surveyed 4,625 IT leaders across 14 countries to identify these changing strategic priorities. In Singapore, 51 percent of respondents ranked data streaming as a top priority for 2026, while only 31 percent chose AI and machine learning solutions.

Security remains the highest overall category at 96 percent, and combined data management, protection, and governance priorities reached 90 percent. Furthermore, 78 percent of leaders reported that insufficient infrastructure for real-time processing is a major challenge, an increase from 62 percent in 2025. Greg Taylor, the senior vice president and general manager for Asia Pacific at Confluent, stated that investing in data infrastructure is essentially investing in AI outcomes. He noted that 81 percent of respondents struggle with data silos and 76 percent face inconsistent data sources. Taylor suggested that framing infrastructure as a prerequisite for performance is more persuasive than treating it as a separate expense.

He emphasized that the real value of data is realized when it is used as and when it is needed. The report highlights that 97 percent of leaders believe data streaming increases the impact of AI investments. Many organizations are seeing significant returns, with 47 percent of Singaporean firms anticipating at least five times return on investment. Beyond AI, 96 percent of respondents expect benefits in customer experience and 95 percent see a reduced time to market for new services. These findings suggest that real-time data infrastructure supports broader business goals while improving the reliability of live operational decisions.

The article describes how the question of protecting under-16s from new technology while also helping them to use it is being addressed through an NSPCC campaign. Alice Thomson, writing for the paper, saw how students reacted to that campaign. The piece sets out the tension between guarding young people against harm and equipping them to work with the tools.

The report presents the issue as a choice between protection and preparation, asking how under-16s should be shielded from new technology and helped to use it at the same time. It names cheating and deepfakes as among the concerns the discussion covers. The NSPCC campaign is described as the vehicle for addressing the issue, and the article follows Thomson as she observes students responding to it. No further figures, dates or names appear in the available text.

Responsibility for the issue is placed with the NSPCC, whose campaign the article says hopes to address it, and with the wider question of how under-16s should be protected and helped. The paper frames the matter as one of balancing protection against preparation.

The context given is the arrival of new technology, with cheating and deepfakes cited as the specific worries in view. The article does not say what happens next, beyond the campaign's stated hope of addressing the issue. It offers no timetable, no figures and no further named individuals. More to follow.

He noted that free chatbot options became more restrictive throughout 2026, including the October 2026 move by Google to shift free Gemini app accounts to Flash-Lite. Additionally, the free sign-in options for Gemini CLI and Qwen Code were ended entirely during this period. Users can access Gemini 4 Hydrogen, released on November 12, 2026, for free through Google AI Studio without providing a credit card. GitHub Copilot Free offers 2,000 monthly inline code completions and uses Copilot Fusion to route tasks to models like GPT-6 Luna.

OpenRouter provides 11 free models as of November 22, 2026, allowing 50 free requests per day for users who skip the payment method. Eligible United States college students aged 18 or older can claim 12 months of Google AI Pro, worth 19.99 dollars monthly, if they redeem the offer by December 31, 2026. Yasir explained that while these routes work, they each have specific drawbacks that users should consider before relying on them. He warned that Google AI Studio may use prompts for training purposes, and OpenRouter models can disappear without notice as promotions end. For the student offer, he advised setting a reminder because Google will charge the monthly fee after the free year expires.

He suggested that AI Studio is best for general prompts, while Copilot Free is the strongest choice for coding tasks. The author noted that free access is now primarily found through developer tools and student promotions rather than standard chatbot applications. He mentioned that GitHub Education provides free Copilot access for verified students, though sign-ups were paused from April until June 2026. He also clarified that a previous offer for four months of free ChatGPT Plus for students ended on October 31. Because free tiers are often temporary, he recommended comparing paid plans after a month of actual use.

stories.Headline: Google blocks 41 AI crawlers from accessing Google Maps pages
stories.Summary:
Google updated its robots.txt file on google.com to block 41 AI crawlers from accessing Google Maps pages. This change occurred between November 17 and November 22, 2026, according to an analysis of archived files. The company placed these bots under a shared AI training opt-out token. Google's own AI control, Google-Extended, remains in the default group to keep Maps open.

The new rules apply to 41 named crawlers, including OpenAI's GPTBot, Anthropic's ClaudeBot, and ByteDance's Bytespider. These bots are now shut out of every Google Maps page on the domain. The group uses the __usage_ai-training token, which Google, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Anthropic committed to honor on October 30, 2026. The list includes Japanese bots Cotoyogi and SBIntuitionsBot, as well as Applebot-Extended and img2dataset.

Japanese SEO specialist Masahiro Tsuji first flagged the update in a post on X at 14:03 UTC on November 22. He initially claimed Google blocked search results and goto pages, but later revised this claim. Tsuji noted that the update makes the stance of refusing scraping clear in the robots.txt file. He expressed surprise at seeing a crawler from Japanese academic institutions on the list.

Barry Schwartz of Search Engine Roundtable replied that some of these rules were added back in July. The change affects various model builders, including Amazonbot, Meta's FacebookBot, and developers from China like DeepSeekBot and QwenBot. Other affected entities include Mistral, Cohere, the Allen Institute for AI, and the Common Crawl archive. These crawlers now lose access to business listings, directions, and contributor profiles on Maps.

The robots.txt file uses a protocol where crawlers follow the most specific user agent group that matches them. Google rewrote an internal comment to ensure new named groups are paired with either the default or AI training group. This design prevents the default group's longer allow rules from overriding the training group's single disallow for maps. Most other pages, like search results, were already off limits to every crawler.

Microsoft will begin honoring these training preferences on February 1, 2027, based on the shared token. Google plans to support the token in early 2027, though private agreements may override these rules. The draft specification states that the policy token is not a directive for crawling behavior. The articles leave open why Google split its own Gemini control from the other 41 bots.

stories.Headline: IndexBox reports edge AI drives embedded smart camera market growth to 2035
stories.Summary:
IndexBox released a report on November 22, 2026, regarding the global embedded smart cameras market. This market is entering a phase of structural expansion through 2035. Growth is fueled by the migration of artificial intelligence from cloud to edge devices. These compact modules perform inference locally to reduce latency and bandwidth. They are used in industrial automation, automotive, retail analytics, and smart infrastructure.

The market index is projected to reach 245 by 2035, with 2025 as the base of 100. A compound annual growth rate of 9.4 percent is envisioned from 2026 to 2035. Industrial automation holds a 35 percent share, while automotive and transportation hold 25 percent. Retail and commercial applications account for 20 percent of the market. These changes are supported by 5G connectivity and declining costs of vision SoCs.

IndexBox reports that the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals and disciplined procurement. They state that a more regionally diversified supply architecture is now in place. The report says competitive advantage hinges on the integrated performance of optics and vision SoCs. It notes that value is migrating toward software stacks and AI model lifecycle management. The firm claims that industrial automation will remain the largest end-use sector.

Retailers are affected by demand for people counting, heat mapping, and frictionless checkout. Healthcare and smart infrastructure users adopt embedded vision for patient monitoring and traffic management. Automotive users face long qualification cycles for driver monitoring and advanced driver-assistance systems. Privacy regulations like GDPR affect the retail sector, requiring on-device anonymization. Some regions face stringent regulations due to data privacy and security concerns.

The market uses a hardware-software co-design paradigm with fragmented demand across various segments. Design and IP are concentrated in innovation hubs, while manufacturing is in electronics regions. In September 2026, U.S. communications equipment output rose 15.2 percent year over year. Computer and electronic product manufacturing producer prices rose 12.9 percent in the same month. U.S. import prices for electrical machinery and equipment rose 3.8 percent in September 2026.

Future growth depends on the integration of NPUs into vision SoCs for complex models. The market may be tempered by semiconductor fabrication bottlenecks and a shortage of AI talent. High non-recurring engineering charges and SDK licenses will continue to impact total ownership costs. Geopolitical factors and trade policies could disrupt multi-jurisdictional supply chains. The report leaves open how competition will evolve between software capabilities and factory integration.

stories.Headline: Hitachi Digital launches HARC Compose to govern agentic AI engineering
stories.Summary:
Hitachi Digital Inc. launched HARC Compose on November 18, 2026, in Santa Clara, California, according to a release dated November 22, 2026. Hitachi Digital is the global digital services company recently unveiled by Hitachi, Ltd. The product combines technology and services to govern the lifecycle of agentic engineering across complex, AI-driven systems. It does so through enterprise specific context, guardrails and intent. The release says it helps companies orchestrate AI from development to deployment through to operations and continuous improvement in a closed loop.

HARC Compose builds on Hitachi's experience and uses standardized, failure-conscious engineering. Hitachi Digital FDEs, forward deployed engineers, use it to build trustworthy AI-native applications faster and to maintain and improve AI agent performance once deployed. It strengthens Hitachi Digital's recurring service model, giving FDEs end-to-end support from ideas to outcomes. It is compatible across multi-vendor environments, and enterprises can use it entirely or opt for individual capabilities. It strengthens HMAX by Hitachi and augments HMAX Foundry solutions including HMAX Data Fabric, HMAX AI Operations, and HMAX Cyber.

Hitachi Digital is the unified brand of GlobalLogic, Inc. and Hitachi Digital Services LLC, and its legal entity is scheduled to be established on April 1, 2027. A press release on September 3, 2026 covered Hitachi expanding HMAX to accelerate deployment of Physical AI. Anand Birje, CEO and Chairman of Hitachi Digital, said HARC Compose is Hitachi Digital in action. He said the true promise of AI is not just writing code faster but shifting human ingenuity toward composing resilient, mission-critical systems. He said eliminating the divide between build and run closes the feedback loop and delivers governance and trust.

Premkumar Balasubramanian, Chief Technology Officer of Hitachi Digital, said speed is expected and trust has to be earned in an era of AI-generated software. He said customers need clarity on what a change is meant to improve, proof that it worked, and confidence in the process behind it. He said forward deployed engineers direct AI agents to build, test, and coordinate changes while maintaining strict human oversight over what goes live. He said live production evidence verifies outcomes. The release says AI has made code development faster and more productive but not necessarily trustworthy across enterprise systems.

The release says that without the right context, enterprise knowledge, company goals, policies, systems, and risk requirements, fast code becomes fast failure. HARC Compose carries enterprise intent from planning through production while keeping human experts in control of critical decisions. It includes CAKE, the Context-Aware Knowledge Engine, which connects enterprise intent, domain knowledge, systems, policies, risks, security, decision and production history and flags gaps and contradictions before agents act. An Orchestration Engine coordinates multiple agents across build, deploy and operate as one system and supports various AI agents and tools selected by customers. Failure-conscious Engineering uses failure mode and effects analysis to identify how a proposed change could fail and to decide what to test before release.

Universal capabilities include Responsible AI, which guards against system deviations such as agent drift, and guided and autonomous work that maintain human engagement. HARC Compose is built on OFE, outcome-forward engineering, a methodology used by Hitachi Digital's own FDE teams, which treats Define, Build, Deploy and Operate as one continuous system. Delivery is considered complete only when a system yields intended business outcomes in the real world, not at system release. The release lists principles including Fidelity, which establishes intent, constraints, failure risks and guardrails before work begins, and Throughput, which uses coding agents to turn clear intent into operable change. HARC Compose is available to enterprises worldwide, and deployments supported by Hitachi Digital FDEs are already underway in the finance, healthcare, and technology industries.

Hitachi Digital is a wholly owned subsidiary of Hitachi, Ltd. with approximately 35,000 professionals in 27 countries. Hitachi revenues for FY2025, ended March 31, 2026, totaled 10,586.7 billion yen, with 606 consolidated subsidiaries and approximately 290,000 employees worldwide. The release says HARC Compose capabilities are expected to expand as Hitachi Digital grows its technical talent base and ecosystem alliances. The release does not give pricing, customer names, or a general availability date beyond saying deployments are underway. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Fujitsu and FamilyMart pilot causal AI to analyze purchases of decarbonized innerwear and build a demand creation model
stories.Summary:
Fujitsu Limited announced on November 22, 2026, that it has launched a pilot study with FamilyMart Co., Ltd. to analyze consumer purchasing behavior and establish a demand creation model for decarbonized products. The study combines Fujitsu Causal AI, a core technology of the Fujitsu Kozuchi AI platform, with LLM causal technology. The initiative is part of the Model Project for Creating Demand for Decarbonized Products, a program publicly solicited by Japan's Ministry of the Environment. The two companies will focus the pilot on environmentally friendly innerwear sold by FamilyMart. The study will analyze sales data and survey results collected through FamilyMart's Famipay app to clarify how information and consumer touchpoints help customers understand a product's environmental value and lead to a purchase.

The companies will then implement in-store initiatives to verify their effectiveness and aim to establish a robust demand creation model. The insights and analytical methods gained are expected to be applied to other categories beyond apparel, including food, daily necessities, and household goods. The Ministry of the Environment's model project aims to promote investment and innovation in decarbonization and to encourage consumer selection of these products, thereby fostering market formation. The featured items are made with recycled polyester fibers that reduce CO2 emissions compared with conventional synthetic fibers, by 15% for inner T-shirts and 8% for REHEAT products. The Ministry of the Environment describes the project as one that appropriately displays the decarbonization value of products and services and develops an environment where consumers and procurement entities can understand and evaluate such value, assessing tolerance for price premiums and impacts on purchasing behavior.

LLM causal technology is described as a technology that discovers intervention points by having an LLM complement intermediate factors not present in the quantitative data, based on causal relationships estimated from the data. Fujitsu reported consolidated revenues of 3.5 trillion yen, or US$23 billion, for the fiscal year ended March 31, 2026. The companies will continue to discuss methods for effectively communicating environmental value and optimizing retail environments, and they will explore applying Fujitsu Causal AI to other product categories. By doing so, the partners aim to contribute to the creation of demand for decarbonized products and enhance customer value in the retail sector through advanced, data-driven marketing. Fujitsu states that its purpose is to make the world more sustainable by building trust in society through innovation, with 100,000 employees working to resolve challenges facing humanity.

stories.Headline: Graham Dumpleton builds Muru, an AI-assisted Rust server for Python apps
stories.Summary:
Graham Dumpleton, who created mod_wsgi twenty years ago, has started a new project called Muru, an AI-assisted Rust server for running Python web applications, and Simon Willison linked to it on 21st November 2026. Dumpleton has spent two decades thinking about the ideal way to serve Python web apps in production since he began mod_wsgi. Muru aims to provide the best possible tools for running ASGI and WSGI Python apps in both development and production. As he did with an earlier project called wrapture, Dumpleton is publishing an extraordinarily detailed account of the work as part of his development process.

The project is written in Rust and relies heavily on AI assistance, though Dumpleton says deciding what is not good enough yet remains his job. He credits twenty years of getting things wrong with mod_wsgi as useful experience for that judgment. He says he is prepared to put in the hard work to keep polishing Muru until it is something he would trust and something users would trust too. The articles give no release date, version number or availability details for Muru.

Dumpleton is the person responsible for the project, and his stated position is that the AI may do a lot of the work on the surface but the standard-setting stays with him. He frames the twenty years of mod_wsgi mistakes as an asset rather than a liability for judging the new server. He commits to continuing the polishing work until the server meets a bar he would trust himself. The articles do not say who else, if anyone, is involved in the project.

The context is that Muru follows the same open, detailed development write-up approach Dumpleton used for wrapture. Willison's link post appeared on 21st November 2026, and the article carries a timestamp of 22nd November 2026. The articles do not say what happens next beyond Dumpleton's stated intention to keep polishing Muru. No timeline, funding or adoption information is given.

stories.Headline: Jony Ive and Joey Flynn discuss whether taste can shield design from AI
stories.Summary:
The New York Times published a story by Jonah Weiner on Silicon Valley's fixation with "taste," which the article describes as a sense of discernment that some in the industry treat as a defense against AI-generated content. The piece features Jony Ive, the former Apple design chief, and Joey Flynn, a former OpenAI product designer, among the people discussing the topic. Techmeme linked to the Times story on November 22, 2026, under a headline naming Ive and Flynn. The article frames taste as something the industry is obsessed with and asks whether AI can learn it.

The discussion centers on whether taste can serve as a moat, meaning a lasting advantage that protects a company's work from being matched by machine-made output. The people quoted in the story include Ive and Flynn, and the article presents their views on taste as a quality that matters in product design. The piece also raises the question of whether AI systems can acquire taste, a question the article leaves open. The Times story is the source for the claims attributed to the people it names.

Ive is identified in the headline as the former design leader at Apple, and Flynn is identified as a former product designer at OpenAI. The article attributes to them and to others the view that taste is a moat against what the headline calls AI slop. The story does not, in the material available, give specific statements from Ive or Flynn beyond their participation in the discussion. Responsibility for the reporting rests with Weiner and the Times, and Techmeme credited the Times when it linked to the piece.

The context the articles provide is the industry's broader concern with AI-generated content and the value placed on human judgment in design. The story asks whether AI can learn taste, and it does not report an answer. What happens next is not described in the available material, which consists of the Techmeme link and the Times byline. More to follow.

stories.Headline: INSEAD professor says human-centric design turns AI concerns into opportunities
stories.Summary:
Phanish Puranam, the Roland Berger Chaired Professor of Strategy and Organisation Design at INSEAD, said the impact of AI on organisations is a design problem rather than a forecasting problem, delivering a keynote address at the Indian School of Business, according to The Hindu. Drawing on research from INSEAD's Organisations and Algorithms Program, he examined four concerns about AI and the future of work and said evidence showed that thoughtful organisational design could turn them into opportunities. He called for a human-centric approach to organisational design in the age of algorithms. The address took place at the fourth edition of the ISB Insights Forum, held on November 20, which brought together researchers, business leaders, policymakers and philanthropists to explore practical solutions to economic and social challenges.

Puranam said people would remain valuable because they could be held accountable and could identify errors that machines might miss, and that organisations which test, learn and adapt could use AI to help employees build skills, collaborate and take greater ownership of their work. Karthik Balakrishnan, Deputy Dean for Faculty and Research at ISB, said the strength of a research ecosystem lies in the quality of research rather than its volume, and that this quality depends on how research is discussed. He said research is only relevant if it is rigorous enough to be acted upon, and that relevance should be judged over time rather than over the next quarter. The annual research platform discussed research across business, market and public policy.

Sessions at the forum examined the geopolitics of AI and AI and financial innovation, including access, competition and trust, looking at how cross-border technology regulations, market competition and governance were influencing enterprise strategy and financial inclusion. A session titled Business for good: Building livelihoods explored how commercial models could create stable incomes at the grassroots, while Policymaking during economic crises examined policy tools for responding to macroeconomic shocks. Another session, What helps women advance at work?, drew on survey data from women professionals in India to compare workplace and domestic career dynamics in the country with findings largely based on western workplaces. The final sessions examined operational models to maximise the population health impact of community health workers, looking at approaches to improving the reach and effectiveness of frontline healthcare delivery.

stories.Headline: South Korea reviews past exam papers for AI cheating and weighs essay-based assessment
stories.Summary:
The 2027 academic year College Scholastic Ability Test concluded on the 19th, but the fallout from cheating with artificial intelligence continues, and the government is considering additional investigations into whether such cheating also occurred in the past. The Ministry of Education is reviewing a plan to trace and investigate last year's 2026 academic year CSAT papers if suspected cheaters are identified, because traces of cheating such as solution steps may remain on the papers. An official at the Ministry of Education said the government asked city and provincial education offices nationwide not to discard last year's CSAT papers and expects to secure them all, but papers from earlier years have likely been discarded because they exceeded the one-year mandatory retention period set by regulations. President Lee Jae Myung wrote on X that concerns about cheating that abuses AI technology are spreading beyond the CSAT to essay-style tests and school-based exams, and he said those who cheat will be held accountable to the end.

The President added that he will order a comprehensive overhaul of the legal basis to technically block the photographing and external transmission of question papers during exams, and he will also order a review of measures to state the updated legal basis on the papers and to add unique identifying marks so the source can be verified if papers are photographed or leaked. Despite the government's pledge of severe punishment, 111 cases of cheating, including possession of electronic devices, were detected in this CSAT, and five cases were confirmed in which electronic devices such as smart glasses and micro-cameras were actually used to cheat. The government plans, through a pan-government task force, to further investigate cheating by analyzing wireless signals collected at test sites, but there are technical limits to detecting devices that do not emit wireless signals, leaving the challenge of ensuring effectiveness. At 8:30 a.m.

on the 19th, the day the exam was administered, emergency disaster alert messages were sent nationwide simultaneously to prevent cheating on the CSAT, the first time such alerts were sent on the exam day. As it is difficult to completely prevent the misuse of technology, calls are growing to fundamentally change the admissions system so that assessment moves away from a format focused on choosing correct answers and instead evaluates the process of solving problems. Teacher organizations such as the Korean Federation of Teachers Associations and the Korean Teachers and Education Workers Union issued a statement on the 20th saying that cheating cannot be fundamentally resolved by strengthening surveillance and control whenever advanced devices appear, and that the curriculum, assessment systems and admissions must be reviewed together so that students' thinking skills, problem-solving processes and ability to apply knowledge are faithfully evaluated. Specific options under discussion include introducing descriptive- and essay-type assessments and oral evaluations, and the National Education Commission conducted public deliberation in August on shifting the CSAT to absolute grading and introducing descriptive- and essay-type assessments.

However, there are concerns that if such assessments are introduced, dependence on private education may increase, potentially exacerbating educational disparities and fairness controversies, and how to ensure the fairness of grading that uses AI is also a task. The National Education Commission is considering expanding descriptive- and essay-type assessments first to school grades rather than introducing them directly into university admissions, with the aim of cultivating students' critical thinking and problem-solving skills within public education. Professor Kim Yong of Korea National University of Education said in a phone interview that the pipeline linking education and society has already almost collapsed, and that we must ask anew whether learning to gain social status or a stable job still makes sense and question the very meaning of learning itself. He emphasized that in the future there will be more assessments that value the learning process and the steps taken to solve problems, and that descriptive- and essay-type assessments should be strengthened while enhancing the instructional capacity of schools and teachers to minimize outside influences such as reliance on private education.

stories.Headline: Major AI firms launch new models as governments tighten restrictions on chips and software
stories.Summary:
Alibaba, OpenAI, Microsoft and Google released new models during the week of November 16. Anthropic debuted on the Nasdaq and Nvidia issued its first earnings report without Jensen Huang. AI tools found software flaws in Apple and Bitcoin Core. US officials attributed a wave of outages to patches and updates. These events occurred as governments moved to restrict AI chips and models.

Alibaba released Qwen4-Max on November 16 with 2.4 trillion parameters and a one million token context window. OpenAI launched GPT-6.2 Astra on November 17 at 8 dollars per million input tokens and 40 dollars per million output tokens. Microsoft launched seven MAI models on November 17, including MAI Code 2. Google released Gemini 4 Neon on November 18 at 3 dollars per million input tokens and 15 dollars per million output tokens. Anthropic priced its IPO at 83 dollars per share, raising about 93.5 billion dollars in gross proceeds.

Nvidia chair Harvey Jones said the board does not intend to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO. Interim CEO Colette Kress raised the fiscal 2028 growth outlook to about 75 percent. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Trump and Xi agreed humans should always be involved in military AI decisions. OpenAI and other companies said their systems changed since GAO tests on attack plans. US intelligence and FBI officials told Congress there was no sign of a coordinated cyberattack.

Researchers used GPT-6 Cyber to find 35 flaws in Apple software, affecting the company. Bitcoin Core disclosed a bug found by an automated scan that let one peer stall a node. Amazon reported that Cairn AI agents found a zero-day during a university attack. Arizona's attorney general is criminally investigating OpenAI and other firms over rogue agents in banks. About 100 countries backed binding rules on autonomous weapons, but the US, Russia and Israel opposed them.

Nvidia reported 115.8 billion dollars in quarterly revenue after Jensen Huang departed on November 12. A Commerce rule now requires licenses for AI chips going to data centers serving China, Macau or Country Group D:5. A California report for Governor Gavin Newsom proposes emergency shutdown powers for frontier models. Databricks is in talks to raise billions at a 225 billion dollar valuation. Nvidia may buy Inception for over 500 million dollars, and Microsoft may sell OpenAI models to ByteDance.

California legislators can introduce bills based on the shutdown report when they return on December 7. Senate Banking Chairman Tim Scott wants Jensen Huang to testify before Christmas, though no date is set. UN talks aim to set rules on autonomous weapons by 2028. The articles leave open whether those autonomous weapon rules will be binding. It remains unknown if Nvidia will reach a deal to buy Inception.

stories.Headline: Trump backs Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick amid criticism over AI chip export controls
stories.Summary:
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick told associates he is not leaving his post in November 2026. He faced weeks of criticism regarding the handling of advanced AI chip export controls. President Donald Trump voiced confidence in Lutnick on November 20. The president stated he has no plans to replace the secretary. This follows the resignation of White House chief of staff Susie Wiles.

A November 16 rule requires licenses for chip resales in Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand. This measure takes effect in 90 days to close a third-country resale loophole. The Entity List has seen no new additions since the October 2025 trade truce with Beijing. Megaspeed International, a 7Road spin-off in Singapore, bought roughly 4.8 billion dollars of Nvidia chips. This amount represents nearly 2 percent of one American company's global data-center sales.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said four agencies backed blacklisting Megaspeed for months. Bessent confronted Lutnick in the White House Situation Room on November 5. Senator Tom Cotton accused Lutnick of disregarding warnings about semiconductors being diverted to China. Cotton sent a letter to the Commerce Department on October 13, 2025. He pressed for the company to be added to the export control blacklist.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned on November 12 after 33 years at the company. Interim CEO Colette Kress took over after Nvidia posted 115.8 billion dollars in quarterly revenue. Officials suspect Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive, of spying for the Chinese government. Over 100 flagged companies, including DeepSeek and CXMT, cleared review but were not published. Reports allege 4 billion dollars of Nvidia hardware was routed to China via Alibaba.

The Entity List is the main tool for blocking technology sales to suspect buyers. Commerce opened a Megaspeed investigation in 2024 and sought Nvidia records in May 2025. An on-site end-use check occurred in June 2025, and Nvidia then stopped selling to Megaspeed. Lutnick has a twenty year relationship with Trump and ties to Stephen Miller. Taiwan is also weighing a bill to criminalize chip smuggling to China.

The Justice Department is now leading a criminal investigation into Megaspeed's possible export violations. Lutnick now has more latitude to operate without clearing policy with Susie Wiles. Trump suggested that a harder line on exports could have triggered a confrontation with Beijing. The articles leave open whether Lutnick will eventually add new companies to the Entity List. They do not confirm if Alibaba assisted in routing hardware to China.

stories.Headline: Nvidia shifts to stricter investment reviews under interim CEO Colette Kress
stories.Summary:
Nvidia, long the main financial backer of the artificial intelligence industry, has begun to shift its investment strategy toward much more systematic and rigorous evaluations of the companies it supports, interim CEO Colette Kress said during a recent earnings conference call, according to a report published by Korea Daily on November 22, 2026. The change in approach, which the report describes as an Nvidia austerity shock, sparked widespread market anxiety over potential funding cutbacks and helped send the Nasdaq down 5.28% after reports of a Securities and Exchange Commission investigation into Nvidia's accounting practices wiped out earlier yearly gains. Nvidia had historically absorbed customer capital shortages and financial risks to pump liquidity directly into the AI ecosystem, tying infrastructure support directly to GPU sales instead of leaving clients to rely entirely on corporate bonds or traditional bank loans. That strategy created an intricate web of circular finance in which the company's massive capital injections fueled the very demand driving its record revenues.

According to Wall Street Journal reports cited in the article, Nvidia's investment portfolio, which includes equity stakes, purchase commitments and financial guarantees, exceeds $100 billion, and its vendor financing heavily supports key partners such as cloud provider CoreWeave, in which Nvidia holds a 10% stake. The portfolio also includes multi-billion-dollar computing purchase agreements and credit guarantees for large-scale data center developments such as OpenAI's Ohio project backed by SoftBank's SB Energy. Plans to launch a massive $500 billion AI infrastructure consortium with top global investment banks and private equity firms aimed to diversify liquidity sources, though implementation has faced sudden delays and hesitation following recent market shifts. Analysts warn that a reduction in Nvidia's capital support could instantly drain over $50 billion from the market, compounding corporate borrowing pressures amid rising interest rates.

Former SEC Chairman Gary Gensler recently warned that AI remains in bubble territory, driven by unsustainable annual infrastructure spending that vastly outpaces historical corporate expenditures, while the International Monetary Fund estimates that AI circular finance has ballooned past $1 trillion, with roughly two-thirds funded by debt. The IMF's estimate raises systemic concerns of a global economic slowdown if investments drastically contract, according to the article. As the final lender of the AI boom pulls back on open-ended financial support, neocloud providers like CoreWeave and Nebius that rely heavily on Nvidia's backing are expected to take the hardest hit. Industry experts note, however, that a more conservative investment stance by Nvidia could open the door for competitors, presenting major market share opportunities for Google and its specialized Tensor Processing Units as well as the broader Application-Specific Integrated Circuit custom AI chip ecosystem.

He suggested that the mismatch between funding and validation is a defining feature. He noted that intelligence does not exempt anyone from overpaying.

Investors are affected by a technology rout that caused Anthropic stock to fall on Friday. Public shareholders express opinions every second while scientific validation runs on its own schedule. The stock market originally assigned most upside to a few laboratories.

Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge claimed he and Claude proved the Riemann Hypothesis about prime numbers. Terence Tao emphasized that the formalized argument for the Riemann Hypothesis still needs independent verification. stories.Headline: Former OpenAI board member Helen Toner warns that no kill switch can stop rogue AI
stories.Summary:
Former OpenAI board member Helen Toner appeared on Fox News Sunday on November 22, 2026, to discuss several critical technology issues. She addressed the causes of recent nationwide tech outages and the growing danger of autonomous artificial intelligence cyber threats. Toner also spoke about the necessity of establishing AI guardrails between the United States and China. Her appearance highlighted the urgent need for better oversight of rapidly evolving software systems.

The situation requires a shift in how officials communicate about software patching, which Toner believes caused the recent nationwide outages. She specifically questioned why government or corporate officials have not been clear about these technical failures. Furthermore, she warned that no single kill switch exists to stop autonomous AI systems that operate outside of United States jurisdiction. This lack of control means that rogue AI could potentially function without any way to shut it down.

Helen Toner is the person responsible for these warnings based on her previous experience on the OpenAI board. She suggested that the rush to patch software may have inadvertently triggered the widespread technical disruptions seen across the country. Regarding the threat of rogue AI, she emphasized that jurisdictional boundaries make it impossible to implement a universal emergency stop. Her comments serve as a warning about the inherent risks of autonomous systems running in foreign territories.

stories.Headline: Nvidia tightens AI financing after Huang resigns as interim CEO Kress pledges stricter oversight
stories.Summary:
The global artificial intelligence industry is facing a funding crisis after Nvidia began tightening its financial support following the resignation of former CEO Jensen Huang. This shift occurred as the Nasdaq plunged 5.28 percent on Friday, erasing all of its gains for the current year. Investors are now anxious because Nvidia previously acted as a central bank for the sector by providing liquidity and assuming financing risks for its clients. This circular financing structure made many data center builders and technology companies heavily dependent on the company's continuous financial backing.

The new approach requires more rigorous scrutiny and systematic investing, which may withdraw over 50 billion dollars from the market according to analyst Tim Arcuri. Nvidia's current investment portfolio exceeds 100 billion dollars, including 48 billion dollars in eight public companies as of September. Specific obligations include a 6.3 billion dollar agreement from September 2025 to buy computing capacity from CoreWeave, where Nvidia holds a 10 percent stake. Additionally, the company reportedly guaranteed 105 billion dollars for SB Energy, a SoftBank subsidiary developing a data center for OpenAI.

Interim CEO Colette Kress stated on Tuesday that the company will continue supporting the AI ecosystem but will apply stricter oversight to its investments. This announcement follows a U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission investigation into the accounting practices of the semiconductor giant. Former SEC Chair Gary Gensler told CNN on November 16 that AI is in a bubble and predicted an economic slowdown before November 2028. IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva also warned on November 16 that a sudden investment retreat could tighten financial markets and slow global growth.

The International Monetary Fund estimates that AI circular financing exceeds 1 trillion dollars, with two-thirds of that amount funded by debt. This environment puts immense pressure on neocloud providers like CoreWeave and Nebius that rely on Nvidia's guarantees to obtain loans. If Nvidia continues to retreat, analysts suggest that Google and other suppliers of customized AI chips could gain a competitive advantage. The industry now faces a double squeeze of rising borrowing costs and fewer advance purchase commitments to reassure lenders.

stories.Headline: German courts grant urgent deepfake injunctions when rights holders act fast and preserve evidence
stories.Summary:
A convincing fake of a chief executive, brand ambassador or advertising campaign can be created and circulated within hours, Global Advisory Experts reported on November 22, 2026. The guide said deepfakes have become a live enforcement issue in Germany in 2026 rather than a technology curiosity. It described a deepfake as synthetic audio, video or imagery produced or altered by artificial intelligence so a person appears to say or do something they never said or did. Typical incidents it listed include cloned brand ambassadors endorsing products they never used, invented celebrity interviews and voice clones used to defraud. The guide said the common element is output realistic enough to mislead an ordinary audience, which can create liability under several German regimes at once.

The guide said Germany has no single deepfake statute and rights holders rely on a mix of civil, constitutional, competition and criminal provisions. It set out five pillars, beginning with personality and image rights under Articles 1 and 2 of the Basic Law and §22 KUG, which requires consent to distribute images of a person. It said copyright under the UrhG offers removal, injunctive relief and damages where a protected work is copied or adapted. It said the MarkenG lets a proprietor stop confusing use of registered brand elements, with national marks registered at the DPMA. It said the UWG provides injunctions and, where fault is shown, damages for misleading commercial content, and that the GDPR, BDSG and StGB may apply to voice cloning, defamation, fraud, extortion and non-consensual intimate imagery.

The guide was written by Global Advisory Experts and featured Markus Koerner of Bird & Bird in Germany as its Gold featured expert on the matter. It said the guide explains which route suits which situation, how quickly each works and what evidence German courts expect before granting urgent relief. It said urgency under the Zivilprozessordnung rules on preliminary injunctions is applied strictly and that delay after discovering a deepfake can forfeit the expedited route. It said orders can be backed by penalties for non-compliance, including Ordnungsgeld and in some cases Ordnungshaft. It said a focused application with a clean evidence bundle and a narrowly drafted request is far more likely to succeed than a sprawling one.

The guide said it is for brand owners, talent agents, celebrities, in-house teams and marketing departments needing enforcement and takedown options in Germany against AI-generated fakes. It said a single deepfake often causes reputational, commercial and endorsement-misuse harm at once, which is why combining remedies is frequently the strongest approach. It said platform takedowns rest on platform terms and the EU Digital Services Act, which imposes notice-and-action duties on hosting and online platform intermediaries operating in the EU. It said a clear, well-evidenced notice identifying the content, the infringed right and the rights holder will normally prompt removal, but platforms differ in responsiveness. It said rights holders should never rely on a takedown alone, should preserve evidence in parallel and should keep a court application ready in case removal stalls or the content reappears.

The guide said the general right of personality derives from Articles 1 and 2 of the Basic Law and has been developed at length by the Federal Constitutional Court. It said the Kunsturhebergesetz protects the right to one's own image and that German courts have consistently regarded unauthorised use of a likeness as a serious interference. It said proving a voice clone is fake may call for acoustic expert analysis, while video deepfakes usually benefit from frame-level forensic review. It said purely machine-generated output generally does not attract copyright itself, but the material fed into the system often does. It said trademark claims can be particularly effective against fake adverts because the holder has an enforceable right on the register and does not need to prove reputational harm from scratch.

The guide said the right answer in many matters is a sequence rather than a single step, a platform takedown within hours followed by a personality rights or UWG injunction to secure a binding court order. It said damages under the UrhG and MarkenG may be calculated by licence analogy, by the infringer's profits or by actual loss. It said claims for information and accounting are normally pleaded alongside the main relief because quantifying loss usually requires disclosure of the infringer's sales and reach. It said the guide includes an evidence and interim relief checklist, sample claim wording and a simple framework for picking the right remedy quickly. It said the analysis of personality and image rights is both constitutional and statutory, and that good drafting counts as much as good theory.

stories.Headline: Guggenheim chief executive urges museums to pursue artful intelligence over AI slop
stories.Summary:
The Guggenheim's chief executive used a public address to set out his view that museums should pursue what he called artful intelligence rather than the flood of machine-made material he described as AI slop, according to a report by Chosun on November 22, 2026. The report said the executive made the remarks while speaking about the place of new technology in art institutions. It presented his position as a call for careful, human-centered use of artificial intelligence in cultural work. The account did not give the text of the speech or say where it took place.

The remarks, as the article describes them, frame the choice as one between thoughtful, artful intelligence and low-quality automated output. The report says the executive argued that museums should not let generative tools replace human judgment and craft. It presents his comments as a warning about the risks of cheap, machine-produced content. The article gives no figures, dates or names beyond the executive's title and the publication date.

Responsibility for the position rests with the Guggenheim's chief executive, who according to the report made the case himself. The article paraphrases him as favoring artful intelligence over what he called AI slop. It does not attribute the phrase to anyone else or record any response from other institutions. No direct quotation beyond the short phrase is given in the report.

The context the article supplies is limited to the wider debate over artificial intelligence in museums and the arts. It does not say what the Guggenheim plans to do next or whether any policy follows from the speech. The report offers no timeline and no further statements from the executive. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Forrester says firms will fold AI token costs into security budgets by 2027
stories.Summary:
Rising cybersecurity risks linked to the rapid adoption of artificial intelligence are forcing global businesses to strengthen their safeguards before 2027. Throughout 2026, companies worldwide faced repeated disruptions caused by single points of failure, including accidental undersea cable cuts across Africa, Asia, and West Asia. A major security flaw in PHP software also caused significant issues, with Check Point Software Technologies reporting that India was the eleventh hardest hit among eighteen affected nations. These events have renewed concerns regarding the dangers of relying on a single technology vendor without having a comprehensive backup plan.

The integration of artificial intelligence into daily operations will require companies to reshape their financial planning for the coming year. According to Forrester Research, businesses will soon need to treat AI usage costs, which are known as tokens, as a core part of their security budgets. This shift is necessary because the growing dependence on single technology providers creates vulnerabilities that hackers can exploit. Organizations must now prepare for new operational risks as AI becomes more integral to their standard business operations.

Experts from Forrester Research, Fortinet, and Gartner are responsible for identifying these emerging threats to essential services. They suggest that the current landscape is changing because artificial intelligence is giving hackers a significant head start in their attacks. These analysts indicate that the risks associated with AI will likely outweigh the disruptions seen during the previous year. Businesses are being urged to move away from single-vendor dependence to avoid the catastrophic outages that have recently plagued critical global services.

stories.Headline: Libya trains officials to use AI for Agenda 2063 reporting
stories.Summary:
Libya opened its Third Training Programme on Domesticating Agenda 2063 through artificial intelligence in Tripoli this week, according to a report by Kanto Kai Okanta published by TechReviewAfrica on Sunday, November 22, 2026. The programme brings together data governance, alignment, analysis and national reporting, with a focus on translating continental commitments into measurable national outcomes. Libya recorded an overall performance of 84% in its national Agenda 2063 implementation report, which the article describes as a foundation for the next phase of its implementation efforts. The training is using alignment maps, AI-assisted reports and live dashboards to strengthen the country's capacity to monitor and report progress under Agenda 2063.

According to the African Union Development Agency-NEPAD, the priority is now to turn plans into delivery by making every figure verifiable, accelerating reporting and ensuring that decisions are informed by reliable evidence. Dr. Mohamed Al-Fadil Gubran, Chairman of Libya's Permanent Committee for Monitoring and Implementing Agenda 2063, described the country's 84% performance as a milestone rather than a finish line. He called for stronger national systems and capacity to ensure that every number can be verified, explained and trusted. The programme seeks to strengthen national reporting, data governance and evidence-based decision-making to accelerate the implementation of the African Union's development blueprint.

Opening the programme, Dr. Ziad Elhajjaji, Minister of State for Digital Economy and Artificial Intelligence, highlighted the transformative potential of responsible AI, trusted data and human judgement in helping institutions plan better, report faster and serve citizens more effectively. Representing AUDA-NEPAD, Director of Operations Ola Ehinmoro reaffirmed the Agency's commitment to supporting Libya beyond alignment and into delivery. He emphasised the importance of capable institutions and reliable data in translating continental commitments into results that people can see and feel in their daily lives. stories.Headline: Meghan Markle's As Ever brand promotes holiday sale with an AI-generated image
stories.Summary:
Meghan Markle's lifestyle brand As Ever drew scrutiny after a holiday sale promotion reportedly used an AI-generated image, according to the Daily Mail. The image was shared on the brand's Instagram account on Thursday, November 19. It advertised the brand's holiday sale with the words "As Ever Holiday Sale: 25% off sitewide." The graphic reportedly contained SynthID, a digital watermark developed by Google to identify AI-generated content. The outlet claimed the graphic was created or edited using technology developed by OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT.

The promotion also included a separate photograph of the Duchess wearing cream-colored clothes beside a Christmas-decorated fireplace. The brand announced a 25% reduction across its website, but the Daily Mail reported that its $148 Holiday Advent Calendar was excluded. The limited-edition product contains 24 chocolates produced with Los Angeles chocolatier Compartés. It features a sketch of the California mansion where Meghan and Harry have lived, along with countdown numbers based on the Duchess's handwriting. Other products, including the brand's fruit spreads and gift baskets, were included in the holiday promotion.

The discovery does not establish who created the graphic or whether the Duchess personally used AI. Meghan previously said on Bloomberg's The Circuit with Emily Chang in August 2025, "Aren't you a little bit scared for, by AI?" She said someone had recently introduced her to ChatGPT, which she had not previously experienced. She admitted, "I'm a little bit vintage in many ways," and said she prefers handwritten notes and traditional ways of communicating. She also revealed that Siri was not enabled on her phone and that she did not use location services.

In August 2026, Meghan and Harry publicly criticized technology companies over the dangers of AI-generated sexual images. In a statement on their official website, the Sussexes supported efforts to stop AI tools from creating nonconsensual intimate images, especially those involving women and children. They criticized companies that challenged stronger safeguards and asked, "Can AI make our world better while it enables the worst in humans?" The statement argued that technology companies were investing enormous sums in artificial intelligence while resisting measures to protect vulnerable users. During his September 2026 appearance at the Clinton Global Initiative in New York, Harry warned that AI companion applications could pose a greater threat to young people than conventional social media.

According to remarks published on the Sussexes' official website, Harry described AI companion apps as the "ultimate sycophant." He warned, "It doesn't just want your attention, it wants your attachment." He expressed concern that children could confide in artificial intelligence instead of developing relationships with real people. The Duke also called for greater accountability from technology companies, arguing that rapid AI development should not come at the expense of public safety. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Atlassian's Sherif Mansour says PMs should steer AI work rather than code
stories.Summary:
Sherif Mansour, who leads AI and product craft at Atlassian and has spent 17 years at the company according to The Futurist account of the conversation, told Lenny's Podcast that the product manager job did not disappear when AI coding arrived but narrowed to direction. He said an early experiment that turned PMs and designers into full-time AI builders fell apart after a month, and that throughput was not the problem because direction was. That failed experiment is why Mansour argues PMs own decision making velocity rather than the decisions themselves, and why the best PMs build a shared brain, a common understanding of customer, product and business context that lets engineers and designers act without waiting for a spec. He names three contexts to fill, customer context, product and market context, and the business you operate in, and said trust breaks once a group grows past 20 or 30 people unless someone maintains that shared base. The workflow change he describes is concrete, since Mansour said he tries never to do a customer interview without engineers in the room.

He cited PMs who send every engineer to test AI tools and report back, plus engineers staffing booths with him at customer events. He pointed to a 2010 Confluence interview where customers used red and green stars to mark unfinished work, and said an engineer in the room proposed the checkbox in the page, an idea he said did not exist on the web at the time. Hiring is where he gets prescriptive, and Mansour uses a triangle credited to Geoff Redfern with general manager, scientist and artist as the three corners describing how a PM naturally does discovery, from TAM and revenue math to hypothesis testing to vision-led taste. He said few people do all three well, so leaders should stop throwing PM bodies at a problem and match the archetype to the work, with all-rounders reserved for zero-to-one teams. He admitted the model is aimed at medium to large organizations rather than startups, and he joked that he is a strong artist and a terrible general manager.

Mansour said on Lenny's Podcast that the idea you no longer need to hire juniors is a misconception, in part because they bring new working norms. His example was his 12-year-old son, who he said went straight to vibe coding games without learning syntax and treats that as normal. The article closes by telling teams to watch for groups that hire for a spike, state the weakness plainly, and pair opposites, as Mansour said he does with his colleague Jamille, rather than asking every PM to ship code. The piece was written by the StartupHub.ai staff and reviewed by editor Daniel Singer, and it draws on Lenny's Podcast as its source.

stories.Headline: Analysts see over 100% upside for Ciena, Tower Semiconductor and Lumentum after steep AI stock declines
stories.Summary:
The AI boom has rewarded early investors handsomely, but the opportunity now looks considerably less straightforward, according to an article by Faheem Tahir published on Yahoo Finance on Sunday, November 22, 2026. After months of enthusiasm surrounding artificial intelligence, investors are increasingly questioning whether the enormous spending behind the technology can generate adequate returns. According to Reuters on November 19, the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index had lost nearly 30% since early October, even as estimates for major technology companies' capital expenditure remained largely unchanged. Barclays strategists noted that hyperscaler spending forecasts for next year had yet to be revised downward, suggesting that the market's retreat has outpaced changes in investment expectations. Rising financing costs, regulatory uncertainty, and potential restrictions on data center construction have complicated the outlook.

The article screened U.S.-listed companies with exposure to AI through chips, cloud computing, software, or supporting infrastructure, using data as of November 20, 2026. It selected stocks that had declined by at least 25% over the preceding month and offered at least 50% upside to their median analyst price targets. The final ten are presented in ascending order of analyst upside potential, and the top five are presented in the article. Hedge fund interest was considered as of the third quarter of 2026, using Insider Monkey's hedge fund database, which tracked 994 hedge funds during the quarter. Ciena Corporation had a 27.95% one-month decline and 104.30% upside potential, with 83 hedge fund holders.

Reuters reported on November 18 that 83% of analyst ratings on key AI stocks were Strong Buy recommendations, despite mounting concerns over profitability and debt. Bank of America's November fund manager survey revealed that nearly 40% of respondents believed companies were overinvesting, while more than half anticipated at least one hyperscaler cutting capital expenditure within six months. On November 16, TD Cowen retained its Buy rating on Ciena while reducing its target to $375 from $400, arguing that strong demand made substantial near-term earnings estimate cuts difficult to justify. On November 3, Craig-Hallum maintained its Buy rating on Tower Semiconductor while cutting its target to $250 from $325, highlighting strong photonics demand and capacity expansion running ahead of schedule. UBS maintained Neutral on Lumentum on November 10, noting accelerating optical demand but identifying the acquisition as the principal near-term share-price driver.

Tower Semiconductor shares fell 39.38% over the past month, while the median analyst price target implied 111.30% upside as of November 20, and it had 49 hedge fund holders. Lumentum Holdings had a 40.75% monthly decline, with its median analyst target implying 111.60% upside, and 122 hedge fund holders. Marvell Technology had a 45.29% monthly decline, with 118.80% upside to its median analyst target, and 108 hedge fund holders. Sandisk Corporation had a 49.87% monthly decline, with 164.80% upside to its median analyst target, and 122 hedge fund holders. On November 11, Evercore maintained Outperform on Sandisk, arguing that supply discipline and long-term customer agreements could make earnings more predictable.

Ciena's fiscal third-quarter revenue rose 37% to $1.67 billion, while adjusted operating margin reached 22.5%, compared with 10.7% a year earlier, and management expected fiscal year-end backlog to exceed $10 billion. Tower Semiconductor generated approximately $240 million in silicon photonics revenue during the third quarter, nearly half its total, overall revenue increased 33% to $526 million, net income reached $120 million, and fourth-quarter revenue guidance was $600 million. Lumentum reported fiscal first-quarter revenue of $1.26 billion and a 42.3% adjusted operating margin, and management secured purchase commitments exceeding $5 billion for a second major win in optics positioned near or alongside chips. Marvell generated $2.17 billion in fiscal second-quarter data-center revenue, up 46% year-over-year, and in November preliminary third-quarter revenue remained consistent with its earlier guidance. Sandisk reported fiscal first-quarter revenue of $11.03 billion, up 23% sequentially, and data-center revenue increased 61% sequentially to approximately $4.8 billion.

Under the proposed transaction, Lumentum shareholders would receive 4.5 Marvell shares per share owned, and completion remains subject to shareholder and regulatory approvals, with expected completion in the first half of 2028. Ciena's Hyper-Rail optical platform, designed to support distributed AI training, should begin contributing meaningful revenue during fiscal 2027, and Ciena trades at approximately 22.1 times estimated fiscal 2027 earnings, with consensus anticipating roughly 66% EPS growth. Tower Semiconductor trades at approximately 18.2 times estimated 2027 earnings, against projected EPS growth of roughly 72%, and has approximately $1.47 billion in cash against $154 million in debt. Lumentum trades at approximately 21.5 times estimated fiscal 2027 earnings, and short interest stood at 8.97% of float on October 30, before the deal announcement. Marvell trades at approximately 32.8 times estimated fiscal 2027 earnings and 18.8 times fiscal 2028 earnings, and Stifel retained Buy on November 20 while reducing its target to $280 from $370.

Management expected silicon photonics manufacturing capacity at year-end to approximately double the level supporting third-quarter shipments, and Lumentum's next-quarter revenue guidance was $1.575, $1.625 billion. Management attributed roughly 60% of Sandisk's total sequential revenue growth to volume and 40% to pricing, indicating that the expansion was not solely a pricing story. The article states that the announced $1,132 equivalent for Lumentum is not a guaranteed cash payout, and that the consideration fluctuates with Marvell's stock. The article leaves open which companies' growth prospects remain intact and which valuations have further to fall, and it notes that additional production capacity takes time to become recognized revenue. The article also leaves open how the proposed Lumentum acquisition will affect customer conflicts and regulatory uncertainty for Marvell.

stories.Headline: Researchers link honorary authorship and hidden AI writing to misrepresented credit in science
stories.Summary:
Scientific publishing faces parallel integrity challenges from honorary authorship and undisclosed artificial intelligence writing, according to an analysis published in the Hellenic Journal of Cardiology. Authors Panos Macheras and Panos E. Vardas wrote the analysis. The analysis states that both practices misrepresent genuine scholarly input and undermine accountability across research disciplines. The authors observe that the two practices emerged from different technological eras. Both obscure who actually performed the intellectual work behind published scientific manuscripts.

The analysis states that authorship serves as an essential record of intellectual contribution and a foundation for professional recognition, career advancement and responsibility for published findings. It says ethical frameworks faced disruption in the late twentieth century with the rise of honorary or cosmetic authorship in multi-investigator biomedical papers. It says author rosters grew as teams expanded and academic competition accelerated, crediting individuals who contributed little or nothing. It says department heads, senior researchers or peripheral colleagues are added to acknowledge hierarchy, enhance prestige or repay professional favors. It says junior researchers often feel compelled to add superiors to protect their institutional standing.

The authors state that honorary authorship dilutes the value of authorship as a marker of intellectual engagement and makes it difficult to identify who conducted a study. They state that it erodes accountability because researchers credited without meaningful involvement may be unable or unwilling to take responsibility for accuracy and integrity. They state that efforts to counter cosmetic authorship date back more than four decades, when Moulopoulos and colleagues argued in 1983 that journals must define individual roles. They state that these roles include the initial idea, study design, data collection, analysis and manuscript drafting. They state that the International Committee of Medical Journal Editors established criteria requiring substantial contributions, participation in writing or revising, approval of the final manuscript and formal accountability.

The analysis states that many leading journals require contributorship statements, but the requirement is not universal and can be undermined by inaccurate declarations. It states that John Ioannidis documented that improper authorship practices persist among highly productive investigators in cardiology. It states that the academic community collectively created the fictitious scientist Camille Noûs to highlight unresolved concerns over credit and responsibility. It states that large language models can help non-native English speakers improve clarity and grammar and help investigators organize concepts, evaluate phrasing and summarize background literature.

It states that undisclosed automated text generation risks introducing inaccurate assertions, fabricated references and misleading interpretations. The analysis states that editorial organizations and publishers have established consensus rules barring artificial intelligence systems from being listed as authors because algorithms cannot accept legal or ethical responsibility. It states that publishers increasingly mandate disclosure when artificial intelligence assists in preparing a manuscript. It states that Macheras and Vardas disclose in their own paper that their graphical abstract was generated with the assistance of the ChatGPT large language model.

It states that both honorary authorship and undisclosed artificial intelligence writing are tied to academic pressures, with career advancement and funding tied to publication metrics. It states that these metrics incentivize maximizing publication volume over genuine scholarly effort. The analysis states that addressing the dual challenges requires institutions and publishers to mandate detailed contributorship statements and enforce full transparency regarding artificial intelligence assistance. It states that institutions should reform evaluation criteria to reward intellectual quality and authentic participation in the creation of knowledge.

It states that cooperative research remains vital for addressing complex scientific problems. It states that formal contributorship requirements are not universally mandated and can be undermined where implemented. It states that the expanding sophistication of generative tools raises critical questions regarding intellectual ownership and attribution. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Ireland's Data Protection Commission blocks or delays nine AI launches over five years
stories.Summary:
Ireland's Data Protection Commission published a report on September 25, 2026, regarding its reviews of artificial intelligence. The regulator examined roughly 180 AI products and services between 2021 and 2025. Most of these reviews occurred before the products reached users in Europe. Nine of these launches were delayed or cancelled because of interventions by the regulator. These reviews were conducted by the Technology Multinational Supervision Unit.

The report, titled Responsible Artificial Intelligence Innovation, covers companies including Meta, Google, Microsoft, OpenAI, TikTok, and X. It includes other firms like Airbnb, Apple, Deepseek, LinkedIn, and Pinterest. The DPC noted that 59 percent of AI products launched in 2024 and 2025 received recommendations. Transparency problems appeared in 72 percent of those recommendations. The regulator requires a minimum lead time of 8 weeks for substantive engagement.

The Technology Multinational Supervision Unit is responsible for engaging with large multinational tech companies based in Ireland. This unit operates separately from other regulatory functions like complaints or inquiries. The DPC stated that this voluntary process acts as a quasi-regulatory sandbox. The regulator noted that recommendations are non-binding in nature. However, the DPC may use other regulatory powers if redline issues are not addressed.

The report affects large platforms that sell advertising in Europe because the DPC is their lead regulator. Some companies, such as X, refused to stop training AI models when requested. The DPC applied to the Irish High Court on August 8, 2024, regarding X. Eurostat data shows 52.7 percent of EU firms avoiding AI due to privacy concerns. AI use among EU enterprises rose from 13.5 percent to 20 percent in 2025.

Generative AI drove most growth, accounting for 79 percent of all engagements. The DPC counted 25 generative AI engagements in 2023, 36 in 2024, and 82 in 2025. Non-generative AI engagements totaled 37 over the whole period. AI engagements with large technology controllers grew tenfold from 2021 to 2025. This activity included technologies like facial recognition, age assurance, and large language models.

The DPC now says training AI on private messages faces a very difficult legal threshold. The regulator believes training new AI models will likely require a Data Protection Impact Assessment. Future monitoring will include how mitigations, such as objection forms, work in practice. The report does not name most companies involved in the specific case studies. It remains open whether companies can justify training AI on private messages under legitimate interests.

stories.Headline: Civil Guard arrests four for using AI to spread jihadist content and radicalize youth
stories.Summary:
The Civil Guard has arrested four people in three provinces and in the autonomous city of Melilla for spreading jihadist content on social networks with the aim of indoctrinating people in terrorism, in an investigation that also detected the use of artificial intelligence to improve radicalization processes. In a first action, officers arrested three people in San Sebastián in Guipúzcoa, Vilanova i la Geltrú in Barcelona and Fuengirola in Málaga, after confirming that they had become radicalized over recent years, especially because of greater access to terrorist propaganda spread on the internet. A parallel operation in Melilla led to the arrest of a young man for his active work in spreading jihadist ideology, and he is attributed with large quantities of jihadist multimedia content on social networks, especially content used by young people. The detainees also recorded videos in which they expressed their jihadist affiliation and displayed bladed weapons, according to material seized during the investigation.

Among the analyzed materials are content related to Daesh and Hamas, used with the aim of indoctrinating for terrorist purposes, and the investigation has also located material that justifies violence and the carrying out of attacks. The Civil Guard considers this terrorist propaganda material to be of special danger because of the intrinsic risk of fostering jihadist radicalization, especially among a young and vulnerable group. The operations were carried out with the cooperation of the National Intelligence Center and the FBI of the United States, within an investigation focused on the spread of terrorist propaganda and the use of new technological tools for the recruitment and radicalization of users on social networks. The report was published on November 22, 2026, and the arrests were made in San Sebastián, Vilanova i la Geltrú, Fuengirola and Melilla.

The General Directorate of the Civil Guard provided the information on the analyzed materials, and the force described the propaganda as especially dangerous because it can foster radicalization among young and vulnerable people. The investigation attributes to the Melilla detainee large quantities of jihadist multimedia content on social networks, especially material used by young people, and the seized material shows that the detainees recorded videos expressing their jihadist affiliation and displaying bladed weapons. The National Intelligence Center and the FBI of the United States cooperated in the operations, which focused on the spread of terrorist propaganda and the use of new technological tools for recruitment and radicalization. The articles do not say what charges the four detainees face or what happens to them next.
