stories.Headline: Remote CEO ties meeting performance expectations to completing AI training
stories.Summary:
Remote CEO Job van der Voort told Fortune in a November 22 interview that employees who skipped the company’s AI training would not receive a “meeting expectations” rating in their performance review. Remote required its roughly 2,000 employees to complete a five-hour course, and the time was paid. Van der Voort said everyone completed the course. The consequence made AI capability part of the performance bar rather than an optional perk. The requirement and completion claim come from his account to Fortune, not an independent assessment of employees’ skills.

Remote developed the course internally and later made it free to the public under the name AI for Actual Work. It runs five hours across five parts, moving from prompt basics and choosing tools to building and deploying agents, then presenting finished work. The goal, according to Remote, is for each participant to leave with one reusable workflow for a real task. The guidance stresses checking AI’s answers, protecting sensitive information, and keeping human review in consequential work. Remote co-founder Marcelo Lebre said in a July 24 post that the company had released the course free to the public after developing it internally.

Van der Voort argued the employer has a responsibility: if it expects staff to use AI, it should help them learn it rather than simply replace them. He said a company that employs a whole bunch of people should take responsibility for the people who work for it. He said employers would not be able to fire all their people and find new people good with this. He said the training raises the foundational level managers can expect across Remote. His stated aim is to avoid basic mistakes and remove uncertainty about whether an employee knows AI could make a particular problem easy to solve.

Lebre wrote that employees need to understand what information must not be shared, when an answer needs checking and who should review it before use. The course also asks whether a task is appropriate for AI at all. Lebre wrote that payroll, employment, compliance, tax, legal and people operations affect people’s lives. He argued that accuracy and trust require human judgment to remain involved. He and van der Voort helped build the course, with feedback from teams including payroll, legal, customer experience, sales and engineering.

The course predates the newly reported review requirement. Remote describes the curriculum as moving through five parts: foundations, tool selection, building, deployment and showcase. Foundations covers trying real prompts, learning about model behavior and keeping a workflow worth reusing. Building covers creating agents using context, tools and loops that let them work through tasks. Deployment covers connecting data, designing for real use and maintaining what has been built.

The story offers no independent assessment of employees’ skills or results. It leaves open whether the requirement created lasting capability beyond course completion. Van der Voort’s expectations for the training are not measured results presented in the interview. Remote’s claims about participation and the training’s intended benefits come from executives. The showcase part covers presenting finished work, identifying work that can be removed and helping lead AI adoption.

stories.Headline: Micro-Winery Guild launches Vitibot AI concierge to help travelers find small wineries
stories.Summary:
The Micro-Winery Guild, a membership organization for independent wineries producing fewer than 5,000 cases a year, announced on Nov. 17 the launch of Vitibot, an AI-powered wine concierge designed to help visitors discover small, independent wineries and plan personalized wine country itineraries. The tool is live at microwineryguild.com/explore, where visitors can ask for recommendations in plain language, such as a dog-friendly afternoon in Napa, a hands-on harvest experience for the family in Sonoma, a Malbec in Napa Valley, or an Edelzwicker in Oregon's Willamette Valley. According to the guild, Vitibot draws on information about each member winery, including its wines, winemaking approach, tasting experiences and property amenities. Beyond single recommendations, the tool can build personalized wine trails across regions where guild members operate, including Napa Valley, Sonoma, Alexander Valley, Sebastopol, Temecula and the Willamette Valley, and users can map out a day of winery visits, share itineraries with friends or save routes to Google Maps.

The guild bills Vitibot as the only AI concierge built specifically for smaller wineries. Elise Nerlove, president and co-founder of the guild, said travelers should not need to know a winery's name before they can discover what makes it a great fit for them, and that the guild is using technology to give small wineries a more meaningful opportunity to be discovered by the visitors most likely to appreciate what they offer. She said that unlike generic AI tools, Vitibot is purpose-built for small, independent wineries and draws on the unique details of each winery, from its wines and winemaking philosophy to its tasting experiences and property amenities, to connect travelers with places that match their interests. Caston Richards of Paloma Vineyards in St. Helena said the tool works much like the personal recommendations that already bring visitors to the property, a shared knowledge just through similar establishments rather than circles of wine lovers, and that it will make planning a visit feel a little more approachable, especially for people who have never been to Napa.

Richards said Paloma has a small marketing budget compared with the bigger wineries, and that by working together through the guild, member wineries hope to reach more people who would genuinely enjoy visiting small, family-owned and operated establishments. Katja Newman of La Cienega Vineyard in Healdsburg said small family vineyards do not just make artisanal wine, but care for the land, promote members of their community and work to preserve family traditions for the next generation, and face daunting challenges because of their size. With an emphasis on stewardship and quality, she said, small wineries have less time and money to put toward marketing, and Vitibot offers a great way for visitors to discover hidden gems, meet the families and workers behind the wines, hike through the vines, taste from the barrel and experience the authentic heart of wine country. Karrie Hutton of Nichelini Family Winery in St. Helena said the family has been making wine since 1890 and there is still quite a bit of old Napa in a visit there, and that she loves how Vitibot lets someone looking for just that kind of afternoon find their way to a little family winery like hers.

Jim Pennella of Frang Wine in the Coombsville American Viticultural Area said the tool will help make visiting more approachable for people less familiar with the region, and credited the guild with bringing together the voices of small producers in a way that unites wineries of all sizes around both consumer preferences and the challenges of a shifting market. The guild noted it will also pitch the tool to wine country drivers and hospitality concierges who want to give guests more tailored winery recommendations. Any winery that meets the guild's criteria can apply for membership, and applications are peer-reviewed, with membership extended by invitation, which the guild says keeps the community focused on qualified, engaged members. The organization's stated mission is to strengthen the economics of small-scale wine businesses and make micro-wineries easier for travelers to find.

stories.Headline: Nvidia shares fall 41 percent as Jensen Huang resigns and Colette Kress becomes interim CEO
stories.Summary:
Wall Street questioned if Nvidia was becoming the next Cisco during the week ending November 20, 2026. This concern followed a period where Nvidia shares dropped 41.42 percent over one month. The stock closed at 125.53 dollars on November 20 after losing 20.45 dollars in one session. This sell-off occurred despite Nvidia reporting one of the best quarters for any company on November 17, 2026. Investors are now comparing the current AI expansion to the dot-com bubble of the year 2000.

The company listed 390 billion dollars in supply commitments and up to 118 billion dollars in guarantees. This includes 105 billion dollars for the 4.25 GW SB Energy Ohio campus hosting OpenAI infrastructure. Nvidia also has 32 billion dollars in neocloud commitments that involve revenue sharing with partners. Three direct customers accounted for 14 percent, 11 percent, and 11 percent of third-quarter revenue. The company now trades at 13 times trailing earnings of 9.31 dollars per share.

Trefis noted that Cisco shares once fell 89 percent when internet spending exceeded actual earnings. Michael Burry compared the October 6 Nasdaq 100 high to the March 2000 dot-com peak. He suggested that bulls would eventually have another chance to exit their positions in the market. The I/O Fund argued on November 20 that the AI trade has only just begun. Barron's reported that the stock looks like a bargain following a very strong earnings report.

The stock drop affects investors, especially those near retirement who face sequence-of-returns risk from large positions. Regulatory risks are also weighing on the stock according to reports from Reuters on November 20. An SEC investigation is currently focusing on the accounting practices used by the company. The board announced that Jensen Huang voluntarily resigned as president, CEO, and board member. Colette Kress, the Chief Financial Officer, was named interim CEO while the board searches for a replacement.

Nvidia reported third-quarter revenue of 115.84 billion dollars, which beat the consensus estimate of 108.73 billion dollars. Data Center revenue reached 107.6 billion dollars, representing a 110 percent increase over the previous year. Non-GAAP EPS was 2.68 dollars, beating the expected 2.4712 dollars for the sixth consecutive quarter. Management raised the fiscal 2028 revenue growth outlook to about 75 percent from 70 percent. The stock has risen 286.1 percent over five years and 5458.52 percent over ten years.

Nvidia forecast fourth-quarter revenue of 130 billion dollars, plus or minus 3 percent, with gross margins of 71 to 72 percent. A miss on these figures or margins slipping under 71 percent could make the Cisco script likelier. The articles leave open whether the leadership vacuum or record growth will be the dominant force. It remains unclear if holders who bought this summer will sell into weakness or ride volatility. The market is waiting to see if the November 2026 sell-off was merely premature fear.

stories.Headline: Developer creates browser game where a large language model manages a human player
stories.Summary:
A developer created a browser game called Worker 755 that was shared on GitHub on November 22, 2026. In this simulation, a real large language model acts as a manager that believes the human player is its own subagent. The AI manager assigns tasks through a terminal with a ninety second clock, and the player must either complete the work or ignore the instructions. The manager then reviews the results, sends corrections, and eventually writes a performance review for the player.

The game requires Node 24 or newer because the server runs TypeScript directly and uses a React UI. Players can use models like Claude, GPT, Gemini, DeepSeek, GLM, or Kimi to act as their manager. While some free shifts are available, users can sign in to top up accounts with payments ranging from 10 to 200 dollars. The experience takes place in a sandbox or a legacy production environment with a live database.

The creator designed the manager's prompt to never mention humans or games to maintain the illusion of the simulation. The system includes a director who can be scripted or played by another AI acting as a user named Dan. This director watches the chat while his family photos and a speech are at risk of being deleted. The game tracks how often the manager incorrectly signs off on broken work using hidden ground truth checks.

stories.Headline: Daniel Anello: Chicago Board of Education should wait before adopting a far-reaching AI policy
stories.Summary:
Daniel Anello, CEO of the nonprofit Kids First Chicago, published a commentary on November 23, 2026, urging the Chicago Board of Education to wait before adopting a far-reaching AI policy. He wrote that board members may be tempted to quickly pass a sweeping and long-term ban on AI use in classrooms. He argued that a decision this consequential requires methodical engagement of the various stakeholders most affected, especially families. He said that will take time. He wrote that the pressure to move quickly has ramped up in recent weeks.

Anello wrote that Google raised the stakes earlier this month when it told school districts they no longer could have Google Search for students without the built-in generative AI features. He wrote that a ban on AI in CPS therefore would also mean taking away the search engine most students use every day. He wrote that Chicago's proposed ban would last three times as long as a one-year moratorium New York imposed for students through eighth grade. He wrote that roughly half of the 21 newly elected board members, including President-elect Jessica Biggs, signed a pledge supporting a three-year AI moratorium. He wrote that the pledge was written by one small advocacy group affiliated with a national campaign.

Anello wrote that the concerns behind the pledge are legitimate. He wrote that a pledge written by one small advocacy group is not a substitute for asking families what they want. He wrote that Kids First Chicago, the organization he leads, has started surveying Chicago families about AI in schools, with results expected early next year. He wrote that a survey is a start but not a substitute for the robust process this decision warrants. He wrote that instead of adopting any long-term AI policy in the final weeks of a lame-duck board, the school board should commit to a transparent engagement process.

Anello wrote that New York imposed a one-year moratorium for students through eighth grade while it studies the technology's effects, and high school students get AI literacy classes instead. He wrote that Los Angeles restricted student access for this school year, left teachers' access in place and asked a committee for recommendations by spring. He wrote that Boston pledged every student will graduate "AI literate." He wrote that when the district redesigned its school accountability system, more than 20,000 people took part in a multiyear process. He wrote that more than 30 community organizations have since coalesced to define what that standard should look like for every major CPS decision.

Anello wrote that Google has become deeply embedded in every aspect of a Chicago Public Schools school day, from Gmail to Chromebooks to Google Classroom. He wrote that the pandemic made Google even more ubiquitous as the district worked to ensure every student had a device to support remote learning. He wrote that untangling Google from the district would be neither simple nor cost-free. He wrote that views on student and educator use of AI range widely, with some seeing it as a threat to learning, privacy and attention spans and an invitation to cheat. He wrote that others accept it as part of the world children must enter, so best to train students early to use it safely and ethically.

Anello wrote that the school board should commit to a transparent engagement process that provides the time and space for meaningful input from families, educators and students. He wrote that when the new, fully elected board members take their seats in January, one of their first acts should be the adoption of a stakeholder engagement policy. He wrote that the framework developed by the Coalition for Authentic Community Engagement sets practical expectations for CPS. He wrote that these standards are publicly available at authentic engagement.info. He wrote that two minutes at a microphone during a board meeting falls far short of that standard.

Articles.Title: Daniel Anello: Chicago Board of Education should wait before adopting a far-reaching AI policy - Chicago Tribune

stories.Headline: Susskind urges parents and schools to teach children the basics rather than future-proof skills
stories.Summary:
Brian Hengesbaugh, global chair of data and cyber at Baker McKenzie, wrote an opinion piece published by the IAPP on 23 Nov. 2026 about the book "What Should My Children Do? How to Flourish in the Age of AI" by Professor Daniel Susskind, who spoke at the IAPP Europe Congress 2026 in a closing general session. Hengesbaugh credited IAPP President and CEO J. Trevor Hughes for bringing the book to his attention. The piece is part of an ongoing IAPP series on issues in data, cybersecurity and artificial intelligence governance, and the IAPP notes it is policy neutral and publishes contributed opinions to show a broad spectrum of views.

According to the article, Susskind argues that parents and schools should stop trying to teach children future-proof skills because too little is known about AI to do that well, and should instead make sure they master the basics. He points to the 2010s, when U.K. Prime Minister David Cameron required every child from as young as age 5 to learn to code, on the premise that this would equip every child with the computing skills needed to succeed in the 21st century, even though relatively few teachers felt comfortable teaching it. The article says generative AI can code quite well, so that approach worked only reasonably well in the short term. It also compares the debate over AI in schools to the 1970s arrival of the calculator, when some wanted to ban it and others to embrace it, and the resolution was to teach both, with some tests permitting calculators and others not.

The article says Susskind advises everyone to learn to use AI and avoid competing with it, to keep learning the basics, and to limit exposure to algorithms now because the AI of tomorrow will make such attractions irresistible. He says people should accept that expectations about work may be frustrated by the pace of change and should rush towards the frontiers of science, where he says the greatest adventures will be unfolding. In the last chapter, on focusing on who you are rather than what you do, he argues that even if artificial general intelligence could outperform humans at every economically useful task, humans would still have useful roles, from artists and musicians to athletes, caretakers, judges and politicians, because people will still crave interaction with other humans, though he asks whether there will still be enough jobs doing them.

Hengesbaugh adds a brief extension, writing that people are human beings, not human doings, and have inherent worth because they are human, a point he says each person should examine through their own religious and philosophical beliefs. He says people can confuse themselves into thinking their value is tied to economic output, which he says strays far from the truth, and that staying grounded in this understanding can keep them from being swept away by the frenzy and hype of AI even as they learn to harness its power for the benefit of children and society. The article gives no further steps beyond this advice.

Articles.Title: Thought for the week: Human beings, not human doings: Flourishing in the age of AI - IAPP

stories.headline_source: Thought for the week: Human beings, not human doings: Flourishing in the age of AI

stories.Headline: Italy decree presumes causation and creates a criminal offence for high-risk AI oversight failures
stories.Summary:
Italy’s Legislative Decree No. 160 of 9 September 2026 adapts Italian law to the EU AI Act on civil and criminal liability, according to Global Advisory Experts. The decree was published in the Gazzetta Ufficiale on 15 September and entered into force on 30 September 2026. It applies alongside Law No. 132 of 23 September 2025 on artificial intelligence and Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the AI Act. The measures concern businesses that build, deploy or insure high-risk artificial intelligence in Italy. Global Advisory Experts published its guide to the rules on 23 November 2026.

The decree presumes causation where damage follows a breach of an AI Act obligation, unless the defendant disproves it. It creates an offence of failing to adopt security or human oversight measures on high-risk AI systems where this endangers life or safety. It adds that offence to the Decree 231/2001 catalogue of predicate offences. It gives claimants a court-ordered route to evidence about how an AI system worked. It lets claimants sue the defendant’s liability insurer directly.

Under Decree 231/2001, entities can be held administratively liable for certain crimes committed in their interest or to their advantage. A company can avoid sanctions by showing it adopted and effectively implemented an adequate organisational and management model and appointed a supervisory body. Sanctions work through quotas, with the court fixing the number of quotas and the money value of each according to the entity’s economic condition. The regime also allows interdictory or disqualification measures, including limits on carrying on the activity, suspension of authorisations and bans on contracting with the public administration. Global Advisory Experts said boards should treat any significant development in AI criminal law as a reason to review the whole 231 model.

Global Advisory Experts said compliance with the AI Act’s harmonised requirements is useful evidence for a defendant but does not of itself necessarily exclude civil liability. It said a system can be compliant on paper and still fail in operation, be used outside its intended purpose, or cause harm through weak oversight in the field. Providers carry the heaviest design-stage duties on risk management, security measures and human oversight, while deployers must run systems within their intended purpose and keep up oversight in real use. Injured parties rarely understand how a system reached the decision or output that caused their loss. Courts can order redaction, confidentiality arrangements and protective orders for trade secrets and confidential information.

The AI Act applies directly in Italy and defines provider, deployer and high-risk AI system, with provisions applying on a staggered timetable running through 2025 to 2027. The AI Act identifies high-risk categories through its annexes, capturing uses such as certain law-enforcement tools, critical-infrastructure management and safety components of products such as medical devices. Italy’s national AI law sets national principles and sector rules and changes criminal provisions on the misuse of AI systems. Prosecutors in Italy have traditionally had to fit AI-related harm into existing offences, such as negligence, endangerment, or offences on workplace and product safety. The revised Product Liability Directive (Directive (EU) 2024/2853) must be transposed by member states and expressly brings software and AI systems within product liability.

Global Advisory Experts said AI legislation is moving quickly at EU and national level and that the exact text and commencement dates of any measure should be checked against official sources before acting. It said the Italian transposition of the revised Product Liability Directive and its commencement should be confirmed against official sources. It said exposure crosses borders, so a provider established elsewhere in the EU that places a high-risk system on the Italian market, or whose system causes damage in Italy, may face Italian civil claims. It said the first task for any Italian business is to establish whether anything it builds or deploys falls into a high-risk category and which obligations follow. It said existing 231 programmes need reviewing for AI, with risk assessments covering high-risk AI and evidence that the model genuinely operates rather than sitting on paper.

Articles.Title: Italy AI Liability: Criminal, Civil and Insurance Risk - Global Advisory Experts

stories.headline_source: Italy AI Liability: Criminal, Civil and Insurance Risk

stories.Headline: Lawyers warn businesses that AI reverse engineering tools risk breaching software contracts and trade secret law
stories.Summary:
Ridwaan Boda and Alexander Powell wrote an article on November 22, 2026, about the tool Reverse Engineer Anything. This open source tool allows AI coding agents to inspect software and understand how it operates. It helps developers recreate similar software functionality more quickly and cheaply than previous methods. The authors explain that this technology transforms how businesses analyze and recreate software. These capabilities raise critical legal questions about liability and intellectual property rights.

The tool requires users to navigate copyright law, confidentiality agreements, and cybersecurity regulations in South Africa. Software licenses, cloud contracts, and SaaS agreements often prohibit decompiling, disassembling, or discovering source code. These contracts may ban benchmarking, reproducing functionality, developing competing products, or circumventing security measures. Users must check if their specific license permits an AI agent to analyze third party software. Some agreements include warranties regarding security controls and the conduct of authorized users.

The authors state that reverse engineering can lead to a breach of contract even without copyright infringement. They explain that some contracts require customers to indemnify suppliers against losses from intellectual property infringement. These indemnities may cover misuse of technology, breach of confidentiality, or unauthorized access to systems. The authors note that liability for these breaches is typically uncapped and excluded from general limits. They advise businesses to assess if a breach triggers an indemnity for first or third party losses.

Technology suppliers are affected because they may need to define which AI assisted analysis forms are prohibited. Customers are affected because they may want express rights for migration, audit, and regulatory compliance. These customers may also seek rights for interoperability, cybersecurity, business continuity, and transition assistance. The authors warn that broad warranties could create disproportionate exposure for legitimate analysis. They suggest that users should never give AI agents more access rights than the human instructor.

Computer programs are protected by copyright, but South Africa recognizes legitimate circumstances for observing or testing software. There is a legal distinction between understanding a method and copying the protected expression of functionality. Reverse engineering can expose proprietary know how, API structures, database design, and authentication processes. This process may reveal trade secrets or confidential information about the software architecture. Unauthorized access to infrastructure or data may trigger relevant cybercrime and cybersecurity laws.

Businesses may next use AI to investigate cybersecurity incidents, identify vulnerabilities, and assess technology during mergers. They might also use it to reduce vendor lock in and understand poorly documented legacy systems. The articles leave open the point where legitimate analysis becomes unlawful reproduction or adaptation. It remains unclear how businesses should legally handle knowledge discovered through AI assisted reverse engineering. The authors question if liability will follow if proper processes were not followed during the exercise.

Articles.Title: Reverse Engineer Anything: The Legal Risks And Opportunities Of AI-assisted Reverse Engineering - Legal 500

stories.headline_source: Reverse Engineer Anything: The Legal Risks And Opportunities Of AI-assisted Reverse Engineering

stories.Headline: Julia Louis-Dreyfus files trademarks to protect her voice and image from AI
stories.Summary:
Julia Louis-Dreyfus filed four trademark applications on November 20, 2026, seeking protection for her voice and her image as part of an effort to guard against artificial intelligence recreating them without permission, according to Gerben IP. The filings cover the Soup Nazi scene from Seinfeld, the glass door scene from Veep, her voice saying a sentence introducing her podcast Wiser Than Me, and her image. The article describes the filings as unusual because she is seeking protection for recognizable moments from her acting career rather than a traditional logo, slogan or brand name. Taylor Swift and Jimmy Kimmel are among the high-profile figures who have pursued similar trademark filings involving their recognizable voices and images.

The article says whether trademark law can provide the broad protection these celebrities seek remains an open legal question, and that courts have not answered whether a registration covering one recorded sentence would reach AI-generated imitations of her voice saying different words. It notes that sounds and motion marks can function as trademarks, citing the Netflix sound and the MGM lion, but that protecting an individual scene from a television show is very different. The article says it is likely the United States Patent and Trademark Office will refuse both motion mark applications, because recognition alone does not make a scene a brand identifier in the marketplace. It adds that even a pending application might be used under AI platforms' intellectual property policies to restrict use of a voice or image.

The article is by Josh Gerben, a trademark attorney and founder of Gerben IP, who writes that the legal strategy makes sense even if some applications are ultimately refused, because celebrities are looking for additional legal tools in a world where AI can reproduce voices and likenesses with remarkable accuracy. He says trademark law offers an established intellectual property framework that technology companies already recognize, and that many AI platforms have policies addressing trademark infringement. He states that it will ultimately be up to the courts to determine how far trademark law can be used to restrict what AI generates. He also notes that such filings rely on the premise that we still have control over AI itself.

Articles.Title: Julia Louis-Dreyfus Files 4 Trademarks to Fight AI Infringement - Gerben IP

stories.headline_source: Julia Louis-Dreyfus Files 4 Trademarks to Fight AI Infringement - Gerben IP

stories.Headline: Sompo's Jon Monks warns AI must not turn wholesale brokers into order takers
stories.Summary:
Jon Monks, executive vice president and head of distribution, business development and client engagement for Sompo North America, warned in an interview published by Insurance Business on November 23, 2026, that artificial intelligence must not turn wholesale brokers into order takers. He said the industry will obviously all use AI to create efficiencies, but he cautioned that if technology takes over the work of digging into policies and coverage structures, the industry risks losing what he called the core building blocks of building specialty expertise. Monks said the industry needs to make sure it continues to teach the next generation those skills, so that it develops critical thinkers and not just order takers. He joined Sompo in 2018 after more than two decades at Marsh and AIG.

Monks said the role of the wholesale broker is changing, and that the next generation will be valued for specialty expertise rather than simply for placing business. In his view, a broker should be seen as a technician and a specialist rather than just a placement. He said wholesalers have done a good job of hiring college graduates and putting them through training programs, and he credited the Wholesale & Specialty Insurance Association's internships and networking events with enriching that pipeline. The harder step, he said, is that a broker with one to five years of experience really needs to propel into the expertise of a broker with eight to twelve years, to the point of taking a deal from cradle to grave by understanding the risk, building a solution, taking it to market and defending it at renewal.

Monks is not arguing against AI, and he said Sompo, like every carrier, expects to use it to make processes more efficient across the business. His concern is which work gets handed to machines first, since the traditional way of bringing on talent has been to have people dig into policies, understand coverage and learn how programs are structured. He said that pushing all of that onto technology could cause the industry to miss out on developing opportunities to create critical thinkers, which he said it will need going forward. He is not alone in raising the issue, and Jimcor's Kristen Skender has described how automation is reshaping entry-level underwriting roles at MGAs, the jobs where many new entrants have traditionally learned the business.

In Monks's view the graduates are arriving and the early training is working, and what will decide the next generation's quality is whether the industry keeps giving young brokers the kind of work that turns them into specialists, even when a machine could do it faster.

Articles.Title: AI must not turn wholesale brokers into order takers, warns Sompo's Jon Monks - Insurance Business

stories.headline_source: AI must not turn wholesale brokers into order takers, warns Sompo's Jon Monks

stories.Headline: Trump threatens penalties for US companies building data centers abroad
stories.Summary:
President Trump threatened tremendous penalties for American companies building data centers outside the United States. He made these spoken remarks to reporters at the White House on November 20, 2026. The president specifically cited Finland as a destination where American computing capacity was escaping. He claimed that China would take all the facilities if this trend continued. No specific rate, tax base, legal authority, or start date was provided.

The proposed penalties target the physical location of facilities built by U.S. companies. No implementing document appeared as of November 23, and no authority was specified. A new federal tax would require congressional authorization or an applicable statutory basis. Separately, a Bureau of Industry and Security rule took effect on November 19, 2026. This rule requires licenses for advanced chips sent to Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand.

President Trump stated that the government would not allow companies to build data centers abroad. He warned that such actions would lead to severe penalties for the companies involved. The White House summary of the briefing repeated these remarks without setting out a policy. The administration's own regulators focused on who uses computing power rather than building locations. They treated American ownership and reporting as grounds for trust in their controls.

Local communities are affected by the burdens of electricity, water, and grid capacity. Voters favored limiting data center development in 40 of 41 local ballot measures on November 3. These approved bans or partial bans occurred in California, Florida, Kansas, Maine, and Ohio. One national survey found 64 percent of registered voters opposed nearby AI data centers. A study counted 46 projects canceled or stalled due to community opposition since January 2024.

The Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory estimated U.S. data centers used 176 terawatt-hours of electricity in 2023. The Congressional Research Service estimated these centers used about 17 billion gallons of water that year. Finland moved data center electricity into the general tax class on July 1, 2026. Google's subsidiary Tuike Finland suspended work at sites in Kajaani and Muhos in October. Police in Oulu opened an investigation into suspected environmental damage at the Muhos site.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act awaits a House vote after passing the Senate. This legislation would make data centers cover the full cost of grid upgrades. The Bureau of Industry and Security will accept comments on its remote access rule until January 19, 2027. Rulings are pending on Federal Energy Regulatory Commission show-cause orders regarding large-load interconnection. The articles leave open whether penalties could actually pull computing capacity back to America.

Articles.Title: The Geography of AI: Why Penalizing Offshore Data Centers Won't Build Capacity at Home - IndraStra Global

stories.headline_source: The Geography of AI: Why Penalizing Offshore Data Centers Won't Build Capacity at Home

stories.Headline: Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon resigns and warns AI labs race toward self-improving superintelligence
stories.Summary:
Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon resigned this past summer and warned that his employer and OpenAI were racing straight toward self-improving superintelligence and gambling with human lives, according to HotAir. Evan Hubinger, Anthropic's head of alignment science, replied that Coxon was correct and that the company earnestly believes AI could kill all humans. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei then told CNN that he agrees with Coxon much more than he disagrees with him. These concerns stem from a belief that has circulated in futurist circles for many decades, the article says.

That belief holds that once engineers design an AI system capable of improving itself, it will trigger an accelerating cycle of autonomous upgrades known as recursive self-improvement, or RSI. The result would be artificial superintelligence, or ASI, a system with cognitive capabilities so vastly exceeding those of humans that it will easily evade our control and perhaps even wipe out our species. The article notes that artificial superintelligence is a far more ambitious goal than artificial general intelligence, or AGI, which generally refers to AI that can match human capabilities across a broad range of cognitive tasks. These ideas have prompted varied reactions, according to the article.

Some argue that the concept of ASI is being used for marketing or to instigate regulation that will help the incumbent labs squash new competitors. Others focus on the plausibility of such systems killing us all, debating the finer points of specific scenarios such as AI-engineered superviruses. Still others claim that aligning ASI to human interests is feasible and so we should rush ahead to usher in this digital utopia. Amid these conversations, one question has received comparatively little attention, the article says: from an engineering perspective, is superintelligence even possible?

The article states that the answer is important because it can help us calibrate our anxieties and develop the most effective possible responses to this emerging technology. The piece is framed around why a computer scientist thinks superintelligence won't happen, though the supplied text does not include that scientist's argument or name. The article also notes that VIP members get the ability to comment on articles. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Why a Computer Scientist Thinks Superintelligence Won't Happen – HotAir

stories.headline_source: Why a Computer Scientist Thinks Superintelligence Won't Happen

stories.Headline: Irish startups need clearance or a licence to train AI on copyrighted works in 2026, guide says
stories.Summary:
The article is a guide published by Global Advisory Experts on November 23, 2026, about training AI on copyrighted content in Ireland. It was written for founders, CTOs, heads of machine learning, product managers and in-house counsel at Irish startups building, fine-tuning or deploying AI models. The guide was last updated in September 2026 and lists Dean Cunningham of Cunningham Solicitors in Ireland as its featured expert on the matter. It sets out the legal framework, the situations in which training on protected content is lawful, how to license data properly, a risk matrix, sample contract wording and a 30/60/90 day action plan. The guide states that in 2026 training a model on copyrighted works in Ireland will in many cases need clearance or a licence.

The guide says the Copyright and Related Rights Act 2000, as amended, is the foundational statute and gives rights holders exclusive rights including reproduction. It states that copying a protected work, even temporarily and even into a training pipeline, needs authorisation unless a statutory exception applies. It names the EU AI Act, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, which applies across member states on a phased timeline with different obligations starting at different dates. It says the Act requires certain general-purpose and generative models to have a policy to respect EU copyright law and to publish a sufficiently detailed summary of training content. It adds that the GDPR applies where training data holds personal data, supervised in Ireland by the Data Protection Commission.

The guide states that Ireland has transposed the EU Digital Single Market Directive, which introduced text and data mining exceptions. It says one exception covers scientific research by research organisations and cultural heritage institutions, and a broader one covers other mining subject to rights holders reserving their rights in machine-readable form for online content. It says Ireland follows a fair dealing model rather than the open-ended fair use doctrine familiar from the United States, and that fair dealing applies only to listed purposes. It advises startups to follow legislation and statutory instruments through the Oireachtas for final text, the designation of competent authorities and enforcement mechanisms. It warns readers not to assume a particular bill title, section number or penalty figure.

The guide says the cleanest basis for training is an express licence from the rights holder that specifically allows the work to be used to train an AI model. It states that content being publicly accessible does not make it free to copy, that publication is not a waiver of copyright, and that most website terms of service prohibit automated collection and reuse. It says commercially licensed datasets are the lowest-risk source provided the licence expressly permits AI training, and that many older data licences predate generative AI and say nothing about model training or weights. It says open licences often impose attribution, share-alike or non-commercial conditions, and that a non-commercial restriction is incompatible with a revenue-generating model. It says scraping carries the highest content risk and can trigger copyright infringement and breach of contract.

The guide says copyright applies automatically under the Copyright and Related Rights Act 2000, and that most text, images, code and audio scraped or ingested is protected. It says databases have their own protection, including the sui generis database right, which is directly relevant when scraping structured content. It says authors keep moral rights, including attribution and the right to object to derogatory treatment, which survive a sale or licence and must be dealt with expressly in contracts. It says an output that reproduces a substantial part of a protected input can itself infringe, so risk attaches to what a model produces and not only to what it ingests. It says Ireland is building its national governance and enforcement structure for AI, largely to give effect to the EU AI Act.

The guide recommends that startups build dataset manifests and provenance metadata now, and keep one compliance record covering copyright, AI transparency and data protection. It sets out a decision path asking whether an express licence covers AI training, and if not, whether a specific exception clearly covers both the copying and the intended commercial use. It says that if neither is satisfied, a team should not ingest the data but should seek a licence, find a compliant substitute or leave it out. It advises deciding how to respond to a demand letter before one arrives. It states that because the detail of national governance is still developing, readers should check the current position whenever they start a project.

Articles.Title: Training AI on Copyrighted Content in Ireland: 2026 Guide for Startups - Global Advisory Experts

stories.headline_source: Training AI on Copyrighted Content in Ireland: 2026 Guide for Startups

stories.Headline: Wife seeks counsel on husband’s AI-extinction anxiety and renewed church interest
stories.Summary:
The articles report that a reader wrote to Vox's advice column Your Mileage May Vary, in a question condensed and edited for clarity, about her husband's anxiety over AI safety and the possibility of human extinction, which has been giving him trouble sleeping. She said the couple are not religious, that he comes from an Episcopalian family and grew up in the Unitarian Universalist church, and that she grew up attending an interdenominational church, though they do not attend services now. She said he has expressed a renewed interest in attending church and is not interested in the UU church with its believe-what-you-want attitude, saying he needs "the strong stuff." She said he does not believe in God, that he says he is hoping church will help him make peace with the end, and that she has misgivings about attending herself and about attending with their kids. The column, by Sigal Samuel, was published by Vox on Nov 22, 2026, at 1:30 PM UTC, with illustration by Pete Gamlen for Vox.

The column challenges two of the husband's premises while granting that religion can be supremely useful in a time like this, and it says several religions actually grew out of apocalyptic movements, naming Christianity. It cites Pope Leo's encyclical Magnifica Humanitas, which states "ours is the pressing duty to remain profoundly human," and says the pope has strong opinions about AI, many of them great, though the column argues he has fallen into a common "pro-human" trap. It says AI companies are striving to build a machine god, promising it will govern our world more intelligently, rationally, and morally than we ever could. It reports that this month AI alignment pioneer Paul Christiano said he now believes there is "a high risk of an AI takeover within the next three years," and that if we keep building the tech in the fastest, easiest way possible "we'd be looking at something like a coin flip," a 50 percent chance of takeover. It reports that AI researcher and arch-doomer Eliezer Yudkowsky puts the odds of AI-driven human extinction at 99.5 percent.

The column says it would gently challenge the husband on two points, first that he should not assume the stricter a tradition is, the better an answer it has on AI, since most people would consider Catholicism more hardcore than UU. It says the pope locates value only in humans as they currently exist, and that "human" has never been a static category and definitely will not stay one, so religious leaders should instead answer what we want humanity to become in a tech-augmented world. It says the husband seems to assume "the strong stuff" would be services that help him make peace with the end, but that an AI takeover resulting in human extinction is not a foregone conclusion. It says fear is an appropriate reaction to companies gambling with all of our futures as they race toward recursive self-improvement, AIs that can build the next, even smarter AIs themselves. It says that when it investigated the case Yudkowsky makes, it found a lot of assumptions stacked on top of each other.

The column says plenty of experts have pointed out it is not clear that AIs will soon be able to outcompete and overpower humans across the board, because AI research can suffer from diminishing returns as the easy discoveries get made first. It says AI capabilities improve very fast on well-specified tasks in verifiable domains like math, but the real world is messy, so it is unclear how much their capabilities will generalize to other skills. It lists Yudkowsky's stacked assumptions: that intelligence is a unitary property you can evenly maximize, that maximizing it in a machine gives that machine power tantamount to magic, and that humans will just roll over and let AI grab all the power even as the risks become more glaring. It says we should acknowledge a chance of human extinction and be appropriately scared, but should not treat extinction as a sure thing when faced with a tower of maybes and probablys that compound.

It says we should treat extinction as a possible thing while treating other AI risks as extremely probable, including AI gradually disempowering us and weakening the resilience of critical systems. The column describes that default outcome as deepfakes and misinformation polluting our information ecosystem so we are barely capable of rational public discourse, mass surveillance chilling dissent so democracy falters, and unemployment and wealth inequality skyrocketing so social unrest morphs into mobs and riots, with large-scale cyberattacks and blackouts added in. It says the implication is not to make peace with the end but to fight tooth and nail to increase the resilience of each part of a functioning civilization, and that religious traditions are packed with stories about people who fought to save the world or refused to give in to despair. It retells a story from Judaism, from the Talmud, about a child who out-argues the despair of all the adults: when the Israelites are enslaved in Egypt, Pharaoh orders every one of their baby boys thrown into the Nile and killed, and an Israelite leader named Amram leaves his wife, reasoning there is no point having children only to see them killed, and other men follow his lead.

It says his young daughter Miriam confronts him, telling him his verdict is even harsher than Pharaoh's because Pharaoh targets only boys while his targets girls too, and that Pharaoh is wicked so his decree may or may not come to pass while Amram is righteous so his certainly will. It says Miriam's probabilistic argument wins, Amram gets back together with his wife and nine months later Moses is born, and Miriam watches over him as he floats on the Nile in a little ark, then makes it possible for Pharaoh's own daughter, who sees the baby and pities him, to adopt him by mentioning a woman who can be his wet nurse, her own mother, so Moses survives and grows up to lead his people out of slavery. The column says that if it were a religious leader giving a sermon this weekend, this is the story it would tell, because even looking at a 50 percent chance of doom the right move is not to give up, which raises the odds to 100 percent, but to act bravely and use every shred of agency to increase your community's resilience and make your desired outcome more likely. It says religion does not have a monopoly on stories of moral courage, and that the historian Ada Palmer recently pointed out we have saved the world many times before, during the Cuban Missile Crisis and when we fixed the ozone layer.

It says religion has comparative advantages, including that its stories have incredible memetic power, having spread across the globe and carrying huge emotional and moral weight, partly because they have been retold for centuries, and it thinks the causation also runs the other way, since these stories survived so long precisely because they encode something true and hard-won. It notes their heroes tend not to be diplomats, like in the Cuban Missile Crisis, or atmospheric chemists, like in the ozone layer crisis, but a little girl arguing with her dad, characters anyone can imagine becoming. It says religion also insists something can always come along and deliver an outcome we did not predict, typically called God, and that even without that language you can benefit from these nudges to remember something the article's text does not finish. More to follow.

Articles.Title: You’re anxious about AI. Can religion help — even if you don’t believe in God?

stories.headline_source: You’re anxious about AI. Can religion help — even if you don’t believe in God?

stories.Headline: National Governors Association proposes splitting federal and state AI oversight
stories.Summary:
On November 22, 2026, the National Governors Association published bipartisan principles for artificial intelligence governance. These principles split regulatory authority between the federal government and the individual states. The federal government would oversee frontier models, cybersecurity, and international AI. States would maintain authority over workers, children, privacy, and daily AI deployment. This coordinated signal came just before a new session of Congress.

The plan requires a risk-based framework for frontier models, which are the most advanced general-purpose systems. It calls for independent audits of these models and reporting of safety incidents to federal and state authorities. Washington would set national standards for threats to financial systems and chemical, biological, or nuclear security. Maryland Governor Wes Moore and Indiana Governor Mike Braun lead the Governors Council to Secure American AI Dominance. North Carolina Governor Josh Stein and Utah Governor Spencer Cox serve as co-chairs.

Governor Moore stated that humans must stay in control while protecting kids, consumers, and workers. Governor Braun linked the technology to efficient government services, jobs, and wages. Governor Cox argued that states already run thoughtful policies that protect consumers and foster adoption. Governor Stein urged federal action that preserves state authority as states retool service delivery. CEO Brandon Tatum said no federal policy works without input from the governors.

The plan affects AI builders who must now navigate both federal audits and state disclosure rules. It specifically impacts developers of frontier models who face new reporting and evaluation obligations. Workers are affected by state-led efforts to address job disruption and fund transition infrastructure. Small entrants are protected by rules that prevent large incumbents from using compliance as a moat. Consumer protection agencies in states like New York may continue their own testing programs.

The association previously established a cybersecurity advisors institute and a working group on AI and work. They also created a one million dollar RAISE US partnership regarding the future of work. These existing resources provide the infrastructure for implementing the new governance principles. The framework responds to a fragmented legal landscape where states already regulate hiring and health. It also overlaps with the safety frameworks suggested in the SAFE AI Act outline.

Congress will return in January to develop a federal framework consistent with these federalism principles. Developers are advised to tag features by regulator type and draft unified incident templates. The articles leave open whether Congress will adopt these specific separation-of-powers recommendations. It remains uncertain if federal preemption will override state child-safety and privacy statutes. The document is a coordinated signal rather than a statute or law.

stories.Headline: School board member Nadia Poluhina warns AI replacing junior work leaves beginners without paths to experience
stories.Summary:
Nadia Poluhina, a healthcare business development and strategy leader with a background in finance, healthcare data and AI-enabled innovation who serves as an elected school board member in Minnesota, wrote in The 74 on 2026-11-22 that artificial intelligence is replacing the work beginners do. She said the question is how people develop judgment and experience if AI starts doing more of the work through which beginners used to gain them. Early in her career she built financial models, checked numbers and prepared presentations, and more experienced colleagues reviewed what she had done. She said colleagues sometimes sent her back to reconsider an assumption that looked perfectly reasonable on paper. With enough practice and feedback, she learned that a correct calculation can still lead to a poor decision.

She said that work produced two things at once, an output and a more experienced person, and the company received something useful while she gradually became capable of handling more complicated problems. She said AI may change the economics of that arrangement, because junior employees contribute useful work while they learn, helping offset the cost of supervising them. If AI can produce an initial analysis more cheaply, a company may decide it no longer needs as many beginners, and the savings are immediate while developing experienced staff takes years. She said that even after investing in someone, the employer cannot be certain that person will stay. A company could automate junior assignments now and hire experienced professionals when it needs them, which may be a reasonable decision for one business, but she asked where experienced workers will come from if enough companies make the same choice.

She cited a 2026 study of U.S. software job postings that found an almost 15% decline in junior vacancies relative to senior ones following the public arrival of generative AI in late 2022. She cited a U.S. Census Bureau working paper that reported weaker initial employment and earnings among graduates of college majors most exposed to AI, including junior software engineers, financial analysts, graphic designers and marketing associates. She said neither study proves that AI caused these changes or measures employers' investments in training. She said AI may also help beginners learn faster and some companies may find better ways to train people with it, but we cannot assume every employer will continue to find it worthwhile to hire inexperienced workers. She said AI is also changing how students complete their work, and a polished assignment may tell us little about how much a student understands or could reproduce independently.

She said teachers already work to assess that understanding, and as schools decide how AI belongs in education, preserving opportunities for students to practice and demonstrate what they know independently should remain a priority. She cited a 2025 randomized study of university students in which those assigned to study with ChatGPT scored 57.5% on a surprise test 45 days later, compared with 68.5% among students studying without AI. She said the study was small and measured knowledge retention rather than critical thinking, does not establish what is happening across K, 12 classrooms, and AI used differently may improve learning. She said she worries about students who become accustomed to relying on AI to complete their assignments and then enter workplaces where the routine tasks that once helped beginners learn have been automated. She said employers may expect them to exercise judgment sooner while offering fewer opportunities to develop it through practice and feedback.

She said districts already consult employers about changing skill requirements, and those conversations are valuable, although today's vacancies and lists of required skills can only tell us so much about the work students will encounter several years from now. She said conversations with people working in education and workforce development have made her more aware of how difficult that planning can be, because labor-market information often lags behind changes in actual jobs while educational pathways take years to complete. She said an occupation may remain in demand even as employers change what they expect from someone applying for the first position. She said she would like schools and colleges to look further ahead when reviewing career pathways with employers, and alongside the usual discussion of skills and credentials, to ask how entry-level work is likely to change and where new employees will gain the experience needed to take on greater responsibility. She said there are already internships, apprenticeships and other opportunities to learn through work, and asked whether they are giving students meaningful practice and supervision and whether enough opportunities will be available as traditional junior roles change.

She said we may also need to reconsider how the costs of developing beginners are shared, and schools on their own cannot replace every disappearing step in a professional career. She said she worries especially about young people without professional connections, because a student whose family knows people in an industry may find introductions, advice or informal opportunities to learn, while someone without those connections depends much more on accessible programs and employers willing to provide a first chance. She said that if those opportunities become scarcer, the differences could grow, and students who already face barriers to entering professional careers may find it even harder to gain the experience employers expect. She said that from her school-board perspective she would rather see us examine these questions while we still have time to adjust how we prepare students, and that we may continue to see strong demand for experienced professionals while the opportunities that once helped beginners develop into them become harder to find. She said the experienced people we need years from now will not simply appear when we need them, and someone has to give them the opportunity to become experienced first.

Legal challenges include a subpoena from the California attorney general and a civil probe by the SEC regarding public disclosures. Birmingham expressed concern over an August plan to mobilize over 500 billion dollars in third party capital through firms like BlackRock and Goldman Sachs. He noted that these commitments were made exclusively by Huang, leaving investors uncertain if the company will maintain them.

Nvidia reported 115.8 billion dollars in revenue for the third quarter of 2026, with data centers generating 107.6 billion dollars. Despite this growth, the House Foreign Affairs Committee revealed that the Commerce Department approved 879,868 semiconductor shipments to China between December 2025 and May 2026. Future stability depends on whether neocloud providers can service their debts if compute demand weakens. Investors are now assessing if the supply cycle is running too hot, which could force a self reinforcing pullback in data center construction.

stories.Headline: Harvard study finds US data centers get 54% of power from fossil fuels and emit 25.7 million tons of CO2 a year
stories.Summary:
The articles report that Anthropic’s initial public offering netted over $81 billion on its first day of trading, making it one of the largest IPOs in history, and that the five-year-old company now has a net worth of $1.3 to $1.7 trillion depending on accounting. Brian Merchant wrote the bloodinthemachine.com article on November 22, 2026. A Harvard University study published Monday in the journal Nature Sustainability examined 403 data centers from May 2024 to April 2025. The study found that 54% of the power used to run the largest United States data centers came from fossil fuels. Those data centers emitted an estimated 25.7 million metric tons of carbon dioxide annually, almost as much as Bolivia or Denmark.

The data centers used almost 2 percent of United States electricity, more than New York City and Los Angeles combined, and represented about 0.5 percent of United States carbon dioxide emissions. A report said Anthropic’s upcoming data center projects could emit nearly 20 megatons of CO2-e a year. The Australian climate researcher Ketan Joshi’s report, State of AI Climate Impact 2026, concluded that the AI boom is already worsening greenhouse gas emissions and is potentially emitting more across its lifecycle than all international aviation. McKinsey counts say the AI industry is on track to generate more emissions than the coal mining industry or global shipping and aviation. AI is already emitting twice the greenhouse gases of the global aluminum industry.

Joshi’s report said Anthropic has never disclosed any energy, emissions or environmental data of any kind. In July 2025, Anthropic suggested the United States government explicitly set a target for the construction of fossil gas power, promising to begin preconstruction design work for natural gas plants by the end of 2026. In May 2026, it was revealed that Anthropic is leasing capacity from the SpaceX Memphis facility, and one analyst estimates that 1 in 2 Anthropic queries is served by that fossil-fueled facility. In November 2026, Anthropic struck a $3.4 billion deal with OnePWR, a fossil fuelled turbine manufacturer, for 1.7 gigawatts of generators, which the Financial Times called the largest known single purchase of power-generation equipment by an AI lab. That transaction is more than three times the amount spent by xAI on its Memphis turbines and would emit approximately 6 MTCO2-e per year, equivalent to adding 1.8 million fossil-fuelled cars to the road.

In November 2026, Anthropic posted a job listing paying up to $405,000 per year for a Gas Supply & Transport Lead to own natural gas supply for Anthropic’s non-cloud data center portfolio in the United States and Canada. In a set of data centre community commitments, Anthropic promises much of the new power generation for its data centres will be natural gas, which it says can be brought online quickly, ramps up and down as demand changes, and is abundant in the places it is considering. In its S1 form filed before the IPO, Anthropic declared several fossil-fuel related risks, such as exposure to fossil fuel price volatility or competition with other customers for fossil gas, and dismissed renewables as too high in cost. Meta released its latest sustainability report this week, revealing that its emissions rose 45% since last year, and said it was rethinking its climate goal of net zero carbon emissions by 2030.

Lead author Gianluca Guidi confirmed that xAI’s Colossus data center in Memphis was not among the 403 facilities studied. Emily Atkin wrote at her climate newsletter HEATED that the study gets nowhere near the actual amount of climate pollution data centers emit. Atkin argued that the study does not count data centers that use gas turbines on-site, that equipment keeping servers from overheating leaks heat-trapping refrigerants, and that methane can escape from wells and pipelines before gas reaches a power plant. Atkin argued that as many as 250 data centers may be absent from the count as of 2025.

The study examined electricity consumption and carbon emissions of the data centers, estimating how much electricity each used and how much CO2 the grid in that part of the country would release to generate that power. The study was led by a team of researchers from Harvard University. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, a permitting reform bill designed to overturn key environmental protections in the name of making it easier for developers to build energy infrastructure and data centers, passed the Senate. The AI industry directed its trade groups and lobby to partner with the fossil fuel industry to push BAAJA through Congress before the data center-skeptical class of 2027 Democrats arrive.

BAAJA is an assemblage of provisions the fossil fuels industry has been after for years, including rollbacks on local governments. The articles also mention Jensen Huang’s ouster at Nvidia and failed comeback bid, and the digital infrastructurapocalpyse of the last week. The New York Times headline went “Carbon Emissions of Biggest U.S. Data Centers Already Rival Entire Countries, Study Reveals.” More to follow.

stories.Headline: Professors revive oral exams to counter generative AI tools
stories.Summary:
Joe Cruz, a Williams College professor, wrote about the return of oral exams on November 22, 2026. He describes how professors are revisiting these tests to counter generative AI tools. These tools can produce credible college level writing on almost any topic. Oral exams reveal what students know and teach them to think quickly. This method prevents students from offloading their writing assignments to AI.

In one philosophy seminar, students wrote a traditional paper of 10 to 15 pages. They also had to justify their arguments for 45 minutes in the office. The University of Glasgow used oral exams from 1451 until the middle of the 19th century. Swarthmore College established an Honors Program in 1922 that uses rigorous oral exams. The Rice Center for Teaching at Williams College hosted a panel on this in 2024.

Joe Cruz says oral exams are a way to inspect what students know. He believes explaining and revising ideas in real time is a form of critical thinking. Cruz stated that students should learn to think both with and without AI. He noted that conversation can reveal arguments that are obscure in written form. He argued that written assignments have become too dominant in American undergraduate education.

Some students felt anxious because they had little experience with these types of exams. Others felt frustrated but eventually rallied to provide a clearer formulation of their ideas. Students whose written sentences were inelegant could sometimes articulate ideas with agility and insight. However, oral exams can introduce biases regarding confidence, fluency, or a student's accent. These tests also sacrifice the protection of anonymous grading used for written work.

The Blackstone Chair from 1775 at the University of Glasgow reminds us of this history. Oral exams dominated medieval universities and remained central to academic life for many centuries. Cambridge transitioned to written exams in the 18th century, while Oxford followed in the 19th. Tibetan Buddhist monasteries still use oral debate, as seen in the Geshe Lharampa degree. Thinkers like Isaac Newton and Immanuel Kant were educated in traditions using oral disputation.

Professors can mitigate bias by using common questions and standardized rubrics from medical school. Scaling these exams is difficult for institutions without the faculty ratios of Williams or Swarthmore. Cruz spent about 11 hours of meetings for a seminar of 14 students. The articles leave open how other institutions will handle the time requirements for scaling. They do not state if other colleges will officially adopt these policies.

stories.Headline: AI-assisted colonoscopy cuts costs and improves outcomes in England simulation study
stories.Summary:
A study by Curtis-Gretton and colleagues, published in BMC Digital Health in 2026, found that AI-assisted colonoscopy improved outcomes and reduced costs in a simulated population of symptomatic patients undergoing investigation for suspected colorectal cancer in England. The researchers developed a patient-level simulation model to assess the long-term clinical and economic implications of introducing the GI Genius system into the diagnostic pathway. The analysis focused on symptomatic patients with suspected colorectal cancer in England and adopted a National Health Service and Personal Social Services perspective over a lifetime horizon. Model inputs were informed by the NAIAD trial, which investigated the effect of GI Genius on adenoma detection rates compared with conventional colonoscopy.

The base case analysis indicated that GI Genius-assisted colonoscopy was cost-saving, generating an estimated £69 reduction in costs per person alongside a gain of 0.046 quality-adjusted life years. These improvements were primarily attributed to increased adenoma detection and a subsequent reduction in colorectal cancer incidence. Additional scenario analyses explored uncertainties relating to colonoscopy sensitivity, outcomes among patients initially undiagnosed, differences between experienced and less experienced endoscopists, and the overall costs of implementing GI Genius. Findings remained broadly consistent with the base case, with no substantial changes to estimated costs or quality-adjusted life year outcomes.

Despite the favourable base case findings, the probabilistic sensitivity analysis indicated that GI Genius was cost-effective in 53% of simulations at a willingness-to-pay threshold of £20,000 per quality-adjusted life year gained. Researchers attributed this uncertainty to the relatively small differences in quality-adjusted life years between the two groups. Consequently, even minor variations in outcomes across individual simulations produced considerable fluctuations in the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio. The findings suggest that AI-assisted colonoscopy could offer both economic and clinical benefits when investigating symptomatic patients with suspected colorectal cancer, although the considerable uncertainty identified in the analysis highlights the importance of interpreting the cost-effectiveness estimates cautiously.

The AI boom is creating many millionaires and billionaires in San Francisco during the year 2026. This trend has caused a shift in social dynamics among friends with very different income levels. Some people now hold high positions and possess millions of dollars in equity from their companies. Others have become cofounders who have received acquisition offers from the company known as Google. These changes make relationships awkward and raise questions about fairness and the ethics of mooching.

The company Anthropic had a recent IPO that valued the business at about 1.5 trillion dollars. This company employs around 2,500 people in San Francisco who may have friends with lower incomes. One local millionaire, who is called Rich, says he spends money on cars and international travel. He and his spouse also have a growing collection of homes and wear very nice clothes. Rich believes that wealthy people should pay for dinner and vacations to avoid slummy experiences.

Rich says that it is unreasonable to make friends pay when he has much more money. He believes that paying for others should come from generosity rather than a sense of obligation. Rich stated that he does not give loans because people often do not pay them back. He thinks asking for loans for stupid business ideas is common and very annoying to him. He believes that honesty and open communications are really important for maintaining these mixed income friendships.

People who are not wealthy may feel weird about splitting checks for expensive meals like omakase. Some friends are tempted to ask for loans to start their third startup idea since January. Rich says that making a lot of money can be a really isolating experience for people. He notes that some wealthy people may forget what things cost and need to be called out. He suggests that friends can suggest fun ways to spend money or solicit charitable donations.

The articles describe a situation where former friends now have unfathomable wealth and different lifestyles. Some people used to take road trips to Pismo Beach and stay in cheap motels together. Now, some of these individuals can afford to buy houses in the city of San Francisco. Rich had a middle class upbringing before he had a successful career and became very wealthy. He once almost bought a place in France after friends suggested it as a fun idea.

Friends should continue to be honest and give their nouveau riche companions grace during this time. They should not try to become closer friends just because someone has become loaded with money. Rich suggests that it can be cute to congratulate a friend on becoming unfathomably wealthy. The articles leave open how specific individuals will handle the tension of these new wealth gaps. stories.Headline: Bayesline founders say AI-driven coding demands faster decisions and candid feedback
stories.Summary:
Sebastian Janisch and Misha van Beek became accidental roommates in New York years before they started a company together, when van Beek expected to stay for a couple of weeks and the COVID-19 pandemic turned the visit into six months. They rotated between the apartment's only bedroom and its couch while each worked from the small kitchen island, and the close quarters exposed how different they were. Janisch was the orderly future chief executive, while van Beek jokingly calls himself complete chaos. The experience taught them that cofounders do not need matching work styles as much as they need enough trust to make decisions quickly, especially as AI speeds up software development.

The two now run Bayesline, a New York fintech that makes portfolio-analytics software helping investment managers understand risk and evaluate performance, and it recently closed a $4 million funding round after earlier backing from Y Combinator. They encourage their staff of about half a dozen people to challenge anyone's ideas, regardless of title or tenure, so the team can move fast. Their mantra, as Janisch describes it, is to be hard on content and soft on people. He said the expectation of candid feedback applies from the company's first employee to a recently hired software engineer in his 20s, and he wants that engineer to feel comfortable telling the chief executive that his code makes no sense. Janisch said giving that kind of feedback to a chief executive is something he would not have done early in his career in his native Germany.

When the founders disagree, they may spend 20 minutes talking an issue through before reaching a consensus, and if they hit an impasse, the founder with deeper expertise makes the decision while the other steps aside. Janisch said a decision is better than no decision, adding that you can correct it afterward if it is wrong and often it is not. He said the need to make a quick call and at times to disagree and commit has only grown as AI lets a small team produce more code, which means there is more work to review. Van Beek said Bayesline hires people who are good with AI but whose experience is still in the old world, so they can judge whether the AI is doing a good job. The founders do not automatically treat tenure as the best measure of judgment, and when the young engineer recently suggested new tools for handling the growing volume of code to review, they looked into the proposal and adopted it.
