stories.Headline: Pictet strategists stay constructive on AI and tech stocks for 2027
stories.Summary:
Pictet Asset Management's chief strategist Luca Paolini and senior multi asset strategist Arun Sai shared their asset allocation outlook for 2027, joined by other wealth managers who offered views on sectors, market capitalisations and regions. The group's stance on investment prospects for 2027 was more positive than it had been a year earlier, according to the outlook. The strategists weighed equities, bonds, alternatives and commodities as they set out how portfolios should be positioned for the year ahead. One wealth manager said she remained reluctant to invest in Brazilian assets, while another pointed to the semiconductor ecosystem that supports the buildout of artificial intelligence capacity. The outlook also touched on record levels of peacetime debt, which the contributors described as not a zero risk for investors.

The 2027 outlook sets out a constructive position on artificial intelligence and technology stocks, with allocations spread across equities, bonds, alternatives and commodities rather than concentrated in a single asset class. The strategists framed the balance of risks around record peacetime debt, which they said is not a zero risk even as they stay positive on the year. The reluctance to invest in Brazilian assets was noted alongside the more favourable view of technology and AI related holdings. The semiconductor ecosystem supporting the AI buildout was cited as a reason for confidence in the sector. The discussion of sectors, market capitalisations and regions indicates that the allocation views are meant to be applied across a diversified portfolio rather than to one market alone.

Paolini and Sai, as chief strategist and senior multi asset strategist at Pictet Asset Management, are the named authors of the outlook, and other wealth managers contributed their own allocation views. One contributor said she was reluctant to invest in Brazilian assets, and another described the semiconductor ecosystem as supporting the buildout. The strategists said the balance of risks should be struck with an appropriate time frame such as the one covered by the outlook. They described record levels of peacetime debt as not a zero risk, a caution that sits alongside their constructive stance. The comments were paraphrased in the coverage rather than given as direct quotations beyond a few words.

The outlook arrives as wealth managers weigh how much of their 2027 allocation should go to AI and technology stocks, and the coverage points readers toward further research on private markets and family offices. Related items listed alongside the outlook include Tiedemann Global's explanation of its investment formula and its view that private markets have more headway, and guidance on how family offices should address private markets when valuations are stretched. A separate item covers bankers' fears that so called Bitcoin treasuries are an accident waiting to happen. The coverage also invites readers to gain access to regular and exclusive research on the global wealth management sector, along with industry events such as breakfast briefings and summits in major wealth management centres and industry awards programmes.

stories.Headline: Experts say AI speeds up planning of cyberattacks on industrial equipment
stories.Summary:
Experts say artificial intelligence has made it faster to plan cyberattacks on industrial equipment, according to a report by Tom Wilson in the Financial Times dated 22 November 2026. The article states that AI helps attackers read manuals and research past accidents more quickly than before. The report was published under the headline that the AI cyber threat is already here. The available text of the article is limited to its headline and summary, because the full piece sits behind a subscription.

The report does not give the names of any attackers, the equipment targeted, or the dates of any incidents in the text available. It also gives no figures on how much faster planning has become or how many attacks have been carried out. The article does not say which manuals or accident records the attackers study. No specific industrial sector or country is identified in the available material.

The experts quoted in the summary attribute the speed-up to AI tools that help attackers work through technical documents and past accident research. The article does not name those experts or set out their remarks beyond that summary. It does not say what the attackers are said to be planning or whether any campaign has been detected. No response from equipment makers, regulators or governments appears in the available text.

The wider context in the summary is that the cyber threat from AI is already present rather than only expected in the future. The article does not say what happens next, whether defences are being changed, or how companies should respond. Because the full article is not available, the details beyond the headline and summary cannot be reported. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Dylan Patel says local permits, not chips, push AI data center gigawatts into 2028
stories.Summary:
SemiAnalysis founder Dylan Patel said data center construction is being throttled by local permitting rather than by GPUs, labor or equipment, and that his firm has already pushed multiple gigawatts of capacity from 2027 into 2028 and more out of 2028 entirely. He made the case on the Sourcery podcast, in an interview published alongside a BigGo Finance report dated 2026-11-20. Patel said the binding constraint is a permit counter in a county office most people could not name. He said his team pushed back multiple gigawatts out of 2027 into 2028, and more gigawatts are slipping out of 2028, for one reason, that permits are just not available. SemiAnalysis tracks every data center in the world, tests chips and models, and employs about 115 people across 15 countries, with offices in New York, Chicago, San Francisco, Oregon, Singapore and Korea.

The delays are spread across thousands of local jurisdictions rather than a single national policy, which Patel said makes them harder to forecast and harder to fix. Texas retains broad leverage through water, wastewater, stormwater, water-consumption rules and air permits, and Patel noted that air permits alone can stop a data center even if it is off-grid and uses almost no water. A poll SemiAnalysis ran with David Shor's team covered every county with a 100-megawatt-plus data center operating, under construction or planned within three years, and found 51% aware one exists in their county today, meaning 49% unaware, and about 40% aware of one planned within three years. Patel pointed to a Louisiana county that raised teacher pay by about $20,000 after a data center's tax revenue arrived. He said all of Elon Musk's data centers use less water than three In-N-Out restaurants, counting embedded water in the supply chain including the fabs making chips and the fuel and turbines generating power against the embedded water in the burgers.

Patel described Texas Governor Gina Hinojosa as publicly constructive, saying she has said she will not stop data centers but will require that they not raise electricity prices and that they be reasonable stewards of water, and he argued both are solvable. He said the harder problem is union labor, because Texas has little union construction labor and mandating it would mean telling electricians and industrial plumbers earning $200,000 or more on data center work that they must join a union, which he suggested is politically unpalatable. He said community opposition is cheaply solvable through direct local compensation, arguing a company could subsidize the power of everyone in a 30 mile radius and it costs like nothing, and could subsidize things and just give people money and it will be fine. He conceded the harms are real but manageable when projects are done properly: noise for an adjacent house, water use if cooling is inefficient, grid price effects if a project gets property tax breaks and buys from the grid, and little lasting local employment after construction ends. He criticized a New York Times bestselling book that he said overstated data center water use by roughly a thousandfold and was later revised, with the original figure still widely cited.

Patel said data centers ranked nowhere among top election issues, where inflation and war with Iran dominated, and that most people hold a vague negative impression formed by online content, some of it reasonable, some completely unreasonable fake astroturfed stuff, and some pushed by external actors. He noted that most jurisdictions that have banned data centers or imposed moratoriums had no meaningful data center capacity to begin with. On space-based data centers he was blunt, saying they solve nothing in the next three to four years and may be further out because the engineering is very hard; he acknowledged Elon Musk is building heavily toward 2028, said he would take the over on that timeline, and allowed roughly a gigawatt in space by around 2030. He said Anthropic crushed it in Q2, OpenAI crushed it in Q3 while Anthropic did only okay, and Anthropic is back on top with Opus 55 and Fable 5.2, while OpenAI keeps delaying releases and Google has re-entered the picture. He said Instinct and Meta's Muse, despite being worse models than OpenAI's, are way better products than OpenAI dots, and attributed part of OpenAI's weakness to an overzealous safety layer called Guardian that blocks actions in its coding and dots products.

Patel described OpenAI's chat interface as badly designed, with separate chat and work sections, a reasoning-effort slider on one side but no pro option on the other, and guessed about 90% of users never toggle models at all; when he beta-tested Meta's Muse he found it clear and intuitive. He said SemiAnalysis runs about $15 million a year on AI, most of the year went to Claude, and over the last few months persistent agents went from zero to 45% of that spend, most of it through Perplexity Computer, which uses Claude and OpenAI models on the back end but offers a better harness. He expected developer tools like Claude Code and CEX to be less sticky because developers switch easily, while enterprise contracts will stick, and said Anthropic has offered enterprise customers a discount conditioned on 70% or more of their AI spend going to Anthropic. He named Sierra and Harvey as growing revenue fast with real ROI, though possibly at high customer acquisition costs, questioned whether inference providers deserve their valuation multiples, noted Harvey's published margins have swung widely, and said he does not know Perplexity's margin on the traffic it intermediates.

He said most startups fail but some will be very successful. Patel has raised a $500 million early-stage fund as a solo general partner, investing at seed and Series A in infrastructure: robotics, silicon, optics, manufacturing, hardware and networking. He would not disclose check sizes, saying disclosure would remove his optionality, and said the fund is a separate company from SemiAnalysis and Catrini and that he will never use the research platform to promote portfolio companies. He said he does not know how to scale an application to a billion users, so he would not be a useful app investor, and that SemiAnalysis employs people who worked at ASML, Applied Materials, Lam Research, TSMC, Intel, Nvidia, Google, Microsoft and Amazon and who have built chips, kernels, compilers, data centers and power plants.

He called out what he sees as a toxic trait among San Francisco and New York investors, believing they know things they don't, and noted hardware investing requires both a great founder and a great idea, whereas application software investing can sometimes ride on the founder alone. He framed his own goals plainly: have fun, make money, try to know everything, influence the people and things that matter, and spend time with family; sourcing comes through his team and friends rather than a formal network, and most inbound pitches are, in his words, boring and wrong. On managing objectivity he said a lot of VCs think they have to be the tail that's wagged by the dog that is their companies, and just because you're invested in something doesn't mean you have to be the tail that's wagged by the dog. Patel acquired Catrini, the research firm he describes as having been right many times and having captured the market's imagination, but keeps it a separate company, and Catrini's director of research, Kyle, retains the dominant voice on what gets published.

When the team asked whether they were still allowed to be bearish on AI after the acquisition, his answer was do whatever you want; he said he isn't there to change their voice but to help them run as a better company. The two firms differ methodologically: SemiAnalysis is numerical and supply-chain-driven, counting data centers, chips, cables, servers, GPUs, fab tools and memory prices, and testing chips, clusters and models on domains including biology, security, cyber and chip design, while Catrini runs experiments, and Patel cited their AI-designed scorpion antivenom, which he said works okay, and their sending someone to the Strait of Hormuz to check on oil shipping. He noted Catrini was super bullish on AI before flipping sharply negative a few months before. The tension between his growing influence and his stated independence is the episode's unresolved question, and the articles leave open what happens next on the pushed-back gigawatts, the fund's check sizes and Perplexity's margin.

stories.Headline: Economist proposes taxing automation investments that displace workers to fund Social Security and Medicare
stories.Summary:
A letter to the editor in the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette on November 22, 2026, at 4:00 a.m. EST addressed tax worker displacement due to artificial intelligence. The writer described an economic transformation made possible by the development and rapid improvement of artificial intelligence. The writer said we have not yet seen much of what AI promises to deliver. The writer said an enormous amount of investment is being made on the expectation that AI will generate more than enough profits to justify those investments.

The writer said many people are worried that those profits will come at their expense and have reason to be worried. In 2019, Daron Acemoglu and Pascual Restrepo published an article entitled “Automation and New Tasks: How Technology Displaces and Reinstates Labor” in the Journal of Economic Perspectives. Their analysis suggests that since 1987 there has been a marked increase in the displacement of labor by automation relative to the increase in employment due to automation. Consequently, the way investments in automation of tasks has been distributed has contributed to a declining share of the nation’s income accruing to labor. The writer said this was not inevitable.

Firms found it more profitable to invest in automation that displaces workers than in machines and computer applications that enhance productivity of existing workers and create demand for new workers, in part because they can save the costs of employer-paid fringe benefits and taxes employers must pay into the Social Security and Medicare Trust Funds. The writer is professor of economics, emeritus, at the University of Pittsburgh. The writer said when workers are displaced, they typically find new employment that pays lower wages and fringe benefits. The writer said this is a loss for those workers and a loss of revenue for governments from wage taxes that support Social Security and Medicare. The writer said these are real costs of automation, but they are not counted by the investing firm as part of their investment.

The writer said a tax on investments that displace workers would correct the bias and direct automation away for job displacement and towards job creation. A second letter to the editor in The Gila Herald on November 19, 2026, at 16:52:24Z was from Mike Diegel of Pima, Arizona. Diegel wrote that he read with interest the Nov. 18 article on Senator Mark Kelly’s new framework to protect Americans from the most advanced AI models. Diegel wrote that Senator Kelly is right about the problem and that companies should not grade their own homework.

Diegel wrote that self-regulation has failed and that oversight that only arrives after an incident is not oversight. Diegel wrote that Kelly’s proposed fix still misses the core issue because it governs the model, not the action. Diegel wrote that Kelly’s framework calls for a rulebook of hazard levels, independent examiners embedded at AI companies to review safeguards as models are built, and testing and liability before and after deployment. Diegel wrote that none of that stops a consequential action at the moment it happens.

Diegel wrote that a test can pass, an examiner can sign off, and a company can disclose a risk, and the AI system can still make the transfer, delete the file, or send the data. Diegel wrote that the danger is not only how smart a model is but what authority it has been given to act. Diegel wrote that a safe model with write access is dangerous and a dangerous model with no authority does nothing. Diegel wrote that his team and he are building Pulpo in Arizona.

Diegel wrote that governance has to sit before execution, as a narrow, one-use permit for that one specific action, with durable evidence afterward. Diegel wrote that no permit means no governed effect and that anything else is monitoring dressed up as prevention. Diegel wrote that he respects Senator Kelly’s intent and his service. Diegel wrote that if we want to protect Americans, we need to govern what AI is allowed to do, not just how it is tested or watched.

stories.Headline: Florida House speaker Sam Garrison creates committee to examine AI risks
stories.Summary:
Florida House Speaker Sam Garrison created a new committee to examine artificial intelligence risks on November 17, 2026, in Tallahassee. This legislative forum will address how governments should respond to technology that advances faster than the rules meant to govern it. The move follows a change in House leadership and renewed debate over the oversight of evolving digital tools. Garrison placed these technology issues among the priorities for the legislature during its two year term. The committee provides a setting for examining AI rather than announcing immediate restrictions on its use.

The Advanced Technology & Digital Security Committee replaces the Information Technology Budget & Policy Subcommittee established under former Speaker Daniel Perez. This standing committee focuses on policy and oversight, while the Appropriations Committee will now handle all budget decisions. Its jurisdiction includes artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, critical infrastructure security, digital privacy, data governance, and digital identity. Michelle Davila was named staff director of the committee on November 9 for the 2026 to 2028 term. These changes were outlined in a memorandum issued by Sam Garrison on November 5.

Speaker Sam Garrison stated that technological disruption could unfold over two or three years instead of a century. He warned that AI might improve so rapidly that humans struggle to understand or control the technology. Garrison urged lawmakers to address these risks, though he did not outline specific legislation during his opening speech. He previously expressed support for federal leadership on AI regulation in April 2026. The speaker compared the current situation to the Industrial Revolution to explain the urgency of the matter.

Governor Ron DeSantis supported an AI Bill of Rights to create consumer protections for personal data and chatbot interactions. This proposal, Senate Bill 482, passed the Senate on March 4 with 35 votes in favor and two against. However, the House rejected that bill on March 13, 2026, and later rejected Senate Bill 2-D on April 29. Former Speaker Daniel Perez favored federal oversight of artificial intelligence rather than state level action. These failed bills left broader consumer protections for AI users unresolved in the state.

Florida's Digital Bill of Rights took effect on July 1, 2024, to establish privacy protections for certain large businesses. Separately, the State Board of Education adopted AI and educational technology rules on September 16, 2026. These rules cover public school districts, charter school boards, and Florida College System institutions regarding student privacy. School districts must finalize their own AI policies by July 1, 2027, for the next school year. Federal officials currently recognize 16 critical infrastructure sectors, including energy, communications, and financial services.

Interim committee weeks begin on November 30, 2026, and the next regular legislative session starts on March 2, 2027. Lawmakers will use this time to review proposals and debate potential changes to technology rules. The articles leave open which specific companies or technologies might face new requirements under future laws. It remains unsettled how state responsibilities will overlap with the national rules currently being examined by Congress. No specific statewide AI law follows automatically from the creation of this new committee.

stories.Headline: Resideo launches AI-powered L7 valve that learns water use and shuts off supply
stories.Summary:
Resideo last week introduced an AI-powered device that it says can learn a household's water-use patterns, flag unusual activity and automatically shut off the water. The product is called the L7 Smart Water Flow Monitor & Shutoff Valve, and it is the newest member of Resideo's First Alert L Series. According to the company, the device can detect leaks as small as four drops per hour. The company's announcement does not disclose pricing or availability information for the new product.

Resideo frames the novelty of the L7 around its AI integration, since smart shutoff valves are not new, according to the article. Paul Vacquier, CEO of the plumbing company Beagle Services, which recently added the L7 to its product offering, said in a statement that the move helps shift the focus from responding to water damage after a loss occurs to identifying issues earlier and potentially reducing the impact. The article does not say what the device requires of a household beyond learning its water-use patterns. The article gives no further details on how the AI works or when the valve will reach customers.

The article does not name anyone at Resideo as responsible for the product or quote any Resideo executive about it. The only person it quotes is Vacquier, whose company, Beagle Services, recently added the L7 to its product offering. The article does not say what happens next for the L7 beyond the company's announcement, and it gives no timeline for pricing or availability. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Organized crime groups steal high value AI hardware during transport to data centers
stories.Summary:
Organized crime groups are stealing artificial intelligence hardware during transport to data centers. These transnational gangs are targeting high value components as the infrastructure boom grows. The thefts have occurred recently, including some in the last few weeks. Criminals are using sophisticated methods to hijack these expensive shipments. This trend is driven by the massive amount of capital entering the industry.

The cargo includes Blackwell chips on pallets worth 15 million to 20 million dollars. Some truckloads moving across the country now carry a value of 100 million dollars. Thieves target generators, transformers, bus bars, and both high and low voltage switchgear. These items are targeted because of scarcity and a large secondary market. The thefts affect the United States and potentially destinations like Russia, Iran, and China.

David Warrick is the executive vice president of enterprise at Overhaul. He stated that the dirt road to the data center is where challenges exist. Warrick said that criminal gangs now buy legitimate trucking companies to gain traction. He noted that these groups operate like cartels with their own finance and HR departments. He believes shippers should treat their hardware shipments as if they were cash.

Hyperscalers and neo cloud providers are affected when stolen components delay contracted compute capacity. These customers worry about brand damage and empty shelves more than the monetary value. Some shippers now use transit vans or box trucks to avoid large losses. Warrick claims that many large thefts never become public due to a level of embarrassment. He mentioned that some losses have reached tens of millions of dollars recently.

The U.S. interstate highway system took 37 years and 650 billion dollars to build. AI infrastructure spending now runs at double that amount every year globally. Thieves use fake paperwork, resprayed trucks, changed license plates, and signal jammers. Overhaul tracks cargo using a data set that adds 200 million data points every month. This system helps identify unscheduled stops and fraudulent pickups to recover stolen loads.

Warrick expects the trend of cargo theft to continue as more money flows into build-outs. He suggests that more work is needed regarding legislation to create punishments that stick. Shippers are encouraged to verify chain of custody and consult with intelligence specialists. The articles do not state if new laws are currently being written. They leave open whether these security changes will successfully deter transnational criminal gangs.

Articles.Title: Cargo Thieves Are Chasing AI Hardware Down the Dirt Road to the Data Center

stories.Headline: Teradyne grows robotics revenue 28% as AI automation demand rises
stories.Summary:
Teradyne is benefiting from growing adoption of artificial intelligence-powered robotics, expanding automation demand and increasing investments in AI data center infrastructure, according to an article published by Zacks Investment Research and carried by Yahoo Finance on November 23, 2026. The article was written by Nilanshi Mukherjee and appeared at 10:04 AM CST. Teradyne's expanding robotics portfolio strengthens its competitive position against KLA and Cohu in the AI space, the article states. Growing investments in physical AI and robot-assisted assembly and testing are creating significant opportunities for the company's Robotics business, according to the article. The article asks whether Teradyne can outpace KLA and Cohu.

In the third quarter of 2026, Teradyne's Robotics revenues increased 28% year over year to $96 million, marking its highest third-quarter revenues on record, the article states. The segment also turned a profit during the quarter, reflecting improving demand and operational performance. Electronics and semiconductor manufacturing has emerged as Robotics' largest vertical, supported by growing automation needs in complex server and rack assembly processes. Teradyne's Universal Robots Gen 7 collaborative robot platform and PolyScope X software are strengthening its competitive position, and these solutions are designed to support physical AI applications and improve automation flexibility across electronics assembly operations. The company is expanding its physical AI ecosystem through partnerships with NVIDIA, Analog Devices, Scale AI, Generalist, Bright Machines and Sereact, collaborations expected to accelerate adoption of intelligent robotics solutions across industrial applications.

Teradyne expects continued Robotics revenue growth in the fourth quarter of 2026, according to the article. Broader automation deployments by a major customer are expected to support growth in 2027, while emerging physical AI applications could create additional opportunities in 2028 and beyond. The article states that Teradyne's expanding AI-powered robotics portfolio, strategic partnerships and growing automation demand strengthen its long-term growth prospects, positioning it favorably against competitors like KLA and Cohu. Teradyne currently carries a Zacks Rank #1 (Strong Buy), the article states. The Zacks Consensus Estimate for fiscal 2026 earnings is pegged at $9.41 per share, which has increased 3.29% over the past 30 days and suggests 137.63% year-over-year growth.

KLA is benefiting from growing demand for AI through its leadership in process control and ability to address growth markets in wafer fab equipment, including high-bandwidth memory and advanced packaging, the article states. Cohu's exposure to AI infrastructure is expanding through adoption of its Eclipse handler and active thermal-control technology for high-power processors, according to the article. Cohu's management raised the estimated annual high-performance computing opportunity pipeline by 18% sequentially to approximately $1 billion in the third quarter of 2026, including about $230 million in qualified opportunities, $440 million in qualification and $330 million in engagement. Cohu also raised its fiscal 2026 high-performance computing revenue outlook to approximately $120 million from $100-$110 million, the article states. Eclipse supports multiple processor generations, helping customers manage capital investment and accelerate production ramps.

Teradyne shares have gained 5.8% year to date, outperforming the Zacks Computer & Technology sector's 6% decline and the Zacks Electronics - Miscellaneous Products decrease of 5.7%, according to the article. Teradyne stock is trading at a premium with a forward 12-month Price/Sales of 5.06X compared with the Computer & Technology sector's 4.27X, and Teradyne has a Value Score of D. The article states that Teradyne is facing stiff competition from KLA and Cohu, and that both companies are expanding their footprint in the AI space. The article originally published on Zacks Investment Research. The article carries a trading disclosure linking to Coinbase and states that Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser.

The article leaves open whether Teradyne can outpace KLA and Cohu in AI, posing the question in its headline without answering it. It gives no date for when Teradyne might outpace its competitors or what measure would settle the comparison. It does not state the size of KLA's or Cohu's AI-related revenues for comparison with Teradyne's $96 million in third-quarter Robotics revenues. It gives no figures for Teradyne's total company results, only the Robotics segment. It does not say what the major customer's broader automation deployments in 2027 involve or name that customer.

stories.Headline: PCS Software’s Villegas says AI should assist dispatchers with repetitive tasks while people make final decisions
stories.Summary:
Danielle Villegas, chief product and technology officer at PCS Software, said on FreightWaves’ What the Truck?!? that artificial intelligence should multiply the efficiency of a dispatch team rather than replace the people on it. She described AI as a tool that takes on repetitive work so dispatchers can spend their time on decisions that matter. Her starting point is the tasks dispatchers repeat every day, such as routine on-time or delayed delivery notifications and load entry. Automating those tasks gives dispatchers room to find more freight and handle exceptions, like a truck breaking down and a replacement driver having to be arranged.

Villegas said the approach changes what AI is for, framing it as a way to expand what a dispatch team can do rather than only as a way to cut costs. She said anyone who has spent time with AI tools knows their limits, and that sometimes AI is confidently wrong when it is wrong. That is why PCS builds its products around human oversight, particularly for consequential decisions, and she said you have to keep the human in the loop especially when dollars or safety are concerned. Rates are the clearest example, because a wrong one lands directly on the bottom line, and her model is for AI to recommend and speed up decisions while a person makes the final call.

To explain why visibility matters, Villegas pointed to the passenger display inside a Waymo, which she said is there to build confidence rather than because the vehicle needs it. She said the same logic applies in freight, where users need to see what the AI is proposing and why. That transparency principle shapes how PCS designed driver assignment in Cortex, which she said draws on more than 40 data elements to recommend which driver should haul which load. Those inputs include dispatcher knowledge, according to the article.

Articles.Title: AI Should Make Dispatchers Better, Not Replace Them, Says PCS Software’s Villegas

stories.headline_source: AI Should Make Dispatchers Better, Not Replace Them, Says PCS Software’s Villegas

stories.Headline: Senate and House urged to pass No Fakes Act banning nonconsensual A.I. replicas of voices and likenesses
stories.Summary:
Three years ago Tom Hanks posted a warning to his millions of fans after a dental plan ran an A.I.-generated ad featuring a younger version of the actor, and he had nothing to do with it. It is not just celebrities who are being impersonated by A.I., because voice actors who were paid a few hundred bucks for recordings they were told were for internal research later found clones of their voices for sale online. A content creator learned on her honeymoon that a YouTube ad was using an A.I. version of her to sell erectile dysfunction supplements. Whether all this is legal is right now an open question, but the opinion article argues it should not be. The article says Hollywood does not need America's leaders to devise a new concept for new circumstances, and that they need to extend and enforce the rules that already exist.

The use of Americans' faces, voices, performances and creative works is already subject to rules at the federal or state level that say, in short, that you need to get permission and you need to pay for the use. That principle has guided the entertainment industry for more than a century, and whether it can continue to protect Americans may be decided in the coming weeks. The No Fakes Act would create a federal prohibition on creating nonconsensual digital replicas of any person's voice or likeness, famous or not. The bill was approved unanimously by the Senate Judiciary Committee in June, and there is momentum to pass it through the full Congress before the end of the year. It is one of the few A.I. bills with true bipartisan support, and the article says the Senate and House should move quickly and deliver the bill to President Trump for signature.

That would ensure Americans retain control of their images and voices in the A.I. era, according to the piece. The writer comes to this issue not as a policymaker but as a practitioner who runs a global talent agency, and part of that job is helping clients license their likenesses and performances, sometimes to A.I. companies. The writer says the agency regularly negotiates those deals and that the bill pending in Congress delivers what the industry needs and what will protect all Americans. Some A.I. companies already follow many of its measures voluntarily, the article states. The article does not say what happens next beyond the push to pass the bill before the end of the year.

Articles.Title: Opinion | Tom Hanks Got A.I.-Cloned. Here’s How We Stop It From Happening to You. - The New York Times

stories.headline_source: Opinion | Tom Hanks Got A.I.-Cloned. Here’s How We Stop It From Happening to You.

stories.Headline: Vietnam urges schools to teach national identity through Vietnamese and AI
stories.Summary:
Báo Thanh niên published an article on 21/11/2026 about educating national identity in the age of AI, carried by Vietnam.vn at 02:14:48Z. The article states that artificial intelligence is changing the way people learn, communicate, and acquire knowledge and culture. It states that English is promoted as a second language in schools, and that education about national identity faces new demands. It states that educating about national identity not only preserves traditional values but also helps the younger generation develop independent and creative thinking based on Vietnamese culture. It states that this helps the younger generation confidently integrate into the global community.

The article states that AI can translate multiple languages, explain cultural differences, and create texts, music, and paintings. It states that technology is increasingly bridging language and geographical gaps, enabling people to access a global wealth of knowledge. It states that national identity is present not only in the traditional ao dai dress, folk songs, festivals, or glorious historical accounts, but also in the Vietnamese language, historical memory, manners, community spirit, compassion, and aspirations for nation-building. It states that identity is not an immutable system of values but continues to develop through reception, creation, and adaptation to the times. It states that schools must help students understand the meaning of tradition, apply positive values to their lives, and be creative based on national culture.

The article states that education in national identity cannot simply stop at imparting knowledge, memorizing historical events, or organizing formal cultural activities. It states that uncreative preservation can lead to the stagnation of tradition, and that embracing the new while forgetting one's roots can cause people to lose their cultural anchor. It states that identity education needs to combine both requirements, helping young people understand where they come from while equipping them with the capacity to dialogue, learn, and contribute to the world. It states that Vietnamese is the foundation and English is the bridge, and that developing foreign languages must go hand in hand with strengthening Vietnamese language proficiency and understanding of national culture. It states that Vietnamese is not only a means of communication but also an environment for shaping thinking, preserving cultural memories, and expressing the Vietnamese soul.

The article states that the ability to use Vietnamese accurately, reason logically, and express independent thoughts is a crucial foundation for lifelong learning. It states that English helps learners access scientific and technological knowledge and human culture, expand cooperation, and introduce Vietnam to the world. It states that the two languages are not opposed but complement each other. It states that the history of Hue National High School from 1896 to 1945 offers a thought-provoking perspective, and that within the French educational environment, with French as the dominant language, the school still contributed to training many generations of patriotic students.

It states that these students included Ho Chi Minh, Tran Phu, Ha Huy Tap, Le Duan, Pham Van Dong, and Vo Nguyen Giap, along with intellectuals and artists such as Dang Thai Mai, Xuan Dieu, Huy Can, Te Hanh, Nguyen Van Thuong, and Tran Hoan, and prominent scientists such as Ta Quang Buu, Ton That Tung, Dang Van Ngu, and Hoang Tuy. The article states that this demonstrates that embracing external knowledge does not equate to losing national identity. It states that language is a tool, knowledge is a resource, while patriotism, character, and social responsibility are formed through the interaction of education, family, living environment, and each individual's awareness. It states that in the age of AI the goal is not just to train people who are proficient in foreign languages, but to cultivate citizens with a strong cultural foundation, independent thinking, the ability to engage in equal dialogue with the world, and the capacity to apply human knowledge to develop the country.

It states that AI necessitates a revolution in the way national identity is taught, and that students can use technology to explore local history, digitize heritage, learn about folklore, compare cultures, and introduce Vietnamese values in multiple languages. It states that in literature classes students can use AI to compare English translations with the original Vietnamese texts, identifying cultural nuances that are difficult to convey between the two languages. The article states that AI can also compose poetry, prose, and music, and pose questions about the differences between machine-generated products and human creations. It states that the Hue City High School Literature Olympiad exam for the 2026-2027 school year raises the issue of creating literary works in the AI era, by placing Xuan Dieu's poem "Going by Boat" alongside poems created by ChatGPT that also write about time.

It states that in history class students can utilize digital resources, verify information, and create products that introduce the nation's history, and that interdisciplinary projects open up opportunities to build online museums, make films about heritage, and create cultural products aimed at an international audience. It states that it is crucial that AI becomes a tool to support critical thinking, not a means to replace human learning, and that copying AI's answers may provide information but does not necessarily lead to deep understanding. It states that schools need to help students learn to ask questions, verify information, identify biases, evaluate products, and take responsibility for their creations. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Educating about national identity in the age of AI. - Vietnam.vn

stories.Headline: Sam Altman backs Jakub Pachocki's plan for industrywide AI development limits
stories.Summary:
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman gave his backing to a proposal for industrywide limits on artificial intelligence development on November 23, 2026. This support follows a plan outlined by OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki on Sunday, November 22. The proposal suggests that rival developers should agree on specific thresholds they will not cross until stronger safety safeguards are established. Altman warned that the capabilities of artificial intelligence could advance faster than companies are able to safely monitor them.

The proposal focuses on a measurement called perplexity, which tracks how accurately models predict the next piece of text. OpenAI reported that GPT-3.5 had a log-perplexity score of around 0.99, while newer models have dropped below 0.8. Pachocki expects potentially transformative capabilities to emerge when scores reach between 0.68 and 0.70, though the exact nature of these changes is unknown. He argues that improvements in this metric have already led to advances in mathematical problem solving and cybersecurity abilities.

Jakub Pachocki is responsible for the proposal and warned that AI could improve its own training methods as early as 2027. He believes this could accelerate development beyond the current capabilities of existing safety measures. Sam Altman endorsed the essay by Pachocki, calling it the most important publication from OpenAI in some time. Altman believes that coordinated restrictions could eventually influence the pace of infrastructure spending and the training of frontier models.

No binding industrywide agreement has been announced among the competing developers at this time. The immediate challenge is whether rivals can agree on enforceable safeguards and common measurement standards. Companies must decide if they can implement these limits without surrendering their own competitive advantages in the market. It remains unclear if other major AI developers will join OpenAI in this effort to slow development.

More to follow.

Articles.Title: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman Gives a Surprising AI Prediction His Backing

stories.headline_source: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman Gives a Surprising AI Prediction His Backing

stories.Headline: New Brunswick communities seek council approval and raise concerns as AI data centers test social license
stories.Summary:
Two communities in New Brunswick are approaching the prospect of AI data center development in different ways, according to an article republished by TechXplore from The Conversation. In Fundy Shores, the mayor has called for new rules governing AI data centers even though no developer has proposed building one in his municipality yet, and the municipality wants future developers to obtain council approval through a rezoning process that would let residents weigh in before construction could proceed. In nearby Saint John, residents have been debating a proposed facility in Lorneville, where at a public meeting they raised concerns about air quality, water consumption and the benefits such a project would bring. After the meeting, one resident told reporters that in their view there is no social license for the project, and the article says the two communities illustrate different points in the debate over social license.

The article describes a social license to operate as the ongoing acceptance of a project by the people affected by it, an informal relationship between a developer and affected communities rather than a formal legal authorization like a government permit. It says the term emerged in the mining industry in the 1990s, when companies recognized that even with government permits in hand, opposition from neighbors could delay or disrupt their operations. As an example, it cites Enbridge's proposed Northern Gateway pipeline, where in April 2014 residents of Kitimat, B.C., voted on the project and 58.4% of those who voted opposed it, after which a political dispute followed about how much weight residents' responses should carry. The article says claims that a project has or lacks a social license often depend on who is speaking for the community and whose views are being counted, since a council resolution, a benefits agreement and a public vote each provide evidence about a different group of people but none necessarily represents everyone affected.

The article says this question of representation is especially important when projects affect Indigenous nations, because First Nations, Inuit and Métis communities have distinct rights, governing institutions and authority to make decisions, and their views cannot be subsumed into municipal consultation or treated as another measure of local opinion. It also warns against treating social license as a one-time decision, noting that before a data center is constructed residents have forecasts and promises to consider, and once a facility opens they can measure those promises against their lived experiences, including how the operator responds when something goes wrong. As an example it cites Sherbrooke, Que., where the city agreed to supply electricity to Bitfarms for a bitcoin mining facility, neighbors soon began complaining to the city about noise, Bitfarms replaced the fans and installed a noise barrier but the problem persisted, and in 2021 the city and the company agreed in principle to move the operation to an industrial park.

The article concludes that a social license is not something a developer keeps indefinitely and largely depends on whether a project continues to meet the expectations of the people affected by it. It says residents' views may change as a project develops and its impacts become clearer, and that a council's approval may allow construction to proceed but does not guarantee lasting community acceptance. It adds that residents must have opportunities to hold operators accountable as they experience the project's effects.

Articles.Title: Who gets to decide whether an AI data center has a 'social license' to operate?

stories.headline_source: Who gets to decide whether an AI data center has a 'social license' to operate?

stories.Headline: METR finds Anthropic accelerates AI progress through AI-driven R&D and solves a 167-year-old math problem
stories.Summary:
On November 5, METR released a report from inside Anthropic, according to investinglive.com on November 23, 2026. Anthropic gave METR unprecedented access to internal data on its AI R&D process from August 12 to October 29. Anthropic restricted some details and METR agreed to those restrictions. The report was released at the same time as the US midterms, during a 5% Nasdaq fall. The article says it was seen as pre-IPO hype and did not get the attention it deserved.

METR is described as the best-placed independent evaluator there is. The article says Anthropic is likely improving its models on well-specified tasks at around twice the rate it did between March 2024 and October 2025. It says a majority of this acceleration is likely attributable to Anthropic's extensive use of AI to do R&D, which it calls close to recursive self-improvement. METR said it did not see evidence for significant bottlenecks that would prevent further capabilities progress due to limits on algorithmic progress, training compute, experiment compute, or data in the next 12 months. METR said it was confident the observed acceleration was not simply the result of faster growth in training compute.

The article attributes the acceleration finding to METR and the R&D explanation to its own assessment. It reports METR's conclusion that there is no wall and that AI will continue to progress at an even-faster pace in the next year. It says Anthropic solved a 167-year-old math problem late last week and that the solution has now been verified. Brian Conrey, described as a leading Riemann specialist, told AFP it is really the biggest thing he thinks has ever happened in mathematics. The article calls the solution a validation of CEO Dario Amodei's promise to cure diseases.

The article says not many people in markets understand the gravity of AI solving the 167-year-old math problem. It says the solution is basically the holy grail of math problems and is likely to unlock entirely new ways of looking at math. It says the implications for scientific discovery, from materials science to medicine, are difficult to overstate. It says the significance of the two developments together is hard to overstate. It says there has most recently been talk about a leap in robotics training from AI.

The article says the market had a meltdown over AI fears this month and that there is a real discussion to have about the economics of the AI spend. It says the real story of AI is the technology itself. It says AI is the most important technology in a generation, or it might not be another technological revolution at all. It says AI may be the technology that accelerates every technological revolution that follows or came before. It says the METR report was released in the midst of the 5% Nasdaq fall.

The article says METR has shown that AI is already accelerating the development of AI itself. It says the Riemann hypothesis breakthrough illustrates the kinds of problems increasingly capable models can tackle. It asks whether the gains will go to memory chip makers, graphics chip makers, power producers or hackers, and calls that an entirely different and difficult discussion. It says the author continues to think the HALO trade is the safest bet on AI. It says the greatest winners from AI may not be the companies selling intelligence but the companies that suddenly find intelligence becoming almost free.

Articles.Title: A look inside Anthropic shows there is no ceiling on AI

stories.Headline: GrantWatch staff verify grants daily and review each listing every 90 to 180 days
stories.Summary:
The article is a personal essay by a GrantWatch writer published on 23 November 2026, reflecting on search and AI changes and a Thanksgiving seating chart. The writer says Google's search updates gave a disastrous May and June. The writer made a seating chart with a turkey in the middle and the head of the table saved for the human who came for an answer. The writer describes SEO, AEO, GEO, AIO and SXO as guests at the table. The writer says the person at the head of the table asks whether the content is clear, trustworthy and useful to them.

The writer says the human wants to know three things: whether there is a grant for their nonprofit, what it takes to apply, and whether it can be done by Friday. The writer says GrantWatch researchers verify grants and add new opportunities every weekday. The writer says researchers check who is eligible, when applications are due, and what the funder actually says. The writer says GrantWatch adds new grants and updates existing grant listings daily. The writer says every grant undergoes a scheduled review every 90 to 180 days to verify its information and availability.

The writer says GrantWatch writers and editors tell readers about the newest grants and explain how to write a grant proposal. The writer says GrantWatch Intelligence and the 12-Stage Grant Pipeline are tools readers can use. The writer says readers with 20 minutes before a board meeting can subscribe to search Human Verified grants. The writer says the staff kept showing up for the people who count on them. The writer says the team will make it through what the writer calls this AI tunnel.

The writer says ChatGPT and Claude showed up already knowing what they want to eat. The writer says there is no choice for anyone writing content right now. The writer gives a prompt asking an AI editor to edit a draft for SEO, AEO, GEO, AIO and SXO while keeping the writer's voice, humor and point of view. The writer says the prompt asks for a clear title and headings, an early answer to the reader's main question, easy-to-verify claims, a flagged source list and an obvious next step. The writer says the prompt asks for light edits and a short list of changes.

The writer says the home office is right across from the dining room. The writer says the acronyms would pull up a chair and turn the mashed potatoes into a featured snippet. The writer says the website and the acronyms can sell GrantWatch subscriptions without the writer this weekend. The writer thanks friends Elli and Mel for having the writer and says the writer is bringing the stuffing, family and a clear mind. The writer says GrantWatch is in good hands.

The writer says the good seat comes with Human Verified grants and invites readers to subscribe and pull up a chair. The writer says GrantWatch is a grant research and management service that does not award grants, distribute grant funding or guarantee an award. The writer says GrantWatch distinguishes open opportunities from upcoming opportunities announced by a funder whose opening date has not arrived or whose complete guidelines are not yet available. The writer says forecasted opportunities are based on advance notices published by funding sources, often government agencies. The writer says projected opportunities are based on GrantWatch's analysis of a funder's documented historical grantmaking cycles and are not necessarily announced by the funder.

stories.Headline: Researchers introduce RISA framework to protect tool using AI agents from prompt injections
stories.Summary:
Researchers introduced Runtime Integrity Safeguards for Agents, known as RISA, to protect tool using large language model agents. This software engineering framework was presented in a study published on November 22, 2026. It addresses runtime integrity problems where indirect prompt injections propagate into side effects or user responses. The system mediates three specific lifecycle boundaries including action authorization, observation incorporation, and response release. RISA coordinates these enforcement efforts through shared provenance, memory, and taint state.

The framework integrates source aware authorization, external resource checks, fact preserving quarantine, response screening, and structured recovery. It was tested using the fixed AgentDojo full 629 attack manifest with DeepSeek V3.2 as agent and guard. RISA reduced the attack success rate from 69.95 percent to 0.16 percent in these specific tests. User Utility under Attack increased from 37.36 percent to 55.17 percent during the same evaluation. Three alternative agents achieved attack success rates between 0.00 percent and 0.32 percent with the guard.

The authors state that runtime policy enforcement, provenance, and recovery are complementary mechanisms for trustworthy tool using systems. They provided the RISA runtime implementation and benchmark integration code in a public GitHub repository. The researchers claim that the system effectively mediates boundaries to prevent untrusted observations from affecting planning context. They noted that blocked action recovery succeeded in 16.0 percent of affected trajectories during testing. The study positions these software engineering tools as essential for securing autonomous agents in production.

Security leaders ask what agents are actually doing and on whose authority they act. CrowdStrike reported responding to over 90 customers after poisoned npm packages hijacked AI tools in August 2025. The CrowdStrike 2026 Global Threat Report warns that adversaries may compromise trusted agents to create malicious insiders. Some experts argue that guardrails alone cannot contain agents that have broad standing access to production. Affected users include developers and business users who turn on agents that inherit their personal privileges.

The articles explain that agents behave non deterministically and may take paths that the requester did not intend. Adversaries can break out from initial access in as little as 27 seconds, causing damage before human intervention. NIST design tenets call for separating an agent's reasoning from the systems that decide its allowed actions. Traditional identity providers were built for human access rather than for autonomous software operating on endpoints. Agents currently often lack verifiable identities and instead use borrowed human credentials or shared service accounts.

Future efforts should include discovering every sanctioned or unsanctioned agent operating across a fleet. Organizations are encouraged to apply least privilege so agents can only perform specific jobs for limited durations. Experts suggest using open standards like SPIFFE to give every agent its own verifiable identity. The articles leave open how to fully integrate these identity controls with existing corporate security infrastructures. They also leave open the specific methods for maintaining records that sit entirely outside an agent's reach.

Articles.Title: RISA: Engineering runtime integrity for tool-using large language model agents

stories.headline_source: RISA: Engineering runtime integrity for tool-using large language model agents

stories.Headline: Peking University researchers develop AI-driven cross-scale simulation for lithium batteries
stories.Summary:
Researchers from the School of Advanced Materials at Peking University and other institutions published a study on November 22, 2026. This team of scientists including Qiliang Zhang, Juntao Zhao, and Chuying Ouyang developed an AI-driven cross-scale simulation for lithium batteries. The project received support from the AI for Science Preferred Program and the National Natural Science Foundation of China. These experts worked across several locations including the Shenzhen Graduate School and the Fujian Science and Technology Innovation Laboratory. The new simulation method addresses the high computational costs that often hinder the development of energy storage.

It aims to fix the insufficient dynamic feedback mechanisms that currently limit the accuracy of battery modeling. The research was funded by the Advanced Materials National Science and Technology Major Project under number 2025ZD0618801. Additional financial support came from the National Natural Science Foundation of China through grant number 12426301. This technical approach integrates artificial intelligence to bridge different scales of material behavior. The authors of the study, who include Genming Lai and Zekai Liu, declared that they have no competing financial interests.

They presented their findings in the journal ACS Nano to show how AI can improve battery simulations. The researchers explained that traditional methods are too expensive and lack the necessary feedback for real-time analysis. By using these new tools, they believe the industry can design more efficient lithium batteries more quickly. This work represents a collaboration between Peking University and the Laboratory of Computational Materials Physics. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Optimal Deep Nonparametric Regression with Uniformly Bounded Lipschitz Constants
stories.Summary:
A paper posted to arXiv on November 22, 2026 by Jiaxin Shi, Ziyuan Chen, Jian Huang and Hansheng Wang sets out a sharp approximation theory for deep ReLU networks held under a split spectral norm product constraint. The authors write that weight norm constraints are widely used to control sensitivity to input perturbations by bounding the Lipschitz constant of neural networks. They add that existing approximation results under fixed bounds on standard norm products are not sufficient to establish optimal statistical rates. Their theoretical result shows that sufficiently smooth Hölder functions can be uniformly approximated to arbitrary accuracy as network depth increases, with the norm-product bound held fixed.

The paper then proposes a penalized least squares estimator for deep nonparametric regression. The authors state that the resulting estimator has a uniformly bounded Lipschitz constant while still reaching the optimal nonparametric rate up to a logarithmic factor. As applications, they establish optimal prediction rates for two-stage learning and give robustness guarantees under adversarial input perturbations. Numerical studies reported in the abstract show the penalized estimator has well-controlled sensitivity to input perturbations and prediction accuracy comparable to classical deep network methods. The work is listed under machine learning in statistics, machine learning in computer science and statistics theory in mathematics.

The abstract names stability under input perturbations as necessary for deep neural network estimators in many applications involving noisy covariates or estimated features. It presents the fixed norm-product bound as the setting in which earlier approximation results fell short of optimal statistical rates. The authors describe their contribution as a sharp approximation theory together with an estimator that keeps the Lipschitz constant uniformly bounded. The abstract does not give the size of the logarithmic factor, the constants involved or the specific numerical results of the studies.

The paper is identified on arXiv as 2611.23979, and the posting page offers a PDF, experimental HTML and TeX source. The abstract does not state where the work has been published or accepted, nor does it give a date for any later version. It also does not say what experiments or applications will follow from the results. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Optimal Deep Nonparametric Regression with Uniformly Bounded Lipschitz Constants

stories.Headline: Researchers present MPG-DPO, a method that personalizes LLM alignment using multidimensional user preference data
stories.Summary:
Zhen-Yu Zhang, Jerry Huang, Gang Niu, Takashi Ishida and Masashi Sugiyama posted a paper to arXiv on November 22, 2026 describing a method for personalizing large language model alignment with multidimensional user preference data. The paper is titled Sample-efficient Personalization of Large Language Model Alignment with Multidimensional User Preference Data and carries the identifier 2611.22210. The authors note that preference alignment has become a central tool for aligning large language models with human values and desired behavior. They add that the online variant of preference alignment can advance model capabilities beyond what static data alone offers by repeatedly generating and labeling new responses with human feedback.

The paper states that costly, time-consuming annotations limit the scalability of online preference alignment, which makes sample efficiency essential. Existing methods typically try to improve sample efficiency by expanding coverage of the response space or by selecting pairs with the highest uncertainty for comparison. The authors argue that although these methods are effective, they quantify uncertainty from the perspective of the language model, which may differ from the uncertainty perceived by the user. They give the example that a pair can appear highly uncertain to the model even when past comparisons from the user already imply a clear ordering.

In response, the authors propose multidimensional preference-guided online direct preference optimization, or MPG-DPO, which uses low-cost multidimensional evaluations from automated verifiers on the user's historical comparisons to build a personalized preference cone that guides response selection for online preference alignment. The method first discards responses that are confidently dominated under the estimated user preference, then selects two responses that are competitive under the retained preference cone yet show the strongest unresolved disagreement. Theoretical analysis in the paper shows that, with high probability, the fraction of queries spent on cone-dominated responses vanishes as learning progresses. Experiments across multiple language model families show that MPG-DPO outperforms strong contenders under matched query budgets.

The paper appears on arXiv, which describes arXivLabs as a framework allowing collaborators to develop and share new features directly on the website. arXiv states that individuals and organizations working with arXivLabs have embraced and accepted its values of openness, community, excellence and user data privacy, and that arXiv is committed to these values and only works with partners that adhere to them. The page also invites ideas for projects that would add value for the arXiv community. The articles do not say what happens next with the method beyond the reported experiments.

Articles.Title: Sample-efficient Personalization of Large Language Model Alignment with Multidimensional User Preference Data

stories.headline_source: Sample-efficient Personalization of Large Language Model Alignment with Multidimensional User Preference Data

stories.Headline: Researchers propose SpatialMind to adapt geometric fusion to spatial task needs in multimodal models
stories.Summary:
Shibin Zhao, Hao Tan, Fan Yang, Haixin Wang, Feilong Chen, Yidong Ma, Chaoyang Zhao, Ming Tang and Jinqiao Wang posted a paper titled SpatialMind: Adaptive Multi-Level Geometric Fusion for Spatial Reasoning in Multimodal Large Language Models to arXiv on 22 November 2026. The paper addresses the limited 3D spatial reasoning of Multimodal Large Language Models, which show promising capabilities in 2D visual understanding. The authors report systematic experiments on multi-level geometric fusion and find that spatial tasks at different cognitive levels, such as distance estimation versus route planning, require geometric representations of different granularities. That finding reveals that a fixed fusion scheme cannot accommodate diverse spatial reasoning requirements, which the authors say earlier approaches either used across all tasks or adopted regardless of task-specific needs. To bridge this gap, the authors propose SpatialMind, a task-adaptive framework for dynamically integrating multi-level geometric representations.

SpatialMind employs GeoFus, a multi-layer geometric fusion module built around a gating network jointly conditioned on textual instructions, visual semantics and geometric representations. This network adaptively modulates the contributions of shallow, intermediate and deep geometric features across the layers of the LLM decoder. The authors further introduce a negative-entropy regularization loss to mitigate gate collapse, and gate visualizations indicate that GeoFus adapts geometric granularity to task requirements. The authors report that experiments demonstrate SpatialMind achieves competitive performance across spatial benchmarks, attaining a state-of-the-art score of 72.3 on VSI-Bench. The paper is listed under Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition and Computational Geometry, and the source code is publicly available at a URL given in the abstract.

The abstract presents the work as a response to the gap left by recent studies that explore integrating 3D reconstruction models into MLLMs. Those approaches, the authors write, either use a single geometric granularity across all tasks or adopt a fixed multi-level fusion scheme regardless of task-specific reasoning requirements. The paper appears on arXiv with the identifier 2611.22415, and the listing offers a PDF, experimental HTML and TeX source, with the abstract page naming all nine authors. The articles give no further details on the benchmarks beyond VSI-Bench, no training details beyond the gating network and the regularization loss, and no publication venue beyond the arXiv posting. The articles also say nothing about planned follow-up work, so what happens next is not stated.

stories.Headline: ClickHouse expands AWS deal to invest $1.5 billion in enterprise AI on AWS
stories.Summary:
ClickHouse announced on Nov. 23, 2026 an expanded five-year strategic collaboration agreement with Amazon Web Services to help enterprises build, observe and secure AI applications on AWS, according to the company. The agreement sets a framework for ClickHouse to invest more than $1.5 billion in potential software, services and solutions on AWS, with increased investment in customer migrations, integrations and go-to-market programs. ClickHouse Cloud is built on AWS and was launched in 2022, and it now serves more than 5,000 customers worldwide. ClickHouse said it has quadrupled its customer count on AWS since signing its first such agreement with AWS in December 2024, and it now holds seven AWS Competencies.

The expanded agreement allows for go-to-market funding from AWS of up to four times the level under the December 2024 agreement, supporting proof-of-concept and migration programs that move analytics, data warehousing, observability and security workloads from legacy systems to ClickHouse Cloud on AWS. ClickHouse will deepen ClickHouse Cloud integrations with Amazon Bedrock, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore and Amazon Quick, so AI agents built on AWS can query live ClickHouse data through the Model Context Protocol, and it will extend that work to new AWS services as they launch. On AWS, ClickHouse will focus its engineering on agentic workloads, including agent observability and evals with Langfuse, transactional state and memory for agents in ClickHouse Managed Postgres, and AI-assisted security operations in ClickHouse Security. ClickHouse Cloud on AWS will continue to run on AWS Graviton by default and expand to additional AWS regions and deployment options.

Aaron Katz, CEO of ClickHouse, said AWS was the foundation for ClickHouse Cloud from the day it launched and that the December 2024 agreement gave the company the structure to expand the collaboration. He said growth on AWS has outpaced the company's estimates, that customers are expanding from real-time analytics into transactions, data warehousing, observability, security and AI engineering, and that they want those workloads on an open, composable foundation. Matt Yanchyshyn, VP of AWS Marketplace and Partner Services, said enterprises are moving AI agents from pilots into production and those agents need fast access to live business data. He said the agreement gives customers more ways to modernize their data infrastructure, connect ClickHouse data to agents built on AWS and put those agents to work.

ClickHouse said ClickHouse Managed Postgres is generally available in ClickHouse Cloud on AWS, ClickHouse Observability is in public beta and ClickHouse Security is in private preview. The company said its remote MCP server connects to Amazon Quick so users can query live ClickHouse data in natural language, that Langfuse integrates with Amazon Bedrock and that ClickHouse Cloud is available in AWS Marketplace. Vaibhav Gupta, VP of Platform Engineering at Sony LIV, said faster visibility translates directly into a better viewer experience and improved platform reliability, and that ClickHouse has become a foundational layer in the company's real-time analytics and observability modernization. He said Sony LIV looks forward to further innovation with AWS services and integrated support for its next generation of large-scale streaming operations. ClickHouse said it will be at AWS re:Invent in Las Vegas from Nov. 30 to Dec. 4 at Booth 706.

stories.Headline: Researchers introduce VEX framework to help AI agents learn computer use from tutorial videos
stories.Summary:
Guangzhi Sun, Zhonghao Zhai, Yixuan Li, and Chao Zhang introduced a new framework called VEX on November 22, 2026, to improve how computer-use agents learn. This system allows agents to learn directly from the audio and visual information found in tutorial videos instead of relying on simple screenshot trajectories. The agents follow a specific watch-act-rewatch paradigm to extract guidance from spoken explanations and visual demonstrations before executing tasks. After performing the actions, the agent verifies its own progress by rewatching its execution as a video to ensure accuracy.

The researchers instantiated this framework as video-SALMONN-VEX, which is a 9B-scale agent built on the video-SALMONN 2 architecture using a Qwen3.5-9B backbone. To enhance performance, they developed Action-Grounded Guide Optimization, a reinforcement learning method that optimizes video-derived guidance for predicting future actions. The team augmented the AgentNet, OSWorld, and CUA-Gym benchmarks with more than 24,000 real-world tutorial videos to provide better training data. These technical changes allow the agent to unify external learning from demonstrations with internal reflection on its own behavior.

The authors reported that video-SALMONN-VEX achieved a 22 percent relative increase in task success over the Qwen3.5 backbone when tested on OSWorld. They also found that the guidance generated by their system improved the performance of Gemini-3.5-flash by 10 percent relatively on the same benchmark. The researchers stated that these results demonstrate the strong potential of using audio-visual understanding as a unified interface for procedural learning. By integrating these capabilities, the agents can better perceive graphical user interfaces and reason over complex instructions to execute tasks.

stories.Headline: G2 finds 46 per cent of companies deploying AI agents in production exceed expected operating costs
stories.Summary:
A G2 report published in October 2026 found that 46 per cent of companies deploying AI agents in production report higher operating costs than they expected, according to TechGig. The overruns stem from three main factors, which are integration work that was not covered in the initial budget, insufficient support after agents go live, and a lack of visibility into costs on a per-agent basis. Gartner's September 2026 forecast projects that global spending on AI agents and assistants will reach US$29 billion in 2026, which shows the growing financial stake in these deployments. The report was covered by TechGig on 22 November 2026. Several studies point to operational friction as a driver of these costs.

MIT NANDA's "The GenAI Divide" from 2025 found that only 5 per cent of organisations successfully implemented generative AI for specific tasks. MuleSoft and Salesforce's Connectivity Benchmark from 2025 surveyed 1,050 IT leaders and found that 95 per cent faced integration challenges when adding AI to existing processes. Deloitte's "State of AI in the Enterprise" from 2026 reported that only 21 per cent of respondents had a mature governance model for AI agents. Together these studies suggest that AI models often struggle when they interact with real-world systems, data, rules and processes. The report says buyers should demand specific provisions from vendors before signing contracts to avoid cost surprises.

These include cost visibility per agent, per session and per call, with execution details that can be recorded and queried through a console and an API. Buyers should also insist on a spending cap per agent that halts execution when the cap is reached, even when the agent runs on the buyer's own provider key. Using one's own provider key, such as for Anthropic, OpenAI or Google, with no vendor markup on tokens, ensures transparent billing directly from the provider. Vendors should also provide regular reports on AI costs and points of attention to decision-makers before the bill arrives. The articles do not say what happens next beyond these recommendations for buyers and vendors.

stories.Headline: Google Antigravity lets developers pick among Gemini 4 and Claude models for coding tasks
stories.Summary:
Google's Antigravity platform gives developers a selection of AI models, including Gemini 4 Hydrogen, Neon, Argon and Carbon, alongside Claude Sonnet and Claude Opus, according to a TechGig guide published on November 22, 2026. The platform also features Orchestrator, which allows two AI models to collaborate on a single task. The guide says the choice of model depends on the complexity of the development task, with simpler models suited to routine work and more capable ones reserved for demanding problems. Gemini 4 Hydrogen is recommended for quick changes, routine coding and simple debugging, while Gemini 4 Neon is better for difficult debugging and complex coding tasks. Antigravity groups its models into categories it calls Everyday Workers, such as Gemini 4, Orchestrators, which pair models together, and Alternative Models from Anthropic.

Orchestrator uses one model for planning and another for implementation, typically Gemini 4 Neon for planning and Gemini 4 Hydrogen for execution. Gemini 4 Carbon is Google's heavyweight option for complex software architecture and major migrations. Claude Sonnet and Opus offer alternative approaches when Google's models are not producing the desired results, particularly for frontend work or in-depth analysis. The platform also lets developers adjust thinking levels for models, from Low for speed to Extra for demanding tasks. The guide recommends a workflow that starts with Hydrogen for small tasks, moves to Neon for complicated problems and uses Orchestrator for substantial feature development.

Developers should prioritise specific prompts, define what should not change and ask for investigation before implementation, according to the article. It also advises working in manageable steps and varying approaches when a prompt fails. The article says developers can optimise their AI-assisted development workflows and resource usage by selecting the appropriate model for each coding task. More to follow.
