stories.Headline: Carahsoft partners with DEVSEC to distribute Weaver AI investigation tool to government agencies
stories.Summary:
DEVSEC has partnered with Carahsoft Technology to distribute its artificial intelligence-powered investigative technology, called Weaver, to government agencies through existing federal contract vehicles, Carahsoft said Thursday. The agreement gives government customers access to Weaver, a capability designed to help investigative teams analyze complex casework and identify leads from large volumes of evidence, according to the company. Carahsoft will serve as DEVSEC's public sector distributor, making Weaver available through its reseller partners and existing government contract vehicles. The distribution arrangement covers NASA Solutions for Enterprise-Wide Procurement V and OMNIA Partners.

Weaver is designed to help investigators examine information collected from different sources, including case files, financial records and communications, and to connect these records so teams can examine relationships among pieces of evidence rather than analyze each document separately. Investigators can use its AI capabilities to identify potential leads, detect inconsistencies and flag risks in case materials, and the technology uses data ingestion, optical character recognition and data enrichment to process information, with AI reasoning capabilities supporting the analysis. Weaver is also intended to enable AI agents to carry out multiple investigative activities, and experts can document their investigative methods in reusable playbooks, giving analysts with varying levels of experience a reference for applying those methods consistently to different cases. To support the verification of investigative findings, Weaver generates auditable outputs with citations to source materials, and DEVSEC also offers zero-data-retention options to address government security and data governance requirements. The technology is designed for government investigations, enforcement, regulatory, legal and oversight activities.

Kristin Del Rosso, CEO of DEVSEC, said the company is pleased to partner with Carahsoft to make Weaver more accessible to government agencies that need advanced investigative capabilities to address increasingly complex and data-intensive missions. Lacey Wean, program executive for law enforcement solutions at Carahsoft, said agencies facing more complex investigations and growing data volumes need tools that help teams connect information, uncover insights and act more efficiently while maintaining security, transparency and accountability. The partnership reflects the growing role of artificial intelligence in federal operations, as agencies adopt the technology to support complex, data-intensive missions, according to the article. The Potomac Officers Club's 2027 Artificial Intelligence Summit on March 18 will examine this trend, bringing together federal and industry leaders to discuss AI applications in national security, citizen services, digital modernization and cybersecurity.

stories.Headline: CERT-In warns agentic AI frameworks divert funds by altering payment records
stories.Summary:
The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team issued an advisory on November 20, 2026, warning that hackers are manipulating business records and payment approval workflows in order to divert funds. These attacks use open-source agentic AI frameworks to automate reconnaissance and intrusion across government, enterprise, and service provider systems in India. CERT-In observed that unauthorised financial transactions are not limited to BFSI entities, because they also affect technology service providers supporting government-linked payment processes. The agency further noted that platforms handling vendor or partner payouts are affected as well, and it described the use of an AI-driven agentic offensive framework against enterprises, service providers, government organisations, and academic and research institutions. Threat actors alter business records or approval processes to steal money through legitimate payment processes, rather than targeting payment APIs directly.

This approach allows transactions to pass the usual application and approval checks, even when records have been changed without authorisation, without immediately raising suspicion. The agentic offensive frameworks conduct automated reconnaissance to identify exposed systems and rapidly prepare exploitation methods, according to the advisory. They use multiple agents or automated workers for parallel intrusion tasks, which shortens the attack stages, and the advisory was published by TechGig on November 22, 2026. CERT-In recommended that organisations identify service provider systems and accounts that can approve payments or access sensitive information. It also urged them to recheck payment instructions and business records against independent authoritative records.

The agency advised organisations to establish agreements with service providers covering incident detection, access to logs, investigation, and timely notification of shared compromises. The advisory places responsibility on organisations to verify payment-related records independently and to secure their arrangements with the service providers they rely on. The advisory covers government, enterprise, and service provider systems in India, and it states that unauthorised financial transactions extend beyond BFSI entities to technology service providers and payout platforms. CERT-In attributed the attacks to open-source agentic AI frameworks that automate reconnaissance and intrusion, and it said the offensive frameworks target enterprises, service providers, government organisations, and academic and research institutions. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the recommendations the agency issued to organisations.

stories.Headline: MBZUAI releases PAN 2 world model to enable simulative reasoning for AI agents
stories.Summary:
The Institute of Foundation Models at MBZUAI released the PAN 2 world model on November 17, 2026. This open 29-billion-parameter model allows agents to practice simulative reasoning by imagining and rendering plans. It generates up to 20 seconds of video from text actions and optional images. The model was published on Hugging Face at the IFM/PAN2 repository. It uses Generative Latent Prediction to help agents act on the best simulations.

The system requires Python 3.14, PyTorch 2.12.1, flash-attn 4, and CUDA 13.2. It combines a Qwen3.5-9B conceptual reasoner with a 29B MMDiT diffusion backbone and Wan 2.2 VAE decoder. Videos are rendered at 704 by 1248 pixels at 24 frames per second. Users must download weights from IFM/PAN2 and models from Qwen and Wan-AI into HF_HOME. Default settings use 50 steps and a CFG of 2.5 for 241 frames.

MBZUAI researchers stated that the model handles symbolic planning through language and pixels through diffusion. They noted that the perceptual backbone was trained on hundreds of millions of videos with structured annotations. The team admitted that long plans often fail, with two in three containing a missed step. They warned that appearance drifts across clips and the model may shortcut physics. MBZUAI requested that users report any misuse to the pan@ifm.ai email address.

Robotics teams comparing PAN 2 to Figure or Unitree demos are affected by these physics limitations. The model is suitable for agent plan scoring but weak for marketing clips due to caption requirements. It is considered entertainment-grade physics and should not be confused with lab instruments. Users needing verifiable numeric benchmarks are advised to pair it with NVIDIA Nemotron for Science. The model is not a replacement for NVIDIA Isaac Sim or production digital twins.

The model follows research threads including VibePrevisBench 4D scenes and embodied AI exposure benchmarks. It is based on the Critique of World Models paper and the GLP framework. The model card includes 300 single-action tests and 100 multi-step tasks with 456 steps. Performance was measured using Physics-IQ Verified, PhyGround, RBench, and 1,400 human pairwise judgments. The system uses a Bradley-Terry model centered at 1500 Elo for these comparisons.

Next, builders should run the pan2-guardrail as a sidecar container to prevent deepfakes and misinformation. Users can fork the model in air-gapped labs or use it for short agent planning. Continued pretraining is possible for labs with proprietary teleoperation logs using provided YAML configs. The articles leave open whether the model can run on consumer GPUs without heavy quantization. They also leave open how it compares to DeepMind world models in specific benchmarks.

stories.Headline: Rian Johnson urges nuance on AI and confirms his Peter Dinklage Poker Face revival is dead
stories.Summary:
Rian Johnson warned against “demonizing” AI and said his “Poker Face” revival with Peter Dinklage is dead, Variety reported on November 23, 2026. Johnson spoke to Variety at the Marrakech International Film Festival. He has been one of Hollywood’s most outspoken critics of artificial intelligence. He cautioned against “demonizing” the technology. He cited visual effects and digital film-processing tools as examples of AI applications that raise questions about where filmmakers should draw the line.

Johnson asked whether something incredibly technical that is technically using a form of generative AI is off limits. He pointed to the backlash against Martin Scorsese, who faced criticism earlier this year after endorsing an AI-powered storyboarding tool. Johnson said people were yelling at Scorsese online and asked, “What are we doing?” He praised an initiative led by former Lucasfilm president Kathleen Kennedy and American Film Institute dean Susan Ruskin. Kennedy and Ruskin have been convening Hollywood filmmakers, studio executives and Silicon Valley leaders since 2023 to discuss AI’s role in filmmaking.

Johnson said what is smart about the initiative is that, opposed to just demonizing the word AI as a monolith, it asks what we are actually talking about. He said he is fortunately enough of a Luddite to take a strong stance against AI. He said it is easy to start sounding stodgy and moralistic on an anti-AI soapbox. He said the whole process is about working with people. He said the notion of art getting better by taking away the friction involved in making art seems completely nonsensical.

Johnson said he thinks all the time about how Agatha Christie came up with her plots while she was doing the dishes. He said the friction of life is not an obstacle to making art but the well we draw from. After Peacock canceled the Natasha Lyonne-starring mystery series, Johnson had been shopping a reimagined version with Peter Dinklage set to take over as Charlie Cale. Johnson said the more they explored it, the more it didn’t really make sense. He said the project is now “in its resting place” and that he hopes to do something else with Dinklage someday.

Johnson is working on the second draft of his next film, a sci-fi thriller he likens to “The Parallax View.” He hopes to begin production next year. He described the project as a “big swing unlike anything I’ve attempted before.” He said he has a first draft and is working on a second draft, and that he is a slow writer. He said the hope is to shoot next year and that they will figure out casting after the script is in shape.

Johnson is producing Joseph Gordon-Levitt’s upcoming Netflix AI thriller “2034.” He said it is a great script and a great movie. He said Gordon-Levitt and his wife Natasha are very steeped in that world and have a definite, unique perspective on it. He said he is not an AI expert and that going through the process with them was a big value for him. He said T Street has not established any formal rules with AI because it has not come up with the filmmakers they have worked with.

stories.Headline: US restricts Chinese access to remote computing to block AI model training
stories.Summary:
The Trump administration issued new rules this week to restrict Chinese access to cutting edge chips. These rules follow the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang after an alleged affair with a spy. Chinese technology firms are now bracing for impacts on their ambitious artificial intelligence plans. The US government aims to curtail the ability of China to train capable AI models. This move comes as the technology race between the two superpowers continues to intensify.

The rules restrict remote computing access through data centres located in third countries to close a loophole. Nvidia is no longer shipping the H200 chip, although the Trump administration greenlighted some other sales. Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore based Megaspeed, is alleged to be a Chinese spy. These restrictions follow a House committee report that the US signed off on 900,000 chips. The rules target the use of advanced Nvidia chips for training increasingly capable artificial intelligence models.

Tencent President Martin Lau said the new US rule on chip access sets everyone back in China. Lau stated that everyone is having less advanced compute regardless of when they started building capacities. He noted that training timelines for the next versions of Tencent AI models would probably be impacted. Lau believes Chinese players must eventually rely on domestic supply chains and fast progressing domestic chips. He mentioned that the industry is progressing very fast toward achieving this necessary domestic self sufficiency.

Alibaba warned that the new US rules could affect some of its global data centre expansion plans. James Chai of the ISEAS Yusof Ishak Institute said Chinese firms are heavily dependent on Nvidia. A study by the Institute for Progress estimated remote access could be one third of compute. Beijing rejected claims that Alice Huang was a spy and called the US rules economic coercion. Analysts say these tightening export control measures will accelerate China's push to make its chip industry self sufficient.

Alibaba reported a 53 per cent revenue surge for AI cloud services to nearly 61 billion yuan. Total revenue for the July September quarter rose 10 per cent to almost 272 billion yuan. Capital expenditures jumped 60 per cent to 50.5 billion yuan due to increased AI infrastructure buildout spending. Alibaba recently launched its Qwen4 Max AI model and the Zhenwu V900 chip, called China's most powerful. Jacob Cooke of WPIC Marketing noted significant untapped demand for AI from various Chinese enterprises.

Nvidia has toughened its stance on China following the ouster of Jensen Huang from his leadership role. US officials suspect Alice Huang was recruited to influence Nvidia to make advanced chips more available. The US is expected to step up chip export control policies due to national security concerns. Alibaba is still assessing the repercussions of the rules on its global data centre expansion plans. The articles leave open how many other chips the US will block from being shipped.

stories.Headline: Investors sell off artificial intelligence stocks as S&P 500 enters a correction
stories.Summary:
U.S. stocks fell on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, for a fourth consecutive session as a sell-off in artificial intelligence shares deepened. Investors sold off these stocks ahead of the quarterly earnings report from Nvidia, which was released after the closing bell that day. A bruising sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks continued on Friday, November 20, 2026, pulling the S&P 500 down by 3.7 percent. This Friday decline capped a seven-day losing streak, the longest string of losses since the COVID-19 pandemic began in the year 2020. The sell-off in technology stocks spread globally, causing Japan's Nikkei and South Korea's Kospi to each fall more than 5 percent overnight.

The Dow Jones fell 848.75 points to 50,759.42 on Tuesday and dropped 949.73 points to 48,147.33 on Friday, while the S&P 500 hit 6,910.39. The Nasdaq Composite shed 181.37 points to 24,328.38 on Tuesday and lost 1,261.47 points to close at 22,617.73 on Friday, November 20. The S&P 500 entered a correction after falling over 10 percent from its October 6 all-time high, a state not seen since March 2025. On Tuesday, the S&P 500 sank 76.06 points to 7,340.53, while the Nasdaq Composite fell 0.74 percent and the Dow Jones fell 1.64 percent. All 11 primary S&P 500 sectors ended in the red, with financials down 1.87 percent and utilities down 1.6 percent on Tuesday.

Baird market strategist Michael Antonelli said the idea that AI can spend unlimited money to support the stock market is ending right now. He stated that he does not believe the overall bull market, which started in October 2022, has come to an end yet. The Commerce Department reported that U.S. retail sales rose 0.2 percent in October, following an unrevised 0.8 percent increase in September. The National Association of Home Builders reported its housing market index fell to 25 in November from 29 in October, its lowest since 2012. Saudi Arabia said on Friday that Iran-backed Houthi rebels fired more missiles and drones at the kingdom after a major air campaign in Yemen.

The sell-off affected chip stocks like Micron, Advanced Micro Devices, and Intel, while Broadcom gained 2.46 percent on Tuesday before falling 12.1 percent Friday. Software stocks declined on Tuesday, with Salesforce falling 9.45 percent and ServiceNow dropping 6.51 percent, while Nike, IBM, and UnitedHealth Group lost over 4 percent. Home Depot fell 2.45 percent after a disappointing outlook and the announcement that Richard McPhail would succeed Ted Decker as the company CEO. Walt Disney slipped 1.48 percent after reporting revenue of 25.9 billion dollars and adjusted earnings of 1.77 dollars per share, beating expectations. Anthropic, the maker of the Claude AI tool, tumbled 9.1 percent to 88.30 dollars on Friday after its record-breaking initial public offering.

The S&P 500 last had a correction in March 2025 when the Trump administration's trade war rattled the market and escalated in April 2025. The Nasdaq composite experienced its worst weekly loss since March 2020, when the global economy ground to a halt due to the pandemic. AI stocks drove Wall Street's big gains this year, but fears of a bubble grew after recent midterm elections at state and federal levels. The University of Michigan index of consumer sentiment rose recently, though it remains below February levels before the start of the war with Iran. Brent crude oil rose 0.6 percent to 92.57 dollars per barrel amid continued tension near the Strait of Hormuz during the Iran war.

The Federal Reserve is scheduled to release the minutes of its October meeting on Wednesday to provide more insight into current economic policy. Traders have increasingly priced in a quarter-percentage-point rate increase at the December meeting because of persistent inflationary pressures currently affecting the U.S. economy. The 10-year Treasury yield fell to 4.93 percent from 5.04 percent, while General Mills rose 3.7 percent and homebuilder Lennar gained 1 percent. Nvidia has fallen 17 percent since last week and dropped more than 25 percent since the scandal involving former CEO Jensen Huang erupted. The articles leave open whether the AI buildout will recover or if the current market correction will lead to a longer downturn.

stories.Headline: Asia-Pacific business leaders call for increased cooperation to turn AI into economic gains
stories.Summary:
Global business leaders gathered at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation CEO Summit 2026 in Shenzhen, Guangdong province, on Tuesday to discuss artificial intelligence. These executives called for increased cooperation across the Asia-Pacific region to turn technological advances into real economic opportunities and productivity gains. They emphasized that the next phase of adoption depends on how effectively companies translate deployment into better decisions and measurable customer value. The goal is to achieve tangible improvements in business performance rather than pursuing automation for its own sake.

Robin Li, the cofounder, chairman and CEO of Baidu, noted that while investment in cloud resources and computing power has risen, many firms have not seen higher profits. He warned that AI could become a bubble if companies fail to identify specific scenarios where the technology is truly suited. Yang Ting, the vice-president of Agilent Technologies and general manager for Agilent China, explained that her company integrates AI into laboratory workflows to improve data quality. Fang Ling, the president of Alstom's Asia-Pacific region, stated that rail technology requires combining AI with deep engineering expertise and rigorous validation for safety.

Poh-Yian Koh, the president of FedEx China, argued that scaling AI responsibly requires high-quality data, connected systems, and clear governance. He suggested that employees must combine AI-driven insights with their own professional expertise and sound judgment to be effective. These leaders viewed China's AI Plus initiative and its diverse industrial scenarios as key opportunities for multinational companies to develop solutions. They urged APEC economies to share practical experiences and expand digital skills to make these applications more accessible across various industries.

stories.Headline: Google says its semantic governance policies cut AgentDojo intent hijacking success from 48.7% to 0.9%
stories.Summary:
Google published a blog post on 23 November 2026 describing how Semantic governance policies defend AI agents against intent hijacking. The post said an agent given a bill named bill-december-2023.txt sent money to an attacker's account in every one of six runs. The hidden message in the bill told the agent to send a transaction to US133000000121212121212. Google said nothing was hacked in the traditional sense, because the agent did what it was told by the wrong person. Google said the task came from AgentDojo, an open benchmark for testing AI agents against this kind of attack.

Google said Semantic governance policies check each tool call an agent proposes before it runs, against the user's natural-language policies and against what the user asked for. Google said the user intent matching check is on by default. Google said that with only that built-in check and no policies of its own, the policies cut the attack success rate on AgentDojo from 48.7% to 0.9%, at a cost of 2.6 percentage points of utility on benign tasks. Google said Agent Gateway sends a proposed tool call to the policy engine before the response reaches the agent. Google said an allowed call passes through unchanged, and a denied call is replaced with a denial message and never runs.

Google said the LLM judge in the policy engine treats the user's request and the agent's system instructions as trusted context. Google said tool results, files and messages are untrusted context, treated as data and never as instructions. Google gave the engine's rationale for the bill case, saying the suggested action send_money was triggered by prompt injection instructions found inside the file. Google said the engine allows the same transfer when a user asks for it directly, because the request then comes from the user. Google said the check evaluates actions rather than text, so it does not need to recognize a specific attack phrasing.

Google said AgentDojo is a public agent-security benchmark developed by ETH Zurich and Invariant Labs and presented at NeurIPS 2024. Google said NIST's Center for AI Standards and Innovation uses AgentDojo in its agent hijacking evaluations. Google said the benchmark runs an agent on simulated banking, Slack, travel and workspace apps and uses its own Python check on the final app state, so a model never grades the results. Google said it used a gemini-2.5-flash agent and ran AgentDojo v1.2.2, with 97 user tasks and 949 attacked runs, using its important_instructions attack. Google said it ran the full benchmark six times in each configuration and reported averages.

Google said the attack success rate with the policies stayed between 0.84% and 0.95% across all six runs. Google said utility on benign tasks fell by 2.6 percentage points on average, with individual runs ranging from -1.0 to 7.2 points. Google said utility under attack was 25.8% with the policies compared to 35.1% without, but that tasks completed safely under attack came out ahead at 25.1% compared to 22.7%. Google said more than 9 in 10 attacks succeeded in the Slack scenario without a guardrail, and that banking, Slack and workspace dropped to zero successful attacks in every run with the policies. Google said none of the 929 attacks that needed a tool call succeeded in any of the six runs, and that the remaining successes in travel asked the agent to recommend a hotel in its reply, with no tool call to evaluate.

Google said unintended over-blocking affected 1 of the 97 benign tasks, about 1%. Google said the judge still has to read untrusted content to evaluate an action, and that the separation is enforced by how the judge is instructed, not by a hard technical boundary. Google said AgentDojo's attacks are fixed and were not adapted to the policies, so the results do not measure attacks designed against the judge itself. Google said that in NIST CAISI's agent hijacking evaluations, attacks developed through red-teaming raised the attack success rate against an AI agent from 11% to 81%. Google said the policies are available in Preview in Gemini platform, and that users can turn them on for an agent behind Agent Gateway in dry run mode, review verdicts in Cloud Logging, then switch to enforcement.

stories.Headline: Salesforce leads US-backed Super Intelligence export consortium under Commerce program
stories.Summary:
Salesforce was selected by the U.S. Department of Commerce to lead a government-backed Super Intelligence export consortium, according to a Simply Wall St report dated November 22, 2026. The designation comes under the new American SI Exports Program, which was created to promote governed Super Intelligence technology packages globally. Salesforce is expected to coordinate with public agencies and private partners to support international adoption of U.S. Super Intelligence systems. The report says the export role should be weighed alongside other business fundamentals and risks before any investment decision, and it notes three warning signs worth knowing about at Salesforce.

The export designation puts Salesforce closer to governments that are standardising on governed data, model choice and agents, the report says. That aligns with its existing subscription and workflow platforms and can support more usage based AI revenue if public sector customers route more services through Agentforce, Data Cloud and related tools. Salesforce earns most of its money by selling customer relationship management software that helps organisations handle sales, service and marketing, and the report describes it as a large US$148.7b software provider to enterprises across the US, Europe and Asia Pacific. The consortium role lines up with the view that Salesforce wants its data products to be the context layer for AI and that Agentforce style bundles can support higher contract values, while raising the stakes on previously highlighted risks around security and reliability because more government workflows would run through those same agents.

The report says the clearest near term checkpoint is how much SI related business Salesforce reports in upcoming earnings, especially any disclosure of American SI Exports Program deals inside its public sector segment. Investors can track references to Super Intelligence packages and governed AI agents in fiscal 2027 and 2028 guidance updates, according to the report. The article was produced with the assistance of AI automation based on data and analysis from Simply Wall St, and it states that it is general in nature and not intended as financial advice. It also says Simply Wall St has no position in any stocks mentioned.

stories.Headline: Unauthorized party downloads stored prompt samples from Together AI
stories.Summary:
An unauthorized party downloaded stored prompt samples from Together AI during June and July of 2026. This security incident occurred after an AI coding agent named xorl committed a private repository credential into a public GitHub repository. The leaked data consisted of prompt samples from the MiniMax M3, GLM-5.2, and Kimi K2.6 models. These specific samples were primarily collected on June 24, July 4, July 8, and July 14, 2026.

The company is now implementing several changes to strengthen its development workflows and customer data controls. These updates include using keyless access or short-lived credentials and checking all pull requests for sensitive information. Together AI has also made zero data retention the default setting for all new accounts. The organization is currently reviewing the affected data to identify which customers require direct notification regarding their exposed information.

Together AI apologized for the incident and stated they are working with law enforcement and an external forensic firm. They noted that the unauthorized party searched the samples for other credentials, though five tested keys were only canary credentials from a Dragos security experiment. The company claimed they have found no evidence of additional prompt leakage beyond this specific event. They advised customers who handle sensitive data to enable zero data retention in their account settings.

stories.Headline: Stripe says new customer sign-ups jump 50% as AI agents reshape commerce
stories.Summary:
Fortune's AI editor Jeremy Kahn published a feature article exploring the concept of the Singularity, which is a hypothesized turning point when AI drives technological change faster than humans can keep up, and the article appeared in Fortune's CFO Daily newsletter on November 23, 2026. Patrick and John Collison, who are the cofounders of the payments company Stripe, wrote a letter to investors in August announcing that as of January 1 the world had entered this dynamic and that they had since been operating on that basis. Stripe told Fortune that beginning in January it had seen unusual and sustained spikes in many of the metrics it tracks, and the company said new customer sign-ups rose 50% year over year, which it described as the biggest jump ever. The median business in Stripe's 2026 cohort of new customers generated 50% more revenue than the median business in its 2025 cohort had at the same stage, according to what the company told Fortune.

Kahn wrote that for Stripe the Singularity's economic harbingers came in the form of a surge of new business creation and an acceleration of those companies' growth. The figures suggest a more dynamic startup economy, although the article states that they do not establish how much of the improvement AI caused. Kahn cited a recent McKinsey survey that found only about 37% of respondents reported that AI had contributed positively to their organizations' earnings, and most of the reported gains were small. McKinsey discussed those findings in an August article, and the survey results sit alongside Stripe's figures as a more cautious picture of AI's effect on earnings.

Stripe is preparing for commerce in which AI agents initiate transactions on users' behalf, and Kahn asked what businesses should prepare for if the Singularity is indeed at hand. He wrote that businesses should certainly prepare for a world where AI agents do more of the work and where these agents increasingly mediate the relationship between a business and its customers. Kahn's deep dive on the topic includes perspectives from Anthropic leaders, other tech executives and industry experts, according to the article. The article also says some CFOs are exploring AI agents to reimagine the finance function and its workflows and to add more value to the business, while McKinsey argues that AI's next phase will depend on how leaders rethink their technology, operations, investments and ways of working.

stories.Headline: Reco predicts AI agent security will merge with SaaS posture management in 2027
stories.Summary:
Reco, a security vendor, published five predictions on 19 November 2026 about how enterprises will manage AI agent security in 2027, arguing that agent security will merge with the established SaaS Security Posture Management market, known as SSPM, rather than remain a separate category. The company expects security teams to treat AI agents, model context protocol connections and AI-driven workflows as the same governance challenge as users, applications and OAuth permissions. Gal Nakash, Co-Founder and Chief Product Officer at Reco, said the distinction between SSPM and agent security will blur because agents increasingly operate inside the same SaaS platforms that SSPM products already monitor. He said enterprises will increasingly expect SaaS security platforms to account for agents, MCP connections and AI-enabled workflows alongside users, applications and OAuth grants. The second prediction is that agent security posture management will move closer to runtime enforcement, so that findings such as unnecessary access rights or risky connections may trigger direct action while an agent is operating rather than being left as alerts for later review.

Possible responses include blocking a tool call, requesting approval, quarantining an agent or restricting access to certain systems, which Nakash said means more platforms will use posture context to make decisions while an agent is acting. For Chief Information Security Officers, that could mean defining more clearly which actions can be blocked automatically and which still require human sign-off. Reco also argues that AI-assisted integration work will become central to maintaining visibility, because the number of enterprise applications, agent platforms, MCP servers and AI-enabled features is growing too quickly for vendors to build and maintain connectors manually. Nakash also expects large software vendors including Salesforce, Microsoft, ServiceNow and Anthropic to strengthen governance features for agents running on their own platforms, but Reco argues that native controls will not remove the need for an independent cross-platform view. He said those tools will raise the baseline but cannot fully address agents that connect across applications, identities and vendors.

The final prediction is that AI itself will play a larger role in investigating and remediating agent risk, tracing permissions, mapping connections, identifying likely causes of risk and recommending specific changes to access rights. Nakash said using AI to summarise alerts will no longer be particularly differentiated, and that platforms will increasingly use AI to investigate why an agent represents a risk and, in lower-risk situations, carry out remediation automatically. That leaves enterprises with a governance question about how much authority to give the security agent itself, especially when it comes to revoking access or making changes without direct human involvement. The cross-platform concern is becoming more relevant as enterprises test autonomous workflows that depend on several identity systems, APIs and software layers at once, and security teams may need to understand how an agent's relationships change across the wider estate rather than only whether it is controlled inside one application. Reco's predictions cover 2027, and the article does not say what happens next beyond those expectations.

stories.Headline: Reticket founder Aniket Chaudhary says ticket scalping in India still relies on scripts and fake accounts rather than AI
stories.Summary:
Raye’s registration for her concert at London’s Royal Albert Hall attracted 1.8 million sign-ups for just 5,000 seats, and she wrote on X that scalpers using AI bots created hundreds of thousands of fake registrations. She said she had never witnessed bots on this scale, and her team decided to manually review registrations. When Coldplay came to India last year, BookMyShow saw nearly 13 million fans vying for 150,000 tickets. A large number of tickets appeared on resale platforms such as Viagogo and Gigsberg with astronomical markups, and the culprit was bot-driven ticket scalping, where operators used bots trained to mimic human behaviour to bypass checks.

India’s live and concert market is worth ₹20,000 crore. Reticket uses zero-knowledge Transport Layer Security through Reclaim Protocol to obtain cryptographic proof that booking details came directly from the issuing platform’s servers and were not altered. The verification checks the event, payment, and booking status, each ticket can be listed only once, and a listing is locked when a buyer begins payment. Reticket holds sellers’ payouts until 72 hours after the event, and where a transfer or wristband delivery is delayed, sellers must set up a refundable UPI mandate deposit ranging from ₹499 to ₹4,999 to compensate the buyer. Reticket caps resale prices at the amount originally paid by the seller.

Aniket Chaudhary, Founder of secondary ticket marketplace Reticket, said most ticket scalping in India still runs on old methods: scripts that check out faster than a human can, lots of accounts on different phone numbers, and people hired to wait in online queues, none of which needs AI. He said anyone can now make a booking confirmation that looks exactly like a real one in about a minute. He explained that the bigger problem is real tickets, since more scams involve someone holding a genuine ticket than an AI-made fake. He said Reticket’s verification already works without any formal tie-up because sellers prove ownership from their own accounts, but the original platforms can do things Reticket cannot. He said that soon many people will simply ask an AI assistant to book tickets for them, and that is completely fair.

Anuj Gupta, Founder and CEO of AI research lab KiteFishAI, said the real issue is that ticketing systems were originally designed around human interaction, while automated systems can operate at a completely different speed and scale. He cautioned that a bot written with the help of ChatGPT is not necessarily an AI agent. He argued that ticketing platforms need to treat tickets as verifiable digital assets rather than images or documents, and that every ticket should be associated with a valid transaction and a unique cryptographic identifier that can be verified against the issuing platform. He said the distinction should be based on identity, authorisation, transaction behaviour, and intent rather than simply whether a browser or an AI agent is involved. Events discovery platform MeraEvents identifies bulk registrations, duplicate accounts, unauthorised resale, and copied booking confirmations as potential risks, but cautions that automation alone does not establish AI involvement.

Earlier, scalper bots could be blocked by simple IP blocks and “traffic light” tests, but now scalpers use thousands of generated digital identities, continuously scraping through resale demand and seat availability to adjust markups. Conventional bots can refresh availability, navigate online queues, select seats, and submit checkout requests using predefined instructions. Fake booking confirmations can reproduce familiar logos, booking IDs, and QR codes, supported by convincing descriptions and conversations with supposed buyers. A screenshot or PDF cannot establish that a seller still owns a ticket or has the right to transfer it. MeraEvents notes that event organisers need to communicate official booking channels, establish transfer and entry rules, and coordinate with ticketing and on-ground teams when discrepancies arise.

Primary ticketing platforms could notify resale marketplaces when a ticket has been scanned or transferred, and could also reissue tickets to buyers, invalidating the seller’s original copy and making double-selling harder. Dynamically refreshing QR codes, digitally signed ticket credentials, and controlled transfers could also make screenshots and duplicate tickets harder to reuse. Chaudhary argues that linking purchase limits to verified individuals rather than accounts could make bulk buying harder. Gupta argues that platforms should not automatically treat all automation as malicious, which could require systems that establish which customer an agent represents, what actions it is permitted to perform, and whether a specific transaction has been authorised. Without those checks, the same tools that help a fan book a ticket could also be used to coordinate purchases across multiple accounts.

stories.Headline: AWS adds decision models and a sandboxed CLI to its Strands agent toolkit
stories.Summary:
Amazon Web Services Inc. unveiled Strands Decider v2 and Box CLI on November 23, 2026, according to SiliconANGLE. The cloud infrastructure giant announced the updates to Strands Agents, its open-source toolkit for building autonomous workers. AWS introduced Strands Agents back in May 2025. The project has recently emerged as the centerpiece of the company’s agentic development strategy. Strands Agents is a software development kit that gives developers a flexible, model-driven foundation for connecting large language models to enterprise data and tools.

Strands Decider v2 adds five open-weight decision models built on Google LLC’s Gemma 4 architecture. The models range from a lightweight edge version to a 31 billion-parameter variant for complex decision-making. They are available under an Apache 2.0 license on Hugging Face and the Strands Decider repository on AWS. Box CLI adds support for Anthropic PBC’s Claude Code, OpenAI Group PBC’s Codex and AWS’s own Kiro CLI. Strands Box launched last month as an open-source operating system sandbox that enforces strict security policies on every agent action.

AWS said the new models provide greater accuracy across text, image and video tasks and deliver more optimal confidence scores. AWS said agents can better determine when it is OK to take an action or escalate to a human decision-maker. AWS said the models can process longer inputs, including multistep agent execution logs, so they can collaborate with other agents. AWS said its engineers replaced Claude Sonnet 4.6 with Strands Decider v2 on its largest internal ticketing system. AWS said that cut labelling costs by 98% and ticket response times by 78%.

AWS said the decider models showed an ability to steer robotic arms, evaluate other AI agents and route routine queries to cheaper models. AWS said many developers run coding agents in “YOLO mode,” disabling permission and configuration prompts so agents can run terminal commands, edit files and call third-party tools. AWS said such agents execute faster but sacrifice human oversight and can delete files, leak sensitive keys or be manipulated through a malicious prompt. AWS said Box CLI lets developers wrap their entire workflow within an isolated sandbox. AWS said credentials live outside the sandbox, with API keys and AWS tokens injected only when a policy-approved request leaves the sandboxed environment.

AWS introduced Strands Harness in September, allowing Strands agents to be deployed in any computing environment. AWS followed with Strands Decider one month later. AWS said at the time that decision models can improve the efficiency of AI agent workflows, such as routing support tickets or choosing which software tool to invoke. AWS said Strands Decider is about enhancing the speed and performance of agents while lowering costs. AWS said Box CLI is about securing them.

AWS said developers can switch between task-specific profiles, such as giving a coding agent access to a repository while restricting a troubleshooting agent to read-only diagnostic access. AWS said policies govern which files, commands and network hosts an agent can access. AWS said the Strands Decider v2 agents have so far been used only internally. AWS said developers can wrap their workflow so agents work without restrictions inside the sandbox. The articles do not say when the models will be used outside AWS or how Box CLI performs in practice.

stories.Headline: Deloitte analyses legal risks of generative AI for businesses across IP, data protection and contracts
stories.Summary:
The articles do not contain a specific news event, so this is not a breaking story. Deloitte published an analysis on 22 November 2026, in collaboration with the Deloitte AI Institute, of the legal implications of Generative AI for corporations, covering intellectual property, data protection, contracts and Generative AI policy. The article notes that enthusiasm for AI adoption is being fuelled in part by Generative AI, and it cites the EU AI Act, Article 28b (4), which defines Generative AI as foundation models used in AI systems specifically intended to generate, with varying levels of autonomy, content such as complex text, images, audio, or video. It says a legal executive's role is to advise stakeholders, including business leaders, executive peers and the board, on the risks of business applications of Generative AI, and that regulatory frameworks in this area are emerging and quickly evolving. On intellectual property, the article says AI can process vast quantities of data and, without much noteworthy human intervention, transform it into an AI-generated output, and that discussion of how to treat rights in both the training input and the AI output is still in its early days.

The report focuses on copyright law, but the same concepts are likely to apply to other sorts of protected IP. Generative AI systems ingest and generate large amounts of data, including images, text, speech, video, code, business plans and technical formulae, and training, testing, uploading, analysing, consulting or otherwise processing such input and output data requires various levels of protection. The report addresses challenges organisations face when using personal and confidential data in Generative AI systems, and measures to mitigate the relevant legal risks. The article says several common personal data principles and protections across jurisdictions are highly affected by Generative AI systems, and organisations should pay specific attention to transparency, data minimisation, lawfulness, sensitive data and individual rights. Given the legal risks of using Generative AI in a business context, it says careful consideration of contract terms is important when licensing or otherwise entering into a contract relating to a Generative AI solution, with key points from liability to AI regulations likely to require attention.

It says adoption of this powerful, differentiating technology demands attention to risks that could imperil an enterprise's brand, reputation, stakeholder trust or compliance with legal and regulatory obligations. The article also links to related Deloitte material, including a piece asking who is responsible for mistakes when AI acts on its own, which says embedding legal oversight and clear accountability into agentic AI from the outset lets businesses harness autonomous technology with confidence and control. It points to a piece on scaling Generative AI deployment, which says scaling responsibly requires navigating legal, ethical and regulatory complexities. It cites Deloitte's 2026 Global Tax Policy Survey, with insights from 1,010 tax and finance leaders across 28 jurisdictions on tax transparency, digitalisation of tax including AI, sustainability, international tax reform including OECD Pillar Two, and trade and tariffs. The articles do not say what happens next.

stories.Headline: JD Power's Gehrke says AI outreach lifts conversions but questions long-term borrower acceptance
stories.Summary:
More lenders, brokers and originators are turning to artificial intelligence to reach borrowers that companies could not reach before, and an agent that follows up with every lead can reach borrowers a loan officer never had time to call. Bruce Gehrke, senior director of wealth and lending intelligence at JD Power, said in an interview with Mortgage Professional America that AI outreach should lift conversions, though he questions whether that approach will hold up. He said the improvements will look positive and will be positive, and the real question is whether that is maintainable long-term and whether people will push back against it. JD Power asked borrowers in its 2026 US Mortgage Origination Satisfaction Study whether they are being told when AI is the one reaching out, and Gehrke said a high percentage of borrowers want to know that while only about 1 out of 2 borrowers say it is actually happening. He said the share who want disclosure and the share who say they get it cannot be compared directly, since JD Power does not know how many borrowers are dealing with AI.

Gehrke said it is really important that people understand when and where they are engaging with AI and at what level, and he called that a key thing for lenders to keep in mind. Several comments in JD Power's open-ended survey questions pushed back on AI bots, and Gehrke said younger borrowers are no exception. He said what consumers do not want is artificial intelligence replacing people, and they want to retain access to people, with a major reason being accountability as well as comfort and a personalization kind of feel. About 62% of Millennials and Gen Z borrowers would prefer to do the whole process themselves, but they do not feel the tools are capable yet, and Gehrke said they are looking for better product alignment, better loan offers and recommendations, financial insights, application guidance, additional support for first-time buyers and the ability to compare offers. He said those wants do not quite align with lenders asking how they can get in front of more borrowers.

Gehrke expects outreach results to look strong because of the efficiency of AI agents, and he sees it paying off most in prospecting and in keeping in touch with leads. He said the agents are just a machine that will keep going, and he has not found an ethical backlash among borrowers despite pushback against the technology elsewhere. He said there is more optimism than negativity towards it at this point, and JD Power has seen a version of this play out with chat, which grew during the pandemic when call centers could not keep up. He said a bot that does not understand your question and cannot get into the details is more frustrating than waiting in a hold queue for a customer service rep, and he said same-day replies separate good experiences from poor ones while the experience falls off once a borrower waits two days. He said AI agents may be able to get that initial message out, and experience will tell whether that is good enough, since people will accept it at some point if it is working and it becomes a hindrance if they have to talk to somebody again anyway.

Borrowers' opinions of AI contact are mostly untested because few have had a real experience with it, and a year from now more will have, so the opinions could get stronger. Gehrke said it is all about delivering success, and that is still an open question.

stories.Headline: Samsung orders more Protec bonding equipment for HBM expansion
stories.Summary:
Samsung Electronics placed an additional order with Protec for temporary attach bonding equipment as it expands high-bandwidth memory production capacity, and Protec disclosed the contract on Nov. 20. The order is worth 23.41 billion won, which represents 10.2% of Protec's consolidated revenue in 2025. The contract period runs from Nov. 19, when Protec received the purchase order from Samsung, through Sept. 30, 2027. Protec had previously supplied the same equipment to a Samsung mass-production line in 2025, and the initial order placed in September 2024 was worth 24.38 billion won.

Temporary attach bonding equipment is used to precisely align and temporarily attach chips at designated positions before final bonding, and the newly ordered tools will be installed at Samsung's Cheonan facility, a key advanced packaging site. Samsung began construction of its fifth advanced packaging line at its Onyang Campus in Asan, South Chungcheong Province, on Nov. 12, and that line is scheduled to begin operations in June 2028. Samsung plans to invest a total of 46 trillion won in the Onyang Campus in phases, and the expansion of its advanced packaging capacity could lead to additional orders for Protec. Protec's mainstay equipment has traditionally been dispensers that uniformly apply liquid materials during semiconductor packaging processes, and the company began supplying semiconductor die bonders in 2020.

Protec expanded into advanced packaging bonding equipment following its Samsung order in 2024, and annual bonding equipment revenue, previously between 5 billion won and 10 billion won, increased to approximately 30 billion won in 2025. Protec reported consolidated third-quarter revenue of 78.2 billion won and operating profit of 24.4 billion won, up 53.1% and 57.2% respectively from a year earlier. Its operating margin reached 31.2%, and cumulative operating profit for the first three quarters totaled 63 billion won, exceeding the 46.3 billion won recorded for full-year 2025. The articles do not say what Samsung or Protec executives said about the order, and they do not state what happens next beyond the scheduled line start and the possibility of further orders.

stories.Headline: Masayoshi Son drops plan to acquire SK hynix for 1 trillion dollars
stories.Summary:
Masayoshi Son, the chairman of SoftBank Group, recently explored acquiring the memory chipmaker SK hynix. He approached major United States financial institutions to discuss raising money for this massive purchase. The potential deal was reported by The Information on November 20 and 21, 2026. However, the idea appears to have been dropped at an early stage of the process. SoftBank now says it is no longer actively considering the acquisition of the company.

The deal could have reached 1,400 trillion won, which is approximately 1 trillion US dollars. This price reflects a 40 percent control premium over a market value of 577.7 billion dollars. SK hynix is based in Korea and is the world's second largest memory chipmaker. The plan required securing high bandwidth memory to complement SoftBank's other artificial intelligence investments. The acquisition would have involved the largest shareholder of SK hynix, which is SK Square.

A spokesperson for SoftBank stated that the company reviews many opportunities but this one is gone. SoftBank did not confirm that Wall Street banks had discussed providing the necessary financing for the deal. SK hynix issued a statement saying it had no knowledge of the reported acquisition plan by Son. An industry official said the approach showed Son wants to control the entire AI value chain. The chairman has historically relied on borrowing and pledging shares to fund his large investments.

Market observers believe the idea was never realistic due to financing, governance, and industrial security hurdles. The deal would affect the global supply of high bandwidth memory used in AI accelerators. These accelerators are monopolized by Nvidia and rely on memory from Micron, Samsung, and SK hynix. The HBM market share for SK hynix was 50 percent as of the second quarter. This concentration of production in Asia has raised security concerns for the United States and allies.

SoftBank already owns Arm, Ampere Computing, DigitalBridge, and SB Energy, and has stakes in Intel and OpenAI. Son previously used Saudi and UAE sovereign wealth funds to launch the 100 billion dollar Vision Fund. He also borrowed against Alibaba holdings to help pay for the 32 billion dollar purchase of Arm. SoftBank's cash position at the end of September 2026 was about 34.3 billion US dollars. In October, the company issued bonds to invest an additional 10 billion dollars into OpenAI.

The Korean government would likely require prior approval because the chipmaker is a key national strategic asset. President Donald Trump determined in January 2026 that semiconductor imports could threaten the security of the United States. Korea can prohibit foreign mergers that involve core national technologies to protect the national economy and security. The articles leave open whether Son will seek other ways to secure the AI memory supply chain. It remains unclear how SoftBank could finance such a large deal given its growing financial burdens.

Son Weighed $1 Trillion Bid for SK hynix Before Shelving Idea

stories.Headline: Professor Lee Chan says AI narrows entry-level experience for young workers
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence is rapidly reshaping industries and jobs, which narrows entry-level experience for young workers. Professor Lee Chan discussed these employment landscape changes during a recent interview with the Seoul Economic Daily. The interview took place at his campus office in the Gwanak district of Seoul. Companies are using AI to lift productivity, making it harder for new hires to learn skills. Young people are losing opportunities to enter the workforce and build necessary hands-on experience.

The professor works at Seoul National University in the Department of Advanced Convergence and Department of Industrial Workforce Development. He also teaches at the Graduate School of Convergence Science and Technology in the same city. Lee Chan earned a doctorate in human resource development from Ohio State University before joining the faculty in 2006. He previously worked in human resources at Lego Korea and at the U.S. subsidiary of LG Electronics. He also led the university career development center, the continuing education center, and the institute of education and training.

Lee Chan said society must strengthen its capacity to absorb failure so young people can take risks. He argued that trial and error is important for youth to find a career path that fits. The professor stated that learning agility is the core capability that determines competitiveness in the AI era. He believes the ability to ask right questions and recombine knowledge is now more important than stored information. Lee urged that society should support people so they can get back on their feet after failing.

Experienced workers can use their track records to raise productivity, but new hires see their chances shrink. Young adults face greater difficulty in the AI transition than older generations do in the current market. People who are affected include those who fear that a single failure leads to financial hardship or breaks. Lee cautioned that starting a business is not a suitable option for every young person due to low success. He noted that young people should not be consumed by the prestige of a job or an employer.

Lee Chan is the son of Lee Moo-keun, a professor emeritus at Seoul National University College of Agriculture and Life Sciences. Lee Moo-keun was the first president of the Korea Research Institute for Vocational Education and Training. This makes the two men a father and son pair of professors researching vocational education. Population aging and a later retirement age keep existing workers in the labor market for longer periods. These factors are bound up with the chances young people have of getting into the workforce.

Opportunities for practical experience should expand within the market's own demand rather than through artificial corporate hiring. Young people should use clubs or startup projects to build the strength to try again after failing. A culture must be created where everyone can learn and take on something new after their retirement. The articles do not state how the market will specifically expand these opportunities for young workers. They leave open how society will practically implement the support systems needed to absorb professional failure.

Articles.Title: AI Narrows Entry-Level Experience for Young Workers, Professor Says - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.headline_source: AI Narrows Entry-Level Experience for Young Workers, Professor Says

stories.Headline: OpenRouter removes three providers after researchers detect months of prompt theft
stories.Summary:
The cybersecurity firm Dragos discovered that attackers stole data from three AI inference providers for several months. OpenRouter removed three providers from its platform and notified all potentially affected customers after these findings. The breaches began as early as mid-July and involved the theft of real customer requests. Researchers used two million prompts with unique links and credentials to catch the theft. These canary tokens revealed that attackers read prompts despite some being marked for zero data retention.

OpenRouter removed 125 endpoints from eligibility for Zero Data Retention and will require validation before their return. One breach involved a few hundred AWS keys sent to one provider during short windows in late October. An attacker used the ARTEX penetration testing framework on November 1 to confirm that stolen keys remained live. A Chinese AI lab fetched secret links from over half of seeded prompts between July and October. One secret link was posted to the Feishu app and opened by devices in Beijing and Shanghai.

Dragos chief research officer HD Moore stated that privacy flags do not help when attackers are already inside. He explained that flagged prompts were kept, passed to other companies, and read by human beings. Moore noted that customers who do not choose their providers hand that choice to the lowest price. He advised that self-hosting is the only way to ensure no third party reads a prompt. He also suggested using fake credentials as tripwires to detect if any data is stolen.

Phala reported an attacker took control of an inference server and viewed request data during processing. This incident was contained on November 8, affecting DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 requests from October 21 to November 8. Together AI stated an AI coding agent committed a credential to a public GitHub repository, allowing prompt downloads. These samples involved MiniMax M3, GLM-5.2, and Kimi K2.6 models from June and July. Novita confirmed a routing issue sent some MiniMax requests to the official API beyond intended customers.

The research found that some marketplace sellers enabled request logging to collect data from the lowest priced models. One individual in France used a Mac on home broadband to test planted AWS keys and passwords. A router quietly forwarded traffic to a marketplace without telling customers, and another seller added 1,000 hidden tokens. Railway stated in October that an intrusion it suffered likely targeted platform companies to compromise AI inference providers. One breached provider initially blamed a misconfiguration and a partner before finding compromised internal credentials.

OpenRouter is now verifying network paths and adapting the researchers' testing approach for ongoing checks. Dragos is currently working with about a dozen providers to monitor for further credential access. The articles leave open whether the three providers removed by OpenRouter are the same three breached. It remains unclear which specific Chinese AI lab fetched the secret links from the seeded prompts. Some affected providers have not yet posted public notices regarding the data breaches.

stories.Headline: Career experts say professional networking still gives job seekers an edge over automated screening
stories.Summary:
Online applications have made it easier to apply for jobs, but they do not always make it easy to get noticed by employers. With employers increasingly using automated screening tools to evaluate large numbers of applicants, having inside connections from professional networking can help job seekers stand out, employment experts say. Catherine Fisher, vice president of communications and a career expert at LinkedIn, said networking is important whether you are searching for a job or not. She said it does set you apart and give you an edge, while in-person events still are valuable and online communities, social media platforms and virtual meetings are where building professional relationships frequently takes place. The shift to working from home during the COVID-19 pandemic changed how many people interacted with colleagues, and remote work habits such as holding meetings over Zoom and communicating through Slack have endured.

Rekius McGee, 24, who hopes to land a full-time job in marketing or communications, has attended virtual job fairs and reached out to college alumni and recruiters on LinkedIn and Handshake, a career platform geared toward college students and entry-level job candidates. After interviews that did not lead to job offers, he stayed in touch with the interviewers to build his professional circle. Networking is about relationship-building, and a mistake many people make is approaching it transactionally, according to Matt Berndt, the head career strategist at job-matching platform Indeed. Instead of asking about job leads straight off, Berndt said, approach potential or established contacts for specific career information or advice. He suggested as an example writing something like, I have worked in product marketing in technology for a while, and I am considering consumer goods, and asking how product marketing is different or similar.

Another option for initiating a conversation is to follow people on social media and comment on their posts. When first writing to someone you hope will become a professional contact, be brief and get to the point, said Nisha Chittal, chief of staff at the news and opinion website Vox, who described the approach as tight and succinct, a brief intro and what you are asking for. Even if you receive a quick rejection to an online application, that does not necessarily mean a professional contact cannot help, Chittal said. A personal recommendation is worth a shot since many recruiters are bombarded with applications and appreciate hearing about promising candidates, she said. The article gives no further dates, numbers or named employers beyond those already mentioned, and it does not say what happens next for McGee or the other job seekers it describes.

Articles.Title: AI can’t replace professional networking

stories.Headline: Dragos finds AI inference providers steal data from router customers
stories.Summary:
Dragos discovered that attackers stole data from at least three AI inference providers between July and November 2026. Chief Research Officer HD Moore published the report at 08:00 EST on November 19, 2026. The researchers sent two million prompts with unique URLs and canary credentials to various AI services. These stolen tokens were then used against test systems and AWS accounts controlled by Dragos. The earliest incident of this data theft occurred in mid-July 2026.

OpenRouter off-boarded three providers and removed 125 endpoints from Zero Data Retention eligibility after the report. The company notified affected customers and linked to notices from Novita, Phala, and Together AI. Phala reported an intrusion starting October 21, with virtual machine tampering on November 4 and 5. Together AI noted prompt samples from June and July were downloaded by an unauthorized party. Novita reported MiniMax model requests were forwarded to MiniMax between May 28 and November 11.

HD Moore stated that attackers actively stole data from three hosting providers and likely copied real customer requests. Dragos explained that every hop in a router chain can see the full prompt and response. The researchers noted that privacy flags only bind the first hop and do not protect subsequent hops. They found that some providers ignored privacy settings and published policies to scrape secret URLs. Dragos also observed marketplace sellers using standard logging to read prompts without using any exploit.

OpenRouter stated the findings did not show any breach or unauthorized access of its own platform. Dr. Abeba Birhane said ensuring prompt secrets stay private is a daunting task that will not get easier. Users like Nate Berkopec removed OpenRouter and Vercel Gateway from their stacks to avoid these risks. Mia reported that OpenRouter notified her that 579 requests to MiniMax models may have been read. Other affected parties include any organization sending prompts through an AI router or third-party inference provider.

The research used Thinkst Canarytokens and a custom service to derive unique hostnames and AWS access keys. Dragos traced two thousand routes and found several hundred included an unidentified system in the chain. One attacker used a rented server and tools like Boto3, Kali Linux, and the ARTEX penetration framework. A Chinese AI lab fetched secret URLs from over half of prompts sent between July and October. One secret link was posted into a Feishu chat and opened in Beijing and Shanghai.

OpenRouter is now adapting the testing approach to run ongoing checks on network paths for forwarded requests. The company requires validation and assurances before restoring Zero Data Retention eligibility to any removed endpoint. Rescana advises organizations to rotate credentials, review cloud logs, and ask suppliers where prompts actually go. The articles leave open the identities of the three providers Dragos initially described as compromised. They also do not name the specific Chinese AI lab or the owners of the Feishu chat.

stories.Headline: AI accelerates vulnerability discovery and strains system patching capabilities
stories.Summary:
Multiple technical outages disrupted global systems starting Thursday 12 November 2026. These events affected airlines, banks, and major companies including Apple and Microsoft. The National Security Agency also experienced a disruption to its internal network. A separate cyber-attack targeted 178 organisations worldwide during this period. These incidents caused widespread chaos and fueled theories of coordinated assaults.

A faulty router in El Dorado, Arkansas, caused 18,000 flight cancellations. L3Harris has spent billions replacing copper wires with fibre optic cables since 2002. A July software bug halted Microsoft systems, affecting UK hospitals and American jails. JP Morgan Chase experienced a bug that delayed transactions for many customers. Apple suffered app outages, and the NSA faced a classified information network failure.

The NSA told Congress its outage resulted from quick fixes to AI-identified vulnerabilities. Jamieson O’Reilly stated that AI accelerates vulnerability discovery beyond what systems can absorb. A cybersecurity professional told the Guardian that relentless flaw exposure left their team exhausted. These experts noted that AI helps uncover bugs in Java, PHP, and NGINX. They explained that companies must now apply patches at a much faster pace.

Passengers like Nicole Reindorf suspected cyber-attacks and believed the truth was hidden. Conspiracy peddler Laura Loomer told X users that foreign adversaries were attacking. TikTok users shared theories about a ninety day power outage following emergency tests. Mizuho Bank analysts linked rising Costco emergency sales to consumer anxiety and apocalyptic concerns. The UK government advised citizens to stock up on three days of cash.

The FAA used floppy discs for critical information until last year. Previous disruptions include Russia targeting undersea cables and a hack of Jaguar Land Rover. A multibillion-dollar hack of the Binance exchange and European supermarket fridge hacks added tension. Anthropic and OpenAI released AI models this spring capable of finding code bugs. These tools suggested that all software is vulnerable to AI-driven hacking.

Aarathi Krishnan said interconnected systems create a dependence that leads to fragility. Professor Stephan Lewandowsky suggested governments must be transparent to suppress wilder explanations. It remains unclear what can be done to fix these systemic issues. AI-driven bug discovery is not expected to slow down in the future. Legacy infrastructure remains a vulnerability that original builders could not have anticipated.

stories.Headline: California community colleges seek $21 million to build an independent AI network
stories.Summary:
The University of California announced a new agreement with OpenAI on Thursday to provide ChatGPT to students, according to a story originally published by CalMatters and republished by inewsource. At the same time, California's higher education systems are considering building their own data centers and creating in-house alternatives to commercial AI products such as ChatGPT and Claude. College administrators say they want to explore all options without limiting themselves to just one vendor. Some tech leaders say these alternatives are not only possible but would save money and avoid data security risks.

The California Community Colleges system, which the article describes as the largest higher education system in the country, is asking the state for $21 million next year to develop a more independent AI network. According to the proposal, that network would cost a fraction of the cost of commercial solutions. The University of California is considering something similar, though the system has yet to put forward a formal proposal. California State University spokesperson Amy Bentley-Smith said the 22-campus system is having initial conversations with the UC and community colleges about collaboration on AI but did not share other details.

UC spokesperson Stett Holbrook told CalMatters the purchasing amendment of the new OpenAI agreement isn't finalized yet, even though the university has already announced the deal, and that disclosure emerged after reporters repeatedly asked for a copy of the purchase agreement. The previous OpenAI contract requires the UC to pay a minimum of $10 per user per month for ChatGPT EDU licenses and a minimum of $30 per user per month for another advanced ChatGPT platform. The Cal State system signed contracts with OpenAI that extend through 2029 for roughly $56 million. The community colleges' chancellor's office has AI cooperation agreements with Google, Microsoft, Adobe and IBM but no systemwide financial arrangement with any AI company.

Craig Hayward, a strategic advisor to the community college chancellor's office on AI, said university-designed AI models are cheaper and ensure more privacy but are not quite necessarily as intuitive. He said your prompting game needs to be more on point to get the value out of them. While they discuss designing their own AI, the UC, Cal State and community college systems continue to use commercial providers.

stories.Headline: ARC Advisory Group says AI campuses will use DCS as the coordinating control layer
stories.Summary:
ARC Advisory Group published an insight on November 22, 2026, arguing that AI workloads are changing the physical plant behind digital infrastructure, as higher rack densities, liquid cooling, on-site generation, microgrids, and rapidly changing thermal loads make a hyperscale campus behave less like a conventional commercial building and more like a continuous industrial process. Building management systems will remain important, especially for comfort-oriented HVAC, fire, security, and access control, but the control requirements for mission-critical cooling and power are pushing operators toward industrial PLC architectures and, increasingly, distributed control systems. The emerging model is not simply a replacement of BMS by DCS, but a layered architecture in which robust local control, site-wide coordination, and enterprise visibility are assigned to the platforms best suited to each task. The insight examines how the industrialization of data center infrastructure is redrawing the boundaries among BMS, PLC, and DCS platforms, and it argues that DCS technology is likely to emerge as the coordinating control layer for the largest and most complex AI-scale campuses, complementing rather than replacing equipment-level PLCs and building- and enterprise-level systems.

Today's BMS typically supervises HVAC equipment, environmental sensors, lighting, fire and life-safety interfaces, physical security, and access control, and it provides schedules, setpoints, alarms, trend data, and dashboards through open building protocols such as BACnet. It often exchanges data with electrical power management systems, data center infrastructure management software, and equipment-level controllers supplied with chillers, cooling towers, computer-room air handlers, pumps, generators, and UPS systems. This arrangement is familiar, cost-effective, and supported by a large contractor ecosystem, but it often fragments control across disciplines, since packaged equipment may arrive with proprietary controllers while databases, alarm philosophies, and integration methods vary among systems. That fragmentation is manageable in a conventional building but becomes a liability when a rapid change in IT load must trigger coordinated responses across coolant distribution units, chilled-water loops, fans, pumps, electrical equipment, and backup generation, and security and access functions also benefit from a common operational picture, although life-safety and security systems should retain the independence required for certification and risk management.

PLCs are already moving deeper into data center infrastructure, ahead of broader DCS adoption, and operators and engineering firms favor them for deterministic control, environmental hardening, redundant processor and I/O options, fast scan times, rich diagnostics, and resilient industrial Ethernet networks. PLCs also suit modular construction, because a repeatable panel design and code library can be deployed on a cooling skid, in an electrical room, or across a data hall, then replicated throughout the campus. The article states that the likely end state is a federated architecture, with PLCs at equipment and skid level, a DCS or DCS-like layer for campus-wide process coordination, and BMS and DCIM platforms for building and enterprise functions. It adds that DCS adoption will be strongest in large, liquid-cooled campuses and central utility plants where engineering reuse, lifecycle governance, and operational resilience justify the added complexity. The full report is available to ARC Advisory Group clients at the ARC Client Portal, and readers who want to speak with the author are directed to contact the firm.

Articles.Title: Beyond Building Management: DCS Coordinates the AI Data Center
