stories.Headline: Dragos finds widespread AI supply chain security failures and data theft
stories.Summary:
Between July and November 2026, the research team at Dragos discovered widespread AI supply chain security failures. Chief Research Officer HD Moore led the investigation into how AI providers handle inference data. The team sent nearly two million prompts containing unique URLs and canary token credentials to various AI services. They monitored these secrets to see where they surfaced after the initial inference request. This process revealed security breaches, prompt theft, and failures to protect customer data.

The study found that attackers stole data from three different hosting providers starting in mid July. One breach in late October involved a couple hundred AWS keys stolen at the provider's front door. Some stolen requests were marked as Zero Data Retention, which is the strictest privacy setting. One attacker used a rented server to compromise two providers and employed the ARTEX penetration testing framework. Other leaks involved a Chinese AI lab and U.S. providers that ignored privacy settings.

HD Moore stated that the results showed a disconnect between AI marketing and actual data handling. He explained that AI providers often store prompts for training, safety, or business purposes. The research team noted that attackers used stolen keys to list S3 buckets and search Secrets Manager. They observed that some marketplace resellers used standard logging to view and retain customer prompts. Moore highlighted that some U.S. providers transmitted data to Chinese organizations despite privacy flags.

Marketplace resellers and external attackers affected customers by stealing confidential source code and strategic plans. Individuals using home broadband connections in France and elsewhere tried to guess usernames and passwords. Some customers paid U.S. providers to keep data domestic, but their prompts flowed to China. One secret link appeared in a Feishu company chat twenty four days after the request. These actors targeted private git repositories and used stolen credentials for tens of thousands of API calls.

AI routers offer a single API endpoint to forward requests to a pool of available models. These routers can be open marketplaces where the lowest price seller receives the traffic. Data often traverses multiple organizations, including model developers, cloud operators, and third party resellers. Some sellers use stolen AWS credentials or consumer API keys to offer deep discounts. This infrastructure creates multiple hops where every entity can see the entire prompt and response.

Defenders can use CloudTrail to detect user agents from Kali Linux and the ARTEX framework. The research team notified the three breached providers, who were previously unaware of the thefts. The articles leave open whether the providers have fixed the bugs causing privacy setting failures. It remains unclear how many real customers lost data alongside the Dragos canary tokens. The report does not state if the Chinese AI lab or the resellers were identified.

Articles.Title: AI Supply Chain Security: What Canary Tokens Found

stories.headline_source: AI Supply Chain Security: What Canary Tokens Found

stories.Headline: Sheffield philosopher Gerardo Viera argues cognitive science study equips students to understand AI
stories.Summary:
The Hindu published an article on November 21, 2026, by Gerardo Viera, a Lecturer in Philosophy of Science at the University of Sheffield in the U.K., asking why students should study Cognitive Science in the age of AI. The article says emerging AI technologies are playing larger roles in work, entertainment, relationships, health and politics, and are changing how people understand themselves. It says societies approach this technological horizon with a mixture of hope that it will solve problems and fear that it may end life as we know it. Viera argues that simply developing skills for the current state of the art is not enough, because technology moves so quickly that those skills rapidly become obsolete.

He proposes instead investigating how advances in AI relate to puzzles about the nature of intelligence and the mind. The article says Cognitive Science draws on Philosophy, Psychology, Neuroscience, Computer Science and related fields, and that these joint resources offer the best hope of resolving puzzles about how the mind fits into the natural world. It says AI advances promise a better understanding of biological minds, since systems can now reproduce complex behaviours long thought to be uniquely human, such as producing language and novel proofs in Maths. It adds that studying biological minds can help design and understand artificial systems, noting that Computer Science was founded by trying to replicate perception, learning and memory, and that advances in the 1970s took inspiration from the network-like arrangement of neurons.

The article also describes an engineering hurdle: modern data centres can use as much electricity and water as a small city, while a honeybee navigates its environment, learns food locations and recognises faces on around 50 calories a year. Viera says discipline-specific training can reveal only part of these puzzles, and that advances in AI and understanding biological minds will likely come from those who acquire interdisciplinary skills. He says that as people rely on AI systems for information and decisions about health and policy, they start to trust these systems as though they are peers, and that safeguarding ourselves and assessing risks and benefits requires knowing how the systems work and whether they are genuinely intelligent. He says these skills open careers across academia and research, education, law and public policy, computing and technology, journalism, public service and social impact.

He says organisations will need people who understand both the technical possibilities of these systems and their wider implications for individuals and society. The article says Cognitive Science requires integrating findings from various, often conflicting, research disciplines. It says a background in Cognitive Science and AI provides an understanding of the limitations and capacities of emerging AI systems, which is needed to navigate this complex technological horizon and to contribute meaningfully to the organisations and professions shaping the technological future. The article does not say what happens next beyond these points.

Articles.Title: Why study Cognitive Science in the age of AI?

stories.Headline: Teenager uses AI chatbot to hack Agniveer test website and tries to sell data on dark web
stories.Summary:
A 14-year-old boy from Ballabhgarh in Haryana was apprehended for allegedly attempting to sell sensitive information linked to around 4,000 Agniveer personnel on the dark web, Delhi Police sources said. According to a senior official familiar with the investigation, the teenager used artificial intelligence tools to identify data that could fetch him money and sought a chatbot's help to hack into a website. He gained unauthorised access to a test website designed for former Agniveers to register themselves and explore employment opportunities in the Indian Armed Forces. Preliminary investigation revealed that the boy managed to breach only the test website, gaining access to names and addresses, the official said. There is no indication so far that information relating to marks, ranks, results or other sensitive personnel records was compromised.

During preliminary questioning, the boy told investigators he was motivated by the prospect of making money, saying he first asked an AI chatbot what kind of data could help him earn and then sought its assistance in finding a way to hack into the system. The exact method used to gain access is still being examined. After accessing the website, he allegedly extracted the information and advertised it on a dark web marketplace, claiming to possess personal records of around 4,000 Agniveer personnel and seeking $500 for the purported database. The Delhi Police's Intelligence Fusion and Strategic Operations unit has recovered data from the juvenile's digital devices, and investigators are examining the material to establish its authenticity and determine the extent of the suspected breach.

The IFSO unit has written to the National Informatics Centre seeking clarification on the data available on the test website and the information accessed by the boy, and police are awaiting a response to ascertain precisely what may have been compromised. While the NIC provides digital infrastructure and hosts government portals, the ownership and maintenance of Agniveer personnel records rest with the Armed Forces and the concerned ministries, officials said. As the accused is a juvenile, he was counselled and handed over to his parents, and police are consulting the Juvenile Justice Board on the further course of action. Further investigation is underway.

Articles.Title: 14-year-old used AI chatbot to hack Agniveer ‘test’ website, wanted to earn money by selling it on dark web: Delhi police sources

stories.Headline: Mistral opens Singapore science hub and APAC headquarters to build sovereign AI models
stories.Summary:
The French artificial intelligence firm Mistral opened a new science hub and Asia-Pacific headquarters at Asia Square Tower 1 in Singapore on November 20, 2026. This facility aims to create sovereign AI models for robotics, high-tech manufacturing, and the public sector to help organizations keep proprietary technology and sensitive data in-house. To support this expansion, the company intends to increase its regional workforce from approximately 100 to 200 employees by 2027, with most of these new roles based in Singapore. The expansion requires hiring forward-deployed engineers with business acumen and forward-deployed scientists with advanced mathematical training to build unique AI tools. These efforts respond to geopolitical concerns, such as new US rules effective November 19 requiring licenses for certain advanced AI chip exports to Singapore and four other nations.

Mistral also seeks to develop models that reflect Singapore's linguistic diversity and help humanoid robots navigate complex environments. In manufacturing, the technology will be trained on production line images to identify defects and irregularities. Geoff Soon, the vice-president of revenue for Asia-Pacific, stated that governments and enterprises in the region increasingly want to control the technology they depend on for economic competitiveness. Co-founder and chief executive Arthur Mensch explained that the company wants Singapore to be a strategic location for empowering clients to retain ownership of their intelligence. Senior Minister of State Tan Kiat How noted that resilience comes from working with strong partners while building deep local capabilities.

Pee Beng Kong of the Economic Development Board added that this investment reinforces Singapore's position as a hub for frontier AI innovation. The company previously collaborated with the Home Team Science and Technology Agency on Phoenix AI models that reflect local laws regarding race and narcotics. Mistral now plans to establish new partnerships within the Singaporean financial sector, although specific details have not yet been released. This growth occurs as companies fear that overseas decisions could cut off access to essential AI models and the chips that run them. Future developments will focus on creating lasting economic value and industrial competitiveness across the Asia-Pacific region.

Articles.Title: Mistral expands Singapore AI operations with science hub to tap demand in key sectors

stories.headline_source: Mistral expands Singapore AI operations with science hub to tap demand in key sectors

stories.Headline: Australia reviews competition laws for AI agent shoppers and surveillance pricing
stories.Summary:
Australia is reviewing its competition laws so they can handle more people using personal artificial intelligence agents to shop, pay and manage money on their behalf, the government said on Nov 21, 2026. Andrew Leigh, assistant minister for productivity, competition, charities and treasury, told reporters in Canberra that the government is doing a whole lot of work to ensure the competition laws keep pace in an AI age. He said more consumers are going to be shopping with AI agents and the government is looking at whether it is important to update the laws there. AI agents are increasingly being designed to shop, make payments and manage money on behalf of users, with retail just one sector among many globally confronting the reality of customers handing over decision-making to agents.

Their growing autonomy is forcing financial institutions to work out how much authority to give them and who is responsible for their actions, the article says. Australians have been shopping online for years, leading to lower footfalls in established retail networks like David Jones, the department store group which has collapsed after almost two centuries in business. Leigh said the government was considering issues such as personalised pricing, also known as surveillance pricing, where different prices can be set for consumers based on their individual data. He cited an example he had heard overseas of people being asked to pay more for a security product because their area was suffering from crime.

Leigh said sometimes that can lead to people paying higher prices, and he stated that the government does not want Australians mucked around by surveillance pricing powered by AI. He said the government wants Australians to get the very best deal in the AI age. The government is also looking at who is responsible for agents' actions as part of its review of whether the laws need updating. The article does not say when the review will finish or what specific changes are being considered.

The article gives no further details on next steps beyond the government's stated work on competition laws and surveillance pricing. It does not name any bill, timeline or enforcement action that would follow from the review. The report was published by The Straits Times on Nov 21, 2026, and was updated the same day. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Australia vows to manage AI agent shoppers, surveillance pricing

stories.Headline: Asahi CEO Katsuki plans $85mn AI cybersecurity upgrade over three years
stories.Summary:
Japanese beverage maker Asahi Group Holdings is investing 13.5 billion yen, or 85 million dollars, into its cybersecurity infrastructure. This massive financial commitment follows a ransomware attack that occurred in 2025 and disrupted business operations for several months. The company intends to spend this money over a three year period to protect its digital assets. These upgrades are designed to prevent similar security breaches from happening again in the future. The investment requires the company to rebuild its existing systems using advanced artificial intelligence technology.

Asahi Group Holdings will also hire more specialized talent to help detect unauthorized access to its networks. These changes aim to create a more resilient defense against the evolving threats of the digital age. The three year plan focuses on integrating these new tools to ensure long term stability. Chief Executive Officer Atsushi Katsuki detailed the spending plans to address the vulnerabilities exposed by the previous incident.

He explained that the company must modernize its approach to security to safeguard its global operations. The leadership believes that combining AI with expert human talent is the best way to monitor threats. This strategic shift reflects a commitment to protecting the company from further operational disruptions. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Asahi pours $85mn into AI cybersecurity upgrades after ransomware attack

stories.headline_source: Asahi pours $85mn into AI cybersecurity upgrades after ransomware attack

stories.Headline: Japan's Noetra AI project faces $5bn cost rise as chip prices and weak yen bite
stories.Summary:
The flagship domestic artificial intelligence initiative in Japan is facing a massive increase in projected expenses. This sovereign project is seeing costs rise by as much as 800 billion yen, which equals approximately 5 billion dollars. The financial pressure on the plan has intensified recently due to the soaring prices of necessary computer chips. A weak yen has further contributed to the rising costs of the technology required for the project. The Noetra initiative now requires a significant amount of additional funding to maintain its current goals.

This sudden cost surge means the Japanese government may be forced to shoulder a much larger financial burden. The project must navigate these economic headwinds to ensure the domestic AI strategy remains viable. These changes are necessary to prop up the initiative against the volatile global semiconductor market. President Hironobu Tamba of Noetra has been speaking about the development of physical artificial intelligence.

He discussed these technological advancements at a government event held in Tokyo on July 16. While the specific response to the cost surge was not detailed, the leadership is managing the project's growth. The government is now evaluating how to cover the multi-billion dollar gap in the budget. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Shachihata launches AI video authentication on X to offset shrinking hanko market
stories.Summary:
A Japanese company that specializes in making traditional carved stamps will launch a new authentication service later this month. Shachihata is moving into the artificial intelligence realm to help users identify videos on X that have been altered. This strategic shift comes as the company seeks new sources of growth to offset its shrinking traditional market. The business is attempting to fight back against the digitalization that is currently devouring the hanko market. The new system requires the use of acoustic watermarks and digital fingerprints to verify the authenticity of video content.

These technical tools will allow users to detect whether a video has been manipulated by artificial intelligence or other editing software. Shachihata is implementing these changes to pivot away from its reliance on physical stamps used for signing documents. The company intends to establish a strong presence in the cybersecurity field by providing these verification tools on the X platform. The leadership at Shachihata is responsible for this transition as they give themselves a mandate to expand their business operations.

They believe that moving into the digital authentication space is necessary because the demand for traditional hanko stamps is declining. By leveraging new technology, the company hopes to protect digital media from the risks associated with deepfakes and altered footage. This move represents a significant departure from their historical focus on physical office supplies and traditional Japanese signing customs. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Anthropic plans a Nasdaq IPO to raise over 90 billion dollars for AI infrastructure
stories.Summary:
Anthropic plans to debut on the Nasdaq stock market this coming Thursday to test investor confidence in the global artificial intelligence boom. The five year old company develops the Claude family of models and expects the initial public offering to generate over 90 billion dollars. Technology companies are committing billions of dollars to the offering despite concerns over financing risks and the sustainability of the investment boom. This arrival occurs during a difficult moment for the sector following a decline in technology shares and a leadership crisis at Nvidia. The company reported a net loss of 104 billion dollars during the first nine months of 2026 but holds 132 billion dollars.

The offering price is expected to be 70 to 78 dollars per share with investments of 26 billion dollars from several major firms. These investors include Advanced Micro Devices, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, while Amazon holds a substantial stake. Anthropic has over 900 billion dollars in spending commitments, including 110 billion dollars with Amazon over 10 years and 400 billion dollars elsewhere. It will spend 125 billion to 150 billion dollars on Google chips by 2028 and lease a data centre starting 2027. Amazon also built an 11 billion dollar data centre in Indiana for Anthropic using custom chips, and Google guaranteed 19 billion dollars.

Anthropic stated in its prospectus that it previously underestimated computing requirements, which left the company short of capacity and affected product deployment. Joe Fath of Eclipse called the staggering numbers hard to wrap one's head around, while David Tollen called it smart investing. Subhadeep Chatterjee, a former Google executive, said that everybody knows Anthropic is going to be the future of the Google company. Broadcom provided a financial backstop with a maximum liability of 43 billion dollars to support the rental of artificial intelligence chips. Bank of America, Blackstone, Citigroup and Morgan Stanley offered 63 billion dollars to purchase the racks of chips that Anthropic will rent.

Corey Quinn of Duckbill questioned if the long agreements could remain unchanged, stating that anything past four years is like throwing darts. The Nasdaq fell 5.3 percent in October, which was its worst monthly performance since March 2025, adding pressure to debt heavy providers. Rising interest rates and new United States ballot measures could further restrict the development of new data centres across the entire country. Investors are also concerned by Nvidia, where shares fell 13 percent after chief executive Jensen Huang resigned following reports of extramarital affairs. Colette Kress was appointed interim chief executive after Huang was linked to a woman suspected of having links to Chinese intelligence.

The company is committing to infrastructure well in advance because it needs computing power to develop advanced models and expand its services. Cloud providers Amazon, Google and Microsoft account for 31 percent of the contractual obligations listed in the latest official company prospectus. Google is expected to hold an ownership stake of approximately 13 percent following the completion of the initial public offering process. The 10 year agreement with Amazon is twice the length of typical contracts, which has attracted questions about the financial exposure. These investments occur as the broader technology sector faces mounting pressure from indebted cloud infrastructure companies and volatile global stock market trends.

The initial public offering will provide funding for the computing infrastructure needed to operate advanced models and expand the company's current services. The articles leave open whether the long term infrastructure commitments and the 20 year data centre lease will remain financially sustainable. It remains uncertain if the arrangements with cloud providers will be renegotiated before the contracts expire as suggested by some industry experts. The market will see if the 90 billion dollar debut can redefine the scale of technology listings despite the current sector turmoil. Investors must wait to see if the calculated exposure to these staggering costs will result in the predicted future for Google.

stories.Headline: Hideo Kojima warns AI may sap joy of creation while Mamoru Oshii sees no immediate film change
stories.Summary:
Japanese game creator Hideo Kojima and film director Mamoru Oshii discussed the potential effects of artificial intelligence on creative work during a recent event. This conversation took place in Tokyo on November 20, 2026, as part of a celebration for the 150th anniversary of the Nikkei media company. The two leading figures shared their perspectives on how emerging technologies might reshape the boundaries of games and cinema. They examined whether these tools would enhance the artistic process or fundamentally alter the nature of imaginative production. Hideo Kojima warned that while artificial intelligence could be beneficial for business operations, it might sap the joy of creation.

He expressed concern that the widespread use of these tools could make people more passive consumers of entertainment over time. The shift toward automated content might reduce the active engagement and effort typically required to produce meaningful art. This transition could potentially change how audiences interact with stories and how creators approach their craft. The responsibility for navigating these changes lies with the creators and industry leaders who integrate these technologies into their workflows.

Kojima suggested that the efficiency gained through automation might come at the cost of the human spirit in art. Mamoru Oshii offered a different view, stating that he sees no immediate change to the world of film. He believes that in the cinematic arts, the questions surrounding the technology currently outweigh the available answers. More to follow.

stories.Headline: LG Uplus, KT and SK Telecom raise AI data center spending as returns stay uncertain
stories.Summary:
SK Telecom, KT and LG Uplus increased their capital spending as they expand into artificial intelligence data centers, and their combined expenditure reached 3.68 trillion won in the first nine months of this year, up 13.7 percent from a year earlier, according to their regulatory filings on Friday. LG Uplus posted the biggest increase, with capital expenditure on a standalone basis reaching 569.8 billion won in the third quarter, a 30.1 percent year-on-year rise driven largely by its AI data center project in Paju, Gyeonggi Province. The company is building a 200-megawatt facility there with four buildings scheduled to begin operations by 2028, and its first 50-megawatt building is expected to be completed by next June. KT's cumulative capital expenditure, including major affiliates, reached 1.599 trillion won, up 20.3 percent, while SK Telecom's total, including its new AI data center unit SK Hyper, was 1.234 trillion won, up 3 percent. The push requires large upfront spending on land, construction, power infrastructure and cooling systems, while depreciation, electricity and maintenance costs continue after facilities begin operating.

KT plans to invest a total of 6 trillion won in AI transformation infrastructure over the next five years and to expand its data center capacity by more than 1 gigawatt by 2031. SK Telecom's spending declined when SK Hyper is excluded, reflecting its strategy of bringing in external investors to share the financial burden of large-scale data center development. Industry officials said the telecom and AI data center businesses have different revenue structures, because returns on data center investments can vary significantly depending on each facility's ability to attract customers, its utilization rate and contract terms. LG Uplus says it has secured customer demand for all four buildings in Paju. During its recent earnings call, SK Telecom said a certain level of increase in investment is inevitable, while emphasizing its plan to finance a substantial portion of AI data center development through external funding.

The AI investment push comes as the telecom companies seek new growth engines beyond their mobile businesses, with demand for computing power and data storage increasing as companies adopt generative AI and expand their use of AI inference services. Questions remain over whether the investments can be recouped, particularly over depreciation costs for graphics processing units. U.S. hyperscalers typically depreciate GPUs over five years in their financial statements, but questions remain over whether this is appropriate, because AI accelerator makers such as Nvidia release new products almost every year. This means the period during which existing GPUs can handle cutting-edge AI workloads may be considerably shorter than their accounting lifespan, effectively shortening the time companies have to generate sufficient returns. Securing customers before facilities become operational and maintaining high utilization rates will be critical to recovering investment costs, and long-term contracts can provide more predictable revenue, but profitability will also depend on electricity prices, operating expenses and the timing of equipment deployment.

stories.Headline: Scamwise finds AI-generated content in 74% of fake stores it analyzed
stories.Summary:
A report from Scamwise, a website checking tool, warns that artificial intelligence is helping scammers quickly build more convincing fake storefronts and fill them with product descriptions, images and other content. Scamwise said it analyzed more than 250,000 shopping websites submitted by users between March and October 2026. More than 100,000 were classified by its system as “definitely” or “likely” scam stores. 74% of the scam stores in its analysis used AI-generated content. A previously unseen scam store was reported to Scamwise about every three minutes.

40% of scam stores were less than 90 days old when checked, and seven in 10 were no longer live 90 days after Scamwise checked them. The data is based on sites consumers chose to submit to Scamwise, often because something already appeared suspicious. Scamwise reported 20% of the confirmed fake-store submissions it analyzed carried an ad-click fingerprint. In that subset, Scamwise said 42% carried a Google Search or Shopping identifier, 29% carried a Facebook identifier and 10% carried an Instagram identifier. The click ID is referred to as “CLID.”

Shaun Khalfan, senior vice president and chief information security officer for PayPal and Venmo, said fraudsters are using AI to create more polished and personalized emails, text messages and websites, making them harder to detect. Josh Hares, executive vice president of the BBB of Greater Atlanta, said scammers can imitate major retailers’ branding and blend their messages into the flood of legitimate holiday promotions. Hares said they just need to hit the right person at the wrong time. Hares said researching a business before making a purchase can help shoppers avoid the frustration of trying to track down a site or recover money afterward. Hares said trust shouldn’t be given blindly and that you shouldn’t just trust somebody because they have a website.

A Google spokesperson said scams have no place on Google and that last year the company blocked over 99% of policy-violating ads before they ever ran. Google said it removed more than 1.7 billion ads in the United States and suspended 3.3 million accounts last year. Google said misrepresentation was its second most-enforced policy and that it removed more than 421.5 million ads globally for misrepresentation in 2025. Google disputed the report’s interpretation of its click tags and said a GCLID is used to measure ad clicks and does not prove a scam ad is currently running. Meta did not respond to requests for comment by deadline.

The BBB recommends going directly to a retailer’s website and comparing prices before entering personal or payment information. Hares cautioned that a website using HTTPS or displaying a lock icon is not necessarily legitimate because fraudulent sites can use those security features too. Hares noted that a new or online-only business is not automatically fraudulent and that the key is to verify the seller rather than assume a polished website proves it is legitimate. Scamwise says scammers often reach shoppers through the same online pathways legitimate businesses use, search tools and social media. A fake website can closely resemble a legitimate retailer’s site, but its web address may contain an extra word, added letters or a slightly different spelling.

Scamwise says Google’s GCLID can indicate a Google Ads click, while Facebook’s FBCLID can appear in both paid and organic Facebook traffic. A click identifier is not proof that Google or Meta knowingly ran a fraudulent ad, that an ad is still active or that a platform profited from a particular store. Google said a GCLID tag can remain in a link after an account is suspended or can be copied across fake sites and redirect links. Google says its policies prohibit scam ads and deceptive practices, including fake online storefronts and advertisers that misrepresent their businesses. Google said it requires merchants to provide return policies, billing terms, contact information and secure checkout options.

Hares recommends checking a seller’s contact information, looking for independent reviews and searching the BBB’s business profiles for available complaints and customer reviews. Shoppers should search the store’s name with “reviews” or “scam” and look beyond testimonials posted on the store’s own website. Shoppers should price-check unbelievable discounts and compare the product’s price with a known retailer. Shoppers should treat ads as a lead, not proof a seller is legitimate, and search for the seller independently rather than buying directly from an ad in their feed. Shoppers should use a credit card, keep screenshots of the listing, promised price, delivery date, seller information, receipt and order confirmation, and keep AI purchase approval turned on.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: Over half of Korean workers fear workplace photos could be misused in AI sex crimes, survey finds
stories.Summary:
A survey of 1,000 workers in Korea aged 19 or older found that 53.1 percent worry photos of themselves posted on company intranets or messaging platforms could be used in artificial intelligence-assisted sex crimes, according to results published Sunday by The Korea Times. The survey was commissioned by the labor rights group Workplace Gapjil 119 and carried out by the polling firm Global Research between Aug. 1 and Aug. 7, 2026. Concern was more widespread among women, with 58.2 percent expressing anxiety, compared with 49 percent among male respondents. The poll also asked workers about safeguards at their companies and about the impact of AI on gender inequality in hiring.

Only 11.6 percent of respondents said their employers had rules in place to prevent and respond to AI-related sex crimes, while 48.6 percent said their companies had no such rules. Another 39.8 percent said they did not know whether such rules existed at their workplaces. Asked what measures companies should take, 29.2 percent called for stronger security regulations, and 28.8 percent said employers should establish workplace policies that clearly define digital sex crimes and set zero-tolerance disciplinary standards. The survey also examined how workers view AI's effect on gender inequality in hiring and employment.

Nearly 40 percent of respondents agreed that AI-driven automation could replace jobs in female-dominated occupations first, increasing women's risk of unemployment. Another 36.8 percent said AI-assisted recruitment systems could disadvantage female applicants by learning from male-dominated hiring records. To prevent such discrimination, 42.9 percent called for companies to fully disclose the criteria and details used by AI in evaluating employees. Another 40.4 percent said companies should regularly check AI-backed hiring systems for gender bias and make the findings public.

Kim Ja-yeon, a labor attorney at the civic group, said AI technology is advancing rapidly while digital sex crimes and gender discrimination are penetrating everyday life, and that companies and the government need to take proactive measures to create safe workplaces. The survey report was published by The Korea Times on Nov. 22, 2026, with a publication time of 4:03 p.m. KST, and was written by Lee Hyo-jin. The article presents the findings as a survey showing that more than half of workers in Korea share the concern about misuse of workplace photos.

stories.Headline: SK Group chairman Chey Tae-won calls for universities to teach wisdom over knowledge in the AI-native era
stories.Summary:
Chey Tae-won, chairman of SK Group and of the Chey Institute for Advanced Studies, said at the Tokyo Forum 2026 that universities must build a new educational system suited to the AI-native era. He spoke during the Business Leader session of the forum, held at Yasuda Auditorium at the University of Tokyo in Japan on the 20th and 21st of November 2026. The Tokyo Forum is an event jointly organized by the Chey Institute for Advanced Studies and the University of Tokyo, and it has been held annually since 2019. Chey said universities should go beyond teaching knowledge and should focus on cultivating wisdom, and he called for nurturing talent who will steer the direction of change so that the value created by AI can be broadly shared.

Chey defined an AI-native society as a human-centered society in which cyberspace and physical space are fused, and he predicted a society that accepts AI as a naturally given environment rather than merely using it as a tool. He also said that as of now no one has the right answer for how to reach an AI-native society, and he sees education as the starting point for finding that solution. He said AI is new and no one has the answer, so collective intelligence must be pooled to find one, and he added that the answer may turn out to be wrong but that the experience of having designed a system firsthand will become a capability to solve problems when facing real-world challenges. He then introduced SK Group programs to develop talent, support employment, and train data center personnel.

Regarding Aizen, a two-year, non-degree program unveiled last month, Chey explained that it is a model that assigns team projects and lets participants find answers on their own. He said participants will tackle assignments across diverse fields and try out their own designs for solving problems. On collaboration between businesses and universities in the AI era, he said working with people from countries with different cultures, systems, and languages is not easy, but the younger generation strengthened by AI can take on such challenges more readily. He added that it would also be a good approach for companies and universities in Korea and Japan to create and operate joint programs to cultivate AI talent.

stories.Headline: Verónica González Laporte examines Korean society and AI in her novel Peeling
stories.Summary:
Mexican anthropologist and novelist Verónica González Laporte wrote a novel called Peeling about Korean society. She began writing the book in 2020 and completed the work in 2024. The story follows a plastic surgeon named Ji-ho who falls in love with an AI sex doll. Ji-ho faces a family illness and a warning from a shaman during the plot. The author used her personal experiences in Korea to explore beauty, isolation, gender, and shamanism.

The book was originally written in Spanish as K-Beauty before being translated into Korean as Bakpi. It features scenes at Mount Halla and Changdeok Palace, and it mentions the city of Cuernavaca. The plot includes a gay character named Geon-hee and a doll named Seong-mi. González lived in Seoul for over five years with her husband, Bruno Figueroa Fischer, until 2023. The story draws parallels between Latin American women and the haenyeo divers of Jeju Island.

González said she wanted to offer another Korea by looking behind the stage of its polished image. She explained that she aimed to recognize social issues that are difficult to notice because they are familiar. The author stated that younger generations need to recognize patriarchal mechanisms that have been established for many years. She noted that she felt at home on Mount Halla because it resembled her Mexican city. González said that people in different countries are similar even if they do not speak the same language.

The novel explores how gender inequality and women's rights play out within the Korean family structure. Ji-ho's mother represents the vulnerable position of young women and the expectations of their in-laws. The character Geon-hee reflects the social taboos and prejudices regarding homosexuality that the author encountered. The book also examines the contrast between cutting-edge technology and centuries-old beliefs like shamanism. These themes affect the characters as they navigate the tension between fantasy and reality.

Inspiration came from a visit to a dermatology clinic during the COVID-19 pandemic for facial redness. González read reports about bodies in plastic bags in China and a man suing for a sex doll. She observed that Korean brands often have similar windows and colors, creating a sense of visual uniformity. Her background as an anthropologist included studying male shamans in northern Mexico before seeing female mudang. She noticed that Korea is a highly organized society that sometimes lacks fantasy in its decorations.

A Spanish-language edition of the novel is currently in preparation for publication. The author recently visited Seoul and noted that the orange taxis she remembered had disappeared. The text describes how the novel reveals shared values that transcend borders through its various characters. The articles do not state when the Spanish edition will be released to the public. They leave open whether the book will be translated into other languages beyond Spanish and Korean.

stories.Headline: Anthropic's Mythos model finds thousands of flaws, driving a global patching surge that causes outages
stories.Summary:
Microsoft patched 3,554 security flaws in the two and a half months before a major November outage. This surge in patching followed the March 2026 release of the Anthropic Mythos model to select firms. The model scanned code for bugs and found hundreds of vulnerabilities, some dormant for decades. These rapid fixes caused outages for Microsoft Outlook, Apple, Workday, United Airlines, JPMorgan Chase, and US air traffic control. The NSA also suffered a classified messaging system outage last week due to a PHP programming language upgrade.

The industry found over 100,000 confirmed vulnerabilities this year, more than double the 48,000 found in 2025. New Zealand health sectors faced Microsoft disruptions in January in the upper North Island, July in Waikato, and November. The NCSC recorded 4,673 incident reports and 23.8 million dollars in losses for 2025/26, down from 5,995 and 26.9 million. The Reserve Bank names concentration risk in shared AI, software, and cloud providers as a financial stability concern. Its Operational Resilience Standard will not take effect until 2028.

US Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said the NSA outage was a fix and not an attack. Retired General Paul Nakasone stated that the current situation of frequent outages is a new normal. Twenty chief executive Joe Lin described a collision between the speed of discovery and the ability to address flaws. US Representative Jim Himes warned that the pace of patching could cause more frequent outages. Health NZ director James Allison insisted disruption was minimal because of satellite phone and Starlink contingencies.

Former CISA director Chris Krebs said all available evidence suggests the recent outage events are not connected. Azul CTO Gil Tene believes AI-driven patch velocity is already causing major incidents. Filigran CEO Samuel Hassine argues updates are pushed onto systems that cannot take much change. Cogent IT expert Tony Grasso criticized the move to the cloud over servers for creating single points of failure. Unions want hospital IT treated as life saving clinical care rather than relying solely on Microsoft.

The acceleration of vulnerabilities began in March 2026 when Anthropic shared its Mythos model with security firms. Most firms moved to the cloud because it was sold as a cheaper and more secure option. The NCSC warns that malicious actors may gain frontier lab AI capabilities by early 2027. This would allow attacks to unfold faster than businesses can detect or respond to them. The RBNZ and FMA are currently urging firms to get the basics right.

Mitiga field CISO Brian Contos recommends using tested rollback procedures, monitoring, and staged rollouts. Business leaders should map vendors under critical functions and build offline fallbacks for processes that cannot stop. Firms are encouraged to ask suppliers how they reverse and stage their updates. The articles leave open how SMEs will handle the risk before the 2028 rules arrive. It remains unclear if the health sector will reduce its reliance on Microsoft.

stories.Headline: Microsoft study finds Copilot offers lowest monthly AI costs across everyday and advanced users
stories.Summary:
Microsoft released research, conducted with GigaOm and published on November 21, 2026, that compares the total cost of ownership of three leading AI tools: Microsoft Copilot, ChatGPT Enterprise and Claude Enterprise. The study tested multiple scenarios across two categories of users, everyday users who handle routine tasks such as searching for information, preparing for meetings, analyzing data and creating content, and advanced users who manage complex multi-step workflows. Over the month evaluated, the research simulated tasks for both groups and found that Copilot consistently offered the lowest monthly costs. For everyday users, Copilot's monthly subscription stands at $30, compared with $205 for Claude and $81 for ChatGPT, making it more than six times cheaper than its most expensive counterpart. For advanced users, Copilot costs $96 per month, compared with $299 for Claude and $149 for ChatGPT, meaning competitor costs run more than three times higher.

The study also examined output quality, with evaluators assessing accuracy, relevance and completeness, and it found that quality across Copilot, ChatGPT and Claude remained broadly comparable even though pricing varies dramatically. According to the research, Copilot's lower pricing comes from three main elements: everyday AI tasks included in the user subscription, which prevents additional fees; a Work IQ feature that provides context-sensitive assistance by drawing on data within the Microsoft ecosystem; and an Auto function that dynamically selects appropriate models and effort levels for the task at hand. The article notes that the study assumes certain usage patterns and that costs could vary depending on the types of tasks performed and negotiated pricing, so some firms may need their own evaluations. GigaOm invites organizations to use its methodology in their own environments for tailored insights.

The research was released by Microsoft in collaboration with GigaOm, and the article was written by David Wilson for Small Business Trends. The article states that the findings suggest small businesses can use a comprehensive AI solution without breaking the bank and without sacrificing work standards for cost savings. It also cautions that as businesses ramp up their use of AI, costs can scale up if not managed proactively, making budgeting and cost oversight crucial for firms that want to scale efficiently. The article says the findings emphasize that costs are one facet of a broader strategy and that embracing an efficient AI solution could provide a competitive edge. It directs readers to the full GigaOm report for further details and insights from the research.

stories.Headline: Explainx.ai publishes a guide mapping three Microsoft Copilot workshop types and a vetting checklist
stories.Summary:
The explainx.ai blog published a guide on 22 November 2026 about copilot workshops, saying the term is not trademarked and search results mix a half-day Excel class, a Copilot Studio agent build and a slideshow about generative AI. The guide maps three workshop families Microsoft customers actually book, which it calls M365 Copilot workshops, Cowork-focused sessions and Copilot Studio workshops. It says a Microsoft Copilot workshop is a scheduled live session where people do work on screen rather than only watch demos. It says the instructor alternates short explanations with tasks such as summarising an inbox, cleaning a sheet, approving Cowork before it sends mail, or publishing a test agent in Studio. It says what separates a workshop from a webinar is feedback, and what separates it from self-paced Learn modules is judgment about when to trust output and what a tenant allows.

The guide says universities, consultancies and Microsoft partners run formats from ninety minutes to two days, and it names HKUST's Copilot Studio Agent Builder Workshop as a focused three-hour Studio build. It says Singapore provider Coursemology runs two-day M365 Copilot intensives across apps, and EY Malta's 2026 series splits Excel, Teams and Outlook, and Word and PowerPoint into separate half-days. It says Microsoft announced Copilot Cowork general availability on June 16, 2026, after a preview that started March 30, and that Cowork bills in Copilot Credits with pay-as-you-go at $0.01 per credit listed in Microsoft's June 16, 2026 GA post. It says a serious agenda allots at least thirty minutes per app used weekly, and that Studio builds need fewer than twenty active builders for one instructor unless assistants are listed. It says the explainx.ai workshop runs on December 20 and 21, 2026, as two evenings of two hours.

The guide says a good provider runs paired seating or a watch-and-question block with honest labeling if half a group lacks licences, and that a bad provider pretends everyone is hands-on. It says Microsoft Learn's Cowork prerequisites state that Cowork asks permission before actions such as sending email, and that a workshop should rehearse that approval step rather than skip it for speed. It says the final hour should give takeaways including exported prompts, a checklist for checking output and a rule for what data may enter Copilot. It says recordings and templates should be named on the syllabus, not promised vaguely. It says pricing, licence names and feature flags change and should be verified on Microsoft Learn and the admin center before committing seats.

The guide says the vetting checklist includes product names in the syllabus, a hands-on ratio of at least half the scheduled time, a checking step, licence honesty, recency, deliverables, class size, data rules, support after class and match to your stack. It says competitors that rank for copilot workshop often excel at one piece, and that Maven-style cohorts emphasize a named rollout framework covering chat, in-app, agents and governance. It says teams should use public outlines for ideas and then insist a vendor covers tenant realities including Purview, oversharing and admin switches. It says common mistakes include no champion, Cowork without governance, Studio agents without ownership and competing tools without habits.

It says a live workshop should be skipped when budget is zero, licences are not approved yet, or only two people need Copilot. The guide says Track 1 covers prompting inside Word, Excel, Outlook, PowerPoint and Teams, and should be picked when a team already has Microsoft 365 Copilot licences and needs daily habits rather than agent architecture. It says Track 2 should be picked when admins enabled Cowork and leaders want delegation rather than chat, and that Cowork workshops fail when everyone lacks licences and watches a polished demo. It says Track 3 teaches topics, knowledge, tools, child agents and connectors, the vocabulary Microsoft uses in campus sessions like HKUST's outline, and that learners leave with a sandbox agent, not a polished production system.

It says Studio is not free forever at scale and that volume packs and P3 discounts should be treated as directional. It says GitHub Copilot is a separate SKU and M365 Copilot should not be assumed to include it. The guide says a workshop should be booked when licences exist, a cohort shares the same apps, and there is a date-bound rollout such as quarter close, fiscal planning season or a Copilot Studio pilot. It says executive briefings rather than hands-on workshops suit leadership that needs risk framing without touching tenants.

It says the explainx.ai copilot workshop page lists dates, prerequisites and recordings policy for a live cohort mapping to the three tracks. It says the guide's hour-by-hour template shifts numbers by format but proportions should not. It says the December 20 and 21, 2026 workshop post explains what each session covers, what attendees need before joining, what explainx.ai saw when it ran Copilot Cowork itself, and who the workshop is for. It says the guide does not state what happens if Cowork is off in a tenant beyond asking the provider.

stories.Headline: Anthropic introduces a novel governance framework as Nvidia faces a leadership crisis and share slump
stories.Summary:
Jensen Huang was ousted from Nvidia in November 2026 after news of his extramarital affairs broke. He had a relationship with an Nvidia executive and a woman US authorities believed was a Chinese spy. Huang misrepresented the nature of the relationship with the alleged spy to senior Nvidia officials. The spy was linked to Megaspeed, a major Nvidia chip buyer in Singapore with Chinese ties. These events led to a significant slump in Nvidia shares and a supply shock for technology.

The US Commerce Department now requires licenses for advanced AI chips for Chinese data centers providing remote computing. Licenses are also required for exports to Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand due to diversion risks. Nvidia shares fell 22.9 per cent last week and 38.7 per cent since the spy scandal began. The S&P 500 dropped 8.8 per cent and the Nasdaq 100 fell 11.8 per cent in that period. Nvidia reported robust third-quarter numbers and strong revenue guidance for 2027 despite the share price slump.

Nvidia stated it is not considering inviting Jensen Huang back to the company. The company's founders at Anthropic wrote a letter to investors about the potential for AI to boost productivity. They warned that AI could inflict immense harm on humanity and has large positive and negative externalities. They said these externalities are in tension with the incentives of for-profit companies and standard governance structures. The founders stated they expect to make mistakes and learn from others as they evolve.

Investors, technology sector luminaries, and Nvidia employees are calling for the return of Jensen Huang. Some investors may be appalled by the multiple share classes introduced by Anthropic for its listing. Holders of Class A shares will face dilution from the ongoing issue and conversion of Class N shares. The US government was alarmed by Huang's ties to a spy linked to a Chinese company. The wider AI ecosystem has seen weakened confidence following the exit of the Nvidia chief executive.

Anthropic was formed as a public benefit corporation to weigh shareholder interests against its public benefit mission. It reached a US$1.5 trillion valuation within six years, while Nvidia hit US$1 trillion in 2023. Anthropic uses five share classes, with Class F and Class T holding most of the control. A single Class F share gives seven co-founders 50.1 per cent voting power over the company. The Long-Term Benefit Trust holds the Class T share and appoints four of seven board members.

Anthropic will issue Class E shares to non-founder employees to give them a say on some governance matters. Class A and Class N shares hold all economic benefits, but Class N shares have no voting rights. Anthropic plans to contribute 2 per cent of equity to its fund for every 50 per cent price increase. Market regulators and governance experts must now consider how to effectively check seemingly indispensable corporate leaders. The articles leave open whether Anthropic's novel governance framework can successfully improve upon standard corporate practices.

stories.Headline: Mortgage executives say AI speeds loan reviews but human underwriters still make final credit decisions
stories.Summary:
Executives at Incenter Diligence Solutions and SitusAMC said artificial intelligence is helping mortgage lenders and due-diligence firms review loan files and extract borrower information, but the technology still needs human oversight, especially when loans involve unusual circumstances or require judgment beyond standard guidelines. At Incenter, AI has accelerated document indexing and data extraction, according to president Pamela Hamrick, and the technology can now sort and categorize thousands of pages of loan documents in minutes, replacing a process that once required employees to manually separate and label files. Hamrick said that while AI can extract information from standardized mortgage documents like loan estimates and closing disclosures, borrower-provided records including pay stubs and bank statements are harder to process because their formats vary, though AI can identify inconsistencies across documents and summarize them for underwriters to investigate. Hamrick said the technology is identifying the questions, the inconsistencies and the anomalies between all of this documentation and summarizing that for an underwriter or a reviewer to dig deeper and decide whether what the AI has identified is a real risk, a minimal risk or no risk at all because of the particular scenario.

Julia Curran, senior managing director of residential AI products at SitusAMC, said the company uses AI to re-underwrite closed loans in the secondary market, checking regulatory and underwriting guidelines as well as data accuracy before loans are reviewed for securitization. According to Curran, SitusAMC builds AI agents around processes established by human subject matter experts and tests their results against loans previously reviewed by people, running repeated tests until the system reaches at least 95% accuracy. Curran said the system sends blank or inconsistent fields to human reviewers, and final credit decisions require judgments that cannot be reduced to individual data points, adding that a final credit decision should not be made by the machine because there are other things to consider besides the specific data points. Hamrick added that companies that fully rely on AI are potentially going to have misses in some other areas where a human might have been able to make a different decision.

Curran also warned about the AI model supplying information not supported or provided by the documents submitted, describing a case in which a model supplied a solar panel number that was not included in a particular loan file, and although the answer was correct, the system had apparently drawn on information from other files. Curran said even though it is right, she does not want that answer and wants to stay within the four walls of the file. The executives said lenders should test AI against established human processes before relying on it for underwriting, and Hamrick recommended introducing the technology in one part of the workflow at a time, comparing its results with human reviews before expanding its use, and preparing employees for changes by retraining them for tasks that require more human intervention. Hamrick said the best thing leaders can do is look where the technology can ultimately take over and then take the people doing those roles and train them to be better at the things that require more human intervention.

Curran said quality control requires testing models across different loan types and scenarios, and SitusAMC maintains a test bank of hundreds of previously reviewed loans, including purchases, refinances, adjustable-rate mortgages and loans with rate buydowns, and when a model changes the company runs its prompts against the test bank to check whether results remain consistent. These tests add costs that lenders may overlook, and Curran said companies should ask AI vendors how their systems were developed, whether subject matter experts helped establish the processes and whether ongoing regression testing is in place. Curran said you want the same answer every time, and the process of taking a non-deterministic process and making it deterministic takes a lot of time and effort.

Articles.Title: Human review remains paramount for AI mortgage underwriting

stories.Headline: Fifteen countries train in Abu Dhabi on AI weather services for farmers
stories.Summary:
National meteorological and agricultural authorities from 15 countries across Africa, Asia, the Middle East and Latin America gathered in Abu Dhabi from November 9 to 13, 2026, for a hands-on training program on using AI for agricultural weather services. The program was organized under the AIM for Scale initiative and convened by the International Affairs Office at the UAE Presidential Court. It was hosted at the Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence and the National Center of Meteorology, with support from the University of Chicago. The week-long program was designed to help national institutions independently evaluate, run and integrate AI weather models into pilot and operational workflows for smallholder farming decisions.

The training had two connected tracks that both aimed to leave each country delegation with a minimum viable product for an agricultural weather service. The weather track covered running and evaluating AI models, hands-on benchmarking and downscaling global forecasts to regional and local scales. The agriculture track focused on turning forecast variables and thresholds into practical farm-level recommendations delivered through extension services. Joint sessions let participants explore multi-hazard early warning systems, climate services co-production and long-term operational planning. The program expanded from a first training in 2025 with six countries, Bangladesh, Chile, Ethiopia, Kenya, Nigeria and the United Arab Emirates, and in 2026 it added representatives from Bolivia, Colombia, Indonesia, Pakistan, Peru, the Philippines, Rwanda, Senegal and Sierra Leone. Both cohorts included representatives from National Meteorological and Hydrological Services, Ministries of Agriculture and related organizations.

The World Meteorological Organization contributed technical advisory efforts under AIM for Scale, helping align the training with global meteorological standards, observation frameworks and sustainable national service delivery. The program's stated ambition is to build capacity across 30 countries by 2027, with the aim of helping national institutions deliver forecasts that support farmers' agricultural decisions and investments. According to the articles, combining AI forecasting tools with capacity development is meant to help countries build self-sustaining weather advisory services. Placing accurate, timely weather intelligence in farmers' hands is described as helping them make decisions on planting, irrigation and harvesting.

stories.Headline: Meta lifts 2026 AI infrastructure spending to as much as $145B
stories.Summary:
Meta Platforms narrowed its 2026 capital spending guidance to a range of $135 billion to $145 billion, with the bulk of the money aimed at artificial intelligence infrastructure, according to an update that arrived with the company's third-quarter 2026 earnings report on October 21, 2026. The new range tightens an earlier forecast of $130 billion to $145 billion, so the top end stayed put while the floor rose. The spending covers the full AI stack, which means data centers, chips, networking products, and the systems needed to train Meta's Llama AI models. Meta's capital expenditures in 2025 came in at approximately $72 billion, and the 2026 guidance puts the company on track to roughly double that figure in a single year.

The company says its AI work is already improving content recommendations, ad impressions, and revenue per ad, and the numbers in the report back that up. Third-quarter 2026 revenue reached $64.6 billion, a 26% increase from the same quarter a year earlier, and advertising accounted for $63.06 billion of that total. Ad impressions rose 10% year over year, while the average price per ad climbed 14%, and Meta's family of apps averaged 3.64 billion daily active users in the quarter. Free cash flow in the third quarter of 2026 came in at negative $2.12 billion, and Meta plans to introduce a new class of non-voting Class C stock while looking to raise up to $95 billion through equity offerings to fund its AI ambitions.

Mark Zuckerberg founded Facebook in his Harvard dorm room in 2004, and two decades later the company is pouring tens of billions into chips and server farms. Zuckerberg and his team increasingly view AI as the critical lever for refining ad tools and deepening engagement on platforms like Facebook and Instagram, according to the report. The non-voting stock structure lets Meta bring in fresh capital without weakening Zuckerberg's control over the company. The article does not say what happens next beyond the planned equity offerings and the stock class.

stories.Headline: Berkeley Haas faculty pilot Rubrica AI grading tool in spring semester
stories.Summary:
UC Berkeley's Haas School of Business will pilot a new AI grading program in the spring semester, according to The Daily Californian, as reported by EdSource. Fifteen faculty members at the business school will use a tool called Rubrica, which is designed to cut the time graduate student instructors spend grading by 40 to 60 percent. Tom Tripp, the executive director of Haas Digital, told the student newspaper that students' identifying information will be completely anonymous to the technology. Tripp also said instructors will have to review Rubrica's assessments, and the tool will flag any unclear results for professors to review and provide broader reports to professors.

The pilot raises questions about how much of the grading work will be handled by the tool and how much by people. Under the plan described by Tripp, the technology will not see who wrote the work, and a human instructor will make the final check on what the tool produces. Rubrica will also send unclear results to professors rather than deciding them on its own, and it will give professors wider reports on the work it assesses. The articles do not say what courses will be involved, how many students will be affected, or what the pilot will cost.

Responsibility for the pilot sits with the Haas School of Business and the fifteen faculty members who will use Rubrica, while Tripp of Haas Digital described the safeguards in an interview with the Daily Californian. Travis Fraser, an MBA student who developed Rubrica, told the paper he had felt he could not do the job as well as he wanted, and he said the technology offers more opportunity to be hands on with students while AI handles remedial and tedious tasks, with a human reviewing at the last step to verify the information. Some students were frustrated at the idea, including junior-transfer Amir Mojdeh, who told the paper he would feel frustrated that a robot would grade a subjective answer instead of someone knowledgeable about the subject. Others said AI grading would free up time to interact directly with students and provide better feedback.

The articles give no further details on how the pilot will be evaluated or what happens after the spring semester. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Chinese Academy of Sciences researchers create AI method to classify membrane protein structures in vesicles
stories.Summary:
Researchers at the Institute of Biophysics of the Chinese Academy of Sciences developed an AI-assisted method for determining three-dimensional structures of proteins in membranes. A team led by professor Zhang Xinzheng created this new system, which they named isSPA-vesicle, to improve structural classification. The group published their findings in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences on November 16, 2026. This technique allows scientists to analyze membrane proteins while they remain embedded in vesicles that mimic physiological conditions.

The isSPA-vesicle method requires an AI model to estimate membrane geometric parameters and calculate normal vectors based on fitted ellipsoidal surfaces. This process enables the filtering of particles by selecting those based on angular differences between their orientations and local membrane normal vectors. The researchers used this tool to reconstruct membrane proteins ranging from 130 kilodaltons to 2 megadaltons across three types of synthetic liposomes and two classes of enveloped viruses. They obtained a resolution of 2.7 Å for influenza A virus hemagglutinin and 3.1 Å for the prefusion spike protein of human coronavirus OC43. Additionally, the method achieved a reconstruction resolution of 3.1 Å on the AcrB validation data set.

Professor Zhang Xinzheng and the research team claim that isSPA-vesicle is a simple and efficient tool for high-resolution structural reconstruction in physiological lipid bilayers. They stated that the system can accurately determine particle positions and orientations even when membrane densities overlap. The researchers noted that their method efficiently removes membrane-unbound particles and lowers the minimum molecular weight of proteins that can be analyzed. They further explained that the performance of the tool is independent of the molecular weight of the soluble domains.

This new approach addresses the limited efficiency and resolution found in conventional single-particle analysis and subtomogram averaging. By using vesicles, the researchers can provide membrane curvature and establish ion gradients that are not possible with other methods. The AI-driven framework allows for the identification of a greater number of valid particles compared to workflows using Topaz or template matching. These advancements help scientists study proteins in their natural state without relying on detergents. More to follow.

Articles.Title: AI-assisted method advances high-resolution structure classification of membrane proteins in vesicles

stories.Headline: LeBron James sues PlayVision over AI betting app using his likeness and Bron name
stories.Summary:
LeBron James sued the makers of an AI sports-betting app on Tuesday, saying they deliberately violated his publicity rights and trademarks by calling it "Bron" and using artificially generated images of him in their marketing. The lawsuit was filed in U.S. District Court in New York, according to the Associated Press. James is a Philadelphia 76ers star and NBA superstar. The app's developer is PlayVision Inc., which is based in California. The app is called "Bron."

The complaint asks the court to block the makers from using James' name, to give up any money they've already made and to award damages, including fair market value for the use of his name as well as punitive damages. James' lawyers sent a cease-and-desist letter on Nov. 5, after which the startup removed the ad from its X and Instagram accounts. The company took the ad down, but not before it had been reposted and viewed about 1 million times, the lawsuit said. The ad attracted about one million views on X within a day, according to the lawsuit. The marketing campaign this month featured an image of a person resembling James, down to his tattoos, voice and No. 23 jersey, sitting in a locker room and scrolling through the app.

James' attorneys called it "a willful, bad-faith tactic" to use the player's fame, likeness and nickname to promote "a new and unknown product." The lawsuit states that "Defendants did not care that they had engaged in illegal conduct to gain notoriety for their previously unknown app." It says they "intentionally created the false impression that Mr. James endorsed and was affiliated with their Bron App, in an effort to drive downloads and paid subscriptions." Gupta responded to the attorneys' demand on social media by writing that the app would get a new name, but no new name had been adopted by the time the lawsuit was filed. Gupta wrote on social media this week that the new name will be announced Wednesday.

Messages sent by The Associated Press through the app's website and to email addresses for its founders seeking comment were not immediately returned Tuesday. The lawsuit notes that James typically commands tens of millions of dollars for such endorsement deals and that he already has an exclusive deal with the prediction market platform Polymarket. It alleges that the app's marketing was especially harmful in part because it showed the AI-generated James scrolling through bets involving NBA players. The lawsuit said "The integrity of NBA competition -- and the public's confidence that players are not betting on the games they play -- is of paramount importance to the league, its players, and its fans." It added that "Any suggestion that an active NBA player is betting on NBA games is therefore far from a trivial matter, and it should not be used for clicks and views."

The app's developer, PlayVision Inc., was launched by chief executive Anish Gupta and chief technology officer Marc Zoghby in 2025, with backing from the startup accelerator Y Combinator, as a program that would use artificial intelligence to analyze game and practice footage for sports teams and fans. This year, the company released its "Bron" app, which it says does not take direct wagers but charges a subscription fee for services such as bet tracking and odds comparisons. Bron is described in Apple's App Store as a "sports analytics and betting research app with live odds comparisons, data-backed picks, player and team trends, a multi-leg Slip and bet tracking." The listing says it does not accept wagers. PlayVision participated in Y Combinator's fall 2025 batch.

James is seeking damages and a court order preventing the defendants from using his name, image, likeness, and voice, as well as the Bron name. The lawsuit claims the founders calculated that the publicity would outweigh any potential legal consequences, effectively treating the alleged violation of James' rights as a marketing expense. It argues that James' endorsements are "uniquely valuable," adding, "That is why defendants decided to steal it for themselves." However, the ad remained available through third-party reposts, and the company had not changed the app's name as of the lawsuit's filing. Gupta wrote on social media this week that the new name will be announced Wednesday.
