stories.Headline: Leading Into 2027: From AI Ambition to Enterprise Value
stories.Summary:
Forvis Mazars published a piece on 23 November 2026 arguing that as organizations move AI beyond isolated pilots, the challenge is no longer simply where to use it, and that leaders must work out how to create meaningful value while managing risk, establishing accountability and enabling innovation. The firm said success looking toward 2027 will require treating AI as an evolving enterprise capability, with strategy, governance, data, implementation and assurance working together across the AI lifecycle, and it set out six actions for organizations to consider. The first is to start with value rather than technology, asking where AI can create meaningful business value and which use cases have the greatest potential, while aligning ambition with risk appetite. It said not every application carries the same potential value or risk, so a productivity tool and a system influencing consequential business decisions may need very different levels of oversight, and governance should reflect those differences. The goal, it said, is not to find more opportunities to use AI but to identify those that add the most value or have the greatest impact and to determine whether the organization is prepared to pursue them successfully.

On readiness, the firm said enterprise readiness covers people, processes and technology, and that AI literacy cannot reside only with data scientists or technology teams, because business leaders and employees need enough understanding to decide when to use AI, how to use it and when human judgment is required. It said accountability must be clear, with organizations determining who owns the AI program and how departments including technology, data, cybersecurity, risk, legal, compliance and internal audit participate, and that as AI changes processes and responsibilities organizations must work out which skills they have, which capabilities they need and how employees will be prepared to work alongside new technologies. It added that trust underlies all of this, since employees and leaders are less likely to embrace AI at scale if they do not understand how it works, where its information comes from, what its limitations are or whether its outputs can be relied upon. The question, it said, is not simply whether an organization can implement AI but whether it is prepared to operate it responsibly and effectively once it does.

On governance, the firm said effective AI governance gives organizations the structure to innovate while managing uncertainty and risk, but it should not stop with a policy or a set of responsible AI principles and has to work at an operational level. That means clear decision-making authority, policies and standards, processes for use-case intake and risk assessment, and visibility into where AI is used across the enterprise, and while an inventory of use cases is a starting point, organizations cannot govern AI they do not know exists. Risk classification can then set the level of governance for each use case, with higher-risk applications possibly requiring more testing, documentation, human oversight or approval than lower-risk productivity tools. The firm also warned that employees can access publicly available AI tools with relative ease, creating the potential for shadow AI, and that AI embedded in existing software and third-party products can make adoption less obvious, so third-party AI needs its own scrutiny of how providers handle data, how systems are hosted, what contractual protections exist and how vendor changes could affect the organization. Governance, it said, should create clarity about where decisions are made, who is accountable and how risks are escalated, and done well it should not prevent innovation but help the organization pursue it with greater confidence.

On data and technology, the firm said data quality, integrity, lineage, privacy and security are critical throughout the AI lifecycle, since poor-quality or incomplete data can affect outputs and weak governance can make it hard to understand where information came from, how it was used and whether it was appropriate for the intended purpose. It said data readiness should be a continuously evolving discipline, with organizations continuing to assess whether the data supporting AI remains appropriate, accurate, secure and representative as models evolve, new data becomes available and use cases expand. Data lineage also matters, it said, because organizations may need to understand where data originated, how it moved through systems, how it was transformed and where it ultimately influenced an AI output, while privacy and cybersecurity add considerations around sensitive information, access, data leakage and external providers. The technology architecture supporting AI must evolve alongside these requirements, the firm said, and organizations may face questions around scalability, interoperability, access and integration as individual experiments become embedded in enterprise workflows.

Articles.Title: Leading Into 2027: From AI Ambition to Enterprise Value

stories.Summary:
SK Group Chairman Chey Tae-won called for Korean and Japanese universities and businesses to jointly develop artificial intelligence talent, speaking at Tokyo Forum 2026 on Saturday. He said education systems and universities need a fundamental redesign for an AI-native society rather than minor curriculum changes. The two-day forum was co-hosted by the Chey Institute for Advanced Studies and the University of Tokyo and began Friday. Its theme was AI as a Transformative Technology: Humanity, Knowledge and Civilization. Chey joined NTT Group Chairman Jun Sawada, Taejae University President Yeom Jae-ho and Sophia University President Miki Sugimura in a discussion moderated by University of Tokyo President Teruo Fujii.

Chey said an AI-native society is not one that simply uses AI but one that accepts AI as an inherent part of its environment. He said new governance and systems are needed because society as a whole, including the current university system, must be designed differently. He called for AI-native universities with entirely new designs and governance structures, adding that minor changes to existing curricula would not be enough. He stressed the importance of collective intelligence, saying even unsuccessful attempts to design new systems could help young people develop problem-solving skills.

He cited SK's initiatives in talent development, employment support and data center workforce training, highlighting AIGEN, a two-year non-degree program launched last month that encourages participants to find solutions through team projects. Asked how companies and universities could cooperate on AI talent, Chey proposed a joint program involving Korean and Japanese institutions. He said there are many opportunities not only between countries but also between companies and universities. He said such a program could create internship and employment opportunities in both countries while nurturing social innovators capable of addressing societal challenges.

In a video welcoming address on Friday, he stressed developing talent capable of guiding change in the AI era. He said people need to ask themselves what problems they want to solve with AI, what new value they want to create and what kind of society they want to build, urging universities to move beyond teaching knowledge and focus on cultivating wisdom. The forum brought together global experts, including French government AI envoy Anne Bouverot and Sakana AI co-founder Ren Ito. The article was published on Nov 22, 2026, and updated the same day.

stories.Headline: Whistleblower alleges a candidate used a calculator to pass a North Chungcheong teacher appointment test
stories.Summary:
An anonymous individual identified as A recently reported that a candidate used a calculator during the Chungbuk teacher appointment test for the 2025 school year. This person claimed that the candidate managed to solve every question on the examination using the device and eventually passed the test. The incident allegedly occurred despite the presence of two supervisors who were tasked with monitoring the examinees in the classroom. Other candidates reportedly informed the supervisor about the calculator use during a break, but the official allegedly ignored the claim.

The situation requires a serious review of the supervision systems used for teacher appointment examinations to prevent future misconduct. This specific case involved the 2025 school year appointment test in North Chungcheong Province where a candidate allegedly cheated. The whistleblower A noted that the supervision was rough because only a few people take this particular test. There are growing concerns that the current management is insufficient to stop candidates from using prohibited electronic devices. This incident has sparked a wider debate about the integrity of professional examinations for educators.

The anonymous author A is responsible for bringing these allegations to light through an online community post on November 22. This person criticized the supervisors for neglecting their duties and claiming they did not see the calculator being used. According to A, the central supervision office stated that the candidate could not be caught because the test had already ended. The whistleblower expressed deep doubt that cheating will be properly prevented in the next appointment test cycle. This individual linked the failure of the supervisors to a general lack of rigor in the testing process.

The controversy comes at a time when the public is buzzing over the use of artificial intelligence glasses to cheat on the CSAT and other professional tests. Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin has reportedly been confused over the specific measures needed to prevent such high-tech cheating. The report suggests that if basic tools like calculators are not caught, more advanced AI technology will pose an even greater threat. There is currently no information regarding official disciplinary actions taken against the candidate or the supervisors involved. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Burger King Korea sells its AI-advertised Chocolate Whopper dessert burger in Seoul
stories.Summary:
Burger King launched the Chocolate Whopper in South Korea, a dessert burger made with brownies, chocolate, and cream cheese mousse, according to Merca 2.0. The product went on sale Thursday, November 19, exclusively at the Flame Ground location in Seongsu, Seoul, the article said. Burger King Korea introduced the item through an advertising campaign that used artificial intelligence, and after releasing AI-generated images and videos, the company published a follow-up announcement confirming the Chocolate Whopper was neither a joke nor a fictional product. Each burger is handmade, only a limited number are available each day, and customers can purchase just one. The Chocolate Whopper is a dessert-inspired take on Burger King's signature burger, designed to preserve its familiar appearance while replacing traditional ingredients with sweet treats.

Instead of beef, it features a chocolate brownie patty, traditional vegetables are replaced with gummies and chocolate pieces, and savory sauces give way to chocolate and raspberry sauces. According to Burger King Korea's official social media posts, the ingredients include chocolate fudge buns, chocolate sauce, dark chocolate shavings, strawberry gummies, milk jelly rings, crunchy chocolate discs, brownies, raspberry sauce, and cream cheese mousse. The Chocolate Whopper costs 9,800 South Korean won per burger, according to Burger King's launch information reported by South Korean media outlets, and each burger is made fresh and available daily starting at 11:00 a.m. while supplies last.

The brand also limits purchases to one per customer and requires the dessert to be consumed on-site, with takeout and delivery not available. In its follow-up announcement, the brand clarified that the product was neither an April Fools' joke nor an AI hallucination, but an actual item it planned to sell. The company released promotional content created with artificial intelligence, explicitly disclosing the use of the technology in its official Instagram posts, and Burger King Korea later confirmed that the Chocolate Whopper was real and would be available at one of its locations. As part of this marketing strategy, the company used technology commonly associated with generating synthetic images to promote a food product it later confirmed was real.

The campaign also illustrates how artificial intelligence can be incorporated into marketing communications, not necessarily to develop a product itself, but to shape its visual presentation and spark consumer curiosity. So far, Burger King has only announced the Chocolate Whopper's availability at Flame Ground Seongsu, its flagship location in South Korea. Burger King's Chocolate Whopper is an example of how a brand can use artificial intelligence to turn an advertising concept into a real consumer experience. What began as a burger that seemed to exist only in AI-generated images has become an actual product available to customers in South Korea.

stories.Headline: AI builds a $75 Thanksgiving menu for six in Houston that rings up at $64.31 at Kroger
stories.Summary:
KPRC 2 News reporter Joy Addison, working with photojournalist Michael Lemons, gave artificial intelligence a challenge to build a Thanksgiving shopping list for six people in Houston with a budget of just $75, and the station published the results on November 21, 2026. The menu had to include a turkey, traditional sides and dessert, and the suggested list included a whole turkey, mashed potatoes, stuffing, green bean casserole, corn, cranberry sauce, dinner rolls and pumpkin pie. AI estimated the cost at $61.75, including a $10 cushion for extra expenses, which would leave $13.25 for anything else the family might need. The station then took the list to Kroger and put together an online cart, and the subtotal came to $64.31, still under budget with $10.69 left to spare. The cart also showed a promotion offering $5 off when shoppers spend $36 on eligible items, but another $26.02 in qualifying products would need to be added to unlock the deal.

Shoppers told the station that grocery prices are hard to ignore, with one saying the prices are pretty much off the charts, and pointing to a McCormick chicken gravy packet that used to cost about $1.99 and was now priced at $3.27. That shopper still believed feeding six people Thanksgiving dinner for $75 is doable, saying the strategy is to look for sales, shop around and take advantage of grocery store specials, and added that using AI for a shopping list had never occurred to them before but might be something to look into. Emily Taylor was not as convinced about the $75 challenge, answering simply no when asked if she thought she could feed six people for that amount. Taylor said sharing the cost with family and friends can help make holiday meals more affordable, and recommended coupons and apps for the right grocery stores as always helpful.

The test showed that AI can help take some of the guesswork out of holiday shopping by giving a menu, organizing the grocery list and helping set a spending target, and the Kroger online cart came in at $64.31, just $2.56 more than AI's estimated spending of $61.75. The station noted that prices and availability can vary and that digital coupons often come with requirements, so shoppers still need to compare prices and make sure they are getting enough food for everyone at the table. With a little planning, some smart shopping and help from technology, keeping Thanksgiving dinner within budget may be more manageable than you think, according to the report. The bottom line, the station said, is that AI won't do the grocery shopping for you, but it might help you make a plan before you hit the aisles.

stories.Headline: Australia AI committee recommends right to control face, voice and likeness
stories.Summary:
Australia's Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence, chaired by Labor MP Jo Briskey with retiring Liberal senator Jonno Duniam as deputy chair, was due to report to parliament on Tuesday with a recommendation that Australians gain a Denmark-style right to control how their face, voice and likeness are used. The committee made that recommendation among 45 others, including weighing in on the controversy about how best to balance the rights of copyright holders with the desire of the Australian government to train artificial intelligence models onshore. In October Denmark proposed an amendment to copyright law, still before its parliament, to give individuals legal rights over their appearance, body and voice against unauthorized AI deepfakes and digital replicas. The proposal is also being pushed in the EU by left-wing parties.

The recommendation would give Australians a right over their face, voice and likeness modeled on the Danish amendment, which is still before Denmark's parliament and would give individuals legal rights over their appearance, body and voice against unauthorized AI deepfakes and digital replicas. The committee's report, due to parliament on Tuesday, makes that recommendation among 45 others and also weighs in on how best to balance the rights of copyright holders with the government's desire to train AI models onshore. Labor and the Coalition joined a bipartisan call for compensation of creatives while incentivizing AI to train onshore. The committee, chaired by Briskey with Duniam as deputy chair, has attempted to find common ground on how to attract AI investment.

Briskey, a Labor MP, chairs the committee and Duniam, a retiring Liberal senator, serves as deputy chair, and the committee has attempted to find common ground on how to attract AI investment. The committee makes the likeness recommendation among its 45 others in the report due to parliament on Tuesday. Labor and the Coalition joined the bipartisan call for compensation of creatives while incentivizing AI to train onshore. The articles do not say what Briskey or Duniam said about the recommendation.

The committee's report is due to parliament on Tuesday, and the articles do not say what happens next beyond that. The Danish amendment is still before Denmark's parliament, and the proposal is also being pushed in the EU by left-wing parties. The articles do not say whether the government has responded to the recommendations or when any of them might be adopted.

stories.Headline: Dubai government deploys over 90 AI applications across 20 entities and releases state of AI report
stories.Summary:
The government of Dubai activated more than 90 artificial intelligence applications across 20 different government entities on November 21, 2026. This large scale deployment represents a significant push to integrate advanced technology into the daily operations of the city's public administration. The initiative aims to modernize how the government functions by utilizing automated systems to handle various administrative tasks. These tools were rolled out simultaneously to ensure a consistent digital transformation across multiple sectors of the local government.

This technological shift requires the integration of smart software into the existing infrastructure of 20 separate government bodies to improve efficiency. The deployment involves the use of over 90 specific AI applications designed to streamline public services and internal government workflows. By implementing these tools, the city intends to change how citizens interact with state services through faster and more accurate digital processing. The state of AI report released alongside this announcement details the specific requirements and the current status of these digital implementations.

Officials from the Dubai government are responsible for this rollout and they stated that the move is part of a broader strategy for innovation. They explained that the goal is to enhance the overall quality of life for residents by making government services more accessible and responsive. The leadership emphasized that adopting these technologies is essential for maintaining the city's position as a global hub for future technology. They believe that the successful integration of these applications will set a new standard for governance in the region.

This deployment follows a series of agreements between the Dubai Immigration and Future Foundation to promote the growth of artificial intelligence and modern technology. The broader context involves a city wide effort to embrace digital transformation and improve the standard of living for all citizens. Future steps will likely involve expanding these AI capabilities to more departments as the government evaluates the performance of the initial 90 applications. The city continues to invest in innovative projects to ensure its infrastructure remains competitive on an international scale.

stories.Headline: Codelco and BHP deploy AI and satellite tools to cut water and energy use in Chilean copper mines
stories.Summary:
Chilean mining companies are integrating artificial intelligence and satellite technology to increase efficiency and protect nature. The state miner Codelco and the global firm BHP have deployed these tools to manage their operations more sustainably. These advancements come as the global demand for copper rises to support the growth of AI data centers. The shift toward smarter mining began with projects like the Lemu Nge satellite launched in August 2024.

The industry must adapt because copper makes up about 83 percent of the weight of materials used in AI infrastructure. S&P Global projects that global copper demand will climb from 28 million tonnes in 2025 to 42 million tonnes by 2040. AI infrastructure alone is expected to contribute nearly 2 million tonnes to this 50 percent increase. Codelco used the Lemu Nge satellite to track over 65 species in the Maitenes-Campiche Wetland and the Roblería del Cobre de Loncha National Reserve. Meanwhile, BHP used machine learning at its Spence and Escondida mines to save 1.1 million cubic meters of water and over 11 GWh of energy.

Carolina Pinilla, the Corporate Director of Environmental Management at Codelco, stated that AI provides a chance to improve environmental oversight in large mines. She noted that the technology helps the company make faster decisions and identify compliance risks before they become serious problems. At Universidad Andrés Bello, Vice-Rector for Digital Transformation Claudia Bascur explained that the Mina Virtual platform allows students to practice safety and operate machinery without real world risks. This immersive system uses an AI agent to monitor student behavior and enforce safety protocols in real time.

The global market could face a shortfall of 10 million metric tons of copper by 2040 if supply does not expand. This gap would represent about 25 percent of the projected demand for the metal. Chile is attempting to close this gap by combining its massive reserves with high tech operational precision. The country continues to deploy orbital technology and machine learning to meet the environmental standards required by global buyers.

stories.Headline: University of Plymouth researchers develop AI that flags bladder cancer risk up to five years early
stories.Summary:
Researchers at the University of Plymouth developed an AI tool that can uncover hidden warning signs of bladder cancer up to five years before diagnosis, identifying 85% of cases in a study involving nearly 70,000 patients. The work was led by Professor Shang-Ming Zhou at the University of Plymouth's Centre for Health Technology. PhD student Xu Wang led the data analysis. The study was published in IEEE Transactions on Biomedical Engineering. The research also involved collaborators from North Bristol NHS Trust and University Hospitals Bristol NHS Foundation Trust.

The team studied electronic medical records from nearly 70,000 patients, covering a 25-year period from 1995 through 2020. The researchers created an AI model called PRECISE-AGZ and used it to investigate 48,261 possible health indicators, from smoking and exercise habits to medication use. The system narrowed the list to 38 features especially useful for predicting bladder cancer risk. The model correctly identified 85% of patients who had bladder cancer and accurately classified 91% of those who did not. The system demonstrated effective detection as early as 12 months before a patient's official diagnosis, and some warning signals could be traced back up to five years.

The AI confirmed the importance of established risk factors including smoking and blood in the urine. It also uncovered unexpected associations, with patients diagnosed with Parkinson's disease or dementia appearing to have a lower risk of bladder cancer, and long-term use of tamoxifen, a breast cancer medication, associated with a higher risk. The findings do not establish that Parkinson's disease or dementia protects against bladder cancer, or that tamoxifen causes it, but raise questions about possible shared biological mechanisms. Among men with benign prostate enlargement, blood in the urine was associated with a lower bladder cancer risk. The system could divide patients into three groups: low-risk below 7% probability, uncertain grey zone of 7-55%, and high-risk above 55%.

Wang said bladder cancer ranks as the ninth most common cancer worldwide, with 614,000 new cases diagnosed in 2022. Wang said no routine screening program exists for the general population, and detection following symptoms relies heavily on invasive cystoscopy procedures. Dr. Helen Winter, Clinical Director for the Somerset, Wiltshire, Avon and Gloucestershire (SWAG) Cancer Alliance, said bladder cancer has a major unmet need in early detection and the prospect of a screening tool is hugely exciting for patients and their families. Winter said it could identify those most at risk more accurately, reduce harm from invasive procedures, and catch cancer earlier. Zhou said the work represents a paradigm shift towards precision screening for bladder cancer.

Bladder cancer kills approximately 220,000 people worldwide each year, and its symptoms can resemble those of far less serious conditions including kidney stones. Under current medical referral guidelines, one of the main warning signs is visible blood in the urine, which can also result from noncancerous problems including kidney stones and prostate conditions. Confirming bladder cancer currently requires cystoscopy, in which a long, thin tube with a small camera inside is moved up the urethra and into the bladder. The examination is invasive, highlighting the need for better ways to identify patients most likely to have the disease. The model performed better at detecting bladder cancer than existing NHS referral guidelines.

The researchers caution that the technology is not yet ready for widespread clinical use. All the patient information used in the study came from the SAIL database in Wales. Zhou said further validation across different healthcare systems is essential before anything is rolled out more widely, and the team would want to investigate other datasets too. Zhou said additional studies would be needed to confirm the causal relationships suggested by the model's predictions. Zhou called it a very exciting early study.

stories.Headline: Applied behavior analysis evolves from Skinner's operant work to debates on compassion and AI
stories.Summary:
Applied behavior analysis began in B. F. Skinner’s laboratory with his 1938 book The Behavior of Organisms, which defined the operant as a basic unit of behavior. Skinner extended that work to people in the 1950s, according to a 2025 National Academies report on autism care for military families. Donald Baer, Montrose Wolf, and Todd Risley published “Some Current Dimensions of Applied Behavior Analysis” in the first issue of the Journal of Applied Behavior Analysis in 1968. In a 1964 case study, Wolf, Risley, and Hortense Mees described treating a young boy, referred to as an autistic child, for tantrums, refusal to wear his glasses, and mealtime problems. Ivar Lovaas at UCLA reported in a 1987 paper in the Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology that 47% of 19 children who received more than 40 hours of one-to-one treatment a week reached normal intellectual and educational functioning, compared with 2% of control children.

The 1968 paper set out seven dimensions: applied, behavioral, analytic, technological, conceptually systematic, effective, and generality. The National Academies report says those dimensions “have guided the field for most of its history.” The 1964 case study’s methods included “mild punishment and extinction,” time-out, and reinforcement. The National Academies calls Lovaas’s program “the catalyst” for the early intensive behavioral intervention models in use today, while noting that “valid concerns arise” about parts of his approach. The Behavior Analyst Certification Board was established as a nonprofit in 1998 to set credentialing standards, and its current Ethics Code for Behavior Analysts has been in force since January 2022.

The code lists “Treat Others with Compassion, Dignity, and Respect” as one of four core principles, and Standard 2.11 makes behavior analysts “responsible for obtaining assent from clients when applicable.” The code defines assent as vocal or nonvocal verbal behavior indicating willingness to participate from people who cannot give informed consent. Justin Leaf and colleagues, in the Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders, evaluated objections from autism rights and neurodiversity advocates, including the Lovaas project’s use of shock, default 40-hour intensity, punishment and extinction procedures, responses to stimming, and claims that ABA is abusive or causes PTSD. They recommended setting intensity individually, including clients and caregivers in choosing goals, measuring social validity and quality of life, and studying long-term and undesired outcomes. “Our field is not infallible, and we should continue to improve and progress our interventions,” the authors wrote.

A 2024 National Academies workshop summary says early practice relied heavily on physical punishment, which drew criticism from autistic self-advocates, and that modern ABA has dropped physical punishment. In late 2023, Ashley Penney and colleagues proposed in Behavior Analysis in Practice that compassion be treated as “an eighth current and essential dimension of ABA,” a proposal that remains the authors’ and not a change to the original framework. In a 2020 proof-of-concept study in Perspectives on Behavior Science, Marc Lanovaz and colleagues trained machine-learning models on simulated single-case graphs, and the models produced fewer false positives and more statistical power than the dual-criteria method, a structured aid for visual analysis. A 2024 systematic review abstract in BJPsych Open compared 25 studies of virtual reality and standard social skills training for autistic children and found no consistently significant differences between the two. The Council of Autism Service Providers has published practice parameters for AI use in ABA covering selection, transparency, consent, monitoring, error reporting, and retirement of AI systems.

The data in the Lanovaz study were simulated, not drawn from clinic records. A review of the AI practice parameters notes that clinicians remain responsible for clinical decisions under BACB codes and that providers should not assume payers will allow or reimburse AI-assisted services. The articles give a timeline: 1938, Skinner publishes The Behavior of Organisms; 1964, the Wolf, Risley, and Mees case study; 1968, Baer, Wolf, and Risley define the seven dimensions; 1987, Lovaas reports his outcome; 1998, the BACB is established; 2022, the BACB Ethics Code takes effect; 2023, Penney and colleagues propose compassion as an eighth dimension. The articles state that nearly 90 years after Skinner’s book the field debates topics such as compassion and artificial intelligence. The articles state that how the field got from one to the other explains much of what payers, providers, and families debate today.

The articles state that any new tool, like any old procedure, has to show it produces socially significant change for the person receiving services. The articles leave open whether payers will allow or reimburse AI-assisted services. The articles leave open whether compassion becomes an eighth dimension of ABA. The articles leave open what further study of long-term and undesired outcomes will show. The articles leave open how the debate over who gets to define socially important change will resolve.

stories.Headline: Times A.I. editor Dylan Freedman drafts his writing on a 1950s typewriter while using A.I. only for reporting
stories.Summary:
Dylan Freedman, the A.I. projects editor for The New York Times, wrote in a Times Insider article published on November 22, 2026, that he uses artificial intelligence in his work every day but never uses it for writing. His job has two parts, enlisting A.I. to help reporters search large collections of documents and multimedia data, such as the Jeffrey Epstein files or President Trump’s speeches, and reporting on developments in A.I. technology. Because he draws a thick line at writing, he composes most of his first drafts on an Olivetti Lettera 22 typewriter from the 1950s, the same model Leonard Cohen used to compose songs and poems. He composed the first draft of the article itself on that typewriter.

Freedman, who was a software engineer at Google before pursuing a journalism degree, described the typewriter as an essential dose of minimalism and a break from crowded browser tabs and blinking terminal windows. He called the machine a technological marvel for translating thoughts into words, noting that it can be used outside without glare and does not need to be recharged. A single ribbon lasts longer than most novels and is cheaper than printer ink, and most mechanical typewriters, made from solid steel, are practically indestructible. The typewriter has few comforts but also no distractions, and using one feels intentional, like taking photographs on a film camera.

Freedman said that typing on the metal machine gives him a rawness that better captures his voice, and that you cannot easily undo, nor should you. He wrote that A.I. is rapidly becoming superhuman at tasks with clear solutions, like coding and math, and that the more he uses A.I., the more he worries about surrendering his cognition. He cited a study published in Nature this year which found that researchers who used A.I. assistance tended to be more productive than their peers but also studied fewer new topics. The article presented these views as his own reasoning and experience rather than as findings about typewriters or writing in general.

The article appeared in Times Insider, a section that explains who The Times is, what it does, and delivers behind-the-scenes insights into how its journalism comes together. Freedman stated in the piece that he uses A.I. heavily for reporting tasks while keeping it out of his writing process, and he offered the typewriter as the tool he relies on for first drafts. The available text of the article does not say what, if anything, follows from his approach for The Times or for other journalists. It also does not describe any further plans, policies or responses connected to the piece.

stories.Headline: A language model writes an ACM column arguing both sides of AI existential risk in one attempt
stories.Summary:
The Communications of the ACM published an opinion column titled “AI and Existential Risk: For Real?” on 23 November 2026, the magazine states. The column was written in February 2026, nearly a year before its publication date, its note says. The text was generated verbatim by a contemporary large language model on the first attempt, without any human post-editing, a human postscript states. The authors say their prompt, reproduced in full in the text, fixed none of the arguments, which the model produced entirely. The note cites the OpenAI, HuggingFace incident and related cases of AI committing spontaneous crimes as recent events.

The prompt asked for an opinion article in three parts, the column states. Part one was a strong case that AI does not constitute an existential risk, of about 400 words, with a fitting quote by a widely known AI researcher. Part two was an intermezzo of about 50 to 80 words with a psychological twist. Part three was a strong case that AI does constitute an existential risk, of about 500 words, directly refuting part one, with a fitting quote by another widely known AI researcher. The prompt asked that the final argument be that humanity gets only one shot at figuring it all out.

The authors say they chose to present the text without disclosure upfront, and that the intent was not to deceive for its own sake. They say the point was to make a simple point visceral rather than abstract. They say the answer to the question of existential risk from AI is far from obvious. They say the same system was able to generate both lines of argument fluently, instantly and in one attempt. They say the question is not only what AI can do to us, but what it can make us believe.

The first half quotes computer scientist Yann LeCun, who said, “You’re going to have to pardon my French, but that’s complete B.S.” The second half quotes computer scientist Geoffrey Hinton, who warned that AI may be used to create “terrible new viruses” and “lethal weapons that decide by themselves who to kill.” The authors say they would not board a plane with a single-digit chance of crashing. They say it would be nice if humanity were not mandatory, unbelted passengers on the plane that is preparing to take off. They say we may be closer to losing control of the steering wheel than we think.

The column says the first half was written by ChatGPT, which it calls an early AI with rather limited capabilities. It includes the sentence: If a weak AI managed to convince you that you shouldn’t worry about AI, maybe you should worry about AI. The authors say there was no superintelligence involved in generating either of the viewpoints. They ask the reader to imagine how convincing the arguments will be once there is. They say AI may give us only one attempt to grab the steering wheel.

The note says the column may already feel anachronistic when read, given the speed of developments in AI in general and recent events in particular. It says extrapolating this anachronism into the future will only reinforce the message. It says many of us are calibrated from times when the timescales for becoming anachronistic were measured in years, often decades. It says the timescale is now down to months. The column ends by asking: Can we do better?

stories.Headline: Threat actors use ARTEX AI framework to automate cyberattacks
stories.Summary:
Nation-state actors and financially motivated threat actors have used an open-source Chinese AI harness called ARTEX to execute cyber attacks. This software was originally developed for penetration-testing purposes but has since been adopted by attackers to automate offensive security tasks. The tool allows these actors to carry out multiple stages of an attack with very little hands-on involvement from a human operator. It represents a growing trend where artificial intelligence makes the exploitation of known vulnerabilities much easier and more efficient.

The ARTEX framework is written in the Go programming language and uses large language models to act as agents. These agents can build a graph of discovered assets and vulnerabilities to determine which targets to investigate next. The system can respond to new information and adjust its approach, such as establishing outside email accounts to bypass CAPTCHA challenges. Microsoft Threat Intelligence researchers described an attack chain that searched GitHub for secrets and extracted data from an Azure Key Vault in about five minutes.

Microsoft researchers are responsible for documenting these capabilities and the speed of the AI-enabled attack chain. They noted that while the underlying attack techniques are not necessarily new, the barrier to carrying out certain attacks is getting lower. The researchers indicated that tasks requiring significant technical knowledge and manual effort can now be completed much faster. They suggested that security teams may have less time to identify and contain intrusions because AI automates different stages of the process.

The broader context involves a sharp rise in cybersecurity incidents, as illustrated by data from the insurance broker Marsh. Marsh reported that client incidents grew from 48 in the last two weeks of May to 105 in the last two weeks of October. To defend against these risks, organizations are encouraged to enforce multi-factor authentication and monitor for unusual Microsoft Graph activity. They should also maintain inventories of approved third-party applications and apply least-privilege access to limit potential damage.

stories.Headline: Market volatility and political headwinds signal a cooling of AI investment
stories.Summary:
Investors in the artificial intelligence business experienced deep anxiety and panic during November 2026. Stocks soared last Thursday after Anthropic went public, but investors began selling by late morning. The market dropped more than 2 percent by the end of that Thursday. Stocks sold off even more sharply on Friday. This left the tech-heavy Nasdaq in negative territory for the year.

Anthropic raised more money in its IPO than any company in history. Nvidia reported that its sales and profits doubled year-over-year and expects 75 percent growth next year. The industry has a backlog of 2.5 trillion dollars in future orders. Nvidia invested 30 billion dollars in OpenAI earlier this year. Anthropic is on track to earn over 80 billion dollars in revenue next year.

Jensen Huang was forced to step down as Nvidia CEO after revelations of multiple affairs. One affair was with a possible Chinese intelligence asset, which created turmoil at the company. President Trump advocated for Huang, and the company reinstated him on Monday morning. Investors bid up Nvidia and other tech stocks following this news. This volatility underscores the current instability of the market.

Democrats won a massive victory in the midterms on a platform of slowing AI data center construction. This approach resonated with voters according to exit polls and creates political headwinds. Many CEOs find the benefits of paying for latest frontier models remain uncertain. Torsten Slok of Apollo Global Management found AI spending is concentrated in a few firms. Slok found no sign that AI boosted productivity growth outside big tech firms.

Investors poured money into AI since OpenAI released ChatGPT in 2022 assuming it would become profitable. Google and Meta spent hundreds of billions of dollars to build out their AI capabilities. AI revenues must exceed 3.5 trillion dollars annually by 2032 for a 10 percent return. Anthropic is projected to spend at least 450 billion dollars in capital expenditures over four years. Goldman Sachs estimated Anthropic will not generate free cash flow until 2030.

AI companies must now convince the rest of the economy to spend massively on their products. The market is signaling that the cash spigot will not be open forever for these firms. Companies may need to slow down if they cannot monetize their data centers and computing power. The articles leave open whether AI will radically reinvent industries like pharmaceuticals. It remains uncertain if the transformation will be a marathon rather than a sprint.

stories.Headline: UAE and Germany guides advise businesses to record human contributions as AI output grows
stories.Summary:
The article reports that businesses across the Emirates now use generative models to produce software, logos, product designs and technical inventions at scale, and that the commercial value of that output depends on whether the law will protect it. Global Advisory Experts published the guide on November 22, 2026, with a last update of October 2026. The guide states that UAE intellectual property legislation was drafted with human creators and inventors in mind, yet a growing share of commercial output is made with, or largely by, software. It sets out what is protected today, where the position is uncertain, how the Ministry of Economy and enforcement bodies are adapting, and what business owners and their advisors should do now. The guide covers the United Arab Emirates only and draws on the UAE statutory framework, Ministry of Economy practice and the international policy work of WIPO.

The guide states that the UAE has not passed one dedicated statute resolving every question, and that existing federal legislation applies while examiner practice adapts step by step. It names Federal Law No. 38 of 2021 on Copyright and Neighbouring Rights, Federal Law No. 11 of 2021 on the Regulation and Protection of Industrial Property Rights, which covers patents and designs, and Federal Law No. 36 of 2021 on Trademarks, all administered through the Ministry of Economy. It says examiners in 2026 apply human authorship for copyright, human inventorship and inventive step for patents, and distinctiveness for trademarks, rather than a special AI rulebook. It states that copyright exists without registration but that the Ministry of Economy runs a voluntary registration system, and that assignment must be in writing as UAE law requires. It advises using priority mechanisms and Patent Cooperation Treaty routes to secure an early filing date while record and claims are refined.

The guide states that UAE patent practice expects a human inventor, that naming an AI system as sole inventor is not supported, and that the applicant must derive rights from a human inventor through employment or assignment. It recommends Pathway A, the cautious route for most filings, naming as inventors the people who framed the problem, set the model's objective, selected and curated data, interpreted results and recognised the inventive outcome. It describes Pathway B as a defensive measure for cases where AI's contribution is truly dominant, building an evidence record of every human decision and preparing a reasoned case on the human contribution to conception. It advises stating the human-defined technical problem and solution clearly in the specification and including worked examples and detail on model configuration, inputs and validation to support enablement. It advises recording contributions as they happen through lab notebooks, code commits, model version logs and decision memos.

The guide states that the most noticeable change in enforcement is operational rather than legislative, with rights holders increasingly using automated tools to detect infringement online and at the border. It says the legal framework for customs seizure and anti-counterfeit action is unchanged, but that authorities and tribunals want provenance and chain of custody, not just screenshots. It states that WIPO's dedicated AI and IP resources track the international policy debate, which is likely to shape UAE practice as cross-border norms settle. It advises asking vendors to warrant that training data and outputs are lawful and to indemnify against third-party infringement claims, and warns that some AI tools reserve rights or give only a limited licence in the output. It states that models trained on huge public datasets may propose solutions overlapping with prior art the applicant has never seen, and that thin or black-box disclosure is a common point of failure.

The guide states that copyright is where AI and intellectual property UAE issues arise first, because generative tools produce text, images, music and code constantly and cheaply. It states that the copyright regime is built around an author, meaning a creator whose intellectual effort shows in the work, and that content generated with no meaningful human creative input is on uncertain ground. It states that where a person conceives, selects, arranges, edits and curates using AI as an advanced tool, the finished work has a strong claim to protection as human-authored, while output from a thin prompt is much less certain. It advises keeping drafts, edits, selection decisions and prompt histories that show the human hand, and treating unedited output with caution as legally fragile until rights are secured by other means. It states that trademark law cares about what a sign does in the market, not who or what created it, and that models often produce marks that are descriptive, generic or close to existing marks.

The guide states that the businesses in the strongest position are those that settled ownership in writing before they deployed the tools, and that every contributor, including employees, contractors, designers and AI vendors, should assign all IP in the deliverables in writing. It advises clearing a mark before adopting it, obtaining a written assignment where a designer, agency or AI vendor was involved, and not assuming that output belongs to whoever ran the tool. It states as a practice note that records showing a mark's originality and development history should be kept to answer any challenge that it is derivative or non-distinctive. It states that the filing strategies, sample clauses and enforcement checklists reflect general patent, trademark and copyright prosecution and enforcement practice in the UAE and the wider GCC, and that points reflecting a practitioner's interpretation rather than a published rule are flagged as practice notes. It states that law numbers and article references can be confirmed through the WIPO Lex national profile for the UAE, and that where the Ministry of Economy publishes filing procedures and guidance, those documents govern how applications are handled in practice.

stories.Headline: Rhombus Power allegedly misleads military commands about its predictive AI capabilities
stories.Summary:
A defense contractor called Rhombus Power allegedly misled military commands about its predictive intelligence capabilities. The company used high-level relationships to gain access across the Pentagon during an artificial intelligence boom. Reporting shows that users of the technology reached very different conclusions about its actual value. The company claimed its product could forecast the military actions of various foreign countries. These claims were used to market the product to several different government customers.

The company marketed the ability to predict North Korean missile launches to South Koreans and U.S. Forces in Korea. It claimed it could predict Chinese military aggression on the India-China border for Indo-Pacific customers. Rhombus Power also claimed it predicted the 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine to the Ukrainian defense minister. The product allegedly used massive data streams from the open internet to anticipate military actions. These data streams included social media, weather, and ship movements.

Kyle Rempfer reported that the company used sleek demos to show percentage chances of incidents. He stated that internal Air Force assessments from Air Mobility Command found the tool had some utility. Rempfer noted that the product did not fulfill the predictive capability that was being marketed. He said the tool did not add to the situational awareness of intelligence analysts. Some combatant commands told the company that it did not deliver as advertised.

Douglas Woodall, the former vice president of warfighting, filed a lawsuit against the company. He alleged that he was terminated in November 2025 after raising internal complaints. Woodall claimed the company falsely inflated its predictive capabilities by using classified information. He alleged that staff used a Special Operations Command contract to access unrelated classified data. This information was allegedly used to check predictions against higher level intelligence findings.

The company used advisors from a strategic consultancy called WestExec to open doors at commands. WestExec was founded by Michelle Flournoy and Anthony Blinken, who joined the Biden administration in 2020. Former commander Vincent Brooks introduced the CEO to two commanders of U.S. Forces Korea. These advisors provided personality details and priorities of commands to help the company sell. The title of advisor allegedly helped the company avoid the stigma of lobbying.

The lawsuit regarding the alleged use of classified information is currently proceeding through the court system. The articles do not state if the company has officially responded to the lawsuit. It remains unclear if other government agencies have conducted similar assessments to the Air Force. The articles do not specify the current status of the Special Operations Command contract. No final determination is given on whether the company committed fraud.

stories.Headline: Hackers use ARTEX AI framework to automate global attacks on government and corporate sectors
stories.Summary:
Chinese hackers and financially motivated attackers have used an open source AI hacking framework called ARTEX to target companies globally. The FBI issued a warning earlier this month stating that these actors have targeted the semiconductor, defense, financial services, legal, telecommunications, healthcare, and government sectors. This tool allows users to connect a preferred large language model from providers like DeepSeek or Anthropic to create multiple agents for different hacking tasks. These agents automate the entire process from reconnaissance to data theft at machine speed, which the FBI says can complete a hack in just a few hours.

The framework is written in Go and requires the user to connect an AI model to automate manual penetration testing steps. The original author, who uses the name Autumn-27, removed the tool from GitHub in October to move it to a closed-source model. However, other individuals such as Jiwoo Jung and a person using the handle Racem continue to host and distribute versions of the code. Jung noted that a user requested the tool be taken down on November 3 after their service was attacked, but he refused based on authorized-use terms.

The creator Autumn-27 stated that the malicious use of the tool runs entirely counter to their original intent and denied any association with the attacks. Racem acknowledged that the harm described by the FBI is real and that unauthorized system entry is a crime, but argued that the responsibility belongs to the operator rather than the tool. Jung added that he encourages security teams to check for indicators of compromise and has provided an email for those attacked. Racem claimed that hosting the tool helps small teams and researchers test their own infrastructure for the cost of API calls.

The FBI and Google's threat intelligence arm have noted that hackers are also using similar multi-agent frameworks including PentAGI, CyberStrikeAI, and CAIRN. Jung explained that agentic tooling has changed the skill level required to hack by compressing tasks that once took days into a few hours. Because the code has been cloned and distributed widely, those hosting the tool believe that deleting repositories will not remove the capability from the internet. Defenders are now encouraged to develop detection signatures to combat the speed of these AI-driven attacks.

stories.Headline: ExperienceFlow launches DATS and signs $500 million MoU with FPT to make Fortune 500 firms Super Intelligence-native
stories.Summary:
ExperienceFlow said on 23 November 2026 that it had launched the Domain AI Transformation Solution, known as DATS, a domain modeling platform that it said turns consulting firms, system integrators and business process outsourcers into Super Intelligence-based domain experts, according to the press release the company issued through PR Newswire. The release said ExperienceFlow also named FPT Software its first DATS Super Intelligence Diamond partner, and that the two companies had signed a $500 million Partnership MoU to transform Fortune 500 enterprises into Super Intelligence-native businesses. According to the release, Alwyn Joseph, ExperienceFlow's new Chief Domain Transformation Officer, signed the MoU with Phuong Dang, Senior Executive Vice President of FPT Software. The release said DATS lets partners fine-tune the Super Intelligence models in ExperienceFlow's Enterprise Digital Nervous System with their proprietary domain expertise, and that the resulting models stay on premises, keep improving and multiply capacity.

According to the release, ExperienceFlow is launching the ExperienceFlow Industry Super Intelligence Transformation Diamond Partnership for a select group of consulting, systems integrator and BPO firms, and a DATS Center of Excellence that turns domain knowledge into products the partners own. The release said the package includes a growth engine for the practice, productization of the partner's own vertical solution, private hardware infrastructure covering the DATS and EDNS platform, compute and ExperienceFlow experts on client pilots, pre-built vertical solutions, full go-to-market support and domain and technology experts working alongside partner teams. The release said DATS is available now to qualified consulting, systems integrator and BPO partners. Under the MoU, the release said, FPT and ExperienceFlow will jointly build industry specific Super Intelligence models for Fortune 500 enterprises, combining FPT's domain expertise and delivery scale with ExperienceFlow's platform.

Giri Athuluru, CEO and co-founder of ExperienceFlow AI, said in the release that the company holds a fundamentally different belief from the GenAI companies trying to eliminate software, consulting, systems integration and BPO companies, and that domain expertise is irreplaceable. He said DATS is the first platform that lets those partners accelerate the differentiation of their expertise, keep it on their own premises and use it to make their clients Super Intelligence-native. Phuong Tran, Senior Executive Vice President of FPT Software, said AI will not replace the services industry but will divide it, and that the firms that lead will be the ones that change how their clients' businesses run. Tran said FPT brings three decades of domain expertise and enterprise transformation experience to build industry-specific solutions on ExperienceFlow's platform, and that across banking and financial services, insurance, supply chain and high technology the companies intend to show the world's largest enterprises what that looks like in practice. Joseph said the firms that know industries best should lead the transformation, and that DATS gives partners AI models built from their own expertise, which they own and continually improve.

The release said Joseph leads ExperienceFlow's DATS business and owns its profit and loss, with responsibility for building, commercializing and scaling the company's domain and vertical solutions and its strategic domain partnerships. It said he has spent more than two decades building and scaling technology businesses, including as President and COO, Deputy CEO, Chief Revenue Officer and board member at public and private companies, and that he was most recently President and COO of Sasken Technologies. The release described ExperienceFlow as building decentralized Super Intelligence that enterprises own and continually improve, grounded in reinforcement learning and continual learning. It described FPT Corporation as a global technology and IT services provider headquartered in Vietnam with operations in more than 30 countries and territories, and said FPT reported total revenue of USD 2.66 billion in 2025 with a workforce of over 54,000 employees across its core businesses.

stories.Headline: Bethany Care Society and Lumenix deploy anonymous sensor platform across 420-suite Calgary care home
stories.Summary:
Bethany Care Society and Lumenix announced on Nov. 23, 2026, a partnership to deploy Lumenix's AIMS platform as the intelligent care infrastructure at Bethany's modernized Bethany Calgary care home, which is under construction and slated for completion in 2027. The site is a 420-suite continuing care home in Calgary's Hounsfield Heights, Briar Hill neighbourhood, built as a small-home model in which 420 private suites with ensuites are grouped into intimate 14-bedroom homes with shared kitchens and living spaces. AIMS, which stands for Artificially Intelligent Monitoring System, will serve as the community's critical operating system and will be embedded throughout the environment. Bethany is described in the announcement as one of Western Canada's largest not-for-profit providers of continuing care and seniors' housing, and Lumenix as a Canadian robotics, digital lighting, data and ambient intelligence company.

The platform replaces several standalone technologies for nurse call, fall prevention and detection, infection control, wandering detection and virtual rounding with a single unified system that can take on more functions as care needs change. AIMS is a privacy-first ambient perception-action platform that uses ceiling-mounted 3D infrared sensors and on-site edge computing to keep continuous, anonymous awareness of a space, detecting risks and prompting a response before a call button is pressed, all without cameras and without capturing personally identifiable images or information. The announcement says AIMS was clinically validated by the Government of Canada and is deployed across leading hospitals in Ontario and Quebec, and that the Bethany partnership extends the platform into Western Canada and the continuing care sector. Under the collaboration, the two organizations will co-develop the operating model for Bethany Calgary, co-create new solutions to longstanding challenges in continuing care delivery, and share what they learn with partners and the sector.

Jennifer McCue, President and Chief Executive Officer of Bethany Care Society, said leading the transformation of how Albertans age well means giving teams every advantage to deliver the best possible care. She said AIMS will become a critical member of the Bethany care team, proactively helping teams recognize risks and care quality issues and respond quickly, so employees can focus on residents and their care. Scott Delaney, Founding Chairman and CEO of Lumenix, said that as Canada's population ages there is a responsibility to better support both the people receiving care and the people who provide it. He said the company's anonymous perception and proactive context-setting technology is already helping Canadian hospitals improve care and support clinical staff, and that Lumenix is honoured to partner with Bethany to bring the approach to continuing and long-term care.

The announcement frames the partnership against Alberta's aging population, noting that one in seven Albertans is over the age of 65 and that this is projected to reach one in five by 2051, increasing demand for seniors' housing and continuing care. For staff, it says, AIMS reduces cognitive load, shortens emergency response times and delivers a continuous, system-wide picture of resident wellbeing, while for residents and families it adds protection and dignity through proactive risk detection and faster response while protecting privacy. The partnership is described as a long-term strategic collaboration focused on advancing the future of continuing care, with the two organizations saying they will deliver tools and care models never before possible. The articles do not say what further steps or timelines follow beyond the 2027 completion of the Bethany Calgary site.

stories.Headline: Nvidia halts chip shipments to China as investors shift focus to AI infrastructure stocks
stories.Summary:
Nvidia halted the shipment of its computer chips to China on November 22, 2026. This action has caused investors to focus more closely on stocks related to artificial intelligence infrastructure. The move comes at a time when technology flows between the United States and China are being questioned. Market participants are now analyzing how this shift in hardware availability will reshape capital flows. The situation requires a closer look at companies that provide the hardware spine for generative artificial intelligence.

This includes designers of processors and accelerators for data centers, as well as builders of server and rack platforms. It also involves the production of memory and interconnect chips that underpin cloud computing. These components are essential for the training and inference of large language models in industrial computing. Sasha Jovanovic reported that this mix of macro and artificial intelligence headlines could meaningfully help or hurt certain large cap stocks.

The author noted that artificial intelligence is no longer just a buzzword used during earnings calls. Instead, it now sits at the crossroads of central bank decisions and new corporate listings. This environment is creating new opportunities for those seeking alternatives before market momentum flies past. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Analyst Jim Handy warns Samsung and SK hynix face a memory price collapse if AI spending slows
stories.Summary:
Jim Handy, founder and general director of Objective Analysis, warned in an interview with The Korea Times that Samsung Electronics and SK hynix could face a sharp memory price decline if hyperscalers reduce their AI spending. He said memory prices could eventually return to 2024 levels as demand weakens. The warning came as shares of Samsung Electronics and SK hynix fell about 33 percent and 34 percent, respectively, over the past three months until Friday. Handy said a downturn could push chipmakers' gross margins from above 80 percent to near zero within roughly two quarters.

Google, Meta, Amazon and OpenAI are spending roughly 40 percent of their revenue on capital expenditures, including AI computing infrastructure, according to Handy. He said such spending is sustainable only if AI demand keeps growing fast enough to justify the investment. Samsung Electronics posted the world's highest quarterly operating profit in the third quarter, helped by higher orders for high-bandwidth memory and other high-end chips as AI server demand increased. Handy said production levels are limited by demand projections made two years earlier, which he said were lower than subsequent demand.

Handy said he does not think AI demand is growing that quickly, so the hyperscalers are likely to slow their spending at some point, and that will cause memory prices to collapse. He said the growth is temporary and prices will fall back to where they were in 2024. Many Korean analysts have focused on rising production levels as the main threat to prices, but Handy argued the more serious risk could come from the demand side if AI investment fails to maintain its current pace. For Samsung and SK hynix, he said, the key risk is no longer simply whether they can keep up with AI-driven demand, but whether that demand will remain strong enough to absorb the enormous amount of capacity and investment being built around it.

stories.Headline: Google cuts 2027 Broadcom TPU shipments by about 1M units and plans more MediaTek chips, Kuo says
stories.Summary:
Google reduced its planned 2027 shipments of Broadcom-designed AI chips while preparing to increase shipments of a MediaTek-designed alternative, according to technology supply-chain analyst Ming-Chi Kuo. Kuo, an analyst at TF International Securities, based the report on an industry survey rather than an official Google announcement. In a recent post, Kuo said his latest industry survey indicated the cut. The report was published on Friday, November 20, 2026. Kuo is best known for his technology supply-chain research.

Kuo said Google had cut planned 2027 shipments of its Broadcom-designed TPU 8i series by approximately 1 million units. That represents roughly 20% of the series' previously expected shipment volume, implying a reduction from approximately 5 million chips to 4 million. Most of the cuts affect the higher-priced 8i Max, also known as Whalefish, according to Kuo. Kuo also reported that Google plans to increase 2027 shipments of the MediaTek-designed TPU 8t series, though the details remain unsettled. The post did not specify the size of that increase.

Kuo linked the change to Google's prioritization of frontier model development, the work involved in building its most advanced AI models. According to his post, Google has repeatedly emphasized in recent months that frontier development receives first call on available computing resources. He characterized the changing TPU shipment mix as an adjustment to that priority amid tight supply chains and data-center power constraints. His post did not provide pricing, contract terms or an estimate of the financial effect on Broadcom. Kuo's post did not provide enough technical or economic detail to establish exactly why Google would favor additional 8t shipments over the affected 8i models.

Market sources indicated Google will bypass longtime partner Broadcom and buy high-bandwidth memory for its own TPUs directly from memory makers, while shifting part of the chip design work to MediaTek. Counterpoint Research outlined the division of work: Google will handle the compute chip design itself, MediaTek will handle the I/O chips for data exchange, and Google will place HBM orders directly. Bernstein estimated in a report that if Google fully adopts the new procurement model, it could save about $50 billion over the TPU product lifecycle. Industry observers said that when a major customer directly controls memory procurement, negotiations over supply prices and contract terms are expected to become more intense. For Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix and Micron, this could mean compressed margins.

In the past, Google handed the design, packaging and HBM procurement for its TPUs to Broadcom as a bundled service. SK Hynix has proposed working with Google to co-develop customized HBM for future TPUs, while Samsung Electronics is seeking an opening through Broadcom, Google's main TPU development partner. One industry source noted that HBM is currently in short supply, so suppliers still hold the upper hand, and some long-term supply contracts have already set price caps. Broadcom shares were down 8.9% on the day amid broad-based selling across the semiconductor sector. The decline should not be attributed solely to the reported shipment changes.

With the shipment changes concerning 2027, the outlook remains subject to revisions. The key questions are how much Google ultimately increases its MediaTek-designed chip orders, whether those gains offset the Broadcom-designed reductions, and what the final mix means for supplier revenue. The post did not specify the size of the 8t increase, leaving it unclear whether additional 8t shipments would fully offset the reduction in the 8i family. The report does not establish the eventual revenue impact for either company. Kuo's findings point to a potential reshuffling within Google's AI-chip supply chain, not clear evidence of a retreat from AI investment.
